**Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim** (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

**Tafsir** (interpretation) **of Surah al-A'raf**

It is Makki (revealed in Makkah), except for eight verses, from His words: ﴿And ask them about the town﴾ up to His words: ﴿And when We raised the mountain above them﴾ [See p. 304 onward.]

Al-Nasa'i narrated from A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Surah al-A'raf in the Maghrib prayer, dividing it between the two rak'ahs. Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq authenticated it.

**Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim**

**Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim**

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾ A Book has been revealed to you, so let there be no constriction in your breast because of it, that you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers. (2)

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾ This was discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah [See vol. 1 p. 154]. Its position is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and "Kitab" (a Book) is its predicate. It is as if he said: "Alif Lam Mim" are letters, "a Book has been revealed to you." Al-Kisa'i said: meaning, "This is a Book."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so let there be no constriction in your breast because of it﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: His words, Exalted is He: ﴿constriction (haraj)﴾ meaning tightness, i.e., your breast should not be constricted by conveying the message. It is narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Indeed I fear that they will crush my head (yathlughu ra'si), so that they leave it like a piece of bread (khubzah)," the hadith. Muslim recorded it. [In the originals it reads "idha yathlughu" in Sahih Muslim; see Sahih Muslim, Book of Paradise, chapter on the attributes by which the people of Paradise and the people of Hell are distinguished. Al-thalgh means to crush; it is said it is striking a wet thing with a dry thing until it breaks. In al-Nihayah: "idhan yathlughu ra'si kama tuthlagh al-khubzah."]

Ilkiya said: its apparent form is a prohibition, but its meaning is the negation of constriction from him, i.e., your breast should not be constricted that they do not believe in it. Your duty is only to convey; you have nothing beyond warning by it, regardless of their faith or disbelief. Similar to it is His words: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself [with grief]﴾ [See vol. 10 p. 353 and p. 63], up to the verse, and His words: ﴿Perhaps you will destroy yourself that they will not be believers﴾ [See vol. 13 p. 89].

The view of Mujahid and Qatadah is that haraj here means doubt, but this is not the doubt of disbelief; it is the doubt of distress. Likewise His words: ﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾ [See vol. 10 p. 353 and p. 63].

It is said that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) while the intended meaning is his community, but this is remote. The pronoun in ﴿منه (from it)﴾ refers to the Qur'an. It is also said that it refers to the warning, meaning: the Book was revealed to you so that you may warn by it, so let there be no constriction in your breast from it. Thus the speech has an inversion (taqdim and ta'khir). It is also said it refers to the denial that the strength of the speech implies, meaning: let there be no tightness in your breast from the denial of those who deny it.

The second: His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and a reminder (dhikra)﴾ may be in the position of nominative, accusative, or genitive. The nominative has two possibilities: the Basran grammarians said it is nominative by an implied subject (mubtada' mudmar). Al-Kisa'i said it is coordinated (ataf) upon "Kitab." The accusative has two possibilities: as an infinitive (masdar), meaning "and remind with it a reminder," according to the Basrans. Al-Kisa'i said it is coordinated upon the pronoun in ﴿anzalnahu (We sent it down)﴾ [In the originals this is as stated; al-Samin said it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "anzal," and called this an error.] The genitive is by analogy with the position of ﴿li-tundhira bihi (that you may warn by it)﴾. Warning is for the disbelievers, and the reminder is for the believers, since they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 3:

There are two issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, meaning the Book and the Sunnah (the prophetic custom and practice). Allah, exalted is He, said: "And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it" [[See vol. 18, p. 17.]]. A group said: this is a command that includes the Prophet ﷺ and his community. The apparent meaning is that it is a command to all people other than him, i.e. follow the religion of Islam and the Qur'an, make lawful what it makes lawful and unlawful what it makes unlawful, comply with its command, and avoid its prohibitions. The verse also indicates the abandonment of following personal opinions (ra'y) in the presence of an explicit text (nass).

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not follow other than Him as protectors﴾. "Other than Him" means apart from Him. The pronoun refers to the Lord, glorified is He, and the meaning is: do not worship alongside Him anything else, and do not take as a protector (wali) whoever has turned away from the religion of Allah. Whoever adopts a school of thought, the adherents of that school are its protectors. It is narrated from Malik ibn Dinar that he read "and do not seek other than Him as protectors" (wa la tabtaghu min dunihi awliya'), meaning, do not seek. The word "awliya'" is not declined (lam yanṣarif) because it contains the feminine ending alif (alif al-ta'nith). It was also said that the pronoun refers to "ma" in His saying: "Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord."

(﴿Little do you remember﴾) "Ma" is superfluous (za'idah). It was also said that with the verb it forms a verbal noun (masdar).

**Qur'an 7:4–5**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed!﴾ *Kam* (how many) is for multiplicity, just as *rubba* (a few) is for paucity. It is in the nominative position as the subject (*mubtada'*, the inchoative), and *ahlaknāhā* (We destroyed it) is the predicate (*khabar*). The meaning is: "And many towns, which are places where people gather, We have destroyed." It is also permissible to read it in the accusative (*naṣb*) by supposing a verb after it, and no verb is to be supposed before it, because the interrogative does not take governance from what precedes it. The first reading is strengthened by His saying: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah!﴾ Had *ahlaknā* not been occupied with the pronoun, the position of *kam* would have been in the accusative governed by it. It is also permissible for *ahlaknāhā* to be a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of *qaryah* (town), and *kam* in meaning is the town itself, so when you describe the town, you have effectively described *kam*. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing﴾, where the pronoun returns to *kam* according to its meaning, since it refers to angels. On this supposition, *kam* cannot be in the accusative position by supposing a verb after it.

﴿So Our punishment came upon it﴾: There is a difficulty with the conjunction by *fa'* (so). Al-Farra' said: *al-fa'* carries the meaning of *al-waw* (and), so sequence is not necessary. It was also said: the meaning is "And how many a town did We intend to destroy, so Our punishment came upon it," like His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾. It was also said: the destruction occurred to some of the people, so the supposition is: "And how many a town, We destroyed part of it, so Our punishment came upon it and We destroyed all of it." It was also said: the meaning is "And how many a town We destroyed, by Our judgment, so Our punishment came upon it." It was also said: "We destroyed it by sending the angels of punishment to it, so Our punishment came upon it, which is annihilation." *Al-ba's* (punishment) is the chastisement that comes upon the soul. It was also said: the meaning is "We destroyed it, and Our destroying them occurred at such and such a time," so the coming of punishment in this case is the destruction itself. It was also said: *al-ba's* is other than the destruction, as we have mentioned. Al-Farra' also related that when the meaning of the two verbs is one or like one, you may place whichever of them you wish first, so the meaning is "And how many a town Our punishment came upon it and so We destroyed it," like *dana fa-qaraba* (he drew near, so he came close) and *qaraba fa-dana*, and *shatamanī fa-asā'a* (he reviled me, so he did evil) and *asā'a fa-shatamanī*, because evil-doing and reviling are one thing. Likewise is His saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾. The meaning, and Allah knows best, is "the moon split, so the Hour drew near," and the meaning is one.

﴿By night﴾: *Bayatan* means at night, and from it comes *al-bayt* (the house), because one spends the night in it. It is said: *bāta yabītu baytan* and *bayatan* (he spent the night).

﴿Or they were taking a noon-rest﴾: That is, *aw hum qā'ilūn*, meaning *aw wa-hum qā'ilūn* (or while they were napping). They found it heavy, so they dropped the *wāw*, as related by al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error; when the reference (*dhikr*) returns, the *wāw* is dispensed with. You say: "Zayd came to me riding, or he is walking," and the *wāw* is not needed. Al-Mahdawi said: they did not say *bayatan aw wa-hum qā'ilūn* because in the sentence there is a pronoun referring back to the first, so the *wāw* was dispensed with. This is the same as al-Zajjaj's meaning. The *aw* here is not for doubt but for distinction (*tafṣīl*), like your saying: "I will surely honour you, being fair to me or unjust." This *wāw* is called by the grammarians *wāw al-waqt* (the *wāw* of time/circumstance).

*Qā'ilūn* is from *al-qā'ilah*, which is *al-qaylūlah* (the noon-rest), namely sleep at midday. It was also said: it is resting at midday when the heat is intense, even if no sleep accompanies it. The meaning is: Our punishment came upon them while they were heedless, either by night or by day.

﴿Their claim﴾: *Al-da'wā* means supplication, and from it comes His saying: ﴿and the last of their prayer﴾. The grammarians related: "O Allah, make us share in the good supplication of those who call upon You." *Al-da'wā* may also mean *al-idde'ā'* (claim). The meaning is: at the time of destruction, they did not sincerely say anything except the acknowledgment that they had been wrongdoers.

*Da'wāhum* is in the accusative position as the predicate of *kāna* (was), and its subject is *illā an qālū* (except that they said), like the verse: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said﴾. It is also permissible for *al-da'wā* to be in the nominative and *an qālū* in the accusative, like His saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn﴾ with *al-birr* in the nominative, and His saying: ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was that they denied﴾ with *'āqibah* in the nominative.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 6–7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ is evidence that the disbelievers will be called to account. And in another revelation: ﴿Then upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 37]. And in Surah al-Qasas: ﴿And the guilty will not be asked about their sins﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 315], meaning when they have settled into the punishment. The Hereafter has stations: a station in which they are questioned for the reckoning, and a station in which they are not questioned. Their questioning is for confirmation, rebuke and exposure. The questioning of the messengers is a questioning to bear witness about them and to make things clear, that is, about the response of the people to them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So that He may question the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 9 and p. 129], as will come. It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ is "the prophets," and ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾ is "the angels who were sent to them." The lam in ﴿Then We will surely question﴾ is the lam of oath, and its real function is emphasis. Likewise (﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾). Ibn Abbas said: "It speaks against them" [the words of al-Tabari: "The book of their deeds speaks for them or against them by their actions"].

﴿And We were not absent﴾, that is, We were witnesses to their deeds. The verse also indicates that Allah, Exalted is He, has knowledge with knowledge.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, verses 8–9:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. *Al-wazn* (the weighing) is the subject (*ibtida'*) and the predicate (*khabar*) is what follows. It is also permissible for *al-haqq* (the truth) to be an adjective (*na't*) of it, with the predicate being *yawma'idhin* (on that Day). It is also permissible to put *al-haqq* in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*). By *al-wazn* is meant the weighing of the deeds of the servants with the scale (*al-mizan*). Ibn Umar said: "The pages of the servants' deeds are weighed." This is the sound view, and it is the one reported in the narrations that follow. It has also been said: the *mizan* is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded. Mujahid said: the *mizan* is the good and bad deeds themselves. Also from him, and from al-Dahhak and al-A'mash: *al-wazn* and *al-mizan* mean justice and judgment, and the mention of weighing is a figure of speech (*darb mathal*), just as you say: "This statement is in the weight (*wazn*) of that and its equivalent (*wizan*)," meaning it is equal to it and matches it, even if there is no actual weighing there. Al-Zajjaj said: this is permissible linguistically, but it is better to follow what has come in the sound chains of transmission concerning the mention of the scale.

Al-Qushayri said: he has spoken well in what he said, for if the *mizan* is interpreted this way, then the *sirat* (bridge) should be interpreted as the path of truth, and Paradise and Hell as what reaches the spirits rather than the bodies, and the devils and jinn as the blameworthy character traits, and the angels as the praiseworthy faculties. The community (*al-ummah*) in the first generation agreed on taking these apparent meanings without *ta'wil* (figurative interpretation). When they agreed on prohibiting *ta'wil*, it became obligatory to take the apparent meaning, and these apparent meanings became established texts (*nusus*).

Ibn Furak said: the Mu'tazilah [[In manuscript Z: al-Imamiyyah.]] denied the scale, on the basis that accidents (*a'rad*) cannot be weighed, since they do not subsist by themselves. Among the theologians (*mutakallimun*) there are those who say that God Most High transforms accidents into bodies and then weighs them on the Day of Resurrection. This is not correct according to us. The correct view is that the scales become heavy by the books in which the deeds are written, and become light by them. A report has been narrated that confirms this, namely that it was reported: "The scale of some of the children of Adam almost becomes light with good deeds, so a written scroll on which is written 'There is no god but Allah' is placed in it, and it becomes heavy." It is thus known that the weight refers to the weight of what the deeds are written upon, not the deeds themselves, and that God, glorified is He, makes the scale light if He wills, and makes it heavy if He wills, by what is placed in its two pans from the pages on which the deeds are written.

In Sahih Muslim, from Safwan ibn Muhriz, who said: a man said to Ibn Umar: "How did you hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) speak about the private conversation (*najwa*) [[He means the private conversation of God Most High with the servant on the Day of Resurrection.]]?" He said: "I heard him say: 'The believer will be brought near to his Lord on the Day of Resurrection until He places His covering (*kanaf*) over him and makes him acknowledge his sins. He will say, "Do you know?" He will say, "O Lord, I know." He will say, "I concealed them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today." Then he will be given the scroll of his good deeds. As for the disbelievers and the hypocrites, they will be called out before the heads of all creation: "These are the ones who lied against Allah."'" His saying "then he will be given the scroll of his good deeds" is evidence that deeds are recorded in scrolls and are weighed.

Ibn Majah related from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man from my community will be called out on the Day of Resurrection before the heads of all creation. Ninety-nine registers (*sijillat*) will be spread out before him, each register as far as the eye can see. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, will say: 'Do you deny any of this?' He will say: 'No, O Lord.' He will say: 'Have my recording scribes wronged you?' He will say: 'No.' Then He will say: 'Do you have an excuse? Do you have a good deed?' The man will be overawed and say: 'No.' He will say: 'Yes, indeed you have good deeds with Us, and no wrong will be done to you today.' Then a card (*bitaqah*) will be brought out for him, in which is written: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger.' He will say: 'O Lord, what is this card with these registers?' He will say: 'You will not be wronged.' The registers will be placed in one pan and the card in the other pan. The registers will rise (*fa-tasha*) and the card will be heavy." Al-Tirmidhi added: "So nothing heavy weighs against the name of Allah." He said: this is a good, strange hadith.

More detailed explanation of this topic will come, God willing, in *al-Kahf* [[See vol. 11, pp. 66 and 293.]] and *al-Anbiya'* [[See vol. 13, pp. 118 and 122.]].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then as for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And as for those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost themselves, for they used to wrong Our signs.﴾ *Mawazinuhu* is the plural of *mizan*, and its original form is *miwzan*; the *waw* was changed to *ya'* because of the kasrah before it. It has been said: it is permissible that there are multiple scales for a single doer, so that each type of his deeds is weighed with one of them. It is also possible that this is a single scale expressed with the plural form, as you say: "So-and-so went to Makkah on mules, and went to Basra on ships." In the revelation there is: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾, and ﴿'Ad denied the messengers﴾ [[See vol. 13, pp. 118 and 122.]], whereas there was only one messenger in one of the two interpretations. It has also been said: *al-mawazin* is the plural of *mawzun* (the weighed thing), not the plural of *mizan*, meaning by *al-mawazin* the weighed deeds. And ﴿whose scales are light﴾ is similar.

Ibn Abbas said: the good and bad deeds are weighed in a scale that has a tongue and two pans. As for the believer, his deed is brought to him in its most beautiful form and placed in the pan of the scale, and his good deeds outweigh his bad deeds. That is His saying: ﴿Then as for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful.﴾ And the deed of the disbeliever is brought in its ugliest form and placed in the pan of the scale, so its weight becomes light until he falls into the Fire. What Ibn Abbas indicated is close to what has been said: God Most High creates every part of the deeds of the servants as a substance (*jawhar*), and the weighing falls upon those substances. Ibn Furak and others rejected this.

In a report: "When the good deeds of the believer are light, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will bring out a card the size of a fingertip (*unmulah*) and put it in the right pan of the scale, in which are his good deeds, and the good deeds will outweigh. Then that believing servant will say to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'May my father and mother be ransomed for you! How beautiful is your face, and how beautiful is your creation! Who are you?' He will say: 'I am Muhammad, your Prophet, and these are your prayers upon me, which you used to send, and I have repaid them to you at the time you most need them.'" Al-Qushayri mentioned this in his tafsir. He also mentioned that *al-bitaqah* (with a kasrah on the *ba'*) is a slip of paper on which the price of goods is written, in the dialect of the people of Egypt. Ibn Majah said: Muhammad ibn Yahya said: *al-bitaqah* is a slip of paper, and the people of Egypt call a slip of paper a *bitaqah*.

Hudhayfah said: the one in charge of the scales on the Day of Resurrection is Jibril (peace be upon him). God Most High says: "O Jibril, weigh between them, and return from some to others." He said: "There is no gold or silver there. If the wrongdoer has good deeds, some of his good deeds are taken and returned to the wronged one. If he has no good deeds, some of the wronged one's bad deeds are taken and loaded onto the wrongdoer, so the man returns with the weight of mountains."

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "God Most High says on the Day of Resurrection: 'O Adam, come forth to the side of the Throne (*kursi*) at the scale, and look at what is raised to you of the deeds of your children. Whoever's good outweighs his evil by the weight of a mustard seed, for him is Paradise. And whoever's evil outweighs his good by the weight of a mustard seed, for him is the Fire, until you know that I do not punish except the wrongdoer.'"

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, verses 8–9:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. *Al-wazn* (the weighing) is the subject (*ibtida'*) and the predicate (*khabar*) is what follows. It is also permissible for *al-haqq* (the truth) to be an adjective (*na't*) of it, with the predicate being *yawma'idhin* (on that Day). It is also permissible to put *al-haqq* in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*). By *al-wazn* is meant the weighing of the deeds of the servants with the scale (*al-mizan*). Ibn Umar said: "The pages of the servants' deeds are weighed." This is the sound view, and it is the one reported in the narrations that follow. It has also been said: the *mizan* is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded. Mujahid said: the *mizan* is the good and bad deeds themselves. Also from him, and from al-Dahhak and al-A'mash: *al-wazn* and *al-mizan* mean justice and judgment, and the mention of weighing is a figure of speech (*darb mathal*), just as you say: "This statement is in the weight (*wazn*) of that and its equivalent (*wizan*)," meaning it is equal to it and matches it, even if there is no actual weighing there. Al-Zajjaj said: this is permissible linguistically, but it is better to follow what has come in the sound chains of transmission concerning the mention of the scale.

Al-Qushayri said: he has spoken well in what he said, for if the *mizan* is interpreted this way, then the *sirat* (bridge) should be interpreted as the path of truth, and Paradise and Hell as what reaches the spirits rather than the bodies, and the devils and jinn as the blameworthy character traits, and the angels as the praiseworthy faculties. The community (*al-ummah*) in the first generation agreed on taking these apparent meanings without *ta'wil* (figurative interpretation). When they agreed on prohibiting *ta'wil*, it became obligatory to take the apparent meaning, and these apparent meanings became established texts (*nusus*).

Ibn Furak said: the Mu'tazilah [[In manuscript Z: al-Imamiyyah.]] denied the scale, on the basis that accidents (*a'rad*) cannot be weighed, since they do not subsist by themselves. Among the theologians (*mutakallimun*) there are those who say that God Most High transforms accidents into bodies and then weighs them on the Day of Resurrection. This is not correct according to us. The correct view is that the scales become heavy by the books in which the deeds are written, and become light by them. A report has been narrated that confirms this, namely that it was reported: "The scale of some of the children of Adam almost becomes light with good deeds, so a written scroll on which is written 'There is no god but Allah' is placed in it, and it becomes heavy." It is thus known that the weight refers to the weight of what the deeds are written upon, not the deeds themselves, and that God, glorified is He, makes the scale light if He wills, and makes it heavy if He wills, by what is placed in its two pans from the pages on which the deeds are written.

And We have certainly established you on the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood; little are you grateful. [Q 7:10]

That is, We made it for you a place of settlement and a cradle, and We prepared for you therein the causes of livelihood. The word ma'ayish (means of livelihood) is the plural of ma'ishah (livelihood), meaning that by which one sustains oneself, such as food and drink, and that by which life is sustained. It is said: 'āsha yaʿīshu ʿaysha<u>n</u>, wa-maʿāshan, wa-maʿīshan, wa-maʿīshatan, wa-ʿīshatan. Al-Zajjaj said: al-maʿīshah is that by which one attains living. According to al-Akhfash and many grammarians, ma'īshah is of the form mif'alah (mafʿalah pattern, i.e., ma-ʿ-ī-sh-ah with the yā' as a root letter). Al-A'raj read "ma'ā'ish" with a hamzah, and Kharijah ibn Mus'ab related it likewise from Nafi'. Al-Nahhas said: the hamzah is a grammatical error (laḥn) that is not permissible, because the singular is ma'īshah, its original form being ma'īshah; an alif of connection (alif al-waṣl) was added, and since both the alif and the yā' are quiescent, there must be a vowelling, for deletion is not possible, and the alif cannot be vowelled, so the yā' was vowelled with what it would have taken in the singular. Its parallel from the waw is manāwir and manāwir (plural of minwar), and maqām and maqāwim, as the poet said:

"And indeed I am the one who upholds the maqāwim (affairs) which Jarir and the client of Jarir did not uphold."

Likewise muṣībah and maṣāwib. This is the preferred form, while the anomalous dialect form is maṣā'ib. Al-Akhfash said: maṣā'ib is permissible because the singular is weak (mu'tall). Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error, for it would necessitate saying maqā'im. Rather, the correct view is that it is like wisādah and isādah. It was also said: hamzah was not permitted in ma'āyish because ma'īshah is of the form mif'alah, so the yā' is original; hamzah occurs only when the yā' is an added letter, as in madīnah and madā'in, ṣaḥīfah and ṣaḥā'if, karīmah and karā'im, wazīfah and wazā'if, and the like.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾. When He mentioned His favors, He mentioned the beginning of His creation. The meaning of creation (khalq) has already been discussed in more than one place [[See vol. 1, pp. 226, 251.]]. "Then We fashioned you" means: We created you as drops of semen (nutfah), then We fashioned you. Then, We inform you that We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others: the meaning is, We created Adam, then We fashioned you in his loins. Al-Akhfash said: "thumma" here carries the meaning of "wa" (and). It has also been said: the meaning of "And We created you" is Adam, peace be upon him, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, then We fashioned you, according to inversion of the order (taqdim wa ta'khir). It has also been said: "And We created you" refers to Adam, mentioned in the plural because he is the father of mankind. "Then We fashioned you" also refers to him, as one says: "We killed you," meaning: we killed your chief. "Then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam." On this view there is neither inversion nor reordering, related also from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said: the meaning is "And We created you," meaning Adam and Eve: Adam from earth and Eve from a rib of his ribs; then fashioning took place after that. So the meaning is: We created your two parents, then We fashioned them; this is the view of al-Hasan. It has also been said: the meaning is, We created you in the loins of Adam, then We fashioned you when We took the covenant from you. This is the saying of Mujahid, related from him by Ibn Juraij and Ibn Abi Najih. Al-Nahhas said: this is the best of the opinions. Mujahid holds that He created them in the loins of Adam, then fashioned them when He took the covenant from them, and then there was the prostration after that. What strengthens this is His saying: "And when your Lord brought forth from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring" [[See p. 313 of this volume.]], and the hadith: "that He brought them forth like particles (ami al-dharr) and took the covenant from them." It has also been said: "thumma" is for reporting, i.e., "And We created you," meaning in the loins of Adam ﷺ, "then We fashioned you," i.e., in the wombs. Al-Nahhas said: this is authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas. I say: all these opinions are possible, and the soundest of them is that which the revelation supports. Allah the Exalted said: "And We created man from an extract of clay" [[See vol. 12, p. 108.]], meaning Adam. And He said: "and from it He created its mate" [[See vol. 4, p. 1.]]. Then He said: "We placed him as a drop in a firm lodging" [[See vol. 12, p. 108.]], the verse. So Adam was created from clay, then fashioned and honored by prostration, and his offspring were fashioned in the wombs of mothers after being created in them and in the loins of fathers. It has already been mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 388.]] that every human is created from a drop and dust, so reflect upon it. Here He said: "We created you, then We fashioned you," and in the end of Surat al-Hashr He said: "He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner" [[See vol. 18, p. 48.]]. So He mentioned fashioning after originating. The explanation of this will come, if Allah the Exalted wills. It has also been said: the meaning of "And We created you" is: We created the spirits first, then We fashioned the bodies last.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾. This is an exception from a different genus (istithna' min ghayr al-jins). It has also been said: it is from the same genus. The scholars differed over whether he was among the angels or not, as has already been explained in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 29.]].

**First issue: the words "mā manaʿaka" (what prevented you).** "Mā" is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, meaning "what (is it that)." This is a question of rebuke. "An lā tasjud" is in the accusative position, meaning "from (prostrating)," and "lā" is extra (*zā'idah*, redundant). In Ṣād (38) the same phrase occurs: *mā manaʿaka an tasjud* [[See vol. 15, pp. 227–228.]]. The poet says:

*Abā jūduhu lā al-bukhlu fa-staʿjalat bihi... naʿam min fatan lā yamnaʿu al-jūda nāʾiluhu*

He meant: "His generosity refused, not stinginess," so he added *lā*. It has also been said that *lā* is not extra, because *manaʿa* contains an element of speech and invitation. It is as if he said: "Who told you not to prostrate?" or "Who invited you to not prostrate?" Just as you say: "I already told you not to do such-and-such." It has also been said that the sentence contains an omission, and the implied meaning is: "What prevented you from obedience and made you need not to prostrate?" The scholars said: what drove him to abandon prostration was arrogance and envy, and he had concealed this in himself when he was commanded. His command came before the creation of Adam, when Allah the Exalted said: *"Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down to him in prostration"* [[See vol. 15, pp. 228 and 227.]]. It was as though a great matter entered him from the words *"fall down to him in prostration."* For "falling down" implies lowering the one who falls and honoring the one to whom he falls. So he concealed in himself that he would not prostrate when he was commanded at that time. When Allah breathed the spirit into Adam, the angels fell down in prostration, while he remained standing among them. By his standing and not prostrating, he revealed what was in his heart. So Allah said: *"What prevented you from not prostrating?"*, meaning: what prevented you from submitting to My command? Thus He brought out the secret of his heart, and he said: *"I am better than him."*

**Second issue:** The words *"idh amartuka"* (when I commanded you) indicate what the jurists say, that a command by its unrestricted form necessarily implies obligation without any indicator, because the blame was attached to abandoning the unrestricted command, which is the Mighty and Majestic One's words to the angels: *"Prostrate to Adam."* This is clear.

**Third issue:** The words *"Qāla anā khayrun minh"* (He said: I am better than him). The meaning is: my superiority over him prevented me from prostrating. Iblis's answer here is an answer in meaning. As when you ask: "Whose house is this?" and the other replies: "Its owner is Zayd." This is not the exact answer, but speech that returns to the meaning of an answer.

*(You created me from fire and created him from clay)*: He saw that fire is nobler than clay, because of its height, its rising, its lightness, and because it is a luminous substance. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Sirin said: "The first to use *qiyās* (analogy) was Iblis, and he erred in the analogy. So whoever measures religion by his own opinion has joined him with Iblis." Ibn Sirin said: "The sun and the moon were only worshipped through analogies." The wise said: "The enemy of Allah erred when he preferred fire over clay, although they are in one rank in that both are created inanimate matter. Clay is better than fire in four respects. First, the substance of clay includes steadiness, calm, dignity, deliberation, forbearance, modesty, and patience. These were what led Adam, peace be upon him, after the happiness that preceded him, to repentance, humility, and supplication, so they brought him forgiveness, election, and guidance. The substance of fire includes lightness, recklessness, sharpness, elevation, and agitation. These were what led Iblis, after the wretchedness that preceded him, to arrogance and persistence in sin, so they brought him ruin, punishment, curse, and misery." Al-Qaffal said so. Second, the report states that the dust of Paradise is pungent musk, while no report states that Paradise contains fire or that Hell contains dust. Third, fire is the cause of punishment, and it is Allah's punishment for His enemies, while dust is not a cause of punishment. Fourth, clay is independent of fire, while fire needs a place, and its place is dust.

I say: there is a fifth possible view, that dust is a place of prostration and a means of purification, as has come in the authentic hadith, while fire is a means of warning and punishment, as Allah the Exalted said: *"This is what Allah threatens His servants with"* [[See vol. 15, p. 243.]]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Obedience was better for Iblis than analogy, so he disobeyed his Lord, and he was the first to analogize by his own opinion. Analogy that opposes a clear text is rejected."

**Fourth issue:** People differed about *qiyās*, between those who affirm it and those who reject it. As for those who affirm it, they are the Companions, the Successors, and the majority of those after them. Worship through it is permissible by reason and has occurred by the Law, and this is the correct view.

Al-Qaffal of the Shafiʿis and Abu al-Husayn al-Basri held that worship through it is obligatory by reason. Al-Nazzam held that worship through it is impossible by reason and by the Law, and some of the Ẓāhirīs rejected it. The first is the correct view. Al-Bukhari said in (*Kitāb al-iʿtiṣām bi-l-kitāb wa-l-sunnah*, The Book of Holding Fast to the Book and the Sunnah): the meaning is that no one is protected except in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Prophet, or in the consensus of the scholars when a ruling is found in them; if it is not found, then analogy. He titled a chapter on this: "Chapter on whoever likens a known principle to a clear principle whose ruling Allah has explained, so that the questioner may understand." He then titled another: "Chapter on rulings known through indicators, and how the meaning of indication and its interpretation." Al-Tabari said: ijtihad, deduction from the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Prophet ﷺ, and the consensus of the community, is the truth that is obligatory and the binding duty of the people of knowledge. Reports from the Prophet ﷺ, and from a group of Companions and Successors, have come with this.

Abu Tammam al-Maliki said: The community agreed on analogy. Among that, they agreed on analogizing gold and silver in zakat. Abu Bakr said: "Release me from my pledge." ʿAli said: "By Allah, we will neither release you nor ask you to resign. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ chose you for our religion, so should we not accept you for our worldly affairs?" So ʿAli analogized the imamate to prayer. The Siddiq analogized zakat to prayer and said: "By Allah, I will not separate what Allah has joined." ʿAli explicitly used analogy regarding the drinker of wine in the presence of the Companions and said: "When he becomes intoxicated, he raves; when he raves, he slanders; so his punishment is the punishment of the slanderer." ʿUmar wrote to Abu Musa al-Ashʿari a letter in which he said: "Understand what occurs to your heart of matters that has not reached you in the Book and the Sunnah. Know the similar cases and the parallels, then measure the matters accordingly. Then aim for what is most beloved to Allah the Exalted and most like the truth in your view." The full hadith was narrated by al-Daraqutni.

Abu ʿUbayda said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding the hadith of the plague, when ʿUmar returned from Sargh [[a place near al-Sham between al-Mughaithah and Tabuk]]: "Are we fleeing from the decree of Allah?" ʿUmar said: "Yes! We flee from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah." Then ʿUmar said to him: "Tell me..." [[See the Muwatta', "Chapter on what has come concerning the plague."]] ... He analogized with him and debated with him by what resembles his question in the presence of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and that is enough for you. As for the reports and the verses of the Qur'an on this meaning, they are many. This indicates that analogy is a principle of the religion and a safeguard of the Muslims, to which the mujtahids return and to which the working scholars turn, so that they derive rulings from it. This is the view of the body of scholars who constitute the proof, and one does not heed whoever departs from it.

As for blameworthy opinion and forced analogy that is forbidden, it is what is not based on these principles mentioned, because that is conjecture and incitement [[In ʿ: "confusion"; in B: "nazgh," meaning instigation.]] from Satan. Allah the Exalted said: *"And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge"* [[See vol. 10, p. 257.]]. Every weak hadith and baseless report that the opponent cites in condemnation of analogy is to be understood as referring to this type of blameworthy analogy, which has no known basis in the Law. The completion of this topic is in the books of legal theory (*uṣūl al-fiqh*).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "Then descend from it"﴾, i.e., from the heaven.

(So it is not for you to be arrogant therein, for its inhabitants are the humble angels.) ﴿So get out, for you are among the debased﴾, i.e., among the abased. This indicates that whoever disobeys his Master is abased. Abu Rawq and al-Bajali said: "﴿Then descend from it﴾" means: from your form in which you are, because he boasted that he was made of fire, so his form was disfigured by darkness and the loss of its brilliance. It was also said: "﴿Then descend from it﴾" means: move from the earth to the islands of the seas, as it is said, "We descended to the land of such-and-such," meaning we moved to it from another place. So it is as if he was expelled from the earth to the islands of the seas, and his authority is there, so he does not enter the earth except in the manner of a thief (in the other manuscript: "al-sari" with a ya), fearing within it until he leaves it. The first opinion is more apparent. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah (see vol. 1, p. 327).

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 7, verses 14–15:

He asked for respite and delay until the Day of Resurrection and the Reckoning. He requested that he not die, because after the Day of Resurrection there is no death. So Allah Most High said: ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi and others said: He was granted respite until the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula), when all creation dies. He had asked for respite until the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya), when people stand before the Lord of the worlds, but Allah refused that for him. And He said: ﴿Until the Day when they are resurrected﴾, and there was no previously mentioned referent of "they who are resurrected," because the story concerns Adam and his offspring; thus the context (al-qarina) indicates that they are the ones who are resurrected.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verses 16–17:

There are three issues here. The first is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Because You have led me astray﴾. Al-ighwa' (leading astray) means causing ghayy (error, deviation) to take hold of the heart. The meaning is: because of what You placed in my heart of error, obstinacy and arrogance. This is because the disbelief of Iblis was not the disbelief of ignorance, but the disbelief of obstinacy and arrogance. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 295.]]. It has been said that the sense of the statement is an oath, meaning: by Your leading me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your path, or in Your path, with the particle elided. The evidence for this view is His words in (Sad): ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 228.]]. It is as if Iblis magnified the value of Allah's leading him astray, because of the power over the servants it entailed, so he swore by it, in order to glorify its status in His sight. It has also been said that the ba' (by) here carries the meaning of the lam (for), as if he said: "for Your leading me astray." It has been said that it means "with" (ma'a), so the meaning is "with Your leading me astray." It has been said that it is an interrogative, as if he asked: "By what did You lead me astray?" On this view it should have been: "Why (bima) did You lead me astray?" It has been said that the meaning is: "Because You have destroyed me by Your curse upon me." Al-ighwa' also means destruction, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So they will meet ghayy﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 125.]], meaning destruction. It has been said: "Because You have misguided me." Al-ighwa' means misguidance and distancing, according to Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: "You have deprived me of Your mercy," and from this is the saying of the poet [[This is the second half of a verse by al-Raqqash; its first half, as in Lisan al-'Arab, root gh-w-y, is: "Whoever meets good, people praise his affair."]]:

"And whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error,"

meaning: whoever is deprived. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is said that a man ghawa, yaghwi, ghayyan, when his affair has become corrupt for him, or when he himself has become corrupt. This is one of the meanings of His words: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 255.]], meaning his life in Paradise became corrupt. It is also said: "ghawa al-fasil," when the young camel does not know its mother's milk.

The second issue: the position of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) is that Allah misguided him and created disbelief in him. For this reason the leading astray in this context is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, and this is the reality. Nothing exists except that it is created by Him and proceeds from His will, the Exalted. The Imamiyyah, the Qadariyyah and others have opposed this, though they obeyed their master Iblis in everything he adorned for them, and did not obey him in this issue. They say: "Iblis erred, and he is prone to error, in that he attributed misguidance to his Lord, may Allah be exalted above that." It is said to them: even if Iblis is prone to error, what will you do with a noble, infallible Prophet, Nuh (peace be upon him), when he said to his people: ﴿My counsel will not benefit you, even if I wished to counsel you, if Allah wills to lead you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 28.]]. It has been narrated that Tawus was approached by a man in the Masjid al-Haram. The man was accused of qadar (the doctrine of human free will against divine decree) and was one of the great jurists. He sat with Tawus, who said to him: "Will you stand up, or be made to stand?" It was said to Tawus: "Do you say this to a jurist?" He said: "Iblis is more learned in jurisprudence than him. Iblis says: 'My Lord, because You have led me astray,' and this man says: 'I lead myself astray.'"

The third issue: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾. That is, by barring them from it and adorning falsehood for them, until they perish as he perished, or go astray as he went astray, or are deprived as he was deprived, according to the three meanings already mentioned for "You have led me astray." The straight path is the way that leads to Paradise. The word "Your path" (siratak) is in the accusative (naṣb, the accusative case) by the elision of "on" (ʿalā) or "in" (fī) from His words "Your straight path," as Sibawayh related: "Zayd struck the back and the belly." He also recited:

"Pliant, with the shaking of the palm its shaft glides,
in it as the fox glides along the path."

[[The verse is by Sa'idah ibn Juwayyah. He means "in the path." In the verse he describes a spear, pliant when shaken, and compares its trembling in itself or in the state of its shaking to the swift, agitated gait of a fox. Al-'asalan is a rapid, agitated movement. Ladn means soft and pliant. (From Sharh al-Shawahid.)]]

Among the best things said in interpreting His words: ﴿Then I will come to them from before them, and from behind them, and from their right and from their left﴾, that is: I will surely turn them away from the truth, make them desire this world, and cast doubt on them concerning the Hereafter. This is an extreme of misguidance, as He said: ﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. 389.]], as already mentioned. Sufyan related from Mansur, from al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah: "from before them" means from their worldly life; "from behind them" means from their Hereafter; "from their right" means their good deeds; "from their left" means their sins. Al-Nahhas said: this is a good view, and its explanation is that the meaning of "then I will come to them from before them" is from their worldly life, until they deny what is in it of signs and the reports of earlier nations. "And from behind them" means from their Hereafter, until they deny it. "And from their right" means from their good deeds and the matters of their religion. This is supported by His words: ﴿Indeed, you used to come to us from the right﴾. "And from their left" means their sins, that is, they follow desires, because he adorns them for them.

﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾, that is, monotheistic and obedient, showing gratitude.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Get out of it﴾, that is, out of the Garden.

(Dhhh) "Madhu'man" means blameworthy. "Al-dha'm" means blame, with the mim lightened [[In some copies: from what precedes it.]]. Ibn Zayd said: "mad'uman" and "madhmuman" are the same; it is said: dha'amtuhu, dhammamtuhu and dhammtuhu, with one meaning. Al-A'mash read "mad'uman". The meaning is one, except that he eased the hamza [[There is no need for this qualification: the hamza is sufficient to distinguish it from dhamm.]]. Mujahid said: "al-math'um" is the one who is banished. The two meanings are close. "Al-madhur" means the one who is removed and driven away, according to Mujahid and others, and its root meaning is pushing away.

(Whoever follows you among them, I will surely fill Hell with all of you together.) The lam is the lam of oath, and the answer is "la-amla'anna Jahannam". It was also said: "liman tabi'aka" is a lam of emphasis, and "la-amla'anna" is the lam of oath. The evidence for this is that outside recitation it is permissible to omit the first lam, but it is not permissible to omit the second. The sentence carries the meaning of a condition and a consequence, that is, whoever follows you, I will punish him. If you said: "Whoever follows you, I will punish him," it would not be permissible, unless you meant "la-u'adhdhibuhu" (I will surely punish him). Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, read "liman tabi'aka minhum" with a kasra on the lam. Some grammarians rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: its estimated meaning, and God knows best, is "for the sake of whoever follows you," as one says: "I honoured so-and-so for your sake." The meaning may also be: the expulsion is for whoever follows you. As for "minkum ajma'in," it means: from you and from the children of Adam, because their mention has already occurred when He said: ﴿And We created you﴾, addressing the children of Adam.

He said to Adam, after Iblis had been expelled from his place in the heaven: "Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden." The meaning of "dwelling" (al-iskan) has already been discussed in Surah al-Baqarah (see vol. 1, pp. 298 and 204), so there is no need to repeat it here. The meaning of "and do not approach this tree" has likewise already been discussed there. All praise is due to Allah.

**Qur'an 7:20:** "Then Satan whispered to them both." That is, *ilayhima* (to them). It was said: from inside the Garden, by the serpent bringing him in. It was also said: from outside, through the power (*al-saltanah*) given to him. This was already discussed in al-Baqarah.

*Al-waswasah* is a faint sound. It is also the inner speech of the soul. One says *waswasat ilayhi nafsuhu waswasatan wa-wiswasan* (with the *waw* kasra). *Al-waswas* (with fatha) is a noun like *al-zilzal*. It is also used for the faint sound of a hunter or dogs, and for the sounds of jewelry. Al-A'sha said:

*You hear from the jewelry a whispering when she turns away,*
*Like the rustling of the 'ishriq plant when the wind stirs it.*

[The 'ishriq is a tree about a cubit high with small seeds. When dry, it makes a sound when the wind blows through it.]

*Al-waswas* is also a name of Satan. Allah the Exalted says: "from the evil of the whisperer who withdraws" (Qur'an 114:4). [See vol. 20, p. 261.]

**"To expose to them"** (*li-yubdiya lahuma*): that is, *li-yuzhira lahuma* (to reveal to them). The *lam* here is *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence), as in His saying: "so that they would become for them an enemy and a grief" (Qur'an 28:8). [See vol. 13, p. 252.] It was also said that it is *lam kay* (the lam of purpose). **"Was concealed"** (*wuriya*): that is, *sutira wa-ghuttiya* (was covered and hidden) from them. In other than the Qur'an, *awra* is permitted, like *aqtat*. **"Of their private parts"** (*min saw'atihima*): the text reads *min 'awratihima* [in some manuscripts]. The private part was named *'awrah* because exposing it distresses its owner. This indicates the ugliness of uncovering it. It was said: their private parts were exposed only to each other, not to others. They had a light (*nur*, meaning a bloom) over them, so their private parts were not seen. Then the light departed. It was also said: it was a garment, which fell off (*tahafata*, meaning fell down). And Allah knows best.

**"Unless you become two angels"** (*illa an takuna malakayn*): *an* is in the accusative position, with the meaning of *illa* (except), by the grammatical construction *karahiyata an* (for fear that), with the noun omitted. This is the view of the Basrans. The Kufans say: *li-'allaa takuna* (so that you do not become). It was also said: the meaning is *illa 'allaa takuna malakayni ta'lamani al-khayra wa-al-sharr* (except that you do not become two angels who know good and evil). It was also said that Adam longed for immortality, because he knew that the angels do not die until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Nahhas said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic showed the excellence of the angels over all creation in more than one place in the Qur'an. Among them is this verse, "unless you become two angels." Among them is also "and I do not say that I am an angel" (Qur'an 6:50). [See vol. 9, p. 25.] And among them is "nor the angels who are brought near" (Qur'an 4:172). [See vol. 6, p. 26.]

Al-Hasan said: Allah preferred the angels by their forms, their wings, and their honor. Others said: He preferred them by obedience and by abstaining from disobedience. Therefore the preference applies in everything. Ibn Furak said: there is no proof in this verse, because it may mean "two angels" in the sense that they would have no desire for food.

The view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Zajjaj, and many scholars is that believers are preferred over the angels. This was already discussed in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 289.] Al-Kalbi said: they (humans) are preferred over all creation, except for a group of angels: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death, because they are among the messengers of Allah. Each group held to apparent evidences from the Law, and the excellence is in the hand of Allah.

Ibn 'Abbas read *malikayni* (with a kasra on the lam), and this is the reading of Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and al-Dahhak. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' denied the kasra on the lam and said: there was no king before Adam (peace be upon him), so that they would become two kings. Al-Nahhas said: with this reading, it is permissible to make the lam sukun (without vowel), but this is not permissible with the first reading, because of the lightness of the fatha.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the accursed one came to them from the direction of kingship. For this reason he said: "Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?" (Qur'an 20:120). [See vol. 11, p. 254.] Abu 'Ubayd claimed that Yahya ibn Abi Kathir's argument from His saying "and a kingdom that does not decay" is a clear proof, but people have abandoned it, so we have abandoned it too. Al-Nahhas said: the reading "illa an takuna mulkayn" (kingship) is an irregular (*shadhdhah*) reading. This statement of Abu 'Ubayd was rejected and considered a gross error. Could Adam (peace be upon him) imagine that he would reach more than the kingdom of Paradise, which is the ultimate goal of seekers? The meaning of "a kingdom that does not decay" is only remaining in the kingdom of Paradise and abiding eternally in it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 21:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he swore to them both﴾, meaning he swore an oath to them both. It is said: "aqsama iqsaman," meaning he swore an oath. The poet said:

*And he swore to her by Allah with full effort, that you are sweeter than the salwa when its honey is gathered* [[Al-salwa: honey. Sharra al-‘asal: he gathered the honey and took it from its place.]]

The form "faa'ala" (qasama) has come from one party, and this refutes the one who said that the form of mufa'ala (participation) is only possible between two. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Ma'idah.

(﴿Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisors﴾) "Lakuma" is not part of the relative clause (sila). The implied meaning is: "Indeed, I am an advisor to you both, among the sincere advisors." This was stated by Hisham al-Nahwi, and a similar point has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah. The meaning of the statement is: "Follow me, I will guide you both," as mentioned by Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 22–24:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he brought them down by deception﴾ — he caused them to fall into ruin. Ibn 'Abbas said: he deceived them by an oath. Adam thought that no one swears by Allah falsely, so [Iblis] deceived them through his whispering and his oath to them. Qatadah said: he swore to them by Allah until he deceived them. The believer may be deceived through Allah [i.e., through an oath by Allah]. Some of the scholars used to say: whoever deceives us by Allah, we are deceived by him. And in a hadith from him (ﷺ): "The believer is ghirr [gullible, one who does not perceive evil] generous, and the wicked person is khibb [crafty, a deceiver] base." The established narration from Abu Hurayrah has "the hypocrite is khibb base" in place of "the immoral person." (Note: ghirr means one who is not alert to evil; khibb, with the kasra or fatha on the kha', is the opposite of ghirr, meaning one who deceives in a corrupting way.)

Nifthawayh recited:

Indeed, the generous man, when you wish, you can deceive him,
and you see the base man, experienced, not deceived.

"Fadallahuma": it is said "adla dalwahu" meaning he lowered his bucket, and "dallahaha" meaning he drew it out. It was also said that "fadallahuma" means he made them bold, from al-dalalah, which is audacity; i.e., he emboldened them to disobedience, so they came out of the Garden.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves some of the leaves of the Garden﴾. In this there are three issues. The first: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿When they tasted the tree﴾ means they ate from it. The disagreement concerning this tree, and how Adam ate from it, has passed in "al-Baqarah" (vol. 1, p. 304). "Their private parts became apparent to them": Hawwa' ate first and nothing befell her; when Adam ate, the punishment took effect, because the prohibition was addressed to both of them, as has passed in "al-Baqarah" (vol. 1, p. 304). Ibn 'Abbas said: the light that had been their garment contracted and became nails on the hands and feet.

The second: "wa-tafiqa" — the fa' may be sukun. Al-Akhfash related "tafiqa yatfiqu," like "daraba yadribu." It is said "tafiqa," meaning he began to do the action. "Yakhsifani": al-Hasan read with a kasra on the kha' and a shaddah on the sad; the original is "yakhtasifani," which was assimilated, and the kha' was given a kasra because of the meeting of two sukuns. Ibn Burayda and Ya'qub read with a fatha on the kha', having transferred the vowel of the ta' onto it. It may also be "yukhassifani" with a damma on the ya', from khassafa yukhassifu. al-Zuhri read "yukhsifani" from akhsafa. Both are transmitted, with the hamzah or the doubling; the meaning is: they cut the leaves and stuck them together so that they might cover themselves with them. From this is "khasf al-na'l" (stitching of the sandal). The khassaf is the one who patches them, and the mikhsaf is the awl. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the leaf of the fig tree. It is related that when Adam, peace be upon him, saw his private parts exposed, he went around the trees of the Garden, seeking a leaf from them with which to cover his nakedness, and the trees of the Garden rebuked him until the fig tree took pity on him and gave him a leaf. "And they began" — meaning Adam and Hawwa' — "to fasten over themselves some of the leaves of the Garden." Allah then rewarded the fig tree by making its outside and inside equal in sweetness and benefit, and gave it two fruits in one year, twice.

It is not impossible that they were commanded to this in the Garden, just as they were told: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾. Sahib al-Bayan related from al-Shafi'i that whoever finds nothing to cover his 'awrah except the leaves of trees is obliged to cover himself with them, because it is a visible covering with which he can conceal himself, as Adam did in the Garden. And Allah knows best.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their Lord called to them: Did I not forbid you from that tree, and tell you that Satan is to you a manifest enemy? They said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers﴾. That is, He said to them: Did I not forbid you? Adam thought that no one swears by Allah falsely, so [Iblis] deceived them through his whispering and his oath to them. Qatadah said: he swore to them by Allah until he deceived them. The believer may be deceived through Allah [i.e., through an oath by Allah]. Some of the scholars used to say: whoever deceives us by Allah, we are deceived by him. Indeed, the generous man, when you wish, you can deceive him,

All the pronouns refer to the earth. He did not mention the waw in "qala" (He said); had he mentioned it, it would also have been permissible [[i.e., in this kind of construction outside the Qur'an.]]. It is like your saying: "Zayd said to 'Amr such-and-such, and he said to him such-and-such."

There are four issues here.

The first concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts﴾. Many scholars said: this verse is evidence for the obligation to cover the 'awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered), because He said, "it covers your private parts." Others said that there is no evidence in it for what they mentioned, but that it indicates only a favour (bounty). I say: the first view is more correct. Covering the 'awrah is among the favours, and so He made clear that He (glory be to Him) made available to His offspring what they can use to cover their 'awrahs, and this indicates the command to cover. There is no disagreement among the scholars on the obligation to cover the 'awrah from people's eyes.

They differed over what the 'awrah is. Ibn Abi Dhi'b said: for a man it is the genitals themselves, the front and the rear, and nothing else. This is the view of Dawud (al-Zahiri), the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir), Ibn Abi 'Ablah [in waw: Ibn 'Atiyya] and al-Tabari, based on Allah's words: "clothing to cover your private parts," "when their private parts became apparent to them," and "to show them their private parts."

In al-Bukhari, from Anas: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ rode his mount [i.e., drove his animal] in the alleys of Khaybar," and in it: "then the izar slipped from his thigh, until I could see the whiteness of the thigh of the Prophet of Allah ﷺ."

Malik said: the navel is not 'awrah, and I dislike that a man should uncover his thigh in the presence of his wife. Abu Hanifa said: the knee is 'awrah, and this is the view of 'Ata. Al-Shafi'i said: neither the navel nor the two knees are 'awrah, according to the sound view. Abu Hamid al-Tirmidhi related that al-Shafi'i had two opinions regarding the navel.

The proof for Malik is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Jarhad: "Cover your thigh, for the thigh is 'awrah." Al-Bukhari recorded it as a suspended narration (ta'liq) and said: the hadith of Anas has a stronger chain, and the hadith of Jarhad is more cautious, so that one may leave the disagreement. This hadith of Jarhad indicates the opposite of what Abu Hanifa said.

It is also narrated that Abu Hurayra kissed the navel of al-Hasan ibn 'Ali and said: "I kiss from you what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to kiss from you." Had the navel been 'awrah, Abu Hurayra would not have kissed it, nor would al-Hasan have allowed him to.

As for the free woman, her whole body is 'awrah except the face and the two palms. Most people of knowledge hold this view. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever wishes to marry a woman, let him look at her face and her palms." And because uncovering it is obligatory in the state of ihram.

Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham said: every part of a woman is 'awrah, even her fingernail. It is narrated from Ahmad ibn Hanbal something similar.

As for the umm al-walad (a slave woman who has borne her master's child), al-Athram said: I heard him, meaning Ahmad ibn Hanbal, being asked about the umm al-walad, how she should pray. He said: she covers her head and her feet, because she cannot be sold, and she prays as the free woman prays.

As for the female slave (amah), the 'awrah of her is what is beneath her breasts, and she may uncover her head and her forearms. It is also said: her ruling is the ruling of the man. It is also said: it is disliked for her to uncover her head and her chest. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to beat the slave women for covering their heads, and would say: "Do not imitate the free women."

Asbagh said: if her thigh is uncovered, she repeats the prayer within its time. Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham said: every part of a slave woman is 'awrah, even her fingernail. This view departs from the sayings of the jurists, because they agree that a free woman may perform the obligatory prayer while her hands and face are uncovered, all of it, while she touches the ground with them. So the slave woman is more entitled to this, and the umm al-walad is in a stricter condition than the slave woman.

A young child has no sanctity regarding his 'awrah. When a girl reaches an age at which she attracts the gaze and is desired, she covers her 'awrah.

The proof of Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers that they should draw their outer garments over themselves﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 241].

The hadith of Umm Salama: she was asked, "What garments should a woman pray in?" She said: "In a shirt (dir') and a wide head-cover (khimar) that conceals the tops of her feet." It has been narrated as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report. But those who stopped it at Umm Salama (as her own statement) are more numerous and more retentive, among them Malik and Ibn Ishaq and others. Abu Dawud said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar raised it, from Muhammad ibn Zayd, from his mother [in b: from his father; he has been narrated from both his father and his mother], from Umm Salama, that she asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Abu 'Umar said: this 'Abd al-Rahman is weak according to them, except that al-Bukhari did record some of his narrations. And the consensus on this matter is stronger than the report.

The second issue concerns the words of Allah: ﴿We have sent down to you clothing﴾. It means the rain that makes the cotton and the flax grow, and that makes the livestock thrive, from which come wool, fur and hair [in the sources: "which" — probably "the livestock which"]. So it is a metaphor, like His words: "And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock" [see vol. 15, p. 234], as will come. It is also said: this sending down was the sending down of the means of clothing together with Adam and Eve, so that it would be an example for others. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "We have sent down to you" means "We created for you," like His words, "And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock," that is, He created them, as will come. It is also said: We inspired you with the method of making it.

The third issue concerns the words of Allah: ﴿and finery (rishan)﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, 'Asim (in the narration of al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi), and Abu 'Amr (in the narration of al-Husayn ibn 'Ali al-Ju'fi) read it as "riyashan." Abu 'Ubayd did not report it except from al-Hasan, and did not explain its meaning. It is the plural of rish, which is what is of wealth and clothing. Al-Farra' said: rish and riyash are like libs and libas. The feathers of a bird (rish al-tair) is what Allah has covered it with. It is also said: it is abundance and a comfortable life. What most lexicographers hold is that rish is whatever covers of clothing or livelihood. Sibawayh recited:

"My finery is from you, and my desire is with you, even if your visits are rare."

Abu Hatim related from Abu 'Ubayda: "He gave the animal its rish," that is, its covering and what is upon it of clothing.

The fourth issue concerns the words of Allah: ﴿And the clothing of taqwa, that is best﴾. He showed that taqwa is the best clothing, as one says:

"When a man does not wear garments of taqwa, he will be exposed, even if he is clothed."

"The best clothing of a man is obedience to his Lord, and there is no good in one who disobeys Allah."

Qasim ibn Malik related from 'Awf from Ma'bad al-Juhani, who said: "The clothing of taqwa" is modesty (haya'). Ibn 'Abbas said: "The clothing of taqwa" is righteous deeds. And from him also: the good bearing in the face. It is also said: what Allah the Mighty and Majestic taught and guided to. It is also said: "The clothing of taqwa" is wearing wool and coarse garments, which are used for humility before Allah the Exalted and in worship to Him, and are better than other garments. Zayd ibn 'Ali said: "The clothing of taqwa" is the coat of mail, the helmet, the arm-guards and the leg-guards, by which one protects oneself in battle. 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr said: it is fear of Allah. It is also said: it is being conscious of the taqwa of Allah in what He commanded and what He forbade. I say: this is the correct view, and to it returns the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Urwa. The saying of Zayd ibn 'Ali is good, for it urges jihad. Ibn Zayd said: it is covering the 'awrah. This involves repetition, since He said first: "We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts." As for the one who said it is wearing coarse garments, as being closer to humility and abandoning showiness, this is an assertion; the eminent scholars used to wear fine garments while maintaining taqwa, as will be explained, if Allah the Exalted wills.

The people of Medina and al-Kisa'i read "libasa" in the accusative, in coordination with the first "libasan." It is also said that it is governed by a hidden verb, meaning "and We sent down the clothing of taqwa." The rest read it in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'). "Dhalika" is its adjective, and "khayrun" is the predicate of the subject. The meaning: "And the clothing of taqwa, the one referred to, which you know, is better for you than the clothing of garments that cover your private parts, and than the finery that We sent down to you. So wear it." It is also said: it is raised by a hidden pronoun, meaning "and it is the clothing of taqwa," that is, it is covering the 'awrah. On this basis the saying of Ibn Zayd is explained. It is also said: the meaning is "and the clothing of taqwa is good," with "dhalika" meaning "huwa" (it). The first grammatical analysis (i'rab) is the best of what has been said about it. Al-A'mash read "wa-libasu al-taqwa khayrun" without "dhalika," and this contradicts the Mushaf.

"That is among the signs of Allah": that is, among the things that indicate that He has a Creator. "Dhalika" is in the nominative as an adjective, or as an apposition (badal), or as an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan).

**First issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾, means: let not Satan divert you from the religion, just as he tempted your two parents by expelling them from the Garden. "Ab" (أَبٌ) is used for the masculine and "abah" (أَبَةٌ) for the feminine. On this basis it was said that "abawan" (أَبَوَانِ) is in the accusative position as a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), describing their state: (having their clothing stripped from them) (ينزع عنهما لباسهما). It may also be a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnaf), in which case one pauses at "from the Garden." "Liyurayahuma" (لِيُرِيَهُما) is in the accusative by the lām of kay (لام كي, the lām of purpose).

﴿Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe﴾. The original form is "yarāʾakum," then the hamza was lightened. "Qabīluhu" (وَقَبِيلُهُ) is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the pronoun, and the separating emphasis (tawkīd) is used to make the conjunction good, as in His saying: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾. This shows that "ra'aytuka wa-ʿAmr" (رأيتك وعمرو) is ugly, and that the pronoun is treated like an explicit noun. In this verse there is also evidence for the obligation to cover the ʿawrah (awrah, the private parts that must be covered), because of His saying: (He strips their clothing from them) (ينزع عنهما لباسهما). Others said: the verse only warns against the loss of blessing, as happened to Adam. This would hold only if it were established that the law of Adam binds us, and the matter is otherwise.

**Second issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He sees you, he and his tribe﴾. "Qabīluhu" (قَبِيلُهُ) means his troops. Mujahid said: it means the jinn and the devils. Ibn Zayd said: "qabīluhu" means his offspring. It was also said: his generation (jīluhu). ﴿From where you cannot see them.﴾ Some scholars said: in this there is evidence that the jinn cannot be seen, because of His saying "from where you cannot see them." It was said: it is possible for them to be seen, since God, when He wills to show them, uncovers their bodies so that they become visible. Al-Nahhas said: "from where you cannot see them" indicates that the jinn are not seen except at the time of a prophet, so that this serves as a sign of his prophethood, because God, mighty and majestic, created them in a form in which they are not seen, and they are seen only when they are transformed out of their forms. That is among the miracles, which occur only in the time of the prophets, may the prayers and peace of God be upon them. Al-Qushayri said: God has established the custom that the children of Adam do not see the devils today. In a report: "Indeed, Satan flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows." And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿who whispers in the breasts of mankind﴾. [See vol. 20, p. 263.] The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the angel has an impulse (lamma), and Satan has an impulse," that is, in the heart. "As for the impulse of the angel, it is a promise of good and an affirmation of the truth; as for the impulse of Satan, it is a promise of evil and a denial of the truth." This has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 3, pp. 329 and 269.] Reports about their being seen have also come down in authentic narrations. Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entrusted me with guarding the zakat of Ramadan, and he mentioned a long story in which he said that he seized the jinni who used to take the dates, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What did your captive do last night?" In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By God, were it not for the supplication of my brother Sulayman, he would have been bound and the boys of the people of Madinah would have played with him." This concerns the ʿifrit (ʿifrīt, a powerful jinni) who suddenly rushed upon him (i.e., appeared before him unexpectedly). It will come in Surah Sad, God willing. [See on His saying: "He said, My Lord, forgive me and grant me..." vol. 15, p. 204.]

﴿Indeed We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾: that is, as an increase in their punishment, and We made them equal in going astray from the truth.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 28:

Al-fahisha (the grave indecency) here, according to the view of most of the exegetes (mufassirun), is their circumambulating the House (the Ka'bah) while naked. Al-Hasan said: it is shirk (associating partners with God) and kufr (disbelief). They argued for this by following their forefathers in taqlid (blind imitation), and by saying that God had commanded them to do it. Al-Hasan said: "And God commanded us to do it." They said: "If God disliked what we are upon, He would have forbidden it to us."

﴿Say: Indeed, God does not command indecency.﴾ This shows that they are arbitrary, and they have no proof that God commanded them to what they claim. The condemnation of taqlid and the condemnation of many of their ignorant beliefs has already passed, and this is one of them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 29–30:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means "There is no god but Allah." It was also said: al-qist means justice, i.e., "Command: justice, so obey Him." There is an ellipsis in the speech.

(And set your faces [toward Him]) That is, turn toward Him in every prayer, toward the qiblah.

(At every place of worship) That is, in whatever mosque you are.

(And call upon Him, sincere to Him in religion) That is, make Him one and do not associate anything with Him.

(As He originated you, you will return) Its parallel is: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ [see p. 42 of this part], and it has already been discussed. The kaf (as) is in the position of a accusative: you will return as He originated you, i.e., as He created you the first time, He will restore you. Al-Zajjaj said: it is connected to what precedes it, i.e., ﴿And from it you will be brought out, as He originated you, you will return﴾.

(A group He guided) "Fariqan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "taʿudun" (you will return), i.e., you will return as two groups: the happy and the wretched. This is strengthened by the reading of Ubayy: "You will return as two groups: a group He guided, and a group upon whom misguidance was due," transmitted from al-Kisai. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said concerning His saying, "A group He guided and a group upon whom misguidance was due": whoever Allah created for misguidance, He makes him end in misguidance even if he does the deeds of guidance; and whoever Allah created upon guidance, He makes him end in guidance even if he does the deeds of misguidance. Allah created Iblis upon misguidance, and he did the deeds of felicity with the angels; then Allah returned him to that upon which He had created him. He said: ﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾. In this there is a clear refutation of the Qadariyyah and those who follow them. It was also said: "fariqan" is governed by "hada" (guided), and the second "fariqan" is in the accusative by an implied verb, i.e., and He misguided a group. Sibawayh recited:

I no longer carry a weapon, nor can I hold the camel's head if it bolts,
And I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain.

[The two verses are by al-Rabiʿ ibn Dabʿ al-Fazari, describing the end of his youth and the loss of his strength.]

Al-Farra said: and if it were in the nominative [it would be permissible], [i.e., in such a construction outside the speech of Allah].

(Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of Allah) ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read "annahum" with a hamzah, meaning "because they".
