**Part 1 of 2**

There are seven issues in this verse.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿O children of Adam﴾. It is an address to all of humankind, even though its specific occasion concerned those Arabs who used to circumambulate the House naked. The ruling is general for every place of prayer, because the consideration is for the generality of the wording, not for the specific occasion (*sabab*, the circumstance of revelation). Some scholars denied that the verse refers to circumambulation, arguing that circumambulation occurs only at one mosque, whereas what applies to every mosque is prayer. This is the view of someone whose understanding of the objectives of the Sharia (*maqasid al-shari'ah*) was obscure. In the Sahih of Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A woman used to circumambulate the House while naked, saying: 'Who will lend me a *tiwaf*?' [[The garment with which one circumambulates. Its form is *tif'al* (*tiqwal*), with a vowel of fatha or kasra.]] She would put it over her private parts, and she would say:

*Today some of it or all of it will show,*
*And whatever shows of it, I will not make lawful.*"

Then this verse was revealed: "Take your adornment at every mosque," with *al-tiwaf* pronounced with a kasra on the *ta'*. This woman was Duba'ah bint 'Amir ibn Qurt, as stated by al-Qadi 'Iyad. Also in the Sahih of Muslim, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, who said: "The Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked, except for the Hums [[The Hums were so named because they were strict (*tahammasu*) in their religion; *al-hamasah* means courage.]]. The Hums were Quraysh and those they had given birth to. They would circumambulate the House naked unless the Hums gave them garments, so men would give garments to men and women would give garments to women. The Hums would not leave Muzdalifah, and all the people would stand at 'Arafat [[In Sahih Muslim: they would reach 'Arafat.]]." In a version other than Muslim's: "They would say, 'We are the people of the Haram; no one of the Arabs should circumambulate except in our garments, and no one who enters our land should eat except from our food.' Whoever among the Arabs had no friend in Mecca to lend him a garment, and no means to hire one, was left with one of two options: either he circumambulated the House naked, or he circumambulated in his own clothes. When he finished his circumambulation, he would cast off his garment, and no one would touch it." That garment was called *al-laqa*. A poet among the Arabs said:

*Enough of sorrow is my companion who stood over it,*
*As if it were a *laqa* before the circumambulators, a forbidden thing.*

They remained in that ignorance, innovation and misguidance until Allah sent His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and Allah revealed: "O children of Adam, take your adornment," to the end of the verse. The Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) caller proclaimed: "Beware, no one may circumambulate the House naked."

I say: As for those who said that the intended meaning is prayer, and that its adornment is sandals, this is based on what Kurz ibn Wabarah narrated from 'Ata', from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said one day: "Take the adornment of prayer." It was asked: "What is the adornment of prayer?" He said: "Wear your sandals and pray in them."

The second issue: the verse indicates the obligation of covering the *awrah* (the parts of the body that must be covered), as previously mentioned. The majority of scholars held that covering it is an obligatory element (*fard*) of prayer. Al-Abhari said it is obligatory in general, and a person must cover it from people's eyes during prayer and at other times. This is the correct view, based on the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying to al-Miswar ibn Makhramah: "Return to your garment and take it, and do not walk about naked." Muslim transmitted it. Isma'il al-Qadi held that covering the *awrah* is one of the recommended practices (*sunan*) of prayer. He argued that if it were an obligation in prayer, a naked person would not be permitted to pray, since every obligatory element of prayer must be performed when one is able, or replaced by its substitute when one is not, or else the prayer is entirely dropped; and this is not the case. Ibn al-'Arabi said: If we say that covering the *awrah* is obligatory in prayer, then if an imam's garment falls and his rear is exposed while he is bowing, and he raises his head and covers it, his prayer is valid. This was stated by Ibn al-Qasim. Sahnun said: Everyone among the followers who looked at him must repeat the prayer. It is also narrated from Sahnun that he must repeat it, and they too must repeat it, because covering the *awrah* is a condition of prayer, so if it is exposed, the prayer is invalidated, just as with purity (*taharah*), which is its root. Qadi Ibn al-'Arabi said: As for those who say their prayer is not invalidated, they have not lost a condition. As for those who say that if he takes it back in its place his prayer is valid, but the prayer of whoever looked at him is invalidated, this is a page that must be erased, and it is not permissible to occupy oneself with it.

In al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i, from 'Amr ibn Salamah, who said: "When my people returned from the Prophet (ﷺ), they said: 'He said: Let the one who has the most memorization of the Qur'an lead you.' So they called me and taught me the bowing and prostration, and I would lead them in prayer, while I wore a patched cloak. They would say to my father: 'Will you not cover your son's backside (*ist*) for us?'" This is the wording of al-Nasa'i. And it is established from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: "The men used to tie their waist-wraps (*izar*) around their necks behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during prayer, because the wraps were so narrow, like children's clothes. Someone said: 'O women's community, do not raise your heads until the men have raised theirs.'" Al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud transmitted it.

The third issue concerns the case where a person sees his own *awrah*. Al-Shafi'i said: If the garment is tight, he should button it or fasten it with something so that the shirt does not gape and the *awrah* is not visible through the collar. If he does not do this and sees his own *awrah*, he must repeat the prayer. This is also the view of Ahmad. Malik permitted praying in a shirt with its buttons undone, when one wears no trousers. This is also the view of Abu Hanifah and Abu Thawr. Salim used to pray with his buttons undone. Dawud al-Ta'i said: If he has a large beard, there is no harm in it. Al-Athram transmitted a similar view from Ahmad. If he is an imam, he should pray only with his cloak (*rida'*), because it is part of adornment. It was said that among the adornments is praying in sandals, narrated from Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ), but this is not authentically established. It was also said that the adornment of prayer is raising the hands during bowing and rising from it. Abu 'Umar said: Everything has an adornment, and the adornment of prayer is the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") and raising the hands. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When Allah grants you abundance, then be generous to yourselves." A man gathers his garments and prays in a waist-wrap and a cloak, in a waist-wrap and a shirt, in a waist-wrap and a *qaba'*, in trousers and a cloak, in trousers and a shirt, in trousers and a *qaba'*, and I think he said: in a *tubban* and a shirt, in a *tubban* and a cloak, in a *tubban* and a *qaba'*. [[The *qaba'* (with fatha) is a garment worn over clothes; it was also said it is worn over a shirt and tied at the waist. The *tubban* (with a damma on the *ta'* and a shadda on the *ba'*) is a small pair of trousers about a span long, covering only the most severe *awrah*.]] Al-Bukhari and al-Daraqutni transmitted it.

The fourth issue concerns His saying, ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: In this verse, Allah permitted eating and drinking as long as it was not extravagance (*israf*) or pride (*makhilah*, meaning arrogance). As for what need requires, namely what satisfies hunger and quenches thirst, it is recommended by both reason and the Sharia, because of what it contains in preserving the self and protecting the senses. For this reason the Sharia prohibited continuous fasting (*wisal*), because it weakens the body, deadens the soul, and weakens one for worship. The Sharia forbids this, and reason rejects it. Whoever restricts himself below the amount needed has no share of righteousness and no portion of asceticism, because what he is deprived of by weakness and frailty, in terms of performing acts of obedience, is greater in reward and greater in recompense. There is a disagreement about what exceeds the amount needed, on two views: it was said to be forbidden, and it was said to be disliked. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is the correct view, for the measure of satiety varies with the differences of lands, times, ages and appetites. Then it was said: there are many benefits in eating little. Among them: a person becomes healthier in body, better in memory, sounder in understanding, sleeps less, and is lighter in spirit. In excessive eating there is the heaviness of the stomach and the foul smell of indigestion [[In 'Ali's text: *nataan li-l-mini'hah*. Al-Jawhari said: *al-infahah* is the rennet (the abomasum).]], and from it various diseases arise, requiring more treatment than the one who eats little needs. Some of the wise said: The greatest medicine is regulating one's food. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained this meaning in a sufficient explanation that dispenses with the words of physicians. He said: "No human fills a vessel worse than the belly. It is sufficient for the son of Adam to have a few morsels that keep his back upright. If he must, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath." Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the hadith of al-Miqdam ibn Ma'd Yakrib. Our scholars said: If Hippocrates had heard this division, he would have marvelled at this wisdom.

It is mentioned that al-Rashid had a skilled Christian physician, who said to 'Ali ibn al-Husayn: "There is nothing in your book about the science of medicine, and knowledge is of two kinds: the knowledge of religions and the knowledge of bodies." 'Ali said to him: "Allah has gathered all of medicine in half a verse of our Book." He said: "What is it?" He said: "The words of the Mighty and Majestic: 'Eat and drink, but do not be excessive.'" The Christian said: "Nothing of medicine has been transmitted from your Messenger either." 'Ali said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered medicine in brief words [[In 'Ali's text: *al-mi'dah bayt al-da'* ... This is the famous version, but it is not a hadith; it is from the words of al-Harith ibn Kaladah, the physician of the Arabs. See *Kashf al-Khulafa'*, vol. 2, p. 214, where there is a discussion about this hadith.]]." He said: "What are they?" He said: "(The stomach is the house of diseases, dieting is the head of every remedy, and give every body what it is accustomed to.)" The Christian said: "Neither your Book nor your Prophet left anything of medicine for Galen."

I say: It is said that treating the sick person is in two halves: half is medicine and half is dieting. If the two are combined, you will see the patient recover and become healthy. If not, then dieting is more beneficial for him, since medicine may benefit when dieting is abandoned, and dieting may benefit even when medicine is abandoned. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The root of every remedy is dieting." What is meant by it, and Allah knows best, is that it suffices in place of every remedy. For this reason it is said that the people of India rely mostly on dieting for their treatment: the patient abstains from eating, drinking and speaking for several days, and then he recovers and becomes healthy.

The fifth issue: Muslim narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The disbeliever eats with seven intestines, and the believer eats with one intestine.'" This is from him (ﷺ) an encouragement to minimize worldly consumption, to be ascetic in it, and to be content with sustenance. The Arabs used to praise little eating and disparage much eating, as one of their poets said:

*A slice of liver is enough for him, if he gets it,*
*Of roasted meat, and the young camel's drink quenches his thirst.* [[The verse is by A'sha Bahilah, lamenting his brother al-Muntashir ibn Wahb al-Bahili. The version in *Lisan al-'Arab* reads: "*yakfihi hazzah fallaz*." The meaning is the same. *Al-Ghamr* (with damma on the first letter and fatha on the second) is a small wound.]]

And Umm Zar' said about Abu Zar''s son [[In 'Ali's text: "daughter" (*ibnah*), meaning: it satisfies her.]]: "And the foreleg of a young kid satisfies him." [[*Al-Jafrah* is a young goat that has reached four months of age.]] And Hatim al-Ta'i, disparaging much eating, said:

*For if you give your belly its desire,*
*And your private parts, both will reach the end of blame together.* [[What is in his *Diwan* is:*
*"And if you give whatever you have..."*
*etc.]]

Al-Khattabi said: The meaning of his saying (ﷺ [[From ʿ.]]), "The believer eats in one intestine," is that the believer takes only what is enough for him, not his full fill. He prefers others over himself and leaves some of his provision for someone else, so what he has eaten satisfies him. The first interpretation is more preferable, and God knows best.

It was said regarding his saying, peace be upon him, "The disbeliever eats in seven intestines," that it is not meant in its general sense, because observation refutes it. There may be a disbeliever who eats less than a believer, and when a disbeliever becomes a Muslim, his eating does not decrease or increase. It was also said that it refers to a specific person: an unbelieving guest was a guest of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is said that he was al-Jahjaha al-Ghifari. It was also said: Thumamah ibn Uthal. It was also said: Nadlah ibn Amr al-Ghifari. It was also said: Basrah ibn Abi Basrah al-Ghifari. He drank the milk of seven sheep. Then in the morning he became a Muslim and drank the milk of one sheep, but he could not finish it. So the Prophet (ﷺ) said that. It is as if he meant: this disbeliever. God knows best.

It was also said: when the heart is illuminated by the light of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), it looks at food with the eye of strengthening oneself for obedience, so it takes from it only the amount needed. When the heart is dark with disbelief, its eating is like that of a beast that grazes until it voids thin dung. [[Al-tholt: the thin part of dung.]]

Scholars disagreed about whether these intestines are literal or not. It was said they are literal, and they have known names among the people of knowledge in medicine and anatomy. It was also said they are metaphors for seven causes by which the glutton eats: he eats out of need, out of hearing [[i.e., the desire of the ear]], smelling, seeing, touching, and tasting, and he increases by [[In ʿ: istitaʿaman.]] acquiring more. It was also said the meaning is that he eats like one who has seven intestines, while the believer, through the lightness of his eating, eats like one who has only one intestine. Thus he shares with the disbeliever a part of his eating, while the disbeliever exceeds him by seven times. The word "intestine" in this hadith means the stomach.

Sixth issue: once this is established, know that it is recommended for a person to wash his hands before and after eating, because of the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Ablution before food and after it is blessing." Likewise it is in the Torah. This was narrated by Zadhan from Salman. Malik disliked washing clean hands, but following the hadith is preferable. A person should not eat food until he knows whether it is hot or cold, because if it is hot he may be harmed. It is narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Cool your food, for hot food has no blessing." It is a sound hadith. This was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah.

He should not smell the food, for that is the behaviour of beasts. Rather, if he desires it he eats it, and if he dislikes it he leaves it. He should make the morsel small and chew it well, so that he is not considered greedy. He should mention God Most High at its beginning and praise Him at its end. He should not raise his voice in praise unless his companions have finished eating, because raising the voice would prevent them from eating.

The etiquette of eating is numerous; this is a summary of it. Some of it will come in Surat Hud, God willing. [[See vol. 9, p. 64.]] There are also well-known etiquettes for drinking, which we have omitted because they are well known. In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Umar, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you eats, let him eat with his right hand, and when he drinks, let him drink with his right hand, for the devil eats with his left hand and drinks with his left hand."

Seventh issue: His saying, Most High, ﴿And do not waste﴾ means in excess of eating. Excess eating leads to excess drinking, which burdens the stomach and holds a person back from serving his Lord and taking his share of voluntary good deeds. If this extends to what prevents him from performing an obligation required of him, it becomes forbidden, and he has been wasteful in his food and drink.

Asad ibn Musa narrated, from the hadith of Awn ibn Abi Juhayfah, from his father, who said: "I ate thareed (bread soaked in broth) with fatty meat, then I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while I was belching [[Tajashshu’: the breathing out of the stomach when it is full.]]. He said: 'Restrain your belching, Abu Juhayfah, for the people who are most satisfied in this world will be the most hungry on the Day of Resurrection.'" Abu Juhayfah never ate until his stomach was full until he died. When he had lunch, he did not have dinner, and when he had dinner, he did not have lunch.

I say: This may be the meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, "The believer eats in one intestine," meaning the one of complete faith. Whoever has excellent Islam and perfect faith, like Abu Juhayfah, reflects on what he will face concerning death and what comes after it, and fear and dread of those terrors prevent him from fulfilling his desires. God knows best.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of "and do not waste" is: do not eat what is forbidden. It was also said: "Wasting is to eat everything you desire." Anas ibn Malik narrated this from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan. It was also said: wasting includes eating after one is already satisfied. All of these are prohibited.

Luqman said to his son: "O my son, do not eat to satiety upon satiety, for if you throw it to the dog, that is better than eating it." Samurah ibn Jundub asked about his son: "What has he done?" They said: "He suffered indigestion yesterday." He said: "Indigestion! " They said: "Yes." He said: "If he dies, I will not pray over him."

It was also said that in the Jahiliyyah the Arabs did not eat fat during their days of Hajj, were content with little food, and circumambulated the Ka'bah naked. So it was said to them: "Take your adornment at every mosque, and eat and drink, and do not waste," meaning by forbidding what God has not forbidden to you.

**Part 1 of 2**

There are four issues here.

**The first issue:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾. This shows that they forbade of their own accord what Allah had not forbidden them. The "adornment" here means fine clothing, when its owner is able to afford it. It was also said that it means all clothing, as was narrated from Umar: "When Allah grants you abundance, then be generous." This has already been mentioned. It is narrated from Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, the teacher of Malik, may Allah be pleased with them all, that he used to wear a khazz (silk) cloak worth fifty dinars. He wore it in winter, and when summer came he gave it in charity, or sold it and gave its price in charity. In summer he wore two garments of cotton from Egypt, dyed with mashq [[A mumashshaq garment is one dyed with mashq, which is a red dye.]], and he would say: "Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?"

**The second issue:** If this is so, then the verse indicates the wearing of fine garments and beautifying oneself with them on Friday and at the festivals, when meeting people, and when visiting brothers in faith. Abu al-Aliyah said: "The Muslims, when they visited one another, would beautify themselves." In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, that he saw a silk garment [[Sira' is spelled with an unvowelled sin, then a kasra, then a yā' with a fatha, then a long alif. It is a type of striped cloth, with yellow stripes or mixed with them, made of silk. The word hulla is pronounced with tanwin, making sira' a descriptive adjective, or without tanwin, making it an idafa construction. Both readings are well known.]] being sold at the door of the mosque. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you bought it for Friday and for the delegations when they come to you?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Only one who has no share in the Hereafter wears this." He did not object to him mentioning beautification; he objected only to the garment being sira'. Tamim al-Dari bought a garment for a thousand dirhams and used to pray in it. Malik ibn Dinar used to wear fine Adeni garments. The garment of Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to be bought for about a dinar. How far is this from one who shuns it and prefers coarse clothing of linen and wool? [He says] "But the garment of piety, that is better" [Qur'an 7:26]. Far from it! Do you think those we have mentioned abandoned the garment of piety? No, by Allah! Rather, they are the people of piety and the possessors of knowledge and discernment, while others are people of claims, whose hearts are empty of piety.

Khalid ibn Shawdhab said: "I witnessed al-Hasan, and Farqad came to him. Al-Hasan took hold of his cloak, pulled him toward himself, and said: 'O Furayqid, O son of the mother of Furayqid! Righteousness is not in this cloak. Righteousness is only what settles in the chest and is confirmed by action.'"

Abu Muhammad, the nephew of Ma'ruf al-Karkhi, entered upon Abu al-Hasan ibn Yasar [[In manuscripts j, w, k and h: Bashshar.]] while wearing a woolen robe. Abu al-Hasan said to him: "O Abu Muhammad, have you made your heart woolen or your body? Make your heart woolen, and wear the Quhi over the Quhi [[Al-Quhi is a kind of white Persian garment, attributed to Quhistan.]]."

A man said to al-Shibli: "A group of your companions have arrived and they are in the congregational mosque." So he went and saw that they were wearing patched garments and rags. He then began to recite:

"As for the tents, they are like their tents,
But I see the women of the tribe are not their women."

Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I dislike wearing rags and patched garments, for four reasons. The first: it is not the dress of the early generations (al-salaf), who only patched out of necessity. The second: it implies a claim of poverty, while a person is commanded to show the effects of Allah's blessings upon him [[In manuscripts j and k: blessing. In a hadith: Allah loves to see the effect of His blessing upon His servant, narrated by al-Tirmidhi.]]. The third: it displays asceticism, which we have been commanded to conceal. The fourth: it is an imitation of those who have strayed from the Shari'ah. And whoever imitates a people is one of them."

Al-Tabari said: "Whoever prefers clothing of hair and wool over clothing of cotton and linen, when the means to it is lawful, has erred. Likewise whoever eats only herbs and lentils instead of wheat bread, or who abandons eating meat out of fear of the arousal of sexual desire." Bishr ibn al-Harith was asked about wearing wool, and it displeased him; his dislike was evident in his face. Then he said: "Wearing khazz and mu'asfar [[A garment dyed with safflower.]] is more beloved to me than wearing wool in cities."

Abu al-Faraj said: "The early generations used to wear garments of medium quality, neither luxurious nor shabby, and they chose the best of them for Friday, for the festivals, and for meeting their brothers. Choosing the best was not considered blameworthy among them. As for clothing that disgraces its wearer, it implies a display of asceticism and a display of poverty, and it is as if it were a tongue of complaint against Allah, the Exalted, and it causes the wearer to be despised. All of this is disliked and forbidden."

If someone says: "Beautifying one's clothing is a desire of the self, and we have been commanded to struggle against it. And it is adornment for people, while we have been commanded that our actions be for Allah, not for people." The answer is: not everything the self desires is blameworthy, and not everything by which one adorns oneself before people is disliked. Rather, one is forbidden from it only when the Shari'ah has forbidden it, or when it is done for show in matters of religion. A person naturally loves to be seen as beautiful, and this is a portion of the self for which he is not blamed. For this reason he combs his hair, looks in the mirror, straightens his turban, and wears a coarse lining of his garment inward while the fine outer side faces outward. None of this is disliked or blameworthy.

Makhul narrated from Aisha, who said: "A group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were waiting for him at the door. He came out wishing to go to them, and there was a water vessel in the house. He began looking into the water and straightening his beard and hair. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you too do this?' He said: '[Yes], when a man goes out to his brothers, let him prepare himself, for Allah is beautiful and loves beauty.'"

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "He who has in his heart an atom's weight of pride will not enter Paradise."

A man said: "A man likes his garment to be fine and his sandal to be fine." He (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is Beautiful and loves beauty. Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people."

The hadiths on this theme are numerous, and all of them point to cleanliness and good appearance. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to us: al-Fadl ibn Dukayn informed us, saying: Mandal related to us from Thawr, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to travel with a comb, a mirror, oil, a tooth-stick (siwak), and kohl.

From Ibn Jurayj: an ivory comb with which he would comb his hair.

Ibn Sa'd said: Qabisa ibn Uqba informed us, saying: Sufyan related to us from Rabi' ibn Subayh, from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would frequently oil his head and comb his beard with water.

Yazid ibn Harun informed us: Abbad ibn Mansur related to us from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a kohl-pot with which he would apply kohl at bedtime, three times to each eye.

**The third issue:** Allah's words: ﴿And the good things of provision﴾. The word *al-tayyibat* (the good things) is a general term for what is good in its acquisition and in its taste. Ibn Abbas and Qatada said: By "the good things of provision" is meant what the people of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic age) prohibited, such as the *bahair* (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released), the *sawa'ib* (animals set free), the *wasa'il* (certain animals, especially sheep, that gave twins), and the *hawami* (stallions set free after siring a set number of offspring). It was also said: the good things are every pleasant kind of food.

Scholars differed on abandoning good things and turning away from pleasures. Some said that this is not among the acts of worship: doing and leaving are equal in what is permissible. Others said that it is not an act of worship in itself, but a means to asceticism in this world, shortening hope in it, and avoiding excessive exertion for its sake; and this is recommended, and what is recommended is an act of worship. Others said, and it is reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "If we wished, we could have made for ourselves *sila'* (roasted meat), *sala'iq* (pastries), and *sinab* (mustard with raisins). But I heard Allah, the Exalted, blame people, saying: ﴿You used up your good things in your worldly life﴾." It is also reported with the letter *ra'* as *sara'iq*; both mean *al-jaradiq* (loaves of bread). *Al-sala'iq* (with a lam) is what sticks of meat and herbs. *Al-sila'* (with a kasra on the sad and a long vowel) is roasted meat. *Al-sinab* is mustard with raisins.

Others distinguished between having all of this with effort and having it without effort. Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn al-Mufaddal al-Maqdisi, the shaykh of our shaykhs, said, and this is the correct view, if Allah wills: it was never reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he abstained from any food because it was good. Rather, he would eat sweets, honey, watermelon, and fresh dates. What is disliked is excessive effort, because of the preoccupation with worldly desires that it brings, distracting from the important matters of the Hereafter. And Allah knows best.

I say: Some Sufis disliked eating good things and based this on the saying of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "Beware of meat, for it has a craving like the craving for wine." The answer is that this statement of Umar was aimed at those he feared would prefer luxury in this world, persist in desires, satisfy the soul with pleasures, forget the Hereafter, and turn wholly to this world. For this reason Umar would write to his governors: "Beware of luxury and the dress of the non-Arabs, and be rough (in your living)." He (may Allah be pleased with him) did not intend to forbid anything Allah had made lawful, nor to prohibit what Allah, blessed is His name, had permitted. The words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are more deserving of being obeyed and relied upon. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ He (peace be upon him) also said: "The master of foods in this world and the Hereafter is meat." Hisham ibn Urwa related from his father, from Aisha, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to eat *tibbikh* (watermelon) with dates and would say: "The heat of this breaks the cold of that, and the cold of that breaks the heat of this." *Tibbikh* is a dialectal variant of *bittikh* (watermelon), and it is a case of metathesis. The refutation of those who prefer eating coarse food has already passed in "al-Ma'ida" (vol. 6, p. 260), and this verse refutes them along with other evidence. And praise be to Allah.

**The fourth issue:** Allah's words: ﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world﴾. That is, they are for them in their rightful sense, through the Oneness of Allah and affirming Him. For Allah bestows blessings and provides. If the one who receives the blessing affirms His Oneness and believes in Him, he has fulfilled the right of the blessing; but if he disbelieves, he has given Satan power over himself. In the authentic hadith: "No one is more patient with harm than Allah: they ascribe a spouse and a child to Him, yet He grants them health and provision." The sentence is complete at "in the life of this world." Then He said *khalisatan* (purely) in the nominative (marfu'), which is the reading of Ibn Abbas and Nafi': "purely on the Day of Resurrection." That is, Allah purifies the good things in the Hereafter for those who believed, and the polytheists have no share in them, as they had a share in them in this world through partnership in it. The meaning of the verse is: "Say: They are shared with others in this world, and they are purely for the believers on the Day of Resurrection." So *khalisatan* is a new clause, as the predicate of an implied subject. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd.

It was also said: the meaning is that these good things that exist in this world are purely for the believers on the Day of Resurrection. Their purity means that they will not be punished or tormented for them. In this case, "in the life of this world" is connected to "believed." Sa'id ibn Jubayr's interpretation points to this.

The rest read it in the accusative (*nasb*) as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) and as a detached qualifier (*qat'*), because the sentence is complete without it. This reading does not permit stopping at "this world." What follows is connected to "for those who believed," as a circumstantial qualifier of it, with the sense: "Say: they are established for those who believed in the life of this world, in the state of their being purely theirs on the Day of Resurrection," as Abu Ali said. The predicate of the inceptive is "for those who believed," and the governing element of the circumstantial clause is the meaning of the verb within the *lam* in "for those who." Sibawayh preferred the accusative because of the fronting of the adverbial phrase.

﴿Thus We detail the verses﴾: that is, as We have detailed for you the lawful and the unlawful, We detail for you what you need.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 33:

There is one issue here. Al-Kalbi said: When the Muslims wore clothes and circumambulated the House, the polytheists (al-mushrikun) went around it [naked], and this verse was revealed. Al-fawahish (the indecencies) are the deeds that are extremely ugly, whether apparent or hidden. Rawh ibn Ubadah narrated from Zakariyya ibn Ishaq, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "What is apparent of them" refers to marrying one's mothers in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), and "what is hidden" refers to fornication (al-zina). Qatadah said: their secret and their open forms. This is open to consideration, for [the verse] mentions sin (al-ithm) and transgression (al-baghy), which indicates that al-fawahish here refers to some of them. If that is so, the most apparent of the fawahish is fornication. And Allah knows best.

(Wa-al-ithm) Al-Hasan said: it is wine (al-khamr). The poet said:

I drank sin until my reason went astray,
Thus does sin take away the minds.

And another said:

We drink sin openly from the cup,
And musk is passed among us as a loan.

[[Al-sawa (ṣuwāʿ): the vessel from which it is drunk. Musta'ar: passed around. That is, we pass it from hand to hand, drinking it.]]

"Wa-al-baghy" is injustice and exceeding the limit in it, which has already been mentioned. Tha'lab said: al-baghy is that a man attacks another man, speaks against him, and oppresses him without right, except when he takes revenge on him with right. The verse separates al-ithm and al-baghy from the fawahish, although they are among them, because of their greatness and vileness; so they are specified by name to emphasize their gravity and to deter from them. Likewise, "and that you associate with Allah" and "and that you say" are in the accusative place as coordinated with what precedes them. A group has denied that al-ithm means wine. Al-Farra' said: al-ithm is what falls short of the prescribed penalty and domineering over people. Al-Nahhas said: as for al-ithm being wine, this is not known; the reality of al-ithm is that it encompasses all disobediences, as the poet said:

I have found that the best of matters is
The fear of God, and the worst of it is al-ithm.

I say: Ibn al-Arabi also denied it and said: "There is no proof in the [first] verse, for if he had said 'I drank the sin' or 'I drank the burden' it would be the same, yet this does not make 'sin' and 'burden' names for wine; likewise al-ithm. What has caused speaking in this manner is ignorance of the language and of the way of deriving meanings from evidence." I say: We have already mentioned it from al-Hasan. Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: wine is sometimes called ithm, and he recited: "I drank the sin..." (the verse), and al-Harawi cited it in his Gharibayn as evidence that wine is ithm. There is no improbability in al-ithm applying to all disobediences and also to wine linguistically, so there is no contradiction. Al-baghy: transgression in wrongdoing; it has also been said: corruption.

There is one issue here: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for every nation there is a term﴾, that is, a appointed time.

(﴿So when their term comes﴾), that is, the time known to Allah, mighty and majestic. Ibn Sirin recited "when their terms come" in the plural. ﴿They cannot delay it by an hour, nor advance it﴾, and the hour is singled out for mention because it is the smallest of the names of time, and it is a temporal adverb (ẓarf zamān). This indicates that the one who is killed is killed at his term (ajal). The term of death is the time of death, just as the term of a debt is the time it falls due. Every thing for which a time is set is its ajal. The ajal of a human being is the time at which Allah knows the living will die in it without fail, and it is a time whose postponement is impossible, since its postponement is not within one's power. Many of the Mu'tazila, except for a few who deviated from them, said: the one who is killed died other than at his appointed term, and that had he not been killed he would have lived. This is an error, because the one who is killed did not die because another killed him; rather he died because of what Allah did in taking his soul at the moment of the blow. If it is said: if he died at his term, why do you kill his striker and exact retaliation from him? It is said to him: we kill him for his transgression and for his disposing of what he had no right to dispose of, not for his death and the departure of the soul, since that is not his act. Were people left, and transgression went without retribution, that would lead to corruption and the ruin of people. This is clear.

O Children of Adam, when there come to you messengers from among you...

Here "in" (إِمَّا) is a conditional particle, and the nūn was added for emphasis because of the attached "mā." It is also said that "mā" is a redundant particle (ṣilah), meaning "if there comes to you." He informs that He sends messengers to them from among themselves, so that their acceptance would be closer.

Al-qaṣaṣ (narration) means following one statement with another.

"My signs" (āyātī) means My obligations (farā'iḍ) and My rulings (aḥkām).

"Whoever fears God and makes amends" is a conditional clause, and what follows is its response. This is also the response of the first conditional, meaning: and whoever among you makes amends between himself and Him. "No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve" is evidence that the believers on the Day of Resurrection will neither fear nor grieve, and no terror or dread will reach them. It is also said that the terrors of the Day of Resurrection may reach them, but their final outcome is security. It is also said that the response of "in yaʾtiyannakum" is what the speech implies, meaning: then obey them, "whoever fears God and makes amends." The first view is the view of al-Zajjaj.

O Children of Adam, when there come to you messengers from among you...

Here "in" (إِمَّا) is a conditional particle, and the nūn was added for emphasis because of the attached "mā." It is also said that "mā" is a redundant particle (ṣilah), meaning "if there comes to you." He informs that He sends messengers to them from among themselves, so that their acceptance would be closer.

"My signs" (āyātī) means My obligations (farā'iḍ) and My rulings (aḥkām).

This is also the response of the first conditional, meaning: and whoever among you makes amends between himself and Him. It is also said that the terrors of the Day of Resurrection may reach them, but their final outcome is security. It is also said that the response of "in yaʾtiyannakum" is what the speech implies, meaning: then obey them, "whoever fears God and makes amends." The first view is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 37:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs?﴾ The meaning is: what injustice is more heinous than fabricating lies against Allah the Exalted and denying His signs. Then He said: (Those will receive their share of what is written [in the Book]), meaning what has been written for them of provision, lifespan and deeds, related from Ibn Zayd. Ibn Jubayr said: [it means] of misery and happiness. Ibn 'Abbas said: [it means] of good and evil. Al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: [it means] of the punishment in proportion to their disbelief. Al-Tabari's preference is that the meaning is: what has been written for them, i.e. what has been decreed for them of good and evil, provision, deeds and term, in accordance with what has preceded from Ibn Zayd, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. He said: Do you not see that He followed that with His words: ﴿until when Our messengers come to them to take their souls﴾, meaning the messengers of the Angel of Death. It has been said: "al-Kitab" here is the Qur'an, because the punishment of the disbelievers is mentioned in it. It has also been said: "al-Kitab" is the Preserved Tablet. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Hulwani related, saying: 'Ali ibn al-Madini dictated to me, saying: I asked 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi about qadar (divine decree), and he said to me: Everything is by qadar, and obedience and disobedience are by qadar, and whoever says that sins are not by qadar has committed a great slander. 'Ali said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi also said to me: Knowledge, qadar and the Book are all the same. Then I presented the words of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi to Yahya ibn Sa'id, and he said: After this, nothing remains, neither little nor much. Yahya ibn Ma'in related: Marwan al-Fazari narrated to us, Isma'il ibn Sumay' narrated to us, from Bukayr al-Tawil, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿those will receive their share of what is written﴾, he said: [It refers to] people who will do deeds for which they must [inevitably] do them. And "hatta" (until) is not a limit (ghayah) here; rather it introduces a new statement about them. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "hatta", "imma" and "illa" are not declined, because they are particles, so they are distinguished from nouns, as in "hublaa" and "sakraa". Al-Zajjaj said: "hatta" is written with a yaa' because it resembles "sakraa", and if it were written with an alif it would resemble "ila". "Imma" is not written with a yaa' because "in" has had "ma" joined to it.

(They will say: Where is what you used to call upon besides Allah?) This is a question of rebuke. The meaning of "tad'un" (you call upon) is "ta'buduna" (you worship).

(They will say: They have vanished from us), meaning they have perished and gone away. It has been said: this occurs in the Hereafter.

(And they will bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers), meaning they will confess to disbelief against themselves.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 38–39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will say: Enter into nations that have passed away before you, of jinn and men, into the Fire﴾. That is, "with nations," so "fi" (in) is used in the sense of "ma'a" (with). This is not impossible, because your saying "Zayd is fi the people" means "with the people." It was also said: it stays on its basic meaning, i.e., enter into their collective. As for the speaker, it was said: it is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, i.e., Allah said, "Enter." It was also said: it is Malik, the keeper of the Fire.

﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾, i.e., the one that preceded it into the Fire, and she is its sister in religion and creed. ﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another therein﴾, i.e., they have gathered together. Al-A'mash read "tada rakū" (تَدَارَكُوا), which is the original form; then assimilation (idgham) occurred, so the alif of connection (alif al-wasl) was needed. Al-Mahdawi related it from Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Nahhas said: Ibn Mas'ud read "ḥattā idhā idāraku" (حَتَّى إِذَا ادَّرَكُوا), i.e., some of them overtook others. ʿIṣma from Abu ʿAmr (read) "ḥattā idhā iddāraku" (حَتَّى إِذَا ادَّارْكُوا) with the alif retained, on the joining of two sukuns. It is related: "hādhān ʿAbd Allāh" (these two are ʿAbd Allāh). And he has two-thirds of the wealth. Also from Abu ʿAmr: "idhā idd āraku" (إِذَا إِدَّارَكُوا) with the alif of connection cut, as if he paused on "idhā" for recollection; then when his pause lengthened, he cut the alif of connection, as one who begins with it. The cutting of the alif of connection has come in poetry, such as his saying:

O soul, be patient, every living one meets [its end], and every two [are destined] to separation.

From Mujahid and Humayd ibn Qays (read) "ḥattā idhi ddāraku" (حَتَّى إِذِ ادَّرَكُوا) with the alif of "idhā" deleted because of the meeting of two sukuns, and the alif after the dal deleted. "Jamīʿan" (جَمِيعاً) is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿The last of them will say to the first of them﴾, i.e., the last of them to enter, who are the followers, to the first of them, who are the leaders. ﴿Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment from the Fire.﴾ The lam in "li-ūlāhum" (لِأُولاهُمْ) is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajal), because they did not address the first of them; rather they said concerning the first of them, "Our Lord, these led us astray." "Ḍiʿf" (ضِعْف) is a like amount added to its like once or more. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that "ḍiʿf" here means the vipers and serpents. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment, and curse them with a great curse﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 249]. There the mention of the double punishment comes in a more dreadful form, along with the rulings that follow from it, God willing. He said, "for each there is a double," i.e., for the follower and the one followed.

﴿But you do not know﴾ according to the reading of the one who reads with the yā' (يَعْلَمُونَ), i.e., each group does not know what the other group has. For if some of those in the Fire knew that another's punishment was greater than his, it would be a kind of consolation for him. It was also said that the meaning with the tā' (تَعْلَمُونَ) is: "but you do not know, O addressees, what they encounter of punishment." It is also permissible that the meaning be: "but you do not know, people of this world, the measure of what they are in of punishment."

﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: You have no superiority over us﴾, i.e., you disbelieved and acted as we did, so you do not deserve any lightening of the punishment. ﴿So taste the punishment for what you used to earn.﴾

﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: You have no superiority over us﴾, i.e., you disbelieved and acted as we did, so you do not deserve any lightening of the punishment. ﴿So taste the punishment for what you used to earn.﴾

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾. That is, for their spirits (arwah). Authentic reports (akhbar sihah) confirm this, and I have mentioned them in my book *al-Tadhkira*. Among them is the hadith of al-Bara' ibn Azib, which, concerning the taking of the soul of the disbeliever, says: "A stench comes out of it, like the foulest carcass found on the face of the earth. They carry it up, and they do not pass by any assembly of angels without the angels saying, 'What is this foul spirit?' They say, 'So-and-so, son of so-and-so,' using the ugliest of the names by which he was called in the world, until they reach the lowest heaven and ask for it to be opened, but it is not opened for them." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "The gates of heaven will not be opened for them," and the verse.

It has also been said that the gates of heaven will not be opened for them when they make supplication. This was said by Mujahid and al-Nakha'i.

It has also been said that the meaning is: the gates of Paradise will not be opened for them, because Paradise is in heaven. This is indicated by His words: ﴿Nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. The camel cannot pass through it, so they will never enter it. This is a definitive proof (dalil qat'i) that does not permit pardon for them. Upon this, all Muslims, those who cannot be attributed with error, have reached consensus (ijma') that Allah, glorified and exalted, will not forgive them, nor any one of them.

Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib said: If someone asks, "How can this be a consensus of the Community, when some of the theologians (mutakallimun) have claimed that the followers (muqallidah) of the Jews, Christians and others among the people of disbelief are not in the Fire?" It is said to him: These are people who denied that the follower (muqallid) is a disbeliever, because of a doubt that entered their minds. They did not claim that the follower is a disbeliever and yet is not in the Fire. Knowing whether the follower is a disbeliever or not is through reasoning (nazar), not through textual stipulation (tawqif) or report (khabar).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "lā tuffataḥu" with a damma on the ya' (yu-), in the masculine form to agree with the plural (tadhkir al-jam'). The rest recited it with the ta' (tuffataḥu), in the feminine form to agree with the group (ta'nith al-jama'ah), as in His words: ﴿the gates being opened for them﴾, where He used the feminine. Since the feminization of "al-abwab" (the gates) is not real (ghayr haqiqi), it is permissible to use the masculine for the plural. This is also the recitation of Ibn Abbas with the ya'.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i lightened (akhaffa) the verb, on the basis that the lightened form applies to both few and many, whereas the doubled form (tashdid) is for multiplication and repetition, one time after another, and nothing else. The doubled form is preferable here, because it is more indicative of the many.

"Al-jamal" means the male camel. Al-Farra' said: "Al-jamal is the husband of the she-camel (naqah)." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said the same when he was asked about the camel, and he said, "It is the husband of the she-camel," as if he considered the questioner ignorant of what all people know. The plural is jimal, ajmal, jamalat and jama'il. It is called jamal only when it is four years old.

In the recitation of Abdullah: "Until the yellow camel (al-jamal al-asfar) passes through the eye of the needle." Abu Bakr al-Anbari mentioned it, saying: My father related to us, Nasr ibn Dawud related to us, Abu 'Ubayd related to us, Hajjaj related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Kathir, from Mujahid, who said regarding the recitation of Abdullah ... and he mentioned it.

Ibn Abbas recited "al-jummal" with a damma on the jim, a fatha on the mim, and a shadda on it. It is the rope of the ship called the qals, and it is a bundle of ropes, the plural of jumlah, as said by Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab. It has also been said: it is the thick rope of hemp. It has also been said: it is the rope by which one climbs the palm tree.

It is also related from him, and from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that "al-jumal" with a damma on the jim and lightening of the mim is also the qals and the rope, as we mentioned just now. It is also related from him "al-jumul" with two dammas, the plural of jamal, like asad and usd, and "al-jumul" like asad and usd.

From Abu al-Sammal: "al-jamli" with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the mim, a lightened form of "jamal."

"Sam al-khiyat" means the hole of the needle, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Every small opening in the body is called sam and summ, and its plural is sumum. The plural of the deadly poison (summ al-qatil) is sima'. Ibn Sirin recited "fi summ" with a damma on the sin.

"Al-khiyat" is that with which one sews. It is said: khiyat and mikhyat, like izar and mi'zar, qina' and miqna'.

"Al-mihad" means the bedding or couch. "Ghawash" is the plural of ghashiyah, meaning fires that will envelop them.

﴿And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the disbelievers. And Allah knows best.
