﴿And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the disbelievers. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ is a parenthetical statement (kalam mu'taridh), meaning: "And those who believed and did righteous deeds, those are the companions of the Garden; they will abide therein forever." And the meaning of "We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity" is that He did not impose upon anyone regarding the maintenance of wives except what he finds and is able to provide, not what his hand cannot reach. And He did not intend to establish that capability (istita'ah) must exist before the act. Ibn al-Tayyib said: its counterpart is "Allah does not burden a soul except with what He has given it" [[See vol. 18, p. 170.]].

Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, commentary on surah 7, verse 43:

Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned among the blessings He bestows on the people of Paradise the removal of rancour from their breasts. Naz' (removal) means extraction, and ghill (rancour) means the hatred lodged in the breast. Its plural is ghilal. That is, We will remove from them in Paradise whatever rancour was in their hearts in the world.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Rancour at the gate of Paradise is like the knees of camels; Allah has removed it from the hearts of the believers."

It is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I hope that I, Uthman, Talhah and al-Zubayr are among those of whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will remove whatever rancour is in their breasts﴾."

It has also been said: the removal of rancour in Paradise means that some of them will not envy others regarding the differences in their ranks. It has further been said that this happens through the drink of Paradise, and for this reason He said: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ (see vol. 19, p. 141), meaning it purifies the impurities from the breasts, as will be explained, if Allah the Exalted wills, in surah al-Insan and surah al-Zumar (see vol. 15, p. 284).

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this"﴾ (that is, to this reward), by His having shown us the way and created guidance for us. This is a refutation of the Qadariyya.

﴿And we would not﴾: the reading of Ibn Amir omits the waw; the rest read it with the waw.

﴿That we might be guided﴾: lam of purpose (lam kay).

﴿Had Allah not guided us﴾: it is in a position of raf' (nominative).

﴿And they will be called﴾: its origin is nudiyu, ﴿that﴾ (an) is in a position of nasb, a lightened form of the heavy (an), meaning that ﴿this is the Garden﴾. It may also be an explanation of what they were called with, since the call is speech, so it has no place in the sentence. That is, it was said to them: ﴿This is the Garden﴾, because they had been promised it in the world; that is, it was said to them: "This is the Garden you were promised." Or it may be said before entering, when they saw it from afar. It has also been said that ﴿tilkumu﴾ means ﹙hadhihi﹚ (this). The meaning of ﴿You have been made to inherit it for what you used to do﴾ is that you inherited its dwellings through your deeds, while your entry into it is by the mercy and bounty of Allah, as He said: ﴿That is the bounty of Allah﴾ (see vol. 5, p. 271).

And He said: ﴿So He will admit them into His mercy and bounty﴾ (see vol. 6, p. 27). In Sahih Muslim: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deed." They said: "Not even you, Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy and bounty." In a non-Sahih report: "There is no disbeliever or believer but he has a place in Paradise and in Hell. When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of Hell enter Hell, Paradise is raised for the people of Hell and they look at their places in it, and it is said to them: 'These are your places had you obeyed Allah.' Then it is said: 'O people of Paradise, inherit them for what you used to do,' and their places are divided among the people of Paradise."

I say: In Sahih Muslim also: "No Muslim man dies but Allah puts in his place in the Fire a Jew or a Christian." This too is an inheritance: He bestows His grace on whom He wills and punishes in His justice whom He wills. In sum, Paradise and its dwellings are attained only by His mercy; so when they enter it by their deeds, they have inherited it by His mercy, and they entered it by His mercy, since their deeds are themselves a mercy from Him to them and a bounty upon them.

The reading ﴿Uriltumuha﴾ is recited without idgham (assimilation), and it is also recited with the idgham of the ta' into the tha'.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire⦆... This is a question of rebuke and reproach.

(An qad wajadna): like "an tilkumu al-jannah," meaning that we have indeed found. It was also said that it is the call itself.

(Fa-adhdhana mu'adhdhinun baynahum): meaning he called out and proclaimed, that is, one of the angels. "Baynahum" is an adverbial expression, as when you say, "I know their midst."

Al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read "ni'im" with a kasra on the ayn, and on this dialect it is permissible to read it with a sukun on the ayn. Makki said: whoever says "ni'im" with a kasra on the ayn intends to distinguish between "na'am," which is an answer particle, and "na'am," which is the name for camels, cattle and sheep. It has been narrated from Umar that he disapproved of "na'am" with a fatha on the ayn in answer, and said: say "ni'im." Na'am and ni'im are two dialects with the same meaning of promise and affirmation. Promise applies when you ask about an affirmed matter, such as your saying: "Will Zayd stand?" and he replies "na'am." Affirmation applies when you report something that has occurred, you say: "such-and-such has happened," and he replies "na'am." When you ask about a negated matter, the answer is "bala," such as your saying: "Did I not honour you?" and he replies "bala." So "na'am" is for answering a question that enters upon an affirmative statement, as in this verse, and "bala" is for answering a question that enters upon a negative, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?⦆ They said: ﴿Yes (bala)⦆ [[See p. 313 of this part.]].

Al-Bazzi, Ibn Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "anna la'nata Allah," which is the original form. The rest read with a light "an" and the raising of la'nah as a subject (mubtada'). So "an" is in a place of nasb in both readings, by dropping the preposition. In the light form it is possible that it has no place in the i'rab, and it is then an explanatory particle (mufassirah), as stated above. It is related from al-A'mash that he read "inna la'nata Allah" with a kasra on the hamza, and this is on the assumption of an implied verb of saying, as the Kufans read ﴿So the angels called to him while he stood praying in the sanctuary: that Allah⦆ [[Thus in the originals. It was mentioned in vol. 4, p. 74 that this is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, so the correct statement is "the two Kufans." Among the irregular readings is that of Ibn Mas'ud.]]. It is narrated that Tawus entered upon Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik and said to him: "Fear Allah and beware of the Day of Proclamation." He said: "And what is the Day of Proclamation?" He said: the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then a proclaimer proclaimed among them: the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers⦆, and Hisham fainted. Tawus said: "This is the humiliation of description, so how will be the humiliation of direct witnessing."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who turn away from the way of Allah﴾ is in the genitive position as a qualifier (na't) of "ẓālimīn" (wrongdoers). It is also permissible to read it in the nominative or accusative, by supposing a subject (ḍamīr) or "a‘nī" (I mean). That is, those who used to bar (yaṣuddūn) people in this world from Islam; so it is from ṣadd (ṣadd), which means prevention (al-man‘). Or they turn away themselves from the way of Allah, meaning they turn aside (yu‘riḍūn); and this is from ṣudūd (ṣudūd, aversion).

(And they seek to make it crooked) (wa-yabghūnahā ‘iwajan): they seek its crookedness and disparage it, so they do not believe in it. This meaning has already passed [[see vol. 4, p. 154.]].

(And they are, concerning the Hereafter, disbelievers) (wa-hum bil-ākhirati kāfirūn): that is, and they were disbelievers in it; the verb "kānū" has been elided, and such elision is common in speech.

﴿وَبَيْنَهُما حِجابٌ وَعَلَى الْأَعْرافِ رِجالٌ يَعْرِفُونَ كُلاًّ بِسِيماهُمْ وَنادَوْا أَصْحابَ الْجَنَّةِ أَنْ سَلامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ لَمْ يَدْخُلُوها وَهُمْ يَطْمَعُونَ﴾ (٤٦)

Ay, between Hell and Paradise, because their mention has preceded: a barrier (ḥājiz), a wall (aswar). It is the wall that God mentioned in His saying: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 245.]].

(﴿وَعَلَى الْأَعْرافِ رِجالٌ﴾) means: upon the ridges of the wall, which are its elevated parts (shurafuh). From this comes ʿurf al-faras (the mane of the horse) and ʿurf al-dik (the comb of the rooster). ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Yazid narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "al-aʿraf is the elevated thing." Mujahid narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "al-aʿraf is a wall that has a crest like the crest of a rooster [[In the manuscripts: Ibn Abi Zayd; the apparent reading is Ibn Zayd. See vol. 12, p. 264.]]." In the lexicon, al-aʿraf means an elevated place, plural of ʿurf. Yahya ibn Adam said: "I asked al-Kisai about the singular of al-aʿraf, and he was silent. So I said: Israʾil narrated to us from Jabir, from Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-aʿraf is a wall that has a crest like the crest of a rooster." He said: "Yes, by God, its singular is ʿarf, and its plural is aʿraf. Boy, bring the paper," and he wrote it down. This statement came in the manner of praise, as He said of them: ﴿men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of God﴾ [[Ibid.]].

The scholars have discussed the people of al-aʿraf in ten opinions:

First: ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shaʿbi, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jubayr said: they are people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: In the Musnad of Khaythamah ibn Sulayman (at the end of the fifteenth part) there is a hadith from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The scales will be set up on the Day of Resurrection, and the good deeds and bad deeds will be weighed. Whoever's good deeds outweigh his bad deeds by the weight of a ṣuwāba [[al-ṣuwāba: the egg of a louse.]] enters Paradise, and whoever's bad deeds outweigh his good deeds by the weight of a ṣuwāba enters the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of God, what about one whose good and bad deeds are equal?" He said: "Those are the people of al-aʿraf, [who did not enter it while they were hoping (to enter)]."

Mujahid said: They are a righteous people, jurists and scholars.

It was said: They are the martyrs; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

Al-Qushayri said: It was said: They are the excellent among the believers and the martyrs. They have finished with occupying themselves with their own souls and have freed themselves to observe the condition of people. When they see the people of the Fire, they seek refuge in God from being returned to the Fire, for in God's power is everything, and the contrary of what is known is possible. When they see the people of Paradise, who have not yet entered it, they hope for their entry into it.

Shurahbil ibn Saʿd said: They are those who are martyred in the way of God, who went out disobedient to their parents. al-Tabari mentioned a hadith on this from the Prophet (ﷺ), that their disobedience and their martyrdom balanced out.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned with his chain of narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And upon the aʿraf are men﴾, that he said: "al-aʿraf is an elevated place above the Sirat (the bridge over Hell). Upon it are al-ʿAbbas, Hamzah, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Jaʿfar Dhu al-Janahayn, may God be pleased with them, who recognize their lovers by the whiteness of their faces and their haters by the blackness of their faces."

Al-Zahrawi related that they are the just witnesses of the Resurrection who testify to people concerning their deeds, and they exist in every nation. al-Nahhas chose this opinion and said: "It is one of the best things said about it, for they are on the wall between Paradise and Hell."

al-Zajjaj said: They are a people of prophets.

It was said: They are people who had minor sins that were not expiated for them by pains and calamities in this world, and who had no major sins; so they are held back from Paradise, so that grief may befall them because of that, which will counterbalance their minor sins.

Salim, the mawla of Abu Hudhayfah, wished to be among the people of al-aʿraf, because his view was that they are sinners.

It was said: They are the children of adultery [[In (another manuscript): the fornicators.]]; al-Qushayri mentioned it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It was said: They are angels appointed over this wall, who distinguish the disbelievers from the believers before their entry into Paradise and Hell; this was mentioned by Abu Mijlaz. It was said to him: "Are angels not called men (rijal)?" He said: "They are males and not females, so it is not far-fetched to apply the word 'men' to them, just as it is applied to jinn in His saying: ﴿and there were men among mankind who sought refuge with men among the jinn﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 8.]]." These angels recognize the believers by their marks and the disbelievers by their marks, and they give good news to the believers of their entry into Paradise, though they have not yet entered it, so they hope for it. When they see the people of the Fire, they pray for themselves for safety from the punishment.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: What necessarily follows from the verse is that upon the aʿraf are men from among the people of Paradise whose entry is delayed, and they experience what has been described of the consideration of the two groups, that is, by their marks, which are the whiteness of the faces and their beauty among the people of Paradise, and their blackness and ugliness among the people of the Fire, and beyond that of knowing the place of these and the place of those.

I say: He withheld from specifying, because of the conflict of reports and details, and God is most knowing of the realities of matters.

Then it was said: al-aʿraf is the plural of ʿurf, which is every high and elevated thing, because by its prominence it is more recognizable than what is low. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-aʿraf is the crest (sharaf) of the Sirat. It was also said: it is the mountain of Uhud, which will be placed there. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: al-Zahrawi mentioned a hadith that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it, and on the Day of Resurrection it will be set up between Paradise and the Fire; upon it will be held back people who recognize each one by his marks; they, if God wills, are among the people of Paradise." He also mentioned another hadith from Safwan ibn Sulaym that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Uhud is upon one of the pillars of Paradise." I say: Abu ʿUmar mentioned from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it, and it is indeed upon a channel from the channels of Paradise."

God's saying: ﴿And they call out to the companions of Paradise﴾: that is, the companions of al-aʿraf call out to the companions of Paradise. ﴿That peace be upon you﴾: that is, they say to them, "Peace be upon you." It was said: The meaning is: "You are safe from punishment." ﴿They have not entered it, while they hope﴾: that is, the companions of al-aʿraf have not entered Paradise, that is, they have not yet entered it. ﴿While they hope﴾: according to this interpretation, it means "while they know that they will enter it." This is known in the lexicon, that ṭamiʿa may mean ʿalima (to know); this was mentioned by al-Nahhas. This is the view of Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas and others, that the intended ones are the companions of al-aʿraf. Abu Mijlaz said: They are the people of Paradise; that is, the companions of al-aʿraf say to them, "Peace be upon you," while the people of Paradise have not yet entered Paradise, and they hope to enter it, [being] believers passing by the companions of al-aʿraf.

The pause is at His saying "Peace be upon you" and at His saying "they have not entered it." Then one begins "while they hope," with the meaning: "while they hope to enter it." It is also permissible for "while they hope" to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning would be: the believers passing by the companions of al-aʿraf did not enter it while hoping, but they entered it not hoping to enter it; so one does not pause at "they have not entered it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning, toward the direction of encounter, which is the direction of facing. The masdar (verbal noun) of the form tif'āl has not come except in two words: tilqā' (تِلْقَاءٌ) and tibyān (تِبْيَانٌ) [[In al-Misbah it is said: "They said that only tibyān and tilqā' and tinḍāl come with a kasra." I say: there is disagreement about this pattern.]]. The rest are with a fatha, such as tasyār (تَسْيَارٌ), tuhmām (تَهْمَامٌ) and tidhkār (تَذْكَارٌ). As for the noun with a kasra, it is numerous, such as tiqsār (تِقْصَارٌ) and timthāl (تِمْثَالٌ).

They said, meaning the companions of the Heights (aṣḥāb al-A'rāf) said:

(Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people.) They asked Allah that He not place them with them, although they knew that He would not place them with them. This is by way of humble supplication, just as the people of Paradise say: ﴿Our Lord, perfect for us our light﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 197.]], and they say: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾, by way of thanks to Allah, mighty and majestic. And they find pleasure in that.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-A'raf (the Heights), verses 48–49:

Allah's words: ﴿And the companions of the Heights (al-A'raf) will call out to men whom they recognise by their marks﴾, meaning, from among the people of the Fire.

(They will say: "Your multitude has not availed you, nor did you used to be arrogant") meaning, for the sake of the world, and your arrogance towards faith.

(Are these the ones) is a reference to a group of the poor believers, such as Bilal, Salman, Khabbab and others.

(Whom you swore) in the world,

(that Allah would not grant them) in the Hereafter,

(mercy). They rebuke them with this. And they were further increased in grief and anguish when they were told (Enter Paradise). Ikrimah recited "dakhalu al-jannah" without an alif, with the dal fatha. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "udkhilu al-jannah" with the kasra on the kha', as a past tense verb in the passive voice, as in Abu Hayyan.

The verse indicates that the companions of the Heights are either angels or prophets, since their statement is a report about Allah the Exalted. As for whoever makes the companions of the Heights to be sinners, the last of their words to the people of the Fire is "nor did you used to be arrogant", and "Are these the ones..." up to the end of the verse is the speech of Allah the Exalted to the people of the Fire, rebuking them for what they had said in the world. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, while the first view is narrated from al-Hasan.

It has also been said: it is the speech of the angels appointed over the companions of the Heights, for the people of the Fire will swear that the companions of the Heights will enter the Fire with them, so the angels will say to the companions of the Heights: "Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve."

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-A'raf (the Heights), verses 48–49:

Allah's words: ﴿And the companions of the Heights (al-A'raf) will call out to men whom they recognise by their marks﴾, meaning, from among the people of the Fire.

(They will say: "Your multitude has not availed you, nor did you used to be arrogant") meaning, for the sake of the world, and your arrogance towards faith.

(Are these the ones) is a reference to a group of the poor believers, such as Bilal, Salman, Khabbab and others.

(Whom you swore) in the world,

(that Allah would not grant them) in the Hereafter,

(mercy). They rebuke them with this. And they were further increased in grief and anguish when they were told (Enter Paradise). Ikrimah recited "dakhalu al-jannah" without an alif, with the dal fatha. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "udkhilu al-jannah" with the kasra on the kha', as a past tense verb in the passive voice, as in Abu Hayyan.

The verse indicates that the companions of the Heights are either angels or prophets, since their statement is a report about Allah the Exalted. As for whoever makes the companions of the Heights to be sinners, the last of their words to the people of the Fire is "nor did you used to be arrogant", and "Are these the ones..." up to the end of the verse is the speech of Allah the Exalted to the people of the Fire, rebuking them for what they had said in the world. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, while the first view is narrated from al-Hasan.

It has also been said: it is the speech of the angels appointed over the companions of the Heights, for the people of the Fire will swear that the companions of the Heights will enter the Fire with them, so the angels will say to the companions of the Heights: "Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise: "Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you"﴾. In this verse there are three issues.

The first: His words ﴿And they call out﴾. It is said that when the people of al-A'raf (the Heights) had entered Paradise, the people of the Fire became hopeful and said: "O our Lord, indeed we have relatives in Paradise, so permit us to see them and speak with them." The people of Paradise do not recognize them because of the blackness of their faces. So they say: ("Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you"). This shows that the son of Adam cannot do without food and drink, even when he is in punishment.

("They say: Indeed Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers") meaning the food and drink of Paradise. Al-ifada (pouring out) means widening, as in the expression afada 'alayhi ni'amahu (he lavished his blessings upon him).

The second: This verse is evidence that giving water to drink is among the best deeds. Ibn 'Abbas was asked: "Which charity is best?" He said: "Water. Have you not seen the people of the Fire, when they cried out to the people of Paradise: 'Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you'?"

Abu Dawud related that Sa'd came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Which charity is most pleasing to you?" He said: "Water." In another narration, Sa'd dug a well and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is for the mother of Sa'd." From Anas, who said: Sa'd said: "O Messenger of Allah, indeed Umm Sa'd used to love giving charity. Will it benefit her if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes, and upon you is water." In another narration, the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah to provide water on her behalf. This indicates that giving water is among the greatest acts of nearness to Allah, exalted is He.

Some of the Tabi'un (the Successors) said: "Whoever has many sins, let him take up giving water." Allah forgave the sins of the one who gave water to a dog, so how much more the one who gives water to a believing man who affirms the oneness of Allah and gives him life.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While a man was walking along a path, he was overcome by thirst, so he went down into a well and drank from it. When he came out, he saw a dog panting and eating the moist earth from thirst. He said: 'This dog has reached the same state that I had reached.' So he filled his leather sock with water, held it in his mouth, climbed up, and gave the dog to drink. Allah thanked him and forgave him." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there a reward for us in animals?" He said: "In every moist liver there is a reward."

[Note: In the narration of al-Bukhari, Ahmad and Ibn Majah, the wording is: "In every hot liver there is a reward."]

The opposite of this is what Muslim related from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A woman was punished because of a cat that she confined until it died; she entered the Fire because of it. She neither fed it nor gave it water when she confined it, nor did she let it go to eat from the creeping creatures of the earth."

[Note: Khashash al-ard (the first kha may be vowelled three ways) means its insects and creeping creatures.]

In the hadith of 'Aisha from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever gives a Muslim a drink of water where water is available, it is as if he freed a slave; and whoever gives a Muslim a drink of water where water is not available, it is as if he gave him life." Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan.

The third: Whoever said that the owner of a pool or a water-skin has more right to his water has derived evidence from this verse, because the meaning of the words of the people of Paradise, "Indeed Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers," is that you have no right to them. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, gave a chapter heading to this meaning: "Chapter: Whoever holds that the owner of the pool and the water-skin has more right to his water." Under this chapter he included, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will surely drive away men from my pool as a stray camel is driven away from the pool."

Al-Muhallab said: There is no disagreement that the owner of the pool has more right to his water, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him: "I will surely drive away men from my pool."

The word الَّذِينَ ("those who") is in the genitive position as a descriptive qualifier (na't) of "the disbelievers." It may also be in the nominative or accusative case by means of an implied (idmar) subject or object. It has been said: it is part of the speech of the people of Paradise. "So today We forget them" means: We leave them in the Fire. "As they forgot the meeting of this their day" means: they abandoned acting upon it and denied it. And "مَا" (ma) is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: "as their forgetting."

(And that they used to deny Our signs) is coordinated with what precedes it, and it refers to their denial.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 52:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an. "Fassalnahu" means: We made it clear, so that whoever reflects upon it may understand it. It was also said: "Fassalnahu" means: We sent it down in parts, gradually.

(Upon knowledge) from Us, in which there is no error or mistake.

(A guidance and a mercy). Al-Zajjaj said: That is, guiding and possessing mercy, so he made it a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in "fassalnahu." He said: It is also permissible to read "hudan wa rahmatun" (in the nominative), meaning: it is guidance and mercy. It was also said: It is permissible to read "hudan wa rahmatin" (in the genitive) as an attribute of "kitab." Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: It is also permissible to read "hudan wa rahmatin" in the genitive as an attributive adjective (na't) of "kitab." Al-Farra' said: Like the verse ﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed﴾ [See p. 142 of this volume.]

(For a people who believe). The believers were singled out because they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 53:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they await anything but its fulfilment?﴾ It is read with a hamza, from āla (to return, to come to pass). The people of Madina pronounce the hamza with lightening (takhfif). Al-nazar here means al-intizar (waiting), i.e. do they wait for anything but what they were promised in the Qur'an of punishment and reckoning? It was also said: "yanzurun" is from al-nazar (looking) toward the Day of Resurrection. So the pronoun in "ta'wilahu" refers to the Book. The outcome (ʿaqibah) of the Book is what God promised in it of resurrection and reckoning. Mujahid said: "ta'wilahu" means its recompense, i.e. the recompense of their denial of the Book. Qatada said: "ta'wilahu" means its outcome (ʿaqibah). The meanings are close to one another.

(On the day its fulfilment comes) i.e. its consequences become manifest on the Day of Resurrection. "Yawm" (the day) is in the accusative, governed by "yaqulu" (they say), i.e. those who had forgotten it before will say, on the day its fulfilment comes:

(Indeed the messengers of our Lord came with the truth. Are there any intercessors for us?) This is an interrogative carrying the sense of wishing (tamanni).

(So that they may intercede) is in the subjunctive because it is the answer to the interrogative.

(for us, or are we to be returned?) Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "or can we be returned?"

(so that we may act differently from what we used to do) Al-Zajjaj said: "nuradd" is coordinated with the meaning, i.e. "Is there anyone to intercede for us, or can we be returned?" Ibn Ishaq read "an nuradda fa-na'mala" with the accusative in both, and the meaning is "unless we are returned," as the poet (it is Imru' al-Qays) said:

"I said to him: do not let your eye weep, for we are only striving for kingship, or we die, and are excused."

Al-Hasan read "aw nuraddu fa-na'malu" with the nominative in both.

(They have lost their souls) i.e. they did not benefit from them, and everyone who does not benefit from his soul has lost it. It was also said: they lost the blessings and their share of them.

(And what they used to fabricate has strayed from them) i.e. what they used to claim, that there is another god with God, has come to nothing.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 54 (part 1 of 2):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. He shows that He alone has the power to bring things into existence, and so He alone is the one who must be worshipped. The original form of *sitta* ("six") is *sidsa*. They wanted to assimilate the *dal* into the *sin*, but the two met at the point of articulation of the *ta'*, so it prevailed over both. If you wish, you may say: one of the two *sin*s was changed into a *ta'*, and it was assimilated into the *dal*. This is because you say in its diminutive *sudaysa*, and in the plural *asdas*, and the plural and the diminutive return nouns to their roots. They also say: "So-and-so came sixth" (*jaa'a fulanun sadisan*, *sadiitan*, *saatan*). Whoever says *sadtan* has changed the *sin* into a *ta'*.

*Al-yawm* ("the day") is the period from the rising of the sun to its setting. If there is no sun, there is no day, said al-Qushayri. He also said: the meaning of "in six days" is "of the days of the Hereafter, each day being a thousand years," to magnify the creation of the heavens and the earth. It was also said: "of the days of this world." Mujahid and others said: the first of them is Sunday and the last of them is Friday.

He mentioned this duration, though had He wished to create them in an instant, He would have done so, for He is capable of saying to them "Be," and they would be. But He wished to teach His servants gentleness and deliberation in affairs, and to show His power to the angels, one thing after another. This is according to those who say that the angels were created before the heavens and the earth. Another wisdom: He created them over six days because for everything with Him there is an appointed term. By this He also shows the forbearance of not hastening punishment upon the disobedient, since for everything with Him there is an appointed term. This is like His saying: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us. So be patient over what they say﴾ [Qaf 50:38–39]. This comes after His saying: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, which were mightier than them in strength﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:6].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then He istawa over the Throne﴾. This is the question of *istiwa'* (being established/rising over), and the scholars have discussed it and given explanations. We have set out the statements of the scholars on it in the book *Al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna wa Sifatihi al-'Ula* ("The Most Excellent Explanation of the Names and Attributes of Allah"), and we mentioned there fourteen opinions.

The majority of the earlier and later scholars hold that, when it is obligatory to declare the Creator, glory be to Him, free of direction (*jiha*) and of being confined in a place (*tahayyuz*), then it follows, along with its necessary implications, according to the general body of the earlier scholars and the leaders among the later ones, that He, blessed and exalted, must be declared free of direction. So He is not in the direction of above according to them, because it follows from this, according to them, that whenever He is specified with a direction, He would be in a place or a space. And place and space entail motion and rest for what occupies space, and change and origination. This is the view of the theologians (*mutakallimun*).

The early pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-awwal*), may Allah be pleased with them, did not assert the negation of direction, nor did they speak of it. Rather, they and the whole community affirmed it for Allah, the Exalted, as His Book has spoken and His messengers have informed. None of the righteous predecessors denied that He is established on His Throne in reality. The Throne was singled out for this because it is the greatest of His creatures. What they did not know is the modality (*kayfiyya*) of the *istiwa'*, for its reality is not known. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The *istiwa'* is known" — meaning linguistically — "the modality is unknown, and asking about this is an innovation (*bid'a*)." Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, said the same. This amount is sufficient, and whoever wants more than this should consult it in its place in the books of the scholars.

In the speech of the Arabs, *istiwa'* means elevation and settling. Al-Jawhari said: "*Istawa* from crookedness" (became straight); "*istawa 'ala zahri dabbatihi*" (he settled upon the back of his mount), i.e., he rested upon it; "*istawa ila al-sama'*" (he turned to the sky), i.e., he intended it; "*istawa*" also means he took control and prevailed. He said:

*Qad istawa Bishrun 'ala al-'Iraqi* ... *min ghayri sayfin wa dammin mihraqi*
(Bishr has taken control of Iraq, without sword and without spilled blood.)

"*Istawa al-rajulu*" means his youth reached its end. "*Istawa al-shay'*" means it became balanced. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr related from Abu 'Ubayda concerning His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful istawa over the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:5]: he said, "*'ala*" (rose above). The poet said:

*Fa-awradtuhum ma'an bi-fayfa'a qafrati* ... *wa qad halaqa al-najmu al-yamani fa-istawa*
(So I brought them to water in a barren desert, when the Yamani star had risen high and stood above.)

That is, it rose and was elevated.

I say: the elevation of Allah and His being high is an expression of the exaltedness of His glory, His attributes and His dominion. That is, there is none above Him in respect of the meanings of majesty that are due to Him, nor is there anyone with Him to whom elevation is shared with Him. Rather, He is *al-'Aliyy* (the Most High) in the absolute sense, glory be to Him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿upon the Throne﴾ — the term (*'arsh*) is a homonym applied to more than one thing. Al-Jawhari and others said: "*al-'arsh*" is the throne of kingship. In the Revelation: ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾ [An-Naml 27:41], and ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾ [Yusuf 12:100]. And *al-'arsh* is the roof of a house. *'Arsh al-qadam* is the part that protrudes from the top of the foot where the toes are. *'Arsh al-simak* is four small stars below al-'Awwa' (a constellation of five stars arranged in a bent line); it is said that it is the rump of the lion. *'Arsh al-bi'r* is covering the well with wood after its lower part has been lined with stones to the depth of a man's height; that wood is the *'arsh*, and its plural is *'urush*. *Al-'Arsh* is also a name for Mecca. And *al-'arsh* means kingship and authority. It is said: "The throne of so-and-so was shattered" (*thulla 'arshu fulanin*) when his kingship, authority and might were gone. Zuhayr said:

*Tadaraktumaa 'Absan wa qad thulla 'arshuhaa* ... *wa Dhubyanu idh dhallat bi-aqdamihaa al-na'lu*
(You rescued 'Abs when its throne was shattered, and Dhubyan when the sandal had humiliated it with its feet.)

The word *'arsh* in the verse may be interpreted as meaning kingship, that is, kingship is settled only for Him, majestic and mighty. This is a good opinion, though it is open to examination, and we have explained it among the opinions in our book.

And praise belongs to Allah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾. That is, He makes it like a covering, i.e., He removes the light of the day so that the maintenance of life in this world is completed by the coming of the night. So the night is for rest, and the day is for livelihood. It is read *yughashshi* with the doubling (*tashdid*), and similarly in *al-Ra'd* (Surah 13). This is the reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i. The rest read it without doubling. Both are dialects: *aghsha* and *ghashsha*. They have unanimously agreed on ﴿so He covered it with what covered it﴾ [An-Najm 53:54] with the doubling, and they agreed on ﴿And We covered them﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:9] (without doubling), so both readings are equivalent. The doubling carries the meaning of repetition and intensification. *Al-taghshiya* and *al-ighsha'* mean clothing one thing with another.

Mention of the day entering upon the night is not made in this verse, so one is sufficient for the other, like ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [An-Nahl 16:81] and ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:26]. Humayd ibn Qays read ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾, and its meaning is that the day covers the night.

(*Yatlubuhu hathithan*) means He seeks it constantly without slackening. And ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (*hal*). The implied sense is: He istawa over the Throne, covering the night over the day. Similarly, ﴿yatlubuhu hathithan﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to the night, meaning He covers the night over the day, seeking it. It is also possible that the clause is a new sentence and not a circumstance. *Hathithan* is either a substitute for the implied *talib* (seeker), or an adjective of it, or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning He seeks it with a swift seeking. *Al-hath* means hastening and speed. *Wallaa hathithan* means "he fled quickly," i.e., hurrying.

(﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars, subjected by His command﴾). Al-Akhfash said: they are conjoined to "the heavens," meaning "and He created the sun." It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir that he read all of them in the nominative (*raf'*), as subjects and predicates.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Surely, to Him belong creation and command﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: the truthfulness of Allah in His report. To Him belongs creation, and to Him belongs command. He created them and commanded them with what He loves. This command entails a prohibition. Ibn 'Uyayna said: "He distinguished between creation and command, so whoever combines them has disbelieved." (*Fa-al-khalq* is the created thing, and *al-amr* is His speech which is not created, and it is His saying "Be" — ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:82].) In His distinguishing between creation and command there is clear evidence against the view of those who say that the Qur'an is created. For if His speech which is a command were created, He would have said: "Surely to Him belongs creation and creation." That would be an incoherent and reprehensible utterance, and Allah is exalted above speaking with what has no benefit. This is also indicated by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾ [Ar-Rum 30:25], and ﴿the sun and the moon and the stars subjected by His command﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:54]. He informed, glory be to Him, that the created things subsist by His command. So if the command were created, it would need another command by which it subsists, and that command would need yet another command, and so on without end. That is impossible. Thus it is established that His command, which is His speech, is eternal and beginningless, not created, so that the subsistence of created things by it may be valid.

It is also indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [Al-Hijr 15:85]. He informed that He created them with truth, meaning the word, which is His saying to the things that come to be: "Be." So if the truth were created, it would not be valid that He created the created things by it, because a creation is not created by a created thing. This is indicated by ﴿And indeed Our word has preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ [As-Saffat 37:171–172], ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:101], and ﴿But the word has come into effect from Me﴾ [As-Sajda 32:13]. All of this is an allusion to precedence in speech regarding eternity, and that requires beginninglessness in existence. This point is sufficient for refuting them.

They have verses which they use as evidence for their position, such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There does not come to them any new reminder from their Lord﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:2], and His saying: ﴿And the command of Allah is a decree decreed﴾ [Al-Ahzab 33:38], and ﴿a thing done﴾ and what is similar to it.

Al-Qadi Abu Bakr said: the meaning of ﴿there does not come to them any reminder﴾ is "any admonition from the Prophet ﷺ, promise, or warning," and "they listen to it while playing," because the admonition and warning of the messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, is a *dhikr* (reminder). Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So remind, for you are only a reminder﴾ [Al-Ghashiya 88:21]. And it is said: "So-and-so is in a *majlis al-dhikr*" (assembly of remembrance/admonition).

As for the meaning of ﴿the command of Allah is a decree decreed﴾ and "a thing done," He, glory be to Him, intends His punishment and vengeance against the disbelievers, His victory for the believers, and what He has decided and decreed of His actions. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until when Our command came﴾ [Hud 11:40]. And He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ [Hud 11:97], meaning his affair, his actions and his ways. The poet said:

*Laha amruha hatta idha ma tabawwa'at* ... *bi-akhfafiha mar'an tabawwa'a madja'a*
(She had her affair until, when she settled with her hooves on a pasture, it settled into a resting place.)

The second issue: when this is established, know that *al-amr* (command) is not at all the same as *al-iradah* (will). The Mu'tazila say: "Command is the very will." This is not correct. Rather, He commands what He does not will and forbids what He wills. Do you not see that He commanded Ibrahim to slaughter his son, and He did not will it from him? And He commanded His Prophet to pray fifty prayers with his community, and He did not will from him except five prayers? And He willed the martyrdom of Hamza, when He says: ﴿and that He may take martyrs from among you﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:140]. And He forbade the disbelievers from killing him, and He did not command them to do it. This is correct and precious in its field, so reflect upon it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 54 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed be Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. "Tabaraka" is on the pattern of "tafa'ala," derived from "al-barakah" (blessing), which means abundance and expansion. It is said: "bורak al-shay'" and "bururak fihi" (the thing was blessed). Ibn 'Arafah said: [it means] Allah is exalted and magnified and raised high. It has also been said: by His name blessing is sought and good fortune is hoped for. The meaning of "Lord of the worlds" has already been discussed in al-Fatihah. [See vol. 1, p. 136.]

**First issue:** Al-Qurtubi says that in this verse there are three questions (masa'il).

**The first question:** God's words, ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, are a command to supplication (du'a') and an act of worship. God then joined to the command attributes that befit it: humility (khushu'), submissiveness (istikana) and entreaty (tadarru'). The meaning of "secretly" (khufyatan) is "inwardly, in the self," so that it stays far from showing off (riya', ostentation). For this reason God praised His prophet Zechariah, peace be upon him, when He said, reporting about him: ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 76.]]. A similar saying is the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: ("The best remembrance is the hidden one, and the best provision is that which suffices"). The Sacred Law affirms that secrecy in acts of righteousness, where no display is involved, is greater in reward than open performance.

This meaning has already been discussed in (Surah) al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 332.]]. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "We met people for whom no deed on earth was done in secret that would become open, ever. The Muslims would strive hard in supplication, yet no voice of theirs could be heard; it was only a whisper between them and their Lord." This is because God Most High says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾. He also mentioned the righteous servant's (of God) act and approved it, saying: ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾.

The followers of Abu Hanifa have used this verse as evidence that saying "Amin" silently is preferable to saying it aloud, since it is a supplication. The discussion of this has already passed in (Surah) al-Fatihah [[See vol. 1, p. 127.]].

Muslim narrated from Abu Musa, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey"—and in another narration, "on a military campaign"—"and the people began to raise their voices in takbir"—and in another narration, "a man, whenever he ascended a hill, would say: There is no god but God." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: ("O people, be gentle with yourselves [[That is, be gentle with them and do not exert yourselves excessively.]], for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and near, and He is with you"). The hadith continues.

**The second question:** The scholars differed about raising the hands in supplication. A group disliked it, including Jubayr ibn Mut'im, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Shurayh saw a man raising his hands and said: "Whom are you reaching for with them? May you have no mother!" Masruq said to a people who had raised their hands: "May God cut them off!" They preferred that when one asks God for a need, he point with his index finger, and they said: "That is sincerity (ikhlas)." Qatadah would point with his finger and not raise his hands. Ata', Tawus, Mujahid and others disliked raising the hands.

The permissibility of raising the hands was narrated from a number of Companions and Successors, and it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ); al-Bukhari mentioned this. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated, then raised his hands, and I saw the whiteness of his armpits." Similar was narrated from Anas. Ibn Umar said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) raised his hands and said: ('O God, I disown before You what Khalid has done')" [[This is Khalid ibn al-Walid, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) sent to the Banu Jadhimah to invite them to Islam. They did not know how to say "We have become Muslims," so Khalid began killing and taking captives among them. The Prophet (ﷺ) was displeased with Khalid for his haste in their affair and his failure to verify their situation. See the Book of Campaigns (Kitab al-Maghazi) in Sahih al-Bukhari.]].

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, he said: "On the day of Badr, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, while his companions were three hundred and seventeen men. The Prophet of God (ﷺ) turned toward the qiblah, stretching out his hands, and began calling out to his Lord..." and he mentioned the hadith. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from him: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) raised his hands, he would not lower them until he had wiped his face with them." He said: "This is a sound, gharib hadith." Ibn Majah narrated from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: ("Indeed your Lord is Modest and Generous; He is shy before His servant when he raises his hands to Him, that He should return them empty"—or he said—"disappointed"). [[The addition is from Sunan Ibn Majah.]]

Those who held the first view used what Muslim narrated from Umarah ibn Ruwaybah, who saw Bishr ibn Marwan on the pulpit raising his hands, and said: "May God disfigure these two hands! I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) do no more than this"—and he pointed with his index finger. They also used what Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah narrated from Qatadah, that Anas ibn Malik told him that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not raise his hands in any supplication except at the prayer for rain (istisqa'), when he would raise them until the whiteness of his armpits was seen.

The first narration has sounder chains and is more reliable than the hadith of Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, for Sa'id's mind had deteriorated in the last part of his life. Shu'bah opposed him in his narration from Qatadah, from Anas ibn Malik, saying in it: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would raise his hands until the whiteness of his armpits was seen."

It has been said that when a calamity befalls the Muslims, raising the hands at that time is beautiful and good, as the Prophet (ﷺ) did at the prayer for rain and on the day of Badr.

I say: Supplication is good in whatever manner is easy, and it is what is required of a person, to show his poverty and need before God, the Mighty and Majestic, and to humble himself and submit before Him. If he wishes to face the qiblah and raise his hands, that is good; and if he wishes not to, that is also fine, for the Prophet (ﷺ) did both as reported in the hadiths. God Most High has said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾, and He did not specify any particular manner, whether raising the hands or otherwise. He also said: ﴿those who remember God standing, sitting and lying on their sides﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 305.]], praising them and not stipulating any state other than what He mentioned. The Prophet (ﷺ) also supplicated in his Friday sermon while not facing the qiblah.

**The third question:** God's words, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, mean: in supplication, even if the wording is general. (The indication here is to this [[What lies between the brackets is as it appears in the original manuscripts, and is probably an addition by a copyist.]].) The transgressor (mu'tadi) is one who goes beyond the limit and commits what is forbidden, and transgression may vary according to what one transgresses in.

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: ("There will be a people who transgress in supplication"). Ibn Majah recorded it from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, who said: Affan narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, Sa'id al-Jurayri informed us, from Abu Nu'amah, that Abdullah ibn Mughaffal heard his son say: "O God, I ask You for the white palace on the right of Paradise when I enter it." He said: "My son, ask God for Paradise and seek refuge with Him from the Fire, for I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: ('There will be a people who transgress in supplication')."

Transgression in supplication takes several forms. Among them is loud shouting and excessive raising of the voice, as has already been mentioned. Among them is that a person supplicates to attain the rank of a prophet, or supplicates for the impossible, and other such excess. Among them is that he supplicates for sin, and other things. Among them is that he supplicates with what is not in the Book or the Sunnah, choosing rhymed phrases and rhymed prose he has found in worthless booklets with no basis and no reliability, making them his habit and abandoning what his Messenger, peace be upon him, supplicated with. All of this prevents the answering of supplication, as has been explained earlier in (Surah) al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 308.]].

His saying, ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set in order﴾ (7:56). On this there is one issue: Allah, glorified is He, forbids every corruption, whether small or great, after order has been established, whether small or great. This is the general ruling according to the sound opinion among the views.

al-Dahhak said: its meaning is, "Do not block [[To 'awwara the waters of a spring means to bury it and seal it up.]] the flowing water, and do not cut down fruit-bearing trees out of harm." It has also been transmitted that cutting off dinars is corruption on the earth, and it has been said that the trading of rulers is corruption on the earth.

al-Qushayri said: the intended meaning is, "Do not associate partners with Allah." So it is a prohibition of shirk, of shedding blood, and of chaos on the earth, and a command to adhere to the sacred laws after their establishment, after Allah had set things right by sending the Messengers and establishing the laws and clarifying the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the one who advanced this view aimed at the greatest corruption after the greatest order, so he singled it out for mention.

I say: what al-Dahhak mentioned is not to be taken in its generality. Rather, it applies when it causes harm to a believer. As for what harms the polytheists, that is permissible, for the Prophet (ﷺ) indeed blocked the water of the old well of Badr [[al-qalib (with a fatha on the qaf): an ancient abandoned well whose owner and digger are unknown, found in the open desert.]] and cut down the trees of the disbelievers. The discussion on cutting off dinars will come, Allah willing, in the commentary on Surat Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 84.]].

﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾ (7:56). This is a command that a person should be in a state of watchfulness, fear, and hope toward Allah, mighty and majestic, so that hope and fear are for the person like two wings for a bird, carrying it along the path of uprightness; if one of them alone is present, the person perishes. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful. And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ (15:49-50) [[See vol. 10, p. 34.]]. Thus He gave hope and instilled fear. So the person calls upon Him out of fear of His punishment and in hope of His reward. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they call upon Us in hope and in fear﴾ (21:90) [[See vol. 11, p. 336.]]. The discussion of this will come. Fear (khawf) is being disturbed by what is not safe from harm, and hope (ta'mil or tama') is anticipating what is loved, said al-Qushayri.

Some scholars said: fear should predominate over hope throughout life, and when death comes, hope should prevail. [[This contradicts what was reported from him, peace be upon him: "If the fear and the hope of a believer were weighed on a scale, neither would outweigh the other," and in another narration, "they would be balanced." It is also reported from Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was dying: "O Allah, You have commanded us to balance between fear and hope, and now my hope in You is the best."]] The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you should die except while thinking well of Allah." Authentic; related by Muslim.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ (7:56). He did not say "qarībah" (feminine). There are seven aspects to this:

The first is that "raḥmah" and "ruḥum" are the same, and they carry the meaning of pardon and forgiveness; this was said by al-Zajjaj and chosen by al-Nahhas.

al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "raḥmah" is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the proper form of a verbal noun is the masculine, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition [mawʿizah]﴾ (2:275) [[See vol. 3, p. 347.]]. This is close to al-Zajjaj's view, because mawʿizah means waʿẓ.

It has been said that by "raḥmah" He meant "iḥsān" (kindness). And since the gender of a word that is not truly feminine may be treated as masculine, this was mentioned by al-Jawhari.

It has also been said that by "raḥmah" here He meant rain. This was said by al-Akhfash, who added: it is permissible to make it masculine, just as some feminine nouns are made masculine. He recited:

*Then no cloud poured forth its rain,*
*and no land grew green with its vegetation.*

[[The verse is by ʿĀmir ibn Juwayn al-Ṭāʾī. It describes a fertile land because of the abundant rain that fell upon it. al-wadq: rain; al-muzna: cloud (from Sharḥ al-Shawāhid).]]

Abu 'Ubayda said: "qarīb" is masculine in agreement with the masculine sense of "place," meaning "a near place." 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: this is an error, for if it were as he said, "qarīb" would have been in the accusative in the Qur'an, as you say, "Indeed Zayd is near to you." It has also been said that it is masculine by way of ascription (nisbah), as if He said: "Indeed the mercy of Allah has nearness," just as you say, "a woman divorced [ṭāliq] and menstruating [ḥāʾiḍ]."

al-Farra' said: when "qarīb" means distance, it may be masculine or feminine; when it means kinship, it is feminine without any disagreement among them. You say: "This woman is my qarībah," meaning a woman of my kin, as mentioned by al-Jawhari. Others quoted from al-Farra': it is said of kinship, "qarībat fulān," but in non-kinship usage both masculine and feminine are permissible; you say: "Your house is qarīb from us," and "So-and-so is qarīb from us." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ (33:63) [[See vol. 14, p. 248.]].

Those who argued for this view said: this is how the Arabs speak, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*Woe to him if he should be left, and there is no mother of Hashim,*
*near, nor al-Basbasa, daughter of Yashkur.*

al-Zajjaj said: this is an error, because the rule for masculine and feminine is that they should follow their verbs.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, verse 57:**

His Exalted saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying, "He covers the night with the day." He mentions another of His blessings, and it indicates His oneness and the establishment of His divinity. The discussion of the wind has already passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 197.]]. *Riyah* is the plural of abundance (jam' kathrah), and *arwah* is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah). The root of *rih* is *rawh*. Whoever says *aryah* as the plural of paucity has been called in error.

"*Bushran*" has seven readings:

The people of the two Sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah) and Abu ʿAmr read *nushuran* with a *damma* on the *nun* and the *shin*, the plural of *nashir* in the sense of attribution (nisbah), meaning "possessing dispersal," so it is like *shahid* and *shuhud*. It may also be the plural of *nashur*, like *rasul* and *rusul*. It is said: "the wind of *nushur*" when it comes from here and from there. *Nushur* carries the meaning of *mansur* (dispersed), like *rukub* in the sense of *markub* (ridden), i.e., "He is the One who sends the winds dispersed."

Al-Hasan and Qatadah read *nushran* with a *damma* on the *nun* and a sukun on the *shin*, lightened from *nushur*, as it is said *kutub* and *rusl*.

Al-Aʿmash and Hamzah read *nashran* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a sukun on the *shin*, as a verbal noun (masdar), whose meaning is governed by what precedes it, as if he said: "He is the One who disperses the winds in dispersal." One says "I spread the thing and it spread out," as though they had been folded and then were spread out at the time of blowing.

It may also be a masdar in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the winds, as if he said, "He sends the winds dispersed," i.e., "giving life," from *anshara Allah al-mayyita fa-nushir* (God gave the dead life and he was revived), just as you say *atana rakdan* (he came to us running), i.e., *rakidan* (running).

It has been said that *nashran* (with a *fatha*) is from *al-nashr*, which is the opposite of *al-tayy* (folding), as we have mentioned. The wind, in its stillness, is like something folded, then it is sent forth from its folding and becomes like something opened. Abu ʿUbayd interpreted it as meaning "scattered in its directions," in the sense that it disperses them here and there.

ʿAsim read *bushran* with a *ba'* and a sukun on the *shin* and tanwin, the plural of *bashir*, meaning the winds bring good tidings of rain. Its witness is His saying: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bringers of good tidings﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 43.]]. The original vowel of the *shin* is a *damma*, but it was made sukun for lightness, as in *rusul* and *rusl*.

It is narrated from him (ʿAsim) *bashran* with a *fatha* on the *ba'*. Al-Nahhas said: It is also read *bushuran*, and *bashr* is the verbal noun of *bashshara*, *yabshuruhu*, meaning *bashshara* (to give good news). These are five readings.

Muhammad al-Yamani read *bushra* on the pattern of *hubla*. And a seventh reading is *bushra* with a *damma* on the *ba'* and the *shin*.

**(Until, when they carry heavy clouds)**: *al-sahab* (the cloud) may be masculine or feminine, and so is every plural that has a *ha'* distinguishing it from its singular. It is permissible to describe it with a singular adjective, so you say *sahab thaqil* (masculine) and *thaqilah* (feminine). The meaning: the wind carried clouds heavy with water, i.e., it made them heavy by their load. It is said: *aqalla fulan al-shay'* (so-and-so lifted the thing), i.e., carried it. "We drove it," i.e., the clouds.

**(To a dead land)**: i.e., there is no vegetation in it. It is said: "We drove it to the land of such-and-such" and "to the land of such-and-such." It has also been said, "for the sake of a dead land," so the *lam* is the *lam* of purpose (lam al-ajal). *Balad* is every place on the earth, whether inhabited or uninhabited, populated or empty. *Al-baldah* and *al-balad* are singular of *al-bilad* and *al-buldan*. *Al-balad* also means a trace (athar), its plural being *abladd*. The poet said:

*"After what decay had covered its traces."* [[This is the second half of a verse by Ibn al-Raqqaʿ. Its first half is: "He recognized the abodes, a guess, and then he visited them."]]

*Al-balad* is also the nest-hollow of the ostrich (udhhi al-naʿam), i.e., the place in the sand where the ostrich lays its eggs, since the ostrich lays them there and has no nest. It is said: "He is more abject than the egg of the *balad*," meaning the ostrich's egg that it leaves behind. *Al-baldah* also means the land: one says "this is our *baldah*," as one says "our *bahrah*" (our sea/ocean). *Al-baldah* is also one of the mansions of the moon, which consists of six stars of the Bow (al-qaws), which the sun enters on the shortest day of the year. *Al-baldah* also means the chest; one says "so-and-so has a wide *baldah*," i.e., a wide chest. The poet said:

*"She knelt down and cast her chest upon the wasteland, few are the voices in it except her low groan."* [[In the original: "after" (baʿd). The correction is from Lisan and the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah. The first *baldah* refers to the part of the chest that lies on the ground; the second to the desert where he made his camel kneel. *Bughām* is the cry of the she-camel, originally that of the gazelle, borrowed for the camel.]]

He means: the she-camel knelt and laid her chest on the ground. *Al-baldah* (with a *fatha* or *damma* on the *ba'*) is also the clear space between the two eyebrows, so these are among the homonymous words (al-alfaz al-mushtarakah).

**(Then We sent down water with it)**: i.e., with the land. It has also been said: "We sent down water from the clouds," because the cloud is the instrument for sending down water. The meaning may also be: "We sent down from it water," like His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of God drink﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 122.]], i.e., from it.

**(Then We brought forth with it fruits of every kind. Thus We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember)**: the *kaf* (in *kadhalika*) is in the accusative position: i.e., like that bringing forth, We will revive the dead.

Al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Abu Razin al-ʿUqayli, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, how does God restore creation, and what is the sign of that in His creation?' He said: 'Did you not pass by the valley of your people barren, then you passed by it and it was stirring, green?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is the sign of God in His creation.'"

It has also been said: the point of the comparison is that their revival from their graves will be by rain that God sends upon their graves, so the graves split open for them, and then the spirits return to them.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Then God will send — or he said, will send down — a rain like a drizzle, and bodies of people will grow from it. Then it will be said: 'O people, come to your Lord, and stop them, for they are to be questioned.'" And he mentioned the hadith. We have mentioned it in full in the book *al-Tadhkirah*, and praise be to God.

This indicates the resurrection and the rising (al-baʿth wa-al-nushur), and to God all matters are returned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 58:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, while that which is bad comes forth only sparingly.﴾ That is, the good land is the good soil. "And the bad" is the soil in which there are stones or thorns, according to al-Hasan. It was also said: the meaning is a comparison. Exalted is He compared the one quick to understand to the good land, and the dull one to the bad land, according to al-Nahhas. It was also said: this is a parable for hearts. A heart that accepts admonition and reminder, and a corrupt heart that turns away from that; al-Hasan also said this. Qatadah said: it is a parable for the believer who acts seeking reward and voluntarily, and the hypocrite who does not seek reward. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (By Him in whose hand is my soul, if any of them knew that he would find a fat bone or two good hooves [[al-mirmah (with the mim vowelled with kasra or fatha): the hoof of a sheep. It was also said: what lies between its hooves.]], he would surely attend the 'Isha' prayer).

"Nakidan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and it means difficult, reluctant to give good. And this is an illustration. Mujahid said: this means that among the children of Adam there are the good and the bad.

Talhah recited "illa nakidan" by dropping the kasra because of its heaviness. Ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "nakadan" with a fatha on the kaf, so it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of "one possessing nakad" (difficulty), as in the verse:

"Indeed it is only advancing and retreating" [[The line is by al-Khansa'. Its first half: "Tarqa'u ma rataat hatta idha adrakat." Al-Khizanah, vol. 1, p. 207.]]

It was also said: "nakidan" with a fatha or a kasra on the kaf has the same meaning, like al-danif and al-danaf, both being dialectal forms.

(Thus do We vary the signs) That is, just as We have varied the signs, meaning the proofs and indications, in refuting polytheism, thus do We vary the signs regarding everything people need.

(For a people who give thanks) He specified the thankful because they are the ones who benefit from this.

**The Qur'anic verse:** "Indeed We sent Noah to his people, and he said, 'O my people, worship Allah.'" (7:59)

*Commentary:* When Allah showed that He is the Creator, the One able to perfect everything, He mentioned the stories of the nations and what they contain of warning to the disbelievers.

The lam in "*laqad*" (indeed) is an emphatic particle that draws attention to an oath. The fa' (then) in "*fa-qala*" indicates that the second event came directly after the first. "*Ya qawmi*" (O my people) is a vocative with the pronoun suffixed. It is also permissible to say "*ya qawmi*" with the original (*yā’*) ending, "*ya qawmiya*."

Nuh was the first of the messengers sent to the earth after Adam, peace be upon them both, by the prohibition of daughters, sisters, paternal aunts and maternal aunts (for marriage).

Al-Nahhas (an-Nahhas, grammarian) said: "He is treated as a diptote (not taking the nunation) because he has three letters." It is also possible that his name is derived from *nāḥa yanūḥu* (to lament), and this meaning and others were already discussed in *Al 'Imran*, so there is no need to repeat it here. [See vol. 4, p. 62.]

Ibn al-Arabi said: "Whoever claims that Idris was before him among the historians has erred. The proof of the error is the authentic hadith about the Night Journey, when the Prophet ﷺ met Adam and Idris. Adam said to him: '*Marhaban bil-nabiyy al-salih wal-ibn al-salih*' (Welcome to the righteous prophet and the righteous son). Idris said to him: '*Marhaban bil-nabiyy al-salih wal-akh al-salih*' (Welcome to the righteous prophet and the righteous brother). Had Idris been the father of Nuh, he would have said, 'Welcome to the righteous prophet and the righteous son.' When he said 'the righteous brother,' this shows that he is connected with him through Nuh, peace be upon them all. No fair-minded person can say anything after this."

Al-Qadi Iyad said: "The reply of the fathers here, such as Nuh, Ibrahim and Adam, was 'Welcome to the righteous son.' Idris was addressed as 'the righteous brother,' as was reported about Musa, Isa, Yusuf, Harun and Yahya, who were not fathers, by agreement regarding the Prophet ﷺ."

Al-Mazari said: "The historians have mentioned that Idris was the grandfather of Nuh, peace be upon them both. If evidence establishes that Idris was also sent as a messenger, then the statement of the genealogists that he was before Nuh is not valid, because of what the Prophet ﷺ reported of Adam's saying that Nuh was the first messenger sent. If no evidence is established, then what they said is permissible, and it is valid to interpret that Idris was a prophet but not a messenger."

Al-Qadi Iyad said: "This may be reconciled by saying that the mission of Nuh was specific to the people of the earth, as he said in the hadith, comprehensively, like our Prophet ﷺ. And Idris was for his own people, like Musa, Hud, Salih, Lut and others."

Some scholars have used as evidence for this the words of Allah: ﴿And indeed Ilyas was among the messengers. When he said to his people, "Will you not fear Allah?"﴾ (37:123–124). It has been said that Ilyas is Idris. It has also been read as "*salamun ʿala idrasin*" (peace upon the Idrasin, i.e., the Idrisiyyin).

Al-Qadi Iyad said: "I have seen that Abu al-Hasan ibn Battal held that Adam was not a messenger, in order to avoid this objection. But the lengthy hadith of Abu Dharr indicates that Adam and Idris were both messengers."

Ibn Atiyya said: "The reconciliation is that the mission of Nuh was well known for reforming people and compelling them to belief through punishment and destruction. So what is meant is that he was the first prophet sent with this characteristic. And Allah knows best."

It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that Nuh, peace be upon him, was sent when he was forty years old. Al-Kalbi said: "Eight hundred years after Adam." Ibn Abbas said: "He remained among his people calling them for a thousand years minus fifty years, as the revelation informs us. Then he lived sixty years after the Flood, until people multiplied and spread."

Wahb said: "Nuh was sent when he was fifty years old." Awn ibn Shaddad said: "Nuh was sent when he was three hundred and fifty years old."

In many hadith books, such as al-Tirmidhi and others, it is stated that all of creation now are descendants of Nuh, peace be upon him. Al-Naqqash mentioned, on the authority of Sulayman ibn Arqam, on the authority of al-Zuhri, that the Arabs, Persians, Romans, the people of Syria and the people of Yemen are from the offspring of Sam ibn Nuh; and the Sind, the Hind, the Zanj, the Habasha, the Zutt and the Nuba, and every black-skinned person, are from the offspring of Ham ibn Nuh; and the Turks, Berbers, the people beyond China, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and the Saqaliba are all from the offspring of Yafith ibn Nuh. All creation are the descendants of Nuh.

Allah's words: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ — the reading "*ghayruhu*" with a *damma* (raised ending) is that of Nafi', Abu Amr, Asim and Hamza, meaning "you have no god other than Him." It is a qualifier (*na't*) according to the position (*mahall*) of the phrase. It has also been said that "*ghayr*" here means "*illa*" (except), meaning "you have no god except Allah." Abu Amr said: "I do not know the *jarr* (genitive, kasra) or the *nasb* (accusative, fatha)." Al-Kisa'i read it with a *khafd* (genitive) according to the position. The accusative is permissible as an exception, though it is not common. However, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted the accusative of "*ghayr*" wherever "*illa*" would be suitable, whether the sentence is complete or not, so they allowed: "*ma ja'a-nī ghayraka*" (no one came to me except you). Al-Farra' said: "It is the dialect of some of the Banu Asad and Qudaa'a." And he recited:

*He was not prevented from drinking from it except that a dove called out*
*In a tall date-palm tree with its fruit clusters.*

[The line is by Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat. *Al-suhuq* means what has grown tall of the doum palm. In *al-Khizana* it is "in its branches" (*ghusun*). *Awqal* means its fruits. See vol. 2, p. 45.]

Al-Kisa'i said: "It is not permissible to say '*ja'a-nī ghayraka*' in an affirmative sentence, because '*illa*' does not occur here." Al-Nahhas said: "According to the Basrans, it is not permissible to put "*ghayr*" in the accusative when the sentence is not complete. That, in their view, is among the most offensive grammatical errors (*lahn*)."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 7, verses 60–62:**

"*al-Mala'*" (الْمَلَأُ) means the most honourable of the people and their leaders. Its explanation has already been given in al-Baqarah [See vol. 3, p. 243.]. *Al-dalal* (الضلال) and *al-dalala* (الضَّلَالَةُ) mean deviating from the path of truth and departing from it. The meaning is: "Indeed, we see you, in your calling to one God, to be in error, far from the truth."

"*Uballigukum*" (أُبَلِّغُكُمْ) is read with the shadda (تشديد) from *al-tabligh*, and without it from *al-iblagh*. It is said that both have the same meaning and are two dialectal forms, like *karramahu* and *akramahu*.

"*Wa-ansahu lakum*" (وَأَنْصَحُ لَكُمْ): *al-nush* means purifying intention from the taints of corruption in dealing with others, as opposed to *al-ghish* (deceit). It is said: *nasahtuhu* and *nasahtu lahu nasihatan wa-nasaahatan wa-nushan*. The form with the preposition *lam* (لَ) is more eloquent. God Most High said: "*Wa-ansahu lakum*." The noun is *al-nasiha*. *Al-nasih* and *al-nasih* (النَّصِيحُ) mean the one who gives advice, and the plural is *nusaha'*. A man described as *nasih al-jaib* means one whose heart is pure. Al-Asma'i said: *al-nasih* is that which is pure of honey and other things, like *al-nasi'*. Everything that is unmixed is *nasah*. Someone who is *intasaha* turns to sincere advice. It is said: "Accept my advice, for I am sincere toward you." *Al-nasih* also means the tailor, and *al-nisah* is the thread with which one sews. *Al-nisahat* also means hides. Al-A'sha said:

"You see the drinkers, all of them intoxicated,
like the hides of the young camels that have been stretched."

*Al-rubah* (الرُّبَحُ) is a dialectal form of *al-rub'* (الرُّبَعُ), which is the young camel. *Al-rubah* is also a bird. Further explanation of this will come in Surah Bara'a [See vol. 8, p. 226.], God willing.

﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people.﴾ (7:64)

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or do you wonder﴾ (7:63). The wāw (the conjunctive "and") is vocalised with a fatḥa because it is wāw al-ʿaṭf (the conjunctive wāw, which links one clause to another). The interrogative alif (alif al-istifhām, the question particle) has entered upon it for taqrīr (affirmation, eliciting an admission). The usual pattern is for the wāw to precede the interrogative particles, except the alif, because of its strength.

﴿that there has come to you a reminder﴾, meaning an admonition, ﴿from your Lord﴾.

﴿through a man from among you﴾, meaning through the tongue of a man. It has also been said that ʿalā (through/upon) here means maʿa (with), that is, with a man. It has also been said that the meaning is: that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord, sent down upon a man from among you, whose lineage you know, that is, a man of your own kind. Had he been an angel, there would likely have been a natural aversion due to the difference in kind.

﴿al-Fulk﴾ (the ship) may be singular or plural. It has been mentioned previously in al-Baqarah (see vol. 2, p. 194).

﴿ʿAmīn﴾ means blind to the truth, as Qatadah said. It has also been said: blind to the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and His power. It is said: "A man is ʿamin with such-and-such," meaning ignorant of it.
