Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 65–69:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to ʿAd [We sent] their brother Hud﴾. That is, and We sent to ʿAd their brother Hud. Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, the son of their father. It was also said: their brother in the tribe. And it was said: that is, a human from among the sons of their father Adam.

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, [it is reported] that "their brother Hud" means "their companion." ʿAd was from the descendants of Sam ibn Nuh. Ibn Ishaq said: ʿAd was the son of ʿAwis ibn Iram ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him. And Hud was Hud ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabah ibn al-Julud ibn ʿAd ibn ʿAwis ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Allah sent him to ʿAd as a prophet. He was among the middlemost of them in lineage and the best of them in ancestry. As for "ʿAd": whoever does not diptote it (lam yasrifhu) makes it the name of a tribe, and whoever diptotes it (sarafahu) makes it the name of a living group. Abu Hatim said: in the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud it is "ʿAdan al-Ula" without an alif. And "Hud" is non-Arabic, and it is declined (infisaf) because of its lightness, since it has three letters. It is also possible that it is Arabic, derived from hada yahudu. The accusative case is by way of apposition (badal). Between Hud and Nuh, as the commentators mentioned, there were seven generations. ʿAd, as it is related, were thirteen tribes, dwelling in the sands, the sands of ʿAlij. They were people of gardens, crops and buildings, and their lands were the most fertile of lands, but Allah became displeased with them and made it into deserts. As it is related, they were in the regions from Hadramawt to Yemen, and they worshipped idols. When his people were destroyed, Hud, along with those who believed with him, went to Mecca, and they remained there until they died.

﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾: that is, in folly and lightness of mind. [The poet] said:

They walked as spears swayed, their upper parts made light by the passing of the scattering winds.

[Note: this is Dhu al-Rummah, describing women.]

This meaning has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah. As for "seeing" here and in the story of Nuh, it was said: it is sight with the eye. And it was said: it is possible that it is meant as opinion, which is the strongest assumption.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh﴾. "Khulafa'" is the plural of khalifah in the masculine sense of meaning, and khala'if according to the wording. He reminded them of a favour by making them the inhabitants of the earth after the people of Nuh.

﴿And He increased you greatly in stature﴾. It may also be read "basṭah" with the sad, because after it there is a ṭa', meaning height in creation and largeness of body. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the tallest of them was a hundred cubits, and the shortest sixty cubits. This increase was over the creation of their forefathers. It was also said: over the creation of the people of Nuh. Wahb said: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and a man's eye would be a nest in which beasts of prey would hatch, and likewise their nostrils. Shahr ibn Hawshab related from Abu Hurayrah who said: a man of the people of ʿAd would take two door-leaves of stone which, if five hundred men of this nation gathered upon them, they could not lift them, and if one of them struck the earth with his foot, it would sink into it.

﴿So remember the favours of Allah﴾: that is, the bounties of Allah. Its singular is ʾilan, ʾilyun, ʾilwun, and ʾalan, like al-ana' whose singular is inan, inyun, inwun and ana.

﴿So that you may prosper﴾. Already mentioned [see vol. 1, p. 181].

Ibn Ishaq said: ʿAd was the son of ʿAwis ibn Iram ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him. And Hud was Hud ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabah ibn al-Julud ibn ʿAd ibn ʿAwis ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Allah sent him to ʿAd as a prophet. He was among the middlemost of them in lineage and the best of them in ancestry. As for "ʿAd": whoever does not diptote it (lam yasrifhu) makes it the name of a tribe, and whoever diptotes it (sarafahu) makes it the name of a living group. Abu Hatim said: in the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud it is "ʿAdan al-Ula" without an alif. And "Hud" is non-Arabic, and it is declined (infisaf) because of its lightness, since it has three letters. It is also possible that it is Arabic, derived from hada yahudu. The accusative case is by way of apposition (badal). Between Hud and Nuh, as the commentators mentioned, there were seven generations. ʿAd, as it is related, were thirteen tribes, dwelling in the sands, the sands of ʿAlij. They were people of gardens, crops and buildings, and their lands were the most fertile of lands, but Allah became displeased with them and made it into deserts. As it is related, they were in the regions from Hadramawt to Yemen, and they worshipped idols. When his people were destroyed, Hud, along with those who believed with him, went to Mecca, and they remained there until they died.

﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾: that is, in folly and lightness of mind. [The poet] said:

They walked as spears swayed, their upper parts made light by the passing of the scattering winds.

[Note: this is Dhu al-Rummah, describing women.]

This meaning has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah. As for "seeing" here and in the story of Nuh, it was said: it is sight with the eye. And it was said: it is possible that it is meant as opinion, which is the strongest assumption.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh﴾. "Khulafa'" is the plural of khalifah in the masculine sense of meaning, and khala'if according to the wording. He reminded them of a favour by making them the inhabitants of the earth after the people of Nuh.

﴿And He increased you greatly in stature﴾. It may also be read "basṭah" with the sad, because after it there is a ṭa', meaning height in creation and largeness of body. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the tallest of them was a hundred cubits, and the shortest sixty cubits. This increase was over the creation of their forefathers. It was also said: over the creation of the people of Nuh. Wahb said: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and a man's eye would be a nest in which beasts of prey would hatch, and likewise their nostrils. Shahr ibn Hawshab related from Abu Hurayrah who said: a man of the people of ʿAd would take two door-leaves of stone which, if five hundred men of this nation gathered upon them, they could not lift them, and if one of them struck the earth with his foot, it would sink into it.

﴿So remember the favours of Allah﴾: that is, the bounties of Allah. Its singular is ʾilan, ʾilyun, ʾilwun, and ʾalan, like al-ana' whose singular is inan, inyun, inwun and ana.

﴿So that you may prosper﴾. Already mentioned [see vol. 1, p. 181].

[Verse 70–72 commentary]

They asked for the punishment with which he had threatened and warned them. So he said to them: "Indeed, there has befallen you [ready punishment]" (qad waqa'a 'alaykum). The meaning of waqa'a is "wajaba" (became due, became obligatory). It is said: "al-qawl wa-l-hukm waqa'a," meaning "wajaba" (the saying and the judgment became due). Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And when the plague fell upon them﴾ [see p. 271 of this part], meaning "nazala bihim" (descended upon them). And His saying: ﴿And when the word has fallen due upon them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 233]. Ar-rijs (the abomination) means the punishment. It has also been said: by ar-rijs is meant the rust (ar-rayn) upon the heart through an increase in disbelief.

(﴿Do you dispute with me over names﴾) meaning the idols which they worshipped, and these had various names. ﴿For which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ meaning no proof for you in worshipping them. Thus "al-ism" (the name) here means "al-musamma" (the named thing). Its parallel is His saying: ﴿They are only names which you have named﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 192]. These names are like al-'Uzza, derived from al-'izz (might), and al-A'azz, and al-Lat; and they possess nothing of might or divinity. Dabir (the root) means the last (remnant). It has already been discussed [see vol. 6, p. 425], meaning: no remnant was left for them.

Thamud was the son of 'Ad, son of Iram, son of Sam, son of Noah. He was the brother of Jadis. They lived in comfort and ease with their means of livelihood, but they defied the command of God, worshipped other than Him, and spread corruption in the land. So God sent to them Salih as a prophet. He was Salih, son of 'Ubayd, son of Asif, son of Kashih, son of 'Ubayd, son of Hadhir, son of Thamud. They were an Arab people. Salih was of the most central of them in lineage and the most excellent of them in nobility. He called them to God, the Exalted, until his beard turned grey [[Al-shamt (with a fatḥa on the mīm): the whiteness of the beard. It is also said: the whiteness of the hair of the head mixed with its blackness.]], yet none followed him except a few weak ones.

"Thamud" is not declined (diptotic), because it became a name for the tribe. Abu Hatim said: it is not declined because it is a non-Arabic name (a'jami). Al-Nahhas [a grammarian] said: this is an error, because it is derived from al-thamad, which is a small quantity of water. The reciters have read ﴿أَلَا إِنَّ ثَمُودَ كَفَرُوا رَبَّهُمْ﴾ [[See vol. 9 p. 59.]] treating it as the name of a tribe. The dwellings of Thamud were al-Hijr [[A place name, the region of Thamud's dwellings.]], between the Hijaz and Syria, extending to Wadi al-Qura, and they were of the descendants of Sam son of Noah. Thamud was named for the scarcity of its water. Its explanation will come, God willing, in the chapter of al-Hijr [[See vol. 10 p. 45 onwards.]].

﴿هذِهِ ناقَةُ اللَّهِ لَكُمْ آيَةً﴾ [This is God's she-camel, a sign for you]. He brought forth for them the she-camel from a hard rock when they asked him for it. She had a day on which she drank all of the water of the valley, and on the other day she gave them, in its place, milk that had never been drunk, sweeter and more delicious than anything. It was sufficient for their needs according to their turns. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿لَها شِرْبٌ وَلَكُمْ شِرْبُ يَوْمٍ مَعْلُومٍ﴾ [For her is a drink, and for you is a drink on a known day] [[See vol. 13 p. 127.]]. The she-camel was attributed to God, Mighty and Majestic, in the sense of the attribution of a creature to its Creator, and this carries the meaning of honour and distinction.

﴿فَذَرُوها تَأْكُلْ فِي أَرْضِ اللَّهِ﴾ [So leave her to eat in God's land]: meaning, her provision and her upkeep are not your responsibility.

**First issue:** Allah's words ﴿And He settled you in the earth﴾. There is an omitted element in it, meaning: He settled you in the earth as dwelling places (manāzil).

(﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾) That is, you build palaces in every place.

(﴿And you hew out the mountains as houses﴾) They made houses in the mountains because of the length of their lifespans, for roofs and buildings would decay before their lives came to an end. Al-Hasan read the vowel on the ḥā' as a fatḥah (taḥsinūna / *tanḥatūna* form as *tanḥatūna*, i.e., with fatḥah), and this is a dialect (lughah). It contains one of the throat letters (ḥurūf al-ḥalq), which is why it follows the pattern *fa'ala yaf'alu*.

**Second issue:** Whoever permits high construction, such as palaces and the like, cites this verse as evidence, along with His words ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [see p. 195 of this part]. It is related that a son of Muhammad ibn Sirin built a house and spent a great deal of wealth on it. This was mentioned to Muhammad ibn Sirin, and he said: "I see no harm in a man building a structure that benefits him." It is also related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah bestows a blessing upon a servant, He loves to see the effect of that blessing upon him." Among the effects of blessing are good building and good clothing. Do you not see that if a man buys a beautiful slave-girl for a great sum, it is permissible, though he could have managed with less? Likewise with building.

Others disliked this, among them al-Hasan al-Basri and others, and they argued with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "When Allah intends evil for a servant, He causes his wealth to be consumed in clay and brick." In another report from him (ﷺ): "Whoever builds beyond what suffices him will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying it upon his neck."

I say: I hold this view, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whatever a believer spends, its replacement is upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except what is spent on building or sin." Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated it, and al-Dāraquṭnī recorded it.

The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The son of Adam has no right to anything beyond these qualities: a dwelling in which he lives, a garment that covers his nakedness, a piece of dry bread and water." It was recorded by al-Tirmidhī.

**Third issue:** Allah's words ﴿So remember the bounties of Allah﴾, that is, His blessings. This indicates that the disbelievers are also granted blessings. The discussion of this has passed in Āl ʿImrān [vol. 4, p. 330].

﴿And do not commit corruption in the earth, causing mischief﴾ has been discussed in al-Baqarah [vol. 1, p. 421]. *Al-ʿithiyy* and *al-ʿuthuww* are two dialects. Al-Aʿmash read *tiʿthaw* with a kasrah on the tā', deriving it from *ʿathiya yaʿthā*, not from *ʿathā yaʿthū*.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾. The second [phrase, "to those who were oppressed"] is a substitute (badal) for the first, because the ones oppressed (al-mustad'afin) are the believers. It is a substitution of part for the whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 77–79:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾. Al-'aqr (hamstringing) is wounding. It was said: it is cutting off a limb that affects the soul. One says 'aqartu al-faras (I hamstrung the horse) when I strike its legs with a sword, and there is khayl 'aqra (a hamstrung horse). And 'aqartu zahr al-dabba (I hamstrung the back of the animal) when I turned its back (i.e., injured it so that it could not carry).

Imru' al-Qays said:

"You say, when the litter tilted with us together: 'You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount!'"

That is, you wounded it and made its back useless. Al-Qushayri said: al-'aqr is the cutting (kashf; in J and K: breaking) of the hamstring of the camel. Then the slaughtering (nahr) was also called 'aqr, because hamstringing is generally the cause of slaughtering. Scholars differed about the one who hamstrung the she-camel, in several opinions. The most sound of them is what is in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Zam'ah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a sermon, and he mentioned the she-camel and mentioned the one who hamstrung it, and he said: (When the most wretched of them rose up, a mighty, wicked (ʿārim: that is, evil and vicious), invincible man among his people (in J: his family) rose up against her, like Abu Zam'ah) and he mentioned the hadith.

It was said his name was Qudar ibn Salif. It was also said: their kingship belonged to a woman called Mulki. She envied Salih when the people inclined to him, and she said to two women who had two lovers who were infatuated with them: "Do not obey them, and ask them to hamstring the she-camel." So they did. The two men went out, drove the she-camel into a narrow place, and one of them shot her with an arrow, and they killed her. The young camel, which was her offspring, came to the rock from which the she-camel had emerged, cried out three times, and the rock split open and it entered it. It is said that it is the beast that will come out to the people at the end of time, as its explanation will come in Surat al-Naml.

Ibn Ishaq said: The young camel pursued four men from among those who had hamstrung the she-camel: Misda' and his brother Dhu'ab. Misda' shot it with an arrow which pierced its heart (intaZama al-sayd means when one stabs or shoots it until it pierces through), then he dragged it by its leg and joined it to its mother, and they ate it along with her. The first account is more sound, for Salih said to them: "Three days remain of your life," and for this reason it cried out three times. It was also said: its hamstringer was alone with eight men, and they are those about whom Allah said: ﴿And there were in the city nine men﴾, as its explanation will come in Surat al-Naml. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So they called their companion, and he took (the sword) and hamstrung (her)﴾. They were drinking, and water was scarce for mixing their drink, and it was the day of the she-camel's milk. One of them stood up, watched the people and said: "I will surely relieve the people of her," and he hamstrung her.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they defied the command of their Lord﴾, that is, they were arrogant. ʿataa yaʿtu ʿutuwwan, that is, he was arrogant. And taʿanna fulan when he did not obey. And al-layl al-ʿatiy: the intensely dark night, related from al-Khalil.

(And they said: "O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with") that is, of the punishment.

(So the earthquake seized them) that is, the severe quake. It was said: it was a mighty cry which tore their hearts apart, as in the story of Thamud in Surat Hud: ﴿in the story of Thamud, the Cry seized them﴾. It is said: rajafa al-shay' yarjifu rajfan wa rajafanan (the thing trembled). And the wind made the trees tremble (arjafat al-rih al-shajar): it moved them. Its origin is movement with sound, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day when the Quaker quakes﴾. The poet said:

"When I saw that the pilgrimage's time had come, and the riding beasts of the people were trembling with the people."

(So they became in their abode) that is, their land. It was said: it is singular in the sense of a genus, and the meaning is: in their dwellings. And in another place He said: ﴿in their homes﴾, that is, in their residences.

(Prostrate) that is, clinging to the ground on their knees and faces, as a bird crouches (yajthum al-ta'ir), that is, they became lifeless from the severity of the punishment. The root of al-judum is for the hare and the like, and the place is majthama. Zuhayr said:

"In it are the oxen and the gazelles walking in succession, and their fawns rising from every resting place."

[Note in source: al-'in with a kasra on its first letter: the cattle, singular a'yan and 'ayna'. Al-aram: the gazelles. Al-atla': their young, singular tala. Khilfa: one group after another. It was said: varied, this one coming and this one going, this one ascending and this one descending. (From the commentary on the Mu'allaqat.)]

It was also said: they were burned by a thunderbolt and became dead in the morning, except for one man who was in the sanctuary of Allah; when he went out of the sanctuary, he was struck by what struck his people.

(Then he turned away from them) that is, upon despairing of them.

(And he said: "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love advisers") It is possible that he said this before their death, and it is possible that he said it after their death, like His peace be upon him saying to the slain of Badr: "Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" It was said: "Do you speak to these corpses?" He said: "You are no more hearing than they, but they cannot answer." The first is more apparent. What indicates it is: (but you do not love advisers), that is, you did not accept my counsel.

One of them stood up, watched the people and said: "I will surely relieve the people of her," and he hamstrung her.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they defied the command of their Lord﴾, that is, they were arrogant. ʿataa yaʿtu ʿutuwwan, that is, he was arrogant. And taʿanna fulan when he did not obey. And al-layl al-ʿatiy: the intensely dark night, related from al-Khalil.

(And they said: "O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with") that is, of the punishment.

(So the earthquake seized them) that is, the severe quake. It was said: it was a mighty cry which tore their hearts apart, as in the story of Thamud in Surat Hud: ﴿in the story of Thamud, the Cry seized them﴾. It is said: rajafa al-shay' yarjifu rajfan wa rajafanan (the thing trembled). And the wind made the trees tremble (arjafat al-rih al-shajar): it moved them. Its origin is movement with sound, and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day when the Quaker quakes﴾. The poet said:

"When I saw that the pilgrimage's time had come, and the riding beasts of the people were trembling with the people."

(So they became in their abode) that is, their land. It was said: it is singular in the sense of a genus, and the meaning is: in their dwellings. And in another place He said: ﴿in their homes﴾, that is, in their residences.

(Prostrate) that is, clinging to the ground on their knees and faces, as a bird crouches (yajthum al-ta'ir), that is, they became lifeless from the severity of the punishment. The root of al-judum is for the hare and the like, and the place is majthama. Zuhayr said:

"In it are the oxen and the gazelles walking in succession, and their fawns rising from every resting place."

[Note in source: al-'in with a kasra on its first letter: the cattle, singular a'yan and 'ayna'. Al-aram: the gazelles. Al-atla': their young, singular tala. Khilfa: one group after another. It was said: varied, this one coming and this one going, this one ascending and this one descending. (From the commentary on the Mu'allaqat.)]

It was also said: they were burned by a thunderbolt and became dead in the morning, except for one man who was in the sanctuary of Allah; when he went out of the sanctuary, he was struck by what struck his people.

(Then he turned away from them) that is, upon despairing of them.

(And he said: "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love advisers") It is possible that he said this before their death, and it is possible that he said it after their death, like His peace be upon him saying to the slain of Badr: "Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" It was said: "Do you speak to these corpses?" He said: "You are no more hearing than they, but they cannot answer." The first is more apparent. What indicates it is: (but you do not love advisers), that is, you did not accept my counsel.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 77–79:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾. Al-'aqr (hamstringing) is wounding. It was said: it is cutting off a limb that affects the soul. One says 'aqartu al-faras (I hamstrung the horse) when I strike its legs with a sword, and there is khayl 'aqra (a hamstrung horse). And 'aqartu zahr al-dabba (I hamstrung the back of the animal) when I turned its back (i.e., injured it so that it could not carry).

Imru' al-Qays said:

"You say, when the litter tilted with us together: 'You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount!'"

That is, you wounded it and made its back useless. Al-Qushayri said: al-'aqr is the cutting (kashf; in J and K: breaking) of the hamstring of the camel. Then the slaughtering (nahr) was also called 'aqr, because hamstringing is generally the cause of slaughtering. Scholars differed about the one who hamstrung the she-camel, in several opinions. The most sound of them is what is in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Zam'ah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a sermon, and he mentioned the she-camel and mentioned the one who hamstrung it, and he said: (When the most wretched of them rose up, a mighty, wicked (ʿārim: that is, evil and vicious), invincible man among his people (in J: his family) rose up against her, like Abu Zam'ah) and he mentioned the hadith.

It was said his name was Qudar ibn Salif. It was also said: their kingship belonged to a woman called Mulki. She envied Salih when the people inclined to him, and she said to two women who had two lovers who were infatuated with them: "Do not obey them, and ask them to hamstring the she-camel." So they did. The two men went out, drove the she-camel into a narrow place, and one of them shot her with an arrow, and they killed her. The young camel, which was her offspring, came to the rock from which the she-camel had emerged, cried out three times, and the rock split open and it entered it. It is said that it is the beast that will come out to the people at the end of time, as its explanation will come in Surat al-Naml.

Ibn Ishaq said: The young camel pursued four men from among those who had hamstrung the she-camel: Misda' and his brother Dhu'ab. Misda' shot it with an arrow which pierced its heart (intaZama al-sayd means when one stabs or shoots it until it pierces through), then he dragged it by its leg and joined it to its mother, and they ate it along with her. The first account is more sound, for Salih said to them: "Three days remain of your life," and for this reason it cried out three times. It was also said: its hamstringer was alone with eight men, and they are those about whom Allah said: ﴿And there were in the city nine men﴾, as its explanation will come in Surat al-Naml. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So they called their companion, and he took (the sword) and hamstrung (her)﴾. They were drinking, and water was scarce for mixing their drink, and it was the day of the she-camel's milk. One of them stood up, watched the people and said: "I will surely relieve the people of her," and he hamstrung her.

"When I saw that the pilgrimage's time had come, and the riding beasts of the people were trembling with the people."

(So they became in their abode) that is, their land. It was said: it is singular in the sense of a genus, and the meaning is: in their dwellings. And in another place He said: ﴿in their homes﴾, that is, in their residences.

(Prostrate) that is, clinging to the ground on their knees and faces, as a bird crouches (yajthum al-ta'ir), that is, they became lifeless from the severity of the punishment. The root of al-judum is for the hare and the like, and the place is majthama. Zuhayr said:

"In it are the oxen and the gazelles walking in succession, and their fawns rising from every resting place."

[Note in source: al-'in with a kasra on its first letter: the cattle, singular a'yan and 'ayna'. Al-aram: the gazelles. Al-atla': their young, singular tala. Khilfa: one group after another. It was said: varied, this one coming and this one going, this one ascending and this one descending. (From the commentary on the Mu'allaqat.)]

It was also said: they were burned by a thunderbolt and became dead in the morning, except for one man who was in the sanctuary of Allah; when he went out of the sanctuary, he was struck by what struck his people.

(Then he turned away from them) that is, upon despairing of them.

(And he said: "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love advisers") It is possible that he said this before their death, and it is possible that he said it after their death, like His peace be upon him saying to the slain of Badr: "Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" It was said: "Do you speak to these corpses?" He said: "You are no more hearing than they, but they cannot answer." The first is more apparent. What indicates it is: (but you do not love advisers), that is, you did not accept my counsel.

**First issue:** The Almighty's words: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people﴾. Al-Farra' said: Lut (لُوطٌ) is derived from their saying, "this is *alyat* (أَلْيَطُ) to my heart," meaning "more closely attached." Al-Nahhas said: Al-Zajjaj said: Some grammarians, meaning al-Farra', claimed that Lut may be derived from *lattu* (لُطْتُ), when I smeared it with clay. He said: This is an error, because foreign names are not derived, like Ishaq (إِسْحَاقَ), so one does not say that it is from *suhq* (السُّحْقُ), which means distance. Lut is diptote (غير منصرف) [[From b, j, k, w and z.]] only because of its lightness, being of three letters with a quiescent middle. Al-Naqqash said: Lut is among the foreign names and is not Arabic. As for *lutu al-hawd* (لُطْتُ الْحَوْضَ, I plastered the basin) and *hadha alyat bi-qalbi min hadha* (هَذَا أَلْيَطُ بِقَلْبِي مِنْ هَذَا), these are correct, but the name is foreign, like Ibrahim and Ishaq. Sibawayh said: Nuh and Lut are foreign names, except that they are light, and therefore they are diptote (صُرِفَتْ). Allah sent him to a nation called Sodom, and he was the nephew of Ibrahim. Its accusative case (نَصْبُهُ) is either by the preceding *arsalna* (أَرْسَلْنا, "We sent"), in which case it is coordinated (مَعْطُوفًا), or it may be accusative in the sense of "remember" (وَاذْكُرْ).

**Second issue:** The Almighty's words: ﴿Do you commit the indecency?﴾, meaning the coming to males. Allah named it "indecency" (الْفاحِشَةِ) to show that it is fornication (زِنًى), just as Allah said: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed it is an indecency﴾ [[See vol. 10 p. 253, p. 42 and vol. 9 p. 81.]]. The scholars differed about what is obligatory upon one who does this, after they agreed on its prohibition. Malik said: He is stoned, whether he is married (أَحْصَنَ) or not. Likewise, the one who is penetrated is stoned if he has reached puberty. It is also narrated from him: He is stoned if he is married, and if he is unmarried he is imprisoned and disciplined. This is the view of 'Ata', al-Nakha'i, Ibn al-Musayyib and others. Abu Hanifa said: The married and the unmarried are both disciplined (يُعَزَّرُ), and this is also narrated from Malik. Al-Shafi'i said: He receives the prescribed punishment for fornication (حَدَّ الزِّنَى), by analogy (قِيَاسًا) with it.

Malik argued by the Almighty's words: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾. That was a punishment for them and a recompense for their deed. If it is said: There is no proof in it for two reasons. First, the people of Lut were punished only for disbelief and denial, like the other nations. Second, their young and old were included in it, which shows it is outside the category of the prescribed punishments (الحُدُودِ). It is said: As for the first, it is an error, for Allah, glorified is He, informed about them that they were upon sins, and He seized them for them, and this is among them. As for the second, among them there was a doer and among them there was one who was pleased, so all were punished for the silence of the majority about it. This is the wisdom of Allah and His way with His servants.

The matter of punishment for the doers remains in force, and Allah knows best. Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whomever you find doing the deed of the people of Lut, kill the doer and the one it is done to." This is the wording of Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah. In al-Tirmidhi's version: "whether he is married or not." Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the unmarried man found committing sodomy (اللُّوطِيَّةِ) that he said: He is stoned. It is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he burned a man called al-Fuja'a when he did the deed of the people of Lut, with fire. This was also the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, for when Khalid ibn al-Walid wrote to Abu Bakr about it, Abu Bakr gathered the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and consulted them. 'Ali said: This sin has not been committed by any nation among the nations except one nation, and Allah did to them what you know. I think he should be burned with fire. So the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that he should be burned with fire. Abu Bakr then wrote to Khalid ibn al-Walid to burn him with fire, and he burned him. Then Ibn al-Zubayr burned them in his time. Then Hisham ibn al-Walid burned them. Then Khalid al-Qasri burned them in Iraq. It is also narrated that seven men were seized in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr for sodomy, and he inquired about them and found four who were married, so he ordered that they be taken out (بِهِمْ) of the Haram, and they were stoned with stones until they died, and he flogged the three. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar were with him and did not object to him. Al-Shafi'i went to this view. Ibn al-'Arabi said: What Malik adopted is more deserving, for its chain is sounder and its basis stronger. The Hanafis held on to the argument that they said: The punishment for fornication is known, so since this disobedience is other than it, it is necessary that it not share its prescribed punishment. They cite in this a hadith: "Whoever places a prescribed punishment where there is no prescribed punishment has transgressed and wronged." Also, it is an intercourse in a private part to which neither making lawful (إِحْلَالٌ) nor marital status (إِحْصَانٌ) is attached, nor the obligation of a dower (مَهْرٍ) nor the establishment of lineage, so no prescribed punishment is attached to it.

**Third issue:** If he has intercourse with an animal (بَهِيمَةً), it has been said: Neither he nor the animal is killed. And it has been said: Both are killed, narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman. In this regard there is a hadith narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has intercourse with an animal, kill him and kill the animal with him." We said to Ibn 'Abbas: What about the animal? He said: I do not think he said that, except that he disliked that its meat be eaten when that deed was done with it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: If the hadith is authentic, then acting upon it is obligatory, and if it is not established, then whoever does that much should seek forgiveness from Allah, and if the ruler disciplines him, it is good. And Allah knows best. It has been said: The killing of the animal is so that it does not bring forth a deformed offspring, so killing it is a benefit for this reason, together with what came in the Sunnah. And Allah knows best. Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: There is no prescribed punishment upon the one who committed fornication with an animal. Abu Dawud said: 'Ata' also said likewise. Al-Hakam said: I think he should be lashed and the prescribed punishment should not be reached with him. Al-Hasan said: He is in the position of the fornicator. Al-Zuhri said: He is lashed one hundred times, whether married or not. Malik, al-Thawri, Ahmad and the people of opinion (أَصْحَابُ الرَّأْيِ) said: He is disciplined (يُعَزَّرُ). This is also narrated from 'Ata', al-Nakha'i and al-Hakam. The reports from al-Shafi'i differed, and this is closer to his school on this matter. Jabir ibn Zayd said: The prescribed punishment is established upon him, unless the animal belongs to him.

**Fourth issue:** The Almighty's words: ﴿No one in the worlds preceded you in it﴾. "Min" (مِنْ) is for the comprehensiveness of the category, meaning that sodomy did not occur in any nation before the people of Lut. The atheists (المُلْحِدُونَ) claim that it existed before them, but the truth is what the Qur'an has reported. Al-Naqqash related that Iblis was the origin of their deed, when he invited them to himself, may Allah curse him, so some of them would have intercourse with others. Al-Hasan said: They used to do that with strangers (الغُرَبَاءِ), and some of them did not do it with others. Ibn Majah narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What I fear most for my nation is the deed of the people of Lut." Muhammad ibn Sirin said: Among the animals there is none that does the deed of the people of Lut except the pig and the donkey.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 81:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed you⁠﴾. Nafi' and Hafs read it as a declarative statement with a single kasra-pointed hamzah, as an explanation of the abomination mentioned before it, so it was not appropriate to introduce the interrogative particle before it, since that would separate what follows from what precedes it. The rest of the readers read it with two hamzahs, in the form of the interrogative whose meaning is reproach, and this was fine because what comes before it and what comes after it are each an independent statement. Abu 'Ubayd, al-Nasa'i and others preferred the first reading, and they argued with the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then if you die, will they be the immortal?⁠﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 287.]] where He did not say "afahum" (will they be...). And He said: ﴿Then if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?⁠﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 226.]] where He did not say "anqalabtum" (will you turn...). This is among the gravest of errors, because they have likened two things that are not alike, for the conditional and its answer are like a single thing, like the subject and predicate, so it is not permissible for there to be two interrogatives in them. Thus it is not permissible to say: "Afa-in mitta afahum", just as it is not permissible to say "a-Zaydun a-muntaliq" (is Zayd... is he going?). The story of Lot, peace be upon him, contains two clauses, so you may make an interrogative of each of them separately. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it was preferred by al-Nahhas, Makki and others. "Shahwatan" (lustfully) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: you desire them with desire. It is also permissible for it to be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). ﴿Nay, you are a people who exceed⁠﴾, its parallel being ﴿Nay, you are a people who transgress⁠﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 132.]], in that by your association of this abomination with shirk.

Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 7, verses 82–83:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your town"﴾, meaning Lot and his followers. The meaning of (yatatahharun) is that they refrain from the act of intercourse in this place of sexual intercourse. It is said: "The man purified himself (tatahhara)," meaning he kept himself free from sin. Qatadah said: "By Allah, they found fault with them without any fault."

(Min al-ghabirin) means "among those who remain" in the punishment of Allah, as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. "Ghabara" is used of a thing when it has passed, and also when it has remained; it is one of the words with opposite meanings (ad-dad). Some people said: the one that has passed is written with the letter ʿayn without a dot (ʿabir), and the one that remains is written with the letter ghayn with a dot (ghabir). Ibn Faris related this in al-Mujmal. [[From b, j, z and k.]] Al-Zajjaj said: "min al-ghabirin" means "among those who were left behind from being saved." It was also said: it is because of her long life. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubaydah holds that the meaning is "among those who lived long," that is, she had grown old. Most in the language hold that al-ghabir means the one who remains, as the rajaz poet said:

"So Muhammad did not cease, since Allah forgave him
what has passed and what remains."

Lot set out with his family, as Allah described, "at a portion of the night" [[See vol. 9, p. 84 onward.]] "Then Jibril, peace be upon him, was commanded, so he inserted his wing beneath their cities, uprooted them, and raised them up until the people of the heaven heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs. Then he turned their upper part to their lower part, and stones of sijjil were rained down upon them." It was said: upon those of them who were absent. And [the punishment] overtook Lot's wife, who was with him, and a stone struck her and killed her. It was mentioned that they were four villages. It was also said: five, in which were four hundred thousand [people]. The story of Lot will come in surah Hud with greater clarity than this, God willing. [[See vol. 9, p. 84 onward.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verses 85–87:

In this passage there are four issues.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿And to Madyan﴾. It has been said regarding Madyan that it is the name of a town and region. It has also been said that it is the name of a tribe, as one says "Bakr" and "Tamim." And it has been said that they are descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim the Friend (al-Khalil) (peace be upon him). Whoever holds that Madyan is the name of a man does not diptote it (i.e. does not treat it as having no nunation), because it is a definite non-Arabic (a'jami) proper name. Whoever holds it to be the name of a tribe or a land is even more entitled not to diptote it.

Al-Mahdawi said: It is narrated that he was the son of Lut's daughter. Makki said: He was the husband of Lut's daughter.

There has been disagreement about his lineage. Ata, Ibn Ishaq and others said: Shu'ayb is the son of Mikil ibn Yashjur ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim (peace be upon him). His name in Syriac was Bayrut, and his mother was Mikail, the daughter of Lut. Al-Sharqi ibn al-Qutami claimed that Shu'ayb was the son of Ayfa ibn Yawbab ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim. Ibn Sam'an claimed that Shu'ayb was the son of Jaza ibn Yashjur ibn Lawa ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

"Shu'ayb" is the diminutive of "Sha'b" or "Shi'b" [[In the Sharh al-Qamus: it is the diminutive of sha'b or ash'ab, as they say the diminutive of aswad is suwayd.]]. Qatada said: He is Shu'ayb ibn Yawbab [[In the manuscript 'a': Thawib.]]. It has also been said: Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn Ayfa ibn Thabit ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim [[These names appear confused in the manuscripts of the original and in the sources available to us, and we have not been able to vouch for their vocalisation.]]. And God knows best.

He was blind [[No messenger of God was blind; rather Shu'ayb, the righteous man and companion of Musa, is said to have been blind, and between them there were three hundred years, since the infallibility of the prophets contradicts what repels one in attributes. Corrected.]], and that is why his people said: ﴿And indeed we see you as weak among us﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 84.]]. He was called "the orator of the prophets" for the excellence of his dialogue with his people. His people were a people of disbelief in God and of cheating in measure and weight.

(﴿There has certainly come to you a clear evidence from your Lord﴾): that is, a proof, namely the coming of Shu'ayb with the message. No miracle for him is mentioned in the Qur'an. It has been said that his miracle is what al-Kisa'i mentioned in the Stories of the Prophets.

The second issue concerns God's words: ﴿And do not deprive the people of their things﴾. Al-bakhs means diminution. It occurs in merchandise through defaming it and making it undesirable, or through deceiving about its value, and through the scheming of excess or deficiency in measure. All of this is consuming wealth falsely, and it was forbidden in the earlier nations and the past ones through the tongues of the messengers (may the blessings and peace of God be upon them all) [[from 'a'.]]. ﴿Sufficient for us is God, and excellent is the Disposer of affairs.﴾

The third issue concerns God's words: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾. It is joined to "and do not deprive". It is a term that encompasses both the subtle and the grave forms of corruption. Ibn Abbas said: Before God sent Shu'ayb as a messenger, the earth was one in which sins were practised, what is forbidden was made lawful in it, and blood was shed in it. He said: That is its corruption. When God sent Shu'ayb and he called them to God, the earth was reformed. And every prophet who is sent to his people is their reformation.

The fourth issue concerns God's words: ﴿And do not sit at every path﴾. He forbade them from sitting on the roads and from obstructing the way that leads to obedience to God, and they used to threaten with punishment whoever believed. The scholars differed about the meaning of their sitting on the roads, in three senses. In this passage there are four issues.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿And to Madyan﴾. It has been said regarding Madyan that it is the name of a town and region. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 88–89:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The eminent ones among his people who were arrogant said: "We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will return to our religion."﴾ Its meaning has already been given. The meaning of "or you will return to our religion" is: you will become part of our religion. It has also been said: the followers of Shu'ayb were upon disbelief before they believed in him, so the meaning is: you will return to us as you were before. Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that "return" (al-'awd) carries the sense of beginning, as one says: "a disliked thing returned to me from so-and-so" (ʿād ilayya min fulān makrūh), meaning it became mine, even if no disliked thing had preceded it; that is, it befell me from him. So Shu'ayb said to them: (Even if we were averse?) meaning: even if we were unwilling, you would compel us to it, namely to leave the homeland or to return to your religion; that is, if you do this, you have committed something monstrous.

(﴿We would have fabricated a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah had rescued us from it.﴾) This is a declaration of despair regarding returning to their religion.

(﴿It is not for us to return to it, except that Allah, our Lord, should will it.﴾) Al-Zajjaj said: that is, except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. He said: this is the view of the people of the Sunnah; that is, a return to disbelief will not occur from us unless Allah wills it. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'). It has also been said: the exception here is by way of submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, as He said: ﴿And my success is only through Allah﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 84.]]. The evidence for this is that what follows it is: ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge; in Allah we have put our trust.﴾ It has also been said: it is like your saying, "I will not speak to you until the crow turns white, and until the camel enters the eye of the needle," while the crow never turns white and the camel does not enter (the eye of the needle [[from z.]]).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾, meaning He knows what has been and what will be. "Knowledge" (ʿilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). "It is not for us to return to it" means: to the town after you have disliked our neighbourhood; rather we will leave your town as emigrants to another. "Except that Allah wills" means He returns us to it. There is some remoteness in this, because one says "returned to the town" (ʿāda li-l-qaryah), not "returned in the town" (ʿāda fi l-qaryah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, meaning: we have relied upon Him. It has already been mentioned in several places [[See vol. 4, p. 189.]].

(﴿Our Lord, open between us and our people in truth﴾) Qatadah said: Allah sent him to two communities: the people of Madyan and the companions of al-Aykah [[al-Aykah: the thick, intertwined trees.]]. Ibn 'Abbas said: Shu'ayb was much given to prayer, and when the persistence of his people in their disbelief and error was prolonged, and he despaired of their reform, he invoked against them, saying: ﴿Our Lord, open between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who open (judgement)﴾ [[Al-Farra' said: fataḥa means "judged" in the dialect of the people of Oman. Al-Tabari.]]. So Allah answered his supplication and destroyed them with the earthquake (al-rajfah).

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-A'raf, verses 90–93:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the chiefs who disbelieved among his people said﴾ means they said to those beneath them.

(﴿If you follow Shu'ayb, you will then surely be losers.﴾) means: destroyed.

(﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾) means the quake. It has also been said: the blast (al-sayhah). And the people of al-Aykah were destroyed by the "shadow" (al-zullah) [[Al-zullah: a cloud in which there was fire, which rained down upon them. It has also been said: a scorching wind (samum). See vol. 13, p. 135.]], as will come.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—it was as if they had never dwelt therein﴾. Al-Jurjani said: it has been said that this is a new sentence, meaning: those who denied Shu'ayb became as though they had never ceased to be dead. "Yaghnaw" means to dwell; it is said: "ghaniytu bil-makan" when I resided in the place, and "ghaniya al-qawm fi darihim" meaning their stay in their home was long. Al-maghna is the dwelling, its plural being al-maghani. Labid said:

"And I dwelt six years before the course of Dahis, had the stubborn soul been granted eternity."

And Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We dwelt for a time in poverty and wealth,
as in time there is both hardship and ease."

("We have experienced the vicissitudes of time, gentle and harsh, / and each of them has poured us a cup of its own" ... "Wealth did not increase us in insolence toward a kinsman, / nor did poverty diminish our noble standing.")

(﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—they were the losers﴾) is a new address, and it is an intensification of blame and rebuke, and a repetition to magnify and exalt the matter. When they said, "Whoever follows Shu'ayb is a loser," Allah said: "The losers are those who uttered this saying."

(﴿So how could I grieve over a disbelieving people?﴾) means: how could I sorrow. One says "asaytu 'ala al-shay'i aswa" (asan), and I am "asin."

And the people of al-Aykah were destroyed by the "shadow" (al-zullah) [[Al-zullah: a cloud in which there was fire, which rained down upon them. It has also been said: a scorching wind (samum). See vol. 13, p. 135.]], as will come.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—it was as if they had never dwelt therein﴾. Al-Jurjani said: it has been said that this is a new sentence, meaning: those who denied Shu'ayb became as though they had never ceased to be dead. "Yaghnaw" means to dwell; it is said: "ghaniytu bil-makan" when I resided in the place, and "ghaniya al-qawm fi darihim" meaning their stay in their home was long. Al-maghna is the dwelling, its plural being al-maghani. Labid said:

"And I dwelt six years before the course of Dahis, had the stubborn soul been granted eternity."

And Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We dwelt for a time in poverty and wealth,
as in time there is both hardship and ease."

("We have experienced the vicissitudes of time, gentle and harsh, / and each of them has poured us a cup of its own" ... "Wealth did not increase us in insolence toward a kinsman, / nor did poverty diminish our noble standing.")

(﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—they were the losers﴾) is a new address, and it is an intensification of blame and rebuke, and a repetition to magnify and exalt the matter. When they said, "Whoever follows Shu'ayb is a loser," Allah said: "The losers are those who uttered this saying."

(﴿So how could I grieve over a disbelieving people?﴾) means: how could I sorrow. One says "asaytu 'ala al-shay'i aswa" (asan), and I am "asin."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 94–95:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not send a prophet into any town⁠﻿ without⁠﻿ ...﴾ There is an ellipsis here, which is: "so its people denied him." ... ﴿except that We seized its people⁠﻿ ...﴾

(with adversity and hardship, that they might humble themselves) The discussion of this has already passed [[see vol. 2, p. 243.]].

(Then We replaced the evil with good) That is, We replaced their barrenness with fertility. ﴿Until they multiplied⁠﻿ (ʿafaw)⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿...⁠﻿ ﴾, meaning they increased in number, according to Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Zayd said: their wealth and their children increased. ʿAfa is among the words with opposite meanings (addad): ʿafa means "increased," and ʿafa also means "was effaced/obliterated." Allah the Exalted informed that He seized them with hardship and with ease, yet they did not take heed and did not give thanks. And they said: "Adversity and ease have touched our fathers too, so we are just like them." So We seized them suddenly (baghtatan), that is, unexpectedly, so that it would be a greater cause of regret.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 96:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if the people of the towns⟩ (ahl al-qura). It is said that a city is called qarya (town/village) because people gather in it, from qaraytu al-ma' idha jama'tahu (I gathered the water, when I collected it). This has been discussed fully in "al-Baqara" (ﷺ... ) .

.

(Had believed) means: confirmed (the truth), (saddaqu).

(And feared God) means: (from) shirk (associating partners with God).

(We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth) means: rain and vegetation. This applies to specific peoples whose mention has preceded, since believers may be tested with hardship of living, and this serves as expiation for their sins. Do you not see that He related about Nuh when he said to his people: ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send down the sky upon you in abundance⟩ [[See vol. 18, p. 301.]], and about Hud: ﴿Then repent to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundance⟩ [[See vol. 9, p. 50.]]. So He promised them rain and plenty specifically. This is indicated by ﴿But they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn⟩, meaning they denied the messengers, whereas the believers confirmed and did not deny.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 97–98:

Allah's saying: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾. The interrogative is for denial, and the fa' (fa, the conjunctive particle) is for coordination. Its parallel is: "Do they then seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam)?" [See vol. 6, p. 214.] By "the towns" is meant Makkah and what surrounds it, because they denied Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: it is general, covering all towns.

﴿That Our punishment should come upon them﴾, i.e., Our chastisement.

﴿By night﴾, i.e., at night, ﴿while they are sleeping﴾.

﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment should come upon them﴾. Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr) and Ibn 'Amir read it with the waw (و) of coordination unvocalized (sukun), in the sense of permission, like His saying: "And do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever" [See vol. 19, p. 146]. "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin." The meaning: "Or be secure from these kinds of punishments," i.e., if you feel secure from one kind of them, you will not feel secure from the other.

It is also permissible for the "aw" (أو) to be for one of two things, as in your saying: "I struck Zayd or 'Amr." The rest read it with a fatha on it followed by a hamza after it. They made it the waw of coordination, into which the alif of interrogation entered, its parallel being: "Whenever they make a covenant, do they [then] break it?" [See vol. 2, p. 39.]

The meaning of ﴿in the forenoon while they are playing﴾ is: while they are occupied with what does not benefit them. It is said of everyone who is occupied with what harms him and does not benefit him that he is a player (la'ib). Al-Nahhas mentioned this. In al-Sihah: "Al-la'b (play) is well known, and al-li'b is like it. He has played (la'iba, yal'abu), and tala''aba means playing again and again. A man who is a telabah (تِلْعَابَة) is one who plays much, and al-tella'ab (التَّلْعَاب), with a fatha, is the verbal noun. And a woman who is la'ub (جارية لعوب) is one who is playful."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does it not become clear to those who inherit the earth﴾ — meaning: does it not make clear (yubayyin).

(to those who inherit the earth) — he means the disbelievers of Makkah and those around them.

(We would have afflicted them) — i.e., We would have seized them (bi-dhunubihim), i.e., for their disbelief and their denial.

(and We seal) — i.e., and We are sealing; so it is a new, independent clause. It was also said: it is coordinated with "We would have afflicted," meaning "We would have afflicted them and [We would] seal," so the past tense has been placed in the position of the future.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the cities﴾, i.e., these cities which We destroyed, and they are the cities of Noah, ʿAd, [[In another manuscript: Noah, ʿAd, Lot and Shuʿayb.]] Lot, Hud and Shuʿayb, previously mentioned.

(We relate) i.e., We recite.

(to you some of their news) i.e., some of their reports. This is a consolation to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the Muslims.

(So they were not to believe) i.e., those disbelievers would not have believed after their destruction even if We had brought them back to life; this is the view of Mujahid. Its parallel is: ﴿And if they were returned, they would revert﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 410.]]. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Rabi said: it was in God's knowledge, on the day He took the covenant from them, that they would not believe in the messengers.

(by that which they had denied before) meaning the day of the covenant, when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam, and they believed unwillingly, not willingly. al-Suddi said: they believed on the day the covenant was taken from them, unwillingly, so they would not truly believe now. It was also said: they asked for miracles, and when they saw them they did not believe in what they had denied before seeing the miracle. Its parallel is: ﴿as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [[See p. 65 of this part.]].

(Thus does God seal the hearts of the disbelievers) i.e., like His sealing of the hearts of these mentioned people, thus God seals the hearts of the disbelievers in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 102:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We found not in most of them any covenant﴾. "Min" (min, here meaning "any" or "a") is redundant (za'idah), and it indicates the sense of genus (jins); were it not for "min", it could be imagined that it refers to a single covenant in meaning. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the covenant taken from them at the time of the dhurr (the primordial seed-state of humanity), and whoever breaks the covenant, it is said to him: "He has no covenant," meaning as if it had never been made with him. Al-Hasan said: the covenant that was enjoined upon them through the prophets, that they should worship Him and not associate anything with Him. It was also said: he intended that the disbelievers are divided, so most of them are those who have no trustworthiness and no fidelity, and among them are those who have trustworthiness along with their disbelief, though they are few. This was narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then after them We sent Musa﴾, i.e., after Nuh, Hud [[So in (ʿ) and in this text. In the rest of the manuscripts: Thamud.]], Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb.

(Musa) i.e., Musa ibn ʿImran. (with Our signs) i.e., with Our miracles.

(but they wronged them) i.e., they disbelieved and did not affirm the signs. And ẓulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. His saying, exalted is He: (so see how was the end of the corrupters) i.e., the final outcome of their affair.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 7, verses 104–112:

﻿[[Reading of Nafi'.]] *Ḥaqīq ʿalā* means *wājib* (obligatory). Whoever reads *ʿalā an lā* (ʿalā ʾallā), the meaning is *ḥarīṣ ʿalā an lā aqūla* (eager that I not say). In the reading of ʿAbd Allah, it is *ḥaqīq an lā aqūla*, with *ʿalā* omitted. It has also been said that *ʿalā* here carries the meaning of *bāʾ* (bi), so that the sense is *ḥaqīq bi-an lā aqūla* (worthy of not saying). The same applies in the reading of Ubayy and al-Aʿmash, *bi-an lā aqūla*, just as you say *ramaytu bi-l-qaws* and *ʿalā al-qaws* (I shot with the bow). Accordingly, *ḥaqīq* in this case means *maḥqūq* (one who is entitled to something). The meaning of *fa-arsil maʿiya Banī Isrāʾīl* is: release them. He had been putting them to hard labour.

﴿So he threw down his staff﴾: the word is used of both physical bodies and abstract meanings, and it has already been discussed earlier. *Al-thuʿbān* is the male of the large snake, the greatest of serpents.

*(Mubīn)*: that is, a serpent with no ambiguity about it.

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾: that is, he brought it out and displayed it. It has been said that it was from his bosom or from his armpit, as in the revelation: ﴿Put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without harm﴾, that is, without leprosy. Moses was dark, very dark-complexioned, then he returned his hand to his bosom and it went back to its original colour. Ibn ʿAbbas said: his hand had a bright light that illuminated what was between the heaven and the earth. It has also been said: his hand would emerge white like snow, shining, and when he drew it back it returned to the likeness of the rest of his body. The meaning of *ʿalīm* (knowing) is: knowing of magic.

*(Min arḍikum)*: that is, from your kingdom, O assembly of the Copts, by his giving precedence to the Children of Israel over you.

﴿So what do you advise?﴾: that is, Pharaoh said: "So what do you advise?" It has also been said that this is from the words of the chiefs, meaning they said to Pharaoh alone: "So what do you advise?", as tyrants and leaders are addressed with: "What do you think about such-and-such?" It is also permissible that they said it to him and to his companions. *Mā* is in the nominative position, with *dhā* in the sense of *alladhī* (which). It is in the accusative position, with *mā* and *dhā* being one word.

﴿They said: Put him off﴾: the people of Medina, ʿAsim and al-Kisāʾī read it without Ḥamzah, except that Warsh and al-Kisāʾī prolonged the vowel of the *hāʾ* (kasra). Abū ʿAmr read it with a sukūn *hamza* and a damma on the *hāʾ*. Both are dialects: it is said *arjaʾtuhu* and *arjaytuhu*, meaning I delayed him. Likewise Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muḥaysin and Hisham read it, except that they prolonged the damma of the *hāʾ*. The rest of the people of Kufa read *arjih* with a sukūn on the *hāʾ*. Al-Farrāʾ said: this is a dialect of the Arabs, who pause on the pronominal *hāʾ* in connected speech when the letter before it is vocalised, as in *hādhihi Ṭalḥah qad aqbalat*. The Basrans rejected this. Qatadah said: the meaning of *arjih* is "detain him." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "delay him." It has also been said that *arjih* is derived from *rajā yarjū* (to hope), meaning: give him hope and leave him hoping. This was related by al-Nahhas from Muḥammad ibn Yazid. The kasra of the *hāʾ* is by assimilation (*ittibāʿ*, vowel harmony). Its damma is permissible on the original form. Its sukūn is a grammatical error (*laḥn*) which is not permissible except in an anomaly (*shudhudh*) of poetry. [[Thus in the originals and in Iʿrab al-Quran of al-Nahhas. It should be noted that this is the reading of the people of Kufa.]]

﴿And his brother﴾: a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) on the *hāʾ*.

﴿Gathering﴾: in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*).

﴿They will bring you﴾: in the jussive, because it is the answer to the imperative (*jawāb al-amr*), and for this reason the *nūn* has been dropped from it. The people of Kufa, except ʿAsim, read *bi-kulli saḥḥār* (every skilled sorcerer), and the rest of the people read *sāḥir*. The two are close in meaning, except that the forms of intensive emphasis (*af ʿāl ashaddu mubālaghah*) are stronger.

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah, it is *ḥaqīq an lā aqūla*, with *ʿalā* omitted. It has also been said that *ʿalā* here carries the meaning of *bāʾ* (bi), so that the sense is *ḥaqīq bi-an lā aqūla* (worthy of not saying). The same applies in the reading of Ubayy and al-Aʿmash, *bi-an lā aqūla*, just as you say *ramaytu bi-l-qaws* and *ʿalā al-qaws* (I shot with the bow). Accordingly, *ḥaqīq* in this case means *maḥqūq* (one who is entitled to something). The meaning of *fa-arsil maʿiya Banī Isrāʾīl* is: release them. He had been putting them to hard labour.

﴿So he threw down his staff﴾: the word is used of both physical bodies and abstract meanings, and it has already been discussed earlier. *Al-thuʿbān* is the male of the large snake, the greatest of serpents.

*(Mubīn)*: that is, a serpent with no ambiguity about it.

Moses was dark, very dark-complexioned, then he returned his hand to his bosom and it went back to its original colour. Ibn ʿAbbas said: his hand had a bright light that illuminated what was between the heaven and the earth. It has also been said: his hand would emerge white like snow, shining, and when he drew it back it returned to the likeness of the rest of his body. The meaning of *ʿalīm* (knowing) is: knowing of magic.

*(Min arḍikum)*: that is, from your kingdom, O assembly of the Copts, by his giving precedence to the Children of Israel over you.

﴿So what do you advise?﴾: that is, Pharaoh said: "So what do you advise?" It has also been said that this is from the words of the chiefs, meaning they said to Pharaoh alone: "So what do you advise?", as tyrants and leaders are addressed with: "What do you think about such-and-such?" The Exalted said: ﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾. The sending (of messengers) is omitted because the listener already knows it.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam said: They were twelve chieftains (naqib), with each chieftain having twenty overseers (ʿarif), and under the hand of each overseer there were a thousand sorcerers. Their leader was Shamʿun, according to the view of Muqatil ibn Sulayman. Ibn Jurayj said: They were nine hundred, from al-ʿArish, al-Fayyum and al-Iskandariyya, in equal thirds. Ibn Ishaq said: They were fifteen thousand sorcerers, and this is narrated from Wahb. It was also said: They were twelve thousand. Ibn al-Munkadir said: Eighty thousand. It was said: Fourteen thousand. It was said: They were three hundred thousand sorcerers from the countryside, three hundred thousand sorcerers from Upper Egypt, and three hundred thousand sorcerers from al-Fayyum and its surroundings. It was said: They were seventy men. It was said: Seventy-three. And God knows best.

It is narrated that they had with them ropes and staffs carried by three hundred camels. Then the serpent swallowed all of that. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi said: When it opened its mouth, its jaw became eighty cubits wide, its lower jaw placed on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. It was also said: The width of its mouth was forty cubits, and God knows best. It made for Pharaoh to swallow him, so he leapt from his throne and fled from it and cried out for help to Musa. So Musa seized it, and behold, it was a staff as it had been. Wahb said: Twenty-five thousand died from fear of the staff.

﴿They said to Pharaoh: Surely for us there will be a reward﴾. That is, a prize and wealth. They did not say "fa-qalu" with the fa', because he meant "when they came, they said." The reading "inna lana" (as a declarative statement) is also recited; it is the reading of Nafi' and Ibn Kathir. They obligated Pharaoh to grant them wealth if they prevailed. Pharaoh said to them: ﴿Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near﴾, that is, among those of exalted rank in our presence, so he added to what they had asked for. It was also said: They were only stating this for themselves as a ruling, that if they prevailed, the reward would be due to them, meaning they said: "The reward is owed to us if we prevail." The rest of the readers recited with the interrogative (a'inna), in the manner of inquiry. They asked Pharaoh whether he would grant them a reward if they prevailed or not, so they did not affirm for Pharaoh that this would happen; they only asked him whether he would do it. He said to them, "Yes," meaning you shall have the reward and nearness if you prevail.

The Companions of Moses (peace be upon him) showed him proper manners, and that was the reason for their faith. According to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', "an" (أَنْ) is in the accusative position, meaning "either you throw (الإلقاء)." A similar usage is the poet's saying:

They said, "Riding," and we said, "That is our custom" [[This is the first half of a verse whose completion is: "or dismounting, for we are a group that dismounts." In manuscript B: "fa-qultu tilka" (I said, "That is...").]]

"Throw," He said. Al-Farra' said: there is an omission in the speech. The meaning is: Moses said to them, "You will never overcome your Lord, and you will never nullify His signs." This is one of the miracles (mu'jiz) of the Qur'an, which no one can match in human speech, and which people are unable to produce. A brief expression gathers many meanings. It was also said that this is a threat, meaning: "Go ahead and throw, and you will see the disgrace that will befall you," since it is not permissible for Moses to command them to practise magic. And it was said: he commanded them to do so in order to make their lies and deception manifest.

"When they threw," that is, the ropes and the staffs, "they bewitched the eyes of the people," that is, they made them imagine things and turned their perception away from its correct understanding, through deception that resembles sorcery and sleight of hand, as its explanation has already been given in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 43.]]. The meaning of "a great (magic)" is great in their estimation, because it was abundant, though it was not truly great. Ibn Zayd said: the gathering was at Alexandria, and the tail of the snake reached beyond the lake. Others said: it opened its mouth and began to devour (تلقف, i.e., swallow up) what they had thrown of their ropes and staffs. It was also said: what they threw were ropes made of leather with mercury in them, so they moved, and they said, "These are snakes."

Hafs read "talqafu" with a sukun on the lam and light pronunciation, taking it as the imperfect of laqifa, yaqlafu. Al-Nahhas said: according to this reading, "tilqafu" is also permissible, since it derives from laqifa. The rest read it with shaddah and a fatha on the lam, taking it as the imperfect of talaqqafa, so it is "tatalaqqafu." It is said: laqiftu al-shay' and talaqqaftuhu when I took it or swallowed it. Talaqqafa, talaqqama and talhama have the same meaning. Abu Hatim said: I have been informed that in some readings it is "talaqqama" with a mim and shaddah. The poet said:

You are the staff of Moses, which has never ceased
Devouring what the sorcerer fabricates.

It is also reported as "talaqqafu."

"What they fabricate," that is, what they lie about, because they came with ropes and put mercury in them until they moved.

Qur'anic commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, verses 123–126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Pharaoh said, "You believed in Him before I gave you permission?"﴾ It is a denial from him against them.

(Indeed, this is a scheme you have devised in the city, to expel its people from it.) That is, there was a prior agreement between you and him in this, so that you might seize control of Egypt. That is, this happened from you in the city of Egypt before you came out into this desert. (But you will come to know.) A threat to them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Pharaoh was the first to crucify, and to cut off hands and feet on opposite sides, the right foot and the left hand, and the right hand and the left foot. This is from al-Hasan.

(And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord.) Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the qaf (taqmu). Al-Akhfash said: It is a dialect; it is said: naqimtu al-amr and naqamtuhu, meaning I disliked it. That is, you resent nothing from us except that we believed in Allah, and He is the Truth.

(When they came to us.) That is, His signs and clear proofs.

(Our Lord, pour upon us patience.) Al-ifraagh means pouring out. That is, pour it upon us at the time of cutting off and crucifixion.

(And cause us to die as Muslims.) It is said: Pharaoh seized the magicians and cut them off on the bank of the river, and that he (i.e., one of them) believed in Musa when six hundred thousand believed.
