(And cause us to die as Muslims.) It is said: Pharaoh seized the magicians and cut them off on the bank of the river, and that he (i.e., one of them) believed in Musa when six hundred thousand believed.

Qur'anic commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, verses 123–126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Pharaoh said, "You believed in Him before I gave you permission?"﴾ It is a denial from him against them.

(Indeed, this is a scheme you have devised in the city, to expel its people from it.) That is, there was a prior agreement between you and him in this, so that you might seize control of Egypt. That is, this happened from you in the city of Egypt before you came out into this desert. (But you will come to know.) A threat to them.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Pharaoh was the first to crucify, and to cut off hands and feet on opposite sides, the right foot and the left hand, and the right hand and the left foot. This is from al-Hasan.

(And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord.) Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the qaf (taqmu). Al-Akhfash said: It is a dialect; it is said: naqimtu al-amr and naqamtuhu, meaning I disliked it. That is, you resent nothing from us except that we believed in Allah, and He is the Truth.

(When they came to us.) That is, His signs and clear proofs.

(Our Lord, pour upon us patience.) Al-ifraagh means pouring out. That is, pour it upon us at the time of cutting off and crucifixion.

(And cause us to die as Muslims.) It is said: Pharaoh seized the magicians and cut them off on the bank of the river, and that he (i.e., one of them) believed in Musa when six hundred thousand believed.

**"And the chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, 'Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land?'"** That is, by causing division and scattering their unity.

**(Will he leave you)** ﴿وَيَذَرَكَ﴾ is read with a fatha on the *ra'* as the answer to the interrogative. The *waw* stands in place of the *fa'* (i.e., it is a *waw* in the sense of *fa'*).

**(And your gods)** ﴿وَآلِهَتَكَ﴾. Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh used to worship idols, so he would worship and be worshipped. Sulayman al-Taymi said: It has reached me that Pharaoh used to worship a cow. Al-Taymi said: I said to al-Hasan, "Did Pharaoh worship anything?" He said, "Yes. He used to worship something that he had hung around his neck." It has also been said that the meaning of "your gods" is "your obedience," just as it is said regarding the verse, ﴿اتَّخَذُوا أَحْبَارَهُمْ وَرُهْبَانَهُمْ أَرْبَابًا مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 199.]] ("They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God"), where it is said: "They did not worship them, but they obeyed them," and so it becomes a figurative expression (*tamthil*).

Nu'aym ibn Maysara read ﴿وَيَذَرُكَ﴾ with a *raf'* (*damma*) on the *ra'*, on the basis of the estimate "and he will leave you." Al-Ash'hab al-'Uqayli read ﴿وَيَذَرْكَ﴾ with a *jazm* (*sukun*), lightened from *yadharuka*, because of the heaviness of the *damma*. Anas ibn Malik read ﴿وَنَذَرُكَ﴾ with a *raf'* and with *nun*. In this reading they reported about themselves that they would abandon worshipping him if Moses were left alive.

Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak read ﴿وَإِلَاهَتَكَ﴾, meaning "and your worship." According to this reading, he used to worship but was not worshipped; that is, he would abandon his worship of you (i.e., they would abandon worship of you).

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: According to the school of those who hold this reading, when Pharaoh said, ﴿أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَى﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 198.]] ("I am your most high lord") and ﴿مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُمْ مِنْ إِلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 288.]] ("I know of no god for you other than myself"), he denied that there was any lord or gods other than himself. So it was said to him, "And [he will leave] you and your *ilaha*," meaning "and he will abandon you and the worship of people for you."

The common reading is ﴿وَآلِهَتَكَ﴾ as mentioned above. It is based on the view that Pharaoh claimed lordship in outward appearance, while he knew that he was himself a created, lordled being. The evidence for this is his statement at the moment of the drowning, ﴿آمَنْتُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا الَّذِي آمَنَتْ بِهِ بَنُو إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 337.]] ("I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe"), but this statement was not accepted from him when he uttered it after the door of repentance had been closed.

Before this state, he had a god that he worshipped secretly, apart from the Lord of the worlds, the Mighty and Majestic. Al-Hasan and others said this.

In the variant recitation (*harf*) of Ubayy it reads: ﴿أَتَذَرُ مُوسَى وَقَوْمَهُ لِيُفْسِدُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَقَدْ تَرَكُوكَ أَنْ يَعْبُدُوكَ﴾ ("Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land, when they have left you [so that they would] worship you?").

It has also been said regarding ﴿وَإِلَاهَتَكَ﴾: it is said that he worshipped a cow, and whenever he found a cow pleasing, he commanded that it be worshipped and said, "I am your lord and the lord of this." For this reason, [the verse about the Samiri] says: ﴿فَأَخْرَجَ لَهُمْ عِجْلًا جَسَدًا﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 232. Note that the verse is about the Samiri.]] ("So he brought forth for them a calf, a body"). This was mentioned by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

Al-Zajjaj said: He had small idols that his people worshipped in order to draw near to him, so they were attributed to him. For this reason he said, "I am your most high lord."

Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: Pharaoh's statement, "I am your most high lord," indicates that they worshipped something other than him.

It has been said that, according to the reading of Ibn Abbas, the intended meaning of *ilaha* is the cow that he used to worship. It has also been said that they meant by it the sun, which they used to worship. The poet said:

*"And we hastened the goddess that she should return [to us]"*

Then he reassured his people and said, **(We will kill their sons)** ﴿سَنَقْتُلُ أَبْنَاءَهُمْ﴾ with *takhfif* (lightened pronunciation), the reading of Nafi' and Ibn Kathir. The rest read it with *tashdid* (doubled), for intensification (*takthir*).

**(And spare their women)** ﴿وَنَسْتَحْيِي نِسَاءَهُمْ﴾, meaning: do not fear them.

**(Indeed, we are above them, dominant)** ﴿وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَاهِرُونَ﴾. He reassured them with these words. He did not say "We will kill Moses," because he knew that he had no power over him. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: Pharaoh was filled with terror of Moses, so whenever he saw him he would urinate like a donkey urinates.

When this reached the people of Moses from Pharaoh, Moses said to them, **(Seek help in God and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He gives it as inheritance to whom He wills)** ﴿اسْتَعِينُوا بِاللَّهِ وَاصْبِرُوا إِنَّ الْأَرْضَ لِلَّهِ يُورِثُهَا مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾. He gave them hope that God would make them inherit the land of Egypt.

**(And the final outcome is for the righteous)** ﴿وَالْعَاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾, meaning: Paradise is for whoever fears God. The "outcome" (*'aqibah*) of anything is its end. However, when it is used without qualification, as in "the outcome is for so-and-so," it is understood in common usage to mean good.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 129:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "We were harmed before you came to us"﴾, that is, at the beginning of your birth, through the killing of the sons and the enslaving of the women.

(And after you came to us) that is, "and now this is repeated against us," meaning the threat that came from Pharaoh. It was also said: the harm from before was their being made to labour for Banu Isra'il in their work until midday, and then being sent away for the rest of the day to earn for themselves. The harm from after was their being made to labour the whole day without food or drink; this was said by Juwaybir. Al-Hasan said: the harm from before and the harm from after were one and the same, namely the taking of the jizya.

(He said: "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land") "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from God is binding; He renewed [in manuscripts B, J, Z and K: "ḥaddada", with a non-dotted letter] the promise for them and made it certain. They were indeed made successors in Egypt in the time of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, and they conquered Bayt al-Maqdis with Yusha' ibn Nun, as has been mentioned earlier. It is narrated that they said this when Musa brought them out and Pharaoh pursued them, so he was behind them and the sea was before them; then God fulfilled the threat by drowning Pharaoh and his people and saving them.

(Then He will see how you act) Its parallels have been mentioned before. That is, He sees the action that merits the recompense, because God does not repay them for what He knows of them, but rather He repays them for what actually occurs from them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 130:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought﴾, meaning barrenness (jadub). This is well known in the language; it is said: "a year (sanah) befell them," meaning drought (jadb). Its implied meaning is "a year of drought." And in the hadith: (O God, make them upon them years like the years of Joseph). Among the Arabs there are those who inflect the nun in al-sinin (i'rab, the grammatical case endings), and al-Farra' recited:

"I see the passing of years has taken from me
as the sirar [[al-sirar and al-srar (with fatha or kasra on the sin in both): the night in which the moon hides at the end of the month.]] takes from the crescent"

Al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh also recited this line with a fatha on the nun, but he recited in this place something that is not permissible other than it, namely his saying:

"And I have passed the head of the forties"

Al-Farra' related from Banu 'Amir that they say: "I stayed with him years, O man," with tanwin (the nunation, unlike the form with no tanwin). He said: Banu Tamim do not apply tanwin and say: "Years passed for him, O man." Sinin is the plural of sanah, and sanah here means drought, not a year (hawl). From it comes "asnata al-qawm," meaning the people suffered drought. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara said:

"'Amr al-'Ula crumbled the bread for his people,
while the men of Makkah were drought-stricken, lean"

﴿Perhaps they may take heed﴾: that is, that they may be admonished and their hearts may be softened.

There are two issues here. The first concerns His words, ﴿When good came to them﴾, meaning fertility and abundance.

(They said, "This is ours") meaning, "We were given it by right."

(But if evil befalls them) meaning drought and sickness. This is the second issue. (They attribute it to Moses) meaning they regard him as a bad omen (yatatayyaru, from tiyarah, "taking omens"). A parallel is His words: ﴿But if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you."﴾ [See vol. 5, p. 282.]

The original form is yataṭayyaru, in which the tā' is assimilated into the ṭā'. Ṭalḥah read tatayyarū as a past-tense verb. The root meaning of tiyarah is drawn from the flight of birds and from driving them away. Its use later became so widespread that anyone who took a bad omen was said to have tatayyara.

The Arabs used to take a favourable omen from the sānih, a bird or animal passing from right to left, and a bad omen from the bāriḥ, one passing from left to right. They also took omens from the cry of the crow, which they interpreted as foretelling separation. They drew conclusions from the calls of birds answering one another, and from their cries at times other than their usual ones. The same applied to gazelles that passed by as sānih or bāriḥ. When a gazelle passed on the bāriḥ side they would say, "Who will give me the sānih after the bāriḥ?" This is a proverb used of a man who mistreats another, and to whom it is said, "He will surely do you good." Its origin is that a man saw gazelles passing on his left, and was told, "They will surely pass on your right for you," and he replied, "Who will give me...", and so on.

However, the strongest of their omens occurred with birds in general, so they applied the term tiyarah to all birds on this basis. The non-Arabs (al-a'ājim) also took omens: they regarded it as a bad sign to see a child being taken to school in the morning, and a good sign to see a child returning from the teacher to his home. They regarded it as a bad sign to see a water-carrier with a full, tied waterskin on his back, and a good sign to see one with an empty waterskin open (his waterskin [in one manuscript: "qirbatuhu"]). They regarded as bad omens a porter loaded with his burden and a beast of burden afflicted with a wiqrah (a fracture in the leg), and as good omens a porter who had set down his load and a beast whose burden had been lifted from it.

Then Islam came with the prohibition of tatayyur and tashā'um (taking bad omens) from whatever bird's voice is heard, whatever it may be and in whatever circumstances. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave the birds in their nests" (muknātihā). Muknāt means their eggs (the word is also vocalised with a fatḥah). Its original meaning is the eggs of locusts. It was also said to mean "their places and dwellings." Shamir said: "The correct reading in his words 'in their muknāt' is that it is the plural of al-maknah and al-malkah, meaning 'settled place'." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also related as makanāt, the plural of makan and makin, the plural of makān (place)."

The reason for this is that many people of the Jāhiliyyah (pre-Islamic period), when they wanted to undertake a matter, would go to a bird in its nest and startle it. If it flew to the right, he would proceed with his need. This was the sānih in their eyes. If it flew to the left, he would turn back. This was the bāriḥ in their eyes. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade this by saying: "Leave the birds in their nests." This is how it appears in the hadith. The grammarians, however, say wukunātihā (with a wāw). Imru' al-Qays said:

"And I set out early while the birds are in their wukunāt."

The wukunah is the name for every nest and hollow. The wakn is the place where a bird lays its eggs and hatches its young, which is a crevice in walls or trees. It is said: "The bird wakana yakinnu wukūnan when they sit on their eggs."

Some Arabs did not regard tatayyur as anything, and they praised anyone who denied it. Al-Muraqqish said:

"I went out in the morning, while I was not going out for the sake of the owl (wāq) or the black crow (ḥātim)*.
So the inauspicious were like the auspicious, and the auspicious like the inauspicious."

* The wāq, with a kasrah on the qāf, is the ṣurad, a large-headed bird, half white and half black, found in trees. The ḥātim is the black crow.

'Ikrimah said: "I was with Ibn 'Abbas when a bird passed, crying out. A man among the people said, 'Good, good!' Ibn 'Abbas said, 'This has neither good nor evil in it.'"

Our scholars said: The sounds of birds have no connection with anything that could be taken as an indication of it, and birds have no knowledge of an event, let alone of a future one, so as to inform anyone about it. No one among people knows the speech of birds, except what Allah the Exalted gave to Sulayman (peace be upon him) of that. Thus tiyarah falls within the category of falsehood. And Allah knows best.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He is not one of us who feigns dreams (tahallum, i.e. claims falsely to have seen a dream), or practises divination (takahhun), or is turned back from his journey by tiyarah." Abu Dawud related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Tiyarah is shirk" (three times). "And there is none among us but [that he has something of it], but Allah removes it through reliance (tawakkul)." [In Abu Dawud's Musnad and some copies of the original: Ibn al-Athir said: "This is how it appears in the hadith, cut short, without the exception stated. That is, except that one may be affected by tiyarah, and aversion may come to his heart. The omission is an abridgement, relying on the listener's understanding... His words 'but Allah removes it through tawakkul' mean that if the thought of tiyarah occurs to him, and he relies on Allah and submits to Him, and does not act on that thought, Allah forgives him and does not hold him to account for it." In another copy: "...and none of us but has taken omens..."]

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever is turned back from his need by tiyarah has committed shirk." It was asked: "What is the expiation of that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "That one of them says: 'O Allah, there is no omen except Your omen, no good except Your good, and there is no god other than You,' and then he proceeds with his need."

In another report: "When one of you experiences that, let him say: 'O Allah, none brings good things except You, none takes away evil things except You, there is no power and no strength except through You.' Then let him go forward, relying upon Allah, for Allah will suffice him for what he finds within himself of that, and Allah the Exalted will suffice him for what concerns him."

The distinction between fa'l (good omen) and tiyarah has already been discussed in Surat al-Ma'idah [see vol. 6, p. 59].

(Indeed, their omen is with Allah) Al-Hasan read ṭayruhum, the plural of ṭā'ir, meaning what has been decreed for them and upon them.

(But most of them do not know) that what befell them of drought and hardships was only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of their sins, and not from Moses and his people.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 132:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever sign you bring us to enchant us with, we will not be believers in you﴾. That is, the people of Pharaoh said to Musa, "Mahma" (whatever). Al-Khalil said: the original form is "ma, ma," the first being a conditional particle and the second being an extra particle of emphasis for the conditional, as it is added to other particles, such as "imma" (either), "haythuma" (wherever), "aynama" (wherever) and "kayfama" (however). They disliked two particles that were identical in pronunciation, so they replaced the first alif with a ha' and said "mahma." Al-Kisa'i said: its original form is "mah," meaning "desist," followed by "ma ta'tina bihi min ayah" (whatever sign you bring us with). It was also said: it is a single independent word, used as a conditional particle, so that what follows it is put in the jussive mood as if it were "in" (if). The answer is ﴿So we will not be believers in you﴾, and (liliastahrana) means "to turn us away from what we are upon." The explanation of this word has already been given in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 200]. It was said: after the sorcerers cast down their staffs, Musa remained among the Copts, prostrating, for twenty years, showing them the signs, until God drowned Pharaoh, and this was their saying.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 133:

There are five issues (masa'il) in this.

The first: Isra'il narrated from Simak, from Nawf al-Shami, who said: Musa (ﷺ) remained among the family of Pharaoh after he overcame the magicians for forty years. Muhammad ibn Uthman ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Minjab: twenty years. He showed them the signs: the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿al-tufan﴾ (the flood), meaning the heavy rain, until they swam in it. Mujahid and 'Ata' said: al-tufan is death. Al-Akhfash said: its singular is tufana. It was also said: it is a verbal noun (masdar), like al-rujhan and al-nuqsan, so no singular is sought for it. Al-Nahhas said: in the language, al-tufan is whatever is destructive, whether death or a torrent, that is, what surrounds them and destroys them. Al-Suddi said: the Children of Israel were not touched by a drop of water, but it entered the houses of the Copts until they stood in the water up to their collarbones [[al-tarakki: the plural of al-taraqwa, a bone that joins the notch of the throat to the shoulder on each side.]], and it lasted over them for seven days. It was also said: forty days. They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to remove it from us, and we will believe in you." So he called upon his Lord, and He lifted the flood from them, but they did not believe. Then Allah made grow for them, that year, vegetation and crops that had not grown before. They said: "That water was a blessing." So Allah sent the locusts upon them, and the locust is the well-known creature, the plural of jarada, both masculine and feminine. If you want to distinguish the gender, you describe it: "I saw a male locust (jarada dhakar)." It ate their crops and fruits, to the point that it would eat the roofs and the doors, until their dwellings collapsed. It did not enter the houses of the Children of Israel at all.

The third: The scholars differed regarding killing the locust when it lands on a land and causes corruption. It was said: it is not to be killed. All the jurists (ahl al-fiqh) said: it is to be killed. Those of the first view argued that it is a great creature of Allah's creation that eats from Allah's provision and the pen (of accountability) does not apply to it, and by what has been narrated: "Do not kill the locust, for it is the greatest army of Allah." The majority argued that leaving them causes the destruction of property, and the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted fighting a Muslim who intends to take property; so when the locust intends to destroy property, it is more fitting that killing it be permitted. Do you not see that they agreed that it is permissible to kill the snake and the scorpion, because they harm people? Likewise the locust. Ibn Majah narrated from Jabir and Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he invoked against the locusts, said: "O Allah, destroy its large ones, kill its small ones, spoil its eggs, cut off its offspring, and seize it by its mouths away from our livelihoods and our provisions, for You are the Hearer of supplication." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, how do you invoke against an army of the armies of Allah by cutting off its offspring?" He said: "Indeed the locust is the sneeze [[al-nathra: like a sneeze.]] of the fish in the sea."

The fourth: It is established in Sahih Muslim, from Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "We fought seven battles with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and we used to eat the locust with him." The scholars did not differ over its being eaten in general, and that if it is taken alive and its head is cut off, it is lawful by agreement, and that this takes the place of slaughter (dhaka) for it. They differed only over whether it requires a cause by which it dies when hunted or not. The majority held that it does not require that, and it is eaten however it dies; its ruling for them is the ruling of fish. This was the view of Ibn Nafi' and Mutarrif. Malik held that it must die by a cause, such as cutting off its heads, its legs, or its wings, and if it dies from that, or it is scalded or thrown into fire, because according to him it is one of the land animals, so its carrion is forbidden. Al-Layth disliked eating dead locusts, except those taken alive and then died, for taking it is its slaughter. This was also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two carrions are made lawful for us, the fish and the locust, and two bloods, the liver and the spleen." Ibn Majah said: Ahmad ibn Mani' narrated to us, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated to us, from Abu Sa'id, who heard Anas ibn Malik say: "The wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) used to give each other locusts on trays." Ibn al-Mundhir also mentioned it.

The fifth: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, created a thousand nations: six hundred of them in the sea and four hundred on the land. The first of these nations to perish will be the locust. When the locust perishes, the nations follow one after another like the string of a necklace when it breaks." Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned it in Nawadir al-Usul and said: The locust became the first of these nations to perish only because it was created from the clay that was left over from the clay of Adam. And nations perish only when the children of Adam perish, because they are subjected to them.

Returning to the story of the Copts: they pledged to Musa that they would believe if the locusts were removed from them. He called upon Allah, and it was removed. But some of their crops remained, so they said: "What remains is enough for us," and they did not believe. So Allah sent upon them the lice, which are the young of the locust swarm (al-daba), as Qatada said. Al-daba is the locust before it flies; its singular is dabaa. A land is madbiyya when the locusts have eaten its vegetation. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-qummal is the weevil that is in the wheat. Ibn Zayd said: the fleas. Al-Hasan said: small black creatures. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-hamnan, which is a kind of tick, its singular is hamnana. So they consumed their animals and crops, and clung to their skins as if they were smallpox upon them, and prevented them from sleep and rest. Habib ibn Abi [[From b, j, and k, and al-Tahdhib.]] Thabit said: al-qummal are the ja'lan [[al-ja'lan (with a kasra on the jim, plural of ja'l, like surad): a black creature of the earth's creatures.]]. In the view of the lexicographers, al-qummal is a kind of tick (qiradan). Abu al-Hasan al-A'rabi al-'Adawi said: al-qummal are small creatures of the kind of ticks, except that they are smaller than them, and its singular is qamla. Al-Nahhas said: this does not contradict what the exegetes said, because it is possible that all these things were sent upon them, since they all share in harming them. Some exegetes mentioned that at 'Ayn Shams [[the capital of Egypt at that time.]] there was a heap of sand, and Musa struck it with his staff and it became lice. The singular of al-qummal is qamla. It was also said: al-qummal is al-qaml (lice), which 'Ata al-Khurasani said. In the reading of al-Hasan, "wal-qaml" with a fatha on the qaf and sukun on the mim. They humbled themselves, but when it was removed from them they did not believe. So Allah sent upon them the frogs, the plural of diфdi' [[al-difda': with a fatha or kasra on the dal and sukun on the fa.]], which is the well-known creature found in water. There is one issue here: the prohibition of killing them is reported. Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah related it with a sahih chain. Abu Dawud related it from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Abd al-Razzaq, and Ibn Majah from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Nisaburi al-Dhuhli, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade killing the surad (a bird), the frog, the ant, and the hoopoe. Al-Nasa'i related from Abd al-Rahman ibn Uthman that a physician mentioned a frog in a medicine in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he forbade killing it. Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq authenticated it. And from Abu Hurayra, who said: the surad is the first bird to fast. When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) went out from Syria to the Haram for the building of the House, al-sakina [[al-sakina: a swift wind, that is, one that passes quickly.]] was with him, and the surad, so the surad was his guide to the place, and al-sakina its measure. When he reached the spot, al-sakina settled on the site of the House and called out: "Build, O Ibrahim, to the measure of my shadow." So the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing the surad because it was Ibrahim's guide to the House, and forbade the frog because it used to pour water on the fire of Ibrahim. When it was unleashed upon Pharaoh, it came and took over all the places, and when it reached the oven, it leapt into it while it was a blazing fire, in obedience to Allah. So Allah made its croaking a glorification (tasbih). It is said that it is the creature that glorifies most. Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: "Do not kill the frog, for its croaking that you hear is glorification." It is related that they filled their beds, their vessels, their food, and their drink; a man would sit with frogs up to his chin, and when he spoke, a frog would leap into his mouth. They complained to Musa and said: "We repent." So Allah removed that from them, but they returned to their disbelief. So Allah sent upon them blood, and the Nile flowed over them as blood. An Israelite would scoop water from it, while a Copt scooped blood. An Israelite would pour water into a Copt's mouth and it would become blood, and a Copt would pour blood into an Israelite's mouth and it would become pure, clear water. [[From b, j, k, and y.]]

(ayatin mufassalat) meaning clear, manifest signs, according to Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: "ayatin mufassalat" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). It is reported that between one sign and the next there were eight days. It was also said: forty days. It was said: a month. For this reason He said "mufassalat" (distinct).

(fastakbaru) meaning they exalted themselves, rising above faith in Allah, may He be exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 134–136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the punishment (al-rijz) fell upon them﴾ — i.e., the torment. It is also read with a ḍammah on the rāʾ; the two are dialects. Ibn Jubayr said: It was a plague (ṭāʿūn) by which seventy thousand of the Copts died in a single day. And it was said: what is meant by al-rijz is the signs mentioned earlier.

(bimā ʿahida ʿindaka) "Mā" is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which), i.e., by what He entrusted to you of knowledge, or by what He singled you out with, so He informed you. It was also said: this is an oath, i.e., by His covenant with you, except that you should pray for us, so "mā" is a supplementary particle (ṣilah). [[Thus it stands in all copies of the original text, and it is evident that it is the verbal-source (maṣdariyyah) particle.]]

(la-in kashafta ʿannā al-rijz) i.e., by your supplication to your God, that He may remove it from us.

(la-nu'minanna laka) i.e., we will affirm you in what you have brought.

(wa-la-nursilanna maʿaka Banī Isrāʾīl) and they had been employing them, as was mentioned earlier. (ilā ajalin hum bālighūhu) meaning their term that had been appointed for them in the drowning.

(idhā hum yankuthūn) i.e., they break what they had pledged upon themselves.

(fa-intaqamnā minhum fa-aghraqnāhum fi al-yamm bi-annahum kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā wa-kānū ʿanhā ghāfilīn) Al-yamm is the sea. "Wa-kānū ʿanhā" — i.e., of the vengeance; it is indicated by "fa-intaqamnā." It was also said: "ʿanhā" refers to the signs, i.e., they did not take heed from them until they became like those who are heedless of them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 137:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We caused the people﴾ means the Children of Israel.

(who were being oppressed) i.e., they were being humiliated through servitude.

(the eastern parts of the earth and its western parts) Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' claimed that the original form was "fi mashariq al-ard wa-magharibiha" (in the eastern parts of the earth and its western parts), and then the "fi" was deleted, so the words became accusative. The apparent meaning is that they inherited the land of the Copts. Thus both words are in the accusative as the direct object (al-maf'ul al-sarih). It is said: "waritu al-mal" and "awrathtuhu al-mal" (I inherited the wealth and I caused him to inherit the wealth). When the verb is transitive by means of the hamza, it takes two objects. The land here is the land of Syria and Egypt. Its eastern and western parts are the directions of east and west within it, so "the land" is specific, according to al-Hasan, Qatadah and others. It was also said: he meant the whole earth, because among the Children of Israel were Dawud and Sulayman, and both ruled the earth.

(which We had blessed) i.e., by bringing forth crops, fruits and rivers.

(And the fair word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience) It is His saying: "And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors" [[See vol. 13, p. 247.]].

(because they were patient) i.e., by their patience over the harm of Pharaoh, and over the command of Allah after they believed in Musa.

(And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been making and what they had been building) It is said: "ʿarasha yaʿrishu" means he built. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: i.e., what they built of palaces and other things. Al-Hasan said: it is the trellising of vines. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "yaʿrushun" with a damma on the ra'. Al-Kisa'i said: this is the dialect of Tamim. Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAblah read "yuʿarrishun" with a shaddah on the ra' and a damma on the ya'.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 138:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to their idols﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yaʿkifūna" with a kasra on the kaf, and the rest read it with a damma. It is said: ʿakafa, yaʿkifu and yaʿkufu, with the same meaning, "to remain at a thing and keep to it." The verbal noun from both is on the pattern ʿukūf. Qatada said: "Those people were from Lakhm, and they were staying at al-Raqqa." It was also said: "Their idols were images of cows, and for this reason al-Samiri brought out a calf for them."

(They said: "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods.") A parallel to this is the statement of the ignorant Bedouins, when they saw a green tree belonging to the disbelievers called Dhat Anwat [[They would hang their weapons on it, that is, they would suspend them.]], which they venerated one day every year. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, make for us a Dhat Anwat just as they have a Dhat Anwat." The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allahu akbar! By Him in whose hand my soul is, you have said what the people of Musa said: 'Make for us a god just as they have gods. He said: Indeed you are a people who act ignorantly' (7:138). You will surely follow the ways of those before you, step by step, exactly as one feather matches another, so much so that even if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it too." [[The qidhdha is the feather of an arrow. Ibn al-Athir said: it is used as a proverb for two things that are alike and do not differ.]] This took place on his journey to Hunayn, as its explanation will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in (the commentary on) Surat Bara'a [[See vol. 8, p. 97.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verses 139–140:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, these people — what they are engaged in is destroyed (mutabbar)﴾. That is, it is doomed to perish. At-tabar (ruin, destruction) is perishing, and every broken vessel is mutabbar. And "amrun mutabbar" means that the worshipper and the worshipped are both doomed to perish. And His saying, ﴿and what they were doing is baseless (batil)﴾: that is, it is going away and vanishing.

﴿...what they used to do.﴾ Kanu (were) here is a superfluous auxiliary (silahra'ida).

﴿He said, "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has favoured you over the worlds?"﴾ 140. That is, I seek for you a god other than Allah, Exalted is He. It is said: baghaytuhu and baghaytu lahu (I sought it for him / I sought him).

﴿And He has favoured you over the worlds﴾ 140. That is, over the worlds of your time. It is also said: He favoured them by destroying their enemy and by the signs with which He specially distinguished them.

ذَكَّرَهُمْ مِنَّتَهُ — "He reminded them of His favour." It is also said: this is an address to the Jews of the time of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "Remember when We delivered your forefathers," as has already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 1, p. 381.]]

**Commentary of al-Qurṭubī (al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qur'ān) on Sūrah al-Aʿrāf (7), verse 142**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We appointed for Mūsā (ﷺ) thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time with his Lord was complete at forty nights﴾. On this verse there are three issues.

**The first issue:** His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And We appointed for Mūsā thirty nights﴾. It is mentioned that among the honours Allah bestowed upon Mūsā (ﷺ) was this, that He promised him a private conversation (munājāh) as an honour to him.

﴿And We completed them with ten﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Masrūq, may Allah be pleased with them, said: these were Dhū al-Qaʿdah and ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. He was commanded to fast the month and to devote himself to worship in it. When he fasted it, he disliked the odour of his mouth and so used the miswāk. It is said: with a stick of carob wood. The angels said: "We used to breathe in from your mouth the scent of musk, and you spoiled it with the miswāk." So ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijjah were added to it.

It is also said: when he used the miswāk, Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: "O Mūsā, I will not speak to you until your mouth returns to what it was before. Do you not know that the fragrance of the fasting person is dearer to Me than the scent of musk?" And He commanded him to fast ten days.

The speech of Allah, may He be exalted, to Mūsā (ﷺ) took place on the morning of the sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr), when He ransomed Ismāʿīl from being slaughtered, and He perfected the Hajj for Muḥammad (ﷺ).

The tāʾ (ha') is dropped from ʿashr (ten) because the counted noun (al-maʿdūd) is feminine.

The benefit of His words, ﴿so the appointed time with his Lord was complete at forty nights﴾, although it is known that thirty and ten make forty, is to prevent the supposition that the meaning is "We completed the thirty with ten of them." So He made clear that the ten are in addition to the thirty.

If it is said: In al-Baqarah He said "forty", and here He said "thirty", so this would be a change of mind (badāʾ). It is said: this is not so. For He said, ﴿and We completed them with ten﴾, and "forty", "thirty" and "ten" are a single statement, not contradictory. He stated the two expressions in detail and in composition: He said "forty" as one composed whole, and He said "thirty", meaning a month consecutively plus ten. All of that is forty, as the poet said:

"Ten and four..."

meaning fourteen, the night of the full moon. This is permissible in the speech of the Arabs.

**The second issue:** Our scholars said: this verse shows that setting a fixed term for an appointment is an established practice, and a meaning of old which Allah established in matters and ordained for the nations, and by which He taught them the measures of deliberation in actions. The first term Allah set was the six days in which He created all created things, ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us﴾ [50:38]. [See vol. 17, p. 23.] We have already explained its meaning earlier in this sūrah in His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. [See p. 218 of this part.]

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: when a term is set for a purpose in which one seeks to attain the object of the term, and the term arrives without it being easy to attain, the term is extended to give insight and an excuse. Allah, may He be exalted, made this clear to Mūsā (ʿalayhi al-salām), so He set for him a term of thirty and then added ten to complete forty. Mūsā (ʿalayhi al-salām) was delayed during these ten days away from his people, and they did not understand the permissibility of deliberation and delay, until they said: "Mūsā has gone astray or forgotten," and they broke his covenant, altered after him, and worshipped a god other than Allah.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: Mūsā said to his people, "My Lord promised me thirty nights to meet Him, and I will leave Hārūn as my successor among you." When Mūsā departed to his Lord, Allah added ten to it, so their trial happened during the ten that Allah added, by what they did of worshipping the calf, as its explanation will come.

Then, an extension added to a term must be determined, just as the term itself is determined. It is not done except by the ruler's judgement (ijtihād) after considering the matters connected with the affair: from time, condition and action. So it is like one third of the previous period, as Allah set the term for Mūsā. If the ruler sees fit to combine the original term and the extension into a single period, it is permitted; but a waiting period (tarabbuṣ) must follow it, because of the excuses that befall human beings. Ibn al-ʿArabī said.

Al-Bukhārī related from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah has left no excuse for a man whose term He delayed until he reached sixty years." [Meaning: He left no place for an excuse for him, since He gave him this long a respite and he did not offer an excuse.]

I say: this is also a basis for the ruler giving warning (iʿdhār) to the one judged, time after time. This was a kindness to creation, and so that the upholding of justice against them would take effect. It is said: aʿdhara fī al-amr, meaning he went to the utmost in it, that is, he gave the ultimate warning after which there is no warning. The greatest warning to the children of Ādam is the sending of messengers to them, so that the proof against them is complete, ﴿And We do not punish until We send a messenger﴾. [See vol. 10, p. 231.] And He said, ﴿And there came to you the warner﴾. [See vol. 14, p. 351.] It was said: they are the messengers. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is white hair. For it comes at the age of maturity, and so it is a sign of leaving the age of youth. He made sixty the limit of the warning because sixty is close to the arena of people's lives, and it is the age of turning back in repentance, humility and submission to Allah, and of awaiting death and meeting Allah. So in it there is a warning after a warning: the first by the Prophet (ʿalayhi al-salām), and the second by white hair, and that is at the completion of forty. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And when he reached forty years, he said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour﴾. [See vol. 16, p. 194.]" So He mentioned, mighty and majestic is He, that whoever reaches forty, it is time for him to know the measure of Allah's favours upon him and upon his parents, and to be thankful for them. [In the text: "yashkuruhā", as found in j and k, which is correct; in aw, z and ā: "yashkurahumā".]

Mālik said: I met the people of knowledge in our city, and they were seeking this world and mixing with people until forty years came upon one of them; then when forty years passed over them, they withdrew from people.

**The third issue:** The verse also shows that dating is done by nights and not by days, by His words, ﴿thirty nights﴾, because the nights are the beginnings of the months. By this the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to report the days; so it is related from ʿĀʾishah that she used to say: "We fasted five with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The non-Arabs (ʿajam) differ in this, and they calculate by days, because their reliance is on the sun.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: the reckoning by the sun is for benefits, and the reckoning by the moon is for the rites (manāsik). For this reason He said, ﴿And We appointed for Mūsā thirty nights﴾.

It is said: ʾarrakhtu tārīkhan and warrakhtu tawrīkhan, two dialects.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And Mūsā said to his brother Hārūn, "Be my successor among my people and set things right"﴾. The meaning: Mūsā said, when he intended to go forth for the private conversation and to be absent in it, to his brother Hārūn: "Be my deputy (khalīfah)." This indicates delegation (al-niyābah).

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say to ʿAlī, when he left him behind in one of his campaigns: "Are you not pleased to be to me in the position of Hārūn to Mūsā, except that there is no prophet after me?"

By this the Rawāfiḍ, the Imāmiyyah and all the other sects of the Shīʿah (Shīʿah: the partisans of ʿAlī) argued that the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed ʿAlī as successor over the entire community, to the extent that the Imāmiyyah declared the Companions to be unbelievers, may Allah disfigure them, because in their view they abandoned the act which was the explicit designation of ʿAlī as successor, and appointed another by their own ijtihād. Among them are those who declared ʿAlī himself to be an unbeliever because he did not rise to seek his right. There is no doubt in the disbelief of these people, and of those who follow them in their saying.

They did not realise that this was a delegation during a lifetime, like an agency (wakālah) which ends by the dismissal of the principal or by his death, and it does not imply that it continues after his death. So on this basis, what the Imāmiyyah and others rely upon is undone. The Prophet (ﷺ) appointed Ibn Umm Maktūm and others as successors over Madīnah, and it did not necessarily follow from that that he was permanently appointed, by consensus. Moreover, Hārūn was made a partner with Mūsā in the very origin of the prophethood, so there is no proof for them in it, as they claim.

And Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and set things right﴾ is a command to reform. Ibn Jurayj said: part of the reform was that he should rebuke the Sāmirī and oppose him. It is also said: that is, be gentle with them, and set their affair right, and set yourself right, that is, be a reformer. ﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾, that is, do not take the path of the disobedient, and do not be a helper of the wrongdoers.

**Allah's words: ﴿When Musa came at Our appointed time﴾**, meaning at the time that had been promised.

**﴿And his Lord spoke to him﴾**, meaning He made him hear His speech without any intermediary.

**﴿He said, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You."﴾** He asked to see Him, longing to behold Him after having heard His speech. **﴿He said, "You will not see Me."﴾** That is, not in this world. It is not permissible to interpret this as meaning that he asked for a great sign so that he could look upon Your power, because he said "at You" (*ilayka*) and Allah replied "You will not see Me." Had he asked for a sign, Allah would have given him what he asked for, just as He gave him the other signs. Musa, peace be upon him, already had sufficient evidence in them to need no other sign, so this interpretation is refuted.

**﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me.﴾** He gave him an example of something stronger and more firm than his own constitution. That is, if the mountain remains firm and still, then you will see Me; but if it does not remain still, then you cannot bear to see Me, just as the mountain cannot bear to see Me. Al-Qadi 'Iyad related from al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib something to the effect that Musa, peace be upon him, saw Allah, and that is why he fell down unconscious; and that the mountain saw its Lord and thereby became crumbled dust, by a perception that Allah created in it. He derived this from Allah's words: ﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me.﴾

Then He said: ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble, and Musa fell down unconscious.﴾ *Tajalla* means to appear, as in your saying *jalawtu al-'arus*, meaning I unveiled the bride; and *jalawtu al-sayf*, meaning I polished the sword and removed its rust, *jila'* in both cases. *Tajalla al-shay'* means the thing was revealed. It was also said: *tajalla amruhu wa qudratuh* (His command and His power became manifest), as said by Qutrub and others.

The reading of the people of Madinah and Basrah is **دَكًّا** (*dakkan*), and its correctness is supported by Allah's words **﴿دُكَّتِ الْأَرْضُ دَكًّا﴾** (*when the earth is pounded to pieces*, 89:21), and by the fact that *jabal* (mountain) is masculine. The people of Kufa read **دَكَّاءَ** (*dakka'*), meaning He made it like a flat, level ground (*ard dakka'*), which is raised ground that does not reach the height of a mountain. The masculine form is *adakk*, and the plural of *dakka'* is *dakka'at* and *dukk*, like *hamra'at* and *humr*. Al-Kisa'i said: *al-dukk* among mountains means the broad ones, whose singular is *adakk*. Another said: *al-dakka'at*, the plural of *dakka'*, are hills of soft earth that are not steep. *Al-didakak* likewise refers to sand that has spread over the ground and not risen up. A *naqa dakka'* is a she-camel without a hump.

In the exegetical literature it is said: the mountain sank into the earth and is still moving in it until now. Ibn 'Abbas said: He made it into dust. 'Ata' al-'Awfi said: into a huge heap of sand.

**﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾**, meaning he lost consciousness, according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah. It was also said: he died. One says *sa'iqa al-rajulu* (the man fainted), so he is *sa'iq*; and *su'iqa* (he was struck unconscious), so he is *mas'uq*. Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: Musa fell down unconscious on Thursday, the Day of 'Arafah, and he was given the Torah on Friday, the Day of Sacrifice. When he recovered he said: **﴿Glory be to You; I repent to You﴾**. Mujahid said: [he repented] of asking to see Him in this world. It was also said: he asked without seeking permission, and therefore he repented. It was also said: he said this out of turning back to Allah and humility before Him when the signs became manifest.

The community (*ummah*) agreed that this repentance was not for a sin, since the prophets are protected from sin. Furthermore, according to the People of the Sunnah and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah*), seeing Allah is permissible. According to the innovators (*mubtadi'ah*), Musa asked on behalf of his people, to make clear to them that it is not permissible; but this does not require repentance. It was said: meaning "I repent to You for killing the Copt," as mentioned by al-Qushayri. The proof that seeing Allah is permissible has already been explained in *al-An'am*. 'Ali ibn Mahdi al-Tabari said: If Musa's request had been impossible, he would not have made it while knowing Allah, just as it would not be permissible for him to say to Him, "My Lord, do You have a consort and a son?" The position of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) and the refutation of them will come in *al-Qiyamah*, if Allah wills.

**﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾**. It was said: among my people. It was said: among the Children of Israel in this age. It was said: [I am the first to believe] that You cannot be seen in this world, because of Your earlier promise in that regard.

In the authentic hadith, from Abu Hurayrah and others, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not make distinctions between the prophets, for people will be struck unconscious on the Day of Resurrection, and I will raise my head and find Musa holding onto one of the pillars of the Throne. I do not know whether he was struck unconscious along with those who were struck, and recovered before me, or whether he was compensated for his first swoon." Or he said: "His first swoon sufficed him."

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ka'b who said: Allah, blessed and exalted is He, divided His speech and His seeing between Muhammad and Musa, may peace and blessings be upon them both. So Musa spoke with Him twice, and Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Him twice.

The Almighty said: ﴿O Musa, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speaking﴾. Al-istifa' means al-ijtiba' (choosing), that is, I have preferred you. He did not say "above the creation" because part of this choosing is that He spoke to him, and He also spoke to the angels and sent him as well as others as messengers. So "above the people" means the people to whom he was sent.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "bi-risalati" (in the singular). The rest read it in the plural. Al-risalah is a verbal noun (masdar), so it may be used in the singular. Whoever reads it in the plural means that he was sent with various kinds of message, so their types differed, and the verbal noun was pluralized because its types differed, as in the line of poetry: "Indeed, the most hateful of voices is the voice of donkeys." [See vol. 14, p. 71.] Here it was pluralized because the kinds of voices and the kinds of those who make them differ, and it was singular in "the voice" because he meant one kind of voice. This indicates that his people did not share in the speaking with him, nor did any of the seventy, as we explained in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 403.]

The Almighty said: ﴿So take what I have given you﴾. This is an indication of contentment; that is, be content with what I have given you.

(And be among the grateful), that is, among those who make manifest My favour to you and My bounty upon you. It is said: "a dabbah shakur" (a grateful beast) when fat appears on it beyond what it is given as fodder. The grateful person is exposed to increase, as He said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾. [See vol. 9, p. 342.] It is narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, remained, after Allah the Mighty and Majestic had spoken to him, for forty nights, and no one who saw him would live except that he died from the light of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah al-A'raf, verse 145:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything﴾. He means the Tawrat (the Torah). It is reported in a report (khabar) that Gabriel (peace be upon him) seized him with his wing and passed him through the heights until he brought him near, so that he heard the scratching of the pen when God wrote the tablets for him. This was related by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim. Mujahid said: the tablets were of green emerald. Ibn Jubayr said: of red ruby. Abu al-Aliyah said: of chrysolite. al-Hasan said: of wood, sent down from the sky. It was also said: of solid rock, which God softened for Moses (peace be upon him), so he cut it with his hand and then split it with his fingers, and it obeyed him as iron obeyed David. Muqatil said: i.e., We wrote for him [[from b, a.]] on the tablets like the engraving of a ring. Rabi' ibn Anas said: the Torah was sent down, and it was seventy loads (wiqr) of a camel. (Wiqr, with a kasra on the waw, means a heavy load; some used it for both heavy and light loads and what lies between them.)

He attributed the writing to Himself as an honour, since it was written by His command. Gabriel wrote it with the pen with which he wrote the Reminder (al-Dhikr), and it was drawn from the River of Light. It was also said: it is writing which God manifested and created on the tablets.

The root of "lawh" (tablet) is (lawh, with a fatha on the lam). God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, on a preserved tablet﴾. It is as if the tablet is where meanings shine forth (talūhu). It is narrated that there were two tablets, and the plural was used because two is considered a plural. It is said: "a man of great tablets" when he has large bones in his hands and feet.

Ibn Abbas said: the tablets broke when he threw them down, and were lifted up except for a sixth of them. It was also said: a seventh remained and six-sevenths were lifted. Thus in what was lifted was the detailing of everything, and in what remained was guidance and mercy.

Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz transmitted with a chain (isnad) from Amr ibn Dinar, who said: It reached me that Musa ibn Imran, the Prophet of God (ﷺ), fasted forty nights. When he threw down the tablets they broke, so he fasted the same number of days again, and they were returned to him.

The meaning of "from everything" is: of what he needs in his religion of rulings and the explanation of the lawful and the unlawful, according to al-Thawri and others. It was also said: it is an expression used for emphasis and not meant to be general. You say: "I entered the market and bought everything," and "with so-and-so is everything." And [the Qur'an says]: ﴿It destroys everything﴾ [[see vol. 16, p. 206]] and ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [[see vol. 13, p. 184]], which has already been mentioned.

﴿An admonition and a detailing of everything﴾: i.e., of everything they were commanded with of rulings, for they did not have ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) [[the exertion of a qualified scholar to derive a legal ruling]]. This specific feature was reserved for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿So take hold of it with strength﴾: there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: So We said to him, "Take it with strength," i.e., with earnestness and energy. Its parallel is ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾, which has already been discussed [[see vol. 1, p. 437]].

﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of it﴾: i.e., they should act upon the commands, avoid the prohibitions, and reflect upon the parables and admonitions. Its parallel is ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [[see vol. 15, pp. 270, 243]]. And He said: ﴿so they follow the best of it﴾ [[see vol. 15, pp. 270, 243]]. Pardon is better than retaliation, and patience is better than vindication. It was also said: the best of it is the obligatory duties and the recommended acts, and the least of it is the permissible.

﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾. Al-Kalbi said: "the abode of the defiant" refers to the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud which they passed by when travelling, and the generations who were destroyed. It was also said: it is Hell, according to al-Hasan and Mujahid, meaning: let it be in your minds, so beware of being among them. It was also said: He meant by it Egypt, i.e., "I will show you the lands of the Copts and the dwellings of Pharaoh empty of them," according to Ibn Jubayr. Qatadah said: the meaning is "I will show you the dwellings of the unbelievers who lived before you, of the tyrants and the Amalekites, so that you may take warning from them," meaning Syria. These two opinions are indicated by ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit﴾ [[see p. 272 of this volume]], and so on. And ﴿We wish to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾, and so on [[see vol. 13, p. 247]], which has already been mentioned.

Ibn Abbas and Qasamah ibn Zuhayr read ﴿I will make you inherit﴾ (sa-uwarrithukum) from the form warratha. This is clear. It was also said: "the abode" means destruction, and its plural is adwar. That is because when God drowned Pharaoh, He revealed to the sea: "Cast their bodies onto the shore." He said: So it did, and the Children of Israel looked at them, and He showed them the destruction of the defiantly disobedient.

**Qur'an 7:146–147**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth without right﴾. Qatadah said: "I will prevent them from understanding My Book." Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah also said this. It was also said: "I will turn them away from believing in them." And it was said: "I will turn them away from benefiting from them, as a recompense for their arrogance." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ (See vol. 18, p. 82). On this view, the "signs" (ayat) are the miracles or the revealed Books. It was also said that the "signs" are the creation of the heavens and the earth, meaning: "I will turn them away from reflecting upon them."

(They are arrogant) means they consider themselves the best of creation. This is a false assumption, and therefore He said: (without right). They do not follow any prophet, nor do they incline to him, because of their arrogance.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it, and if they see the way of guidance, they will not take it as a way, but if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way﴾. This refers to these arrogant people. He informed about them that they abandon the path of rectitude and follow the way of error and misguidance, that is, they take disbelief as their religion. Then He gave the reason, saying: (That is because they denied Our signs), that is, that treatment which I inflicted upon them was because of their denial.

(And they were heedless of them) means that by their failure to contemplate the truth they were like the heedless. It may also mean that they were heedless of what they would be recompensed with, as it is said: "How heedless is so-and-so of what is intended for him."

Malik ibn Dinar read *wa-in yurawu* with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'* in both occurrences, meaning: He will do that to them. The people of Madinah and the people of Basra read *sabīla al-rushd* with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'* and sukun on the *shīn*. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read *al-rashad* with a *fatḥa* on both the *rā'* and the *shīn*. Abu 'Ubayd said: Abu 'Amr distinguished between *al-rushd* and *al-rashad*, saying: *al-rushd* is in righteousness, and *al-rashad* is in religion.

Al-Nahhas said: "Sibawayh held that *al-rushd* and *al-rashad* are like *al-sukhṭ* and *al-sakhaṭ*, and al-Kisa'i said the same. The correct report from Abu 'Amr differs from what Abu 'Ubayd said." Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: Nasr ibn 'Ali narrated to us from his father, from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', who said: "When *al-rushd* occurs in the middle of the verse, it is with sukun; when it occurs at the end of a verse, it is with a vowel." Al-Nahhas said: By "the end of a verse" he means something like ﴿And facilitate for us from our affair a right course (rashadan)﴾ (See vol. 10, p. 358). So, according to him, the two are two dialects with one meaning, except that he gave this one a *fatḥa* so that the verse endings would agree.

It is said: *rashada* (yarshudu) and *rashuda* (yarshudu). Sibawayh also related *rashida* (yarshadu). The true meaning of *al-rushd* and *al-rashad* in the language is that a person attains what he desires, and it is the opposite of failure.
