Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 148:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the people of Musa took, after him,﴾ meaning: after his departure to the Mount (al-Tur).

(min huliyyihim) This is the reading of the people of Madina and the people of Basra. The people of Kufa, with the exception of 'Asim, read "min hiliyyihim" with a kasra on the ha'. Ya'qub read "min halyihim" with a fatha on the ha' and with takhfif (lightening of the yā'). Al-Nahhas said: the plural of ḥilyun (ḥilī, ḥilyun) is ḥilī and ḥiliyy, like thady and thudiyy and thidiyy. The original form is ḥuluwiyy; the waw was assimilated into the yā', so the lām took a kasra because it neighbours the yā', and the ḥā' may take a kasra because of the kasra of the lām. Its damma is according to the original form.

(ʿijlan) is an object (maf'ul).

(jasadan) is an adjective (naʿt) or a substitute (badal).

(lahu khuwar) is in the nominative as a subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). It is said: khāra yakhūru khuwāran, meaning he bellowed; likewise jaʾara yajʾaru juʾāran. It is also said: khawira yakhwaru khawaran, meaning he became cowardly and weak.

It is narrated in the accounts of the calf that al-Samiri, whose name was Musa ibn Zafar, is ascribed to a village called Samira. He was born in the year the sons were slain, and his mother hid him in a mountain cave, and Jibril nourished him, so he recognised him for that. When he crossed the sea on a mare in heat (wadiq) [[i.e., one desiring the stallion]] to get ahead of Pharaoh into the sea, he took a handful of the trace of the horse's hoof. This is the meaning of His saying: "So I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger" [20:96]. [[See vol. 11, p. 238.]]

Musa had promised his people thirty days. When he delayed in the additional ten and thirty nights had passed, he said to the Children of Israel, and he was obeyed among them: "Indeed, with you are ornaments from the ornaments of the family of Pharaoh." They had a festival in which they adorned themselves, and they borrowed ornaments from the Copts for that day. When Allah brought them out of Egypt and the Copts drowned, that jewellery remained in their hands. Al-Samiri said to them: "It is forbidden to you; so bring what you have and we will burn it." It was also said: this jewellery is what the Children of Israel had taken from the people of Pharaoh after the drowning, and that Harun said to them: "The jewellery is spoil, and it is not lawful for you," so he gathered it in a pit he had dug, and al-Samiri took it. It was also said: they borrowed the jewellery on the night they intended to leave Egypt, and they gave the Copts the impression that they had a wedding or a gathering. Al-Samiri had heard their saying: "Make for us a god as they have gods" [see p. 273 of this part]. Those gods were in the likeness of cattle, so he fashioned for them a calf with a body, that is, solid, but they used to hear a lowing from it. It was also said: Allah turned it into flesh and blood. It was also said: when he cast that handful of dust into the fire upon the jewellery, it became a calf with a lowing, and it lowed one single lowing and did not repeat it. Then he said to the people: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot" [20:88]. He means: he forgot it here and went seeking it and strayed from it. So they said: "Come, let us worship this calf." Allah said to Musa while he was communing with Him: "Indeed We have tested your people after you, and al-Samiri has misled them" [20:85]. Musa said: "O Lord, this al-Samiri brought out for them a calf from their jewellery. Who made for it a body?" – meaning flesh and blood – "and who made for it a lowing?" Allah, glorified is He, said: "I did." He said: "By Your might and Your majesty, none misled them but You." He said: "You have spoken the truth, O Wisest of the wise." This is the meaning of His saying: "It is nothing but Your trial" [[See vol. 11, p. 232 and p. 294 of this part.]].

Al-Qaffal said: al-Samiri devised by hollowing out the calf and placing it against the wind, until there came from it something imitating the lowing, and he gave them the impression that it had become so because of the dust placed in the body, which he had taken from the dust of the hooves of Jibril's horse. This is speech full of incoherence [[In B and Y: mutahafit (incoherent).]]. Al-Qushayri said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾ shows that the one worshipped must be characterised by speech.

﴿And does not guide them to a way﴾ meaning, a path to proof.

﴿They took it﴾ meaning, as a god.

﴿And they were wrongdoers﴾ meaning, wronging themselves in taking it [[In Z: their taking it.]]. It is also said: and they became wrongdoers, meaning polytheists, by making the calf a god.

﴿Wa-lammā suqita fī aydīhim﴾ means: after Musa returned from the appointed meeting (al-miqat). It is said of one who is remorseful and bewildered, "He has been made to fall into his hand [suqita fi yadihi]." Al-Akhfash said: it is said *suqita fi yadihi* and *ususqita*. As for one who says *saqata fi aydīhim* in the active form, its meaning according to him is "the remorse fell." This is related by al-Azhari, al-Nahhas and others.

Remorse is in the heart, but the hand is mentioned because it is said of one who obtains something, "such-and-such a matter has come into his hand," since dealing with things is generally done by the hand. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾. Also, although remorse settles in the heart, its effect appears in the body, because the remorseful person bites his hand and strikes one of his hands against the other. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he began to turn over his palms over what he had spent therein﴾, meaning he regretted. And ﴿On the Day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾, meaning out of regret. The remorseful person places his chin in his hand. It has also been said that its origin is from *al-isti'sar* (taking someone captive), which is when a man strikes another man or throws him down and casts him from his hands to the ground in order to capture him or bind him; so the one thrown down is "fallen upon" by the one who fell.

(﴿Wa-ra'aw annahum qad ḍallū﴾) That is, they were overtaken [in manuscripts B and Y: "ibtalaw", they were tested] by disobedience to Allah.

(﴿Qālū la-in lam yarḥamnā rabbunā wa-yaghfir lanā lanakūnanna mina al-khāsirīn﴾) They began to acknowledge servitude and to seek forgiveness. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: ﴿la-in lam tarḥamnā rabbanā wa-taghfir lanā﴾ with the *ta'* as address (the second person). This carries the sense of seeking help, humble submission, earnest entreaty and supplication in asking and invoking. *Rabbanā* with the accusative (*naṣb*) is by omitting the vocative (*nidā'*). It is also more eloquent in supplication and submission. So their reading of both is more expressive of humility and supplication, and therefore it is preferable.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 150–151 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾ (150). "Ghadbana" is not declined because its feminine is "ghadba," and because the alif and nun in it are equivalent to the two feminine alifs in your saying "hamra'" (red). It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). "Asifan" means intensely angry. Abu al-Darda' said: "Al-asaf is a station beyond anger, more severe than it." It is "asif," "asaf," "asfan," and "asuf." Al-asif also means grieved. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: he returned grieved over the conduct of his people. Al-Tabari said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed him before his return that they had been tested with the calf, and therefore he returned angry. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Musa, peace be upon him, was among the greatest of people in anger, but he was quick to return (al-fay'a) [[al-fay'a (with fatha or kasra on the fa'): the state of returning from a thing that a person has been involved in and engaged with.]], so "that for this." Ibn al-Qasim said: I heard Malik say: "When Musa, peace be upon him, became angry, smoke rose from his cap, and the hair of his body raised his robe. This is because anger is an ember that blazes in the heart." For this reason the Prophet ﷺ commanded whoever became angry to lie down; if his anger did not subside, he should perform ghusl, for his lying down extinguishes it and his washing puts it out. The quickness of his anger was the reason he slapped the Angel of Death and gouged out his eye. This has already been discussed in al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 122.]], what the scholars say about it. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: Musa, peace be upon him, permitted himself this because he was the interlocutor of Allah, as if he saw that whoever dared against him or extended a hand to harm him, the matter was grave. Do you not see that he argued with Him, saying: "From where will You take my soul? From my mouth, though I have conversed with my Lord with it! Or from my hearing, though I have heard the speech of my Lord with it! Or from my hand, though I have taken the Tablets from Him with it! Or from my foot, though I stood before Him speaking to Him at Mount Sinai! Or from my eye, though my face has shone with His light!" So he returned to his Lord, silenced. In Abu Dawud's Musannaf, from Abu Dhar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: "If one of you becomes angry while standing, let him sit; if the anger leaves him, well, otherwise let him lie down." It is also related from Abu Wa'il al-Qass, who said: We entered upon 'Urwah ibn Muhammad al-Sa'di, and a man spoke to him and angered him. He stood, then returned after having performed wudu', and said: My father related to me from my grandfather 'Atiyyah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Anger is from Satan, and Satan was created from fire, and fire is extinguished only by water; so when one of you becomes angry, let him perform wudu'."

His saying, the Exalted: (Evil is what you have done in my stead after me) (150): a rebuke from him to them, meaning: how evil is the deed you did after me. It is said: "khalafahu" with what is disliked, and it is also said regarding good. It is said of him: "khalafahu bi-khayr aw bi-sharr fi ahlihi wa qawmihi ba'da shukhusihi" (he left him in good or evil in his family and people after his departure).

(Have you hastened the command of your Lord) (150): meaning, you preceded it. Haste (al-'ajalah) is advancing a thing before its time, and it is blameworthy. Speed (al-sur'ah) is doing a thing at its first appropriate time, and it is praiseworthy. Ya'qub said: It is said "'ajiltu al-shay'" meaning I preceded it, and "a'jaltu al-rajul" meaning I asked him to hasten, i.e., I compelled him to haste. The meaning of "amra rabbikum" (the command of your Lord) is the appointed time of your Lord, i.e., the promise of forty nights. It was also said: "Did you hasten the wrath of your Lord?" It was also said: "Did you hasten to worship the calf before a command from your Lord came to you?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he threw down the Tablets﴾ (150). There are two issues in this. The first: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he threw down the Tablets﴾ (150), meaning, because of the anger and grief that overtook him when he saw his people devoted to worshipping the calf, and his brother's neglect of their affairs. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this. Hence it is said: "The report is not like seeing with one's own eyes." There is no regard for what is related from Qatadah, if it is authentically transmitted from him, nor is it correct that his throwing the Tablets was because of what he saw in them of the excellence of the community of Muhammad ﷺ, and that this did not belong to his own community. This is a wretched view that should not be attributed to Musa ﷺ. It has already been mentioned from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Tablets broke, and that the detail was lifted from them while the guidance and mercy remained in them. The second: Some ignorant Sufis have used this as evidence for the permissibility of throwing garments when their ecstasy over music becomes intense. Then some of them throw them intact, and some tear them and then throw them. He said: "These are in a state of absorption, so they are not blamed, for Musa, peace be upon him, when grief overcame him over his people's worship of the calf, threw the Tablets and broke them, and he did not know what he had done." Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi said: Who can authenticate that Musa, peace be upon him, threw them with the throw of one who breaks? What is mentioned in the Qur'an is that he "threw" (alqa) them, so from where do we know that they broke? Even if it were said that they broke, from where do we know that he intended to break them? Even if we authenticated that about him, we would say he was in a state of absorption, to the extent that if a sea of fire were before him, he would wade into it. Who can authenticate such absorption for these people, when they recognize the singer from others and guard against a well if there were one before them? Moreover, how can the states of the prophets be compared with the states of these fools? Ibn 'Aqil was asked about their ecstatic movements and the tearing of their garments, and he said: "It is an error and forbidden, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the squandering of wealth." Someone said to him: "But they do not understand what they are doing." He said: "If they attend these places knowing that ecstasy overcomes them and removes their reason, they are sinful for what they inflict upon themselves of tearing and other ruin. The address of the Law does not drop from them, for they were addressed before attending to avoid this place which leads to that. Just as they are forbidden from drinking intoxicants, so too is this ecstasy that the Sufis call wajd: if they are truthful that it contains a drunkenness of nature, and if they are lying, they corrupt even while sober. There is no safety in it in either state, and avoiding the places of suspicion is obligatory."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he seized his brother by the head, drawing him toward himself﴾ (150), meaning by his beard and forelock. Harun was three years older than Musa, peace be upon them both, and was more beloved to the Children of Israel than Musa, because he was gentle in anger. Regarding Musa's seizing his brother by the head there are four interpretations. The first: that this was customary among them, just as the Arabs used to seize a man by the beard of his brother and companion as honor and reverence, so it was not in the manner of humiliation. The second: that this was only so that he could privately tell him of the revelation of the Tablets to him, since they had been revealed to him during this private communion, and he wanted to conceal them from the Children of Israel before the Torah. Harun said to him: "Do not seize me by the beard or the head," lest his secret be confused for the Children of Israel with humiliation. The third: he did this to him because it occurred to his mind that Harun was inclined with the Children of Israel in what they did concerning the calf, and such a thing is not permissible for prophets. The fourth: he took his brother to him so that he might learn what was with him, and Harun disliked that lest the Children of Israel think he had humiliated him, so his brother made clear to him that they had oppressed him, meaning the calf-worshippers, and "they nearly killed him," meaning they came close to it. When he heard his excuse, he said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother," meaning: forgive me for the anger because of which I threw the Tablets, and forgive my brother, because he thought him negligent in denouncing them, though no negligence had come from him, that is, forgive my brother if he fell short. Al-Hasan said: All of them worshipped the calf except Harun, for if there had been a believer other than Musa and Harun, he would not have limited himself to saying "My Lord, forgive me and my brother," but would have prayed for that believer too. It was also said: he sought forgiveness for himself for his act toward his brother, doing this out of his anger against him, since he had not joined him to inform him of what had happened so that he could return and set matters right among them. Hence he said: "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?" (20:92–93), and so on. Harun explained that he only stood firm out of fear for his own life from being killed. The verse indicates that one who fears being killed for himself when changing wrong may remain silent. The explanation of this has already been given in Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 47.]]. Ibn al-'Arabi: In it is evidence that anger does not alter rulings, as some people claim, for Musa, peace be upon him, did not let his anger change any of his actions; rather, they proceeded on their course: the throwing of a tablet, the reproach of a brother, and the slapping of an angel. Al-Hadawi: because his anger was for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and his silence toward the Children of Israel was out of fear that they would fight one another or scatter.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: Son of my mother﴾ (150). He was the son of his mother and father, but this is a word of gentleness and tenderness. Al-Zajjaj said: It was said that Harun was Musa's brother by the mother, not by the father. It is read with fatha and kasra on the mim. Whoever reads with fatha makes "ibn umma" one word, like "khamsata 'ashara" (fifteen), so it is like your saying: "O fifteen, come forward." Whoever reads with kasra makes it an annexation to the first-person pronoun, then deletes the annexed ya' because the structure of the vocative is on deletion, and leaves the kasra on the mim to indicate the annexation, like his saying: "O My servants" (39:10). What indicates this is Ibn al-Sumayqa's reading "Ya ibna ummi" with the ya' retained in its original form. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd said: "Ibn umma" with fatha, its estimate being "ya ibna ummaha." The Basrans said: this view is wrong, because the alif is light and is not deleted, but the two nouns were made one noun. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim said: "Ibn umma" with kasra, as you say "ya ghulam, ghulam, aqbil," and this is an anomalous dialect and reading with it is remote. This only applies to what is annexed to you; but for what is annexed to something annexed to you, the correct form is to say "ya ghulam ghulami" and "ya ibn akhi." They permitted "ya ibn umma" and "ya ibn 'amm" because they are common in speech. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas said: But it has a good and fine construction, in which "ibn" with "umm" and with "amm" is made one name, just as in your saying "ya khamsata 'ashara aqbilu," so the ya' is deleted as it is deleted from "ya ghulam." "Indeed the people deemed me weak" (7:150): they humiliated me and counted me weak. "And they nearly killed me," meaning they came close to it. "Do not let the enemies rejoice over me" (7:150): do not make them glad. Shamatah (gloating) is joy at what befalls your brother of calamities in religion and in worldly life, and it is forbidden and prohibited. In a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not show gloating over your brother, lest Allah grant him health and afflict you." The Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge from it and say: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the evil of decree, from the snare of misery, and from the gloating of enemies." Al-Bukhari and others recorded it. The poet said:

When time drags its heavy burdens over people, it brings down others as well.
So say to those who gloat over us: Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we met.

Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an (Commentary on surah 7, verses 150–151, part 2 of 2):

Mujahid and Malik ibn Dinar read "tashmatu" with a fatha on the ta' (tashmata) and a fatha on the mim, and "al-a'da'" in the nominative (al-a'da'u). The meaning is: do not do to me what would make the enemies rejoice, that is, let them not rejoice at something you do to me. It is also related from Mujahid that he read "tashmata" with a fatha on both (the ta' and the mim) and "al-a'da'a" in the accusative. Ibn Jinni said: the meaning is "fa-la tashmat bi anta ya Rabb" (so do not let the enemies rejoice over me, You, O Lord). This is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿Allah mocks at them﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 207] and similar. Then he returned to the intended meaning and supplied a verb, governing "al-a'da'" in the accusative, as if he said: "wa la tushmit bi ya, al-a'da'" (and do not make the enemies rejoice over me).

Abu Ubayd said: I have also related from Humayd: "fa-la tushmit" with a kasra on the mim. Al-Nahhas said: there is no sound basis for this reading, because if it were from shamita, it would have to be "tashmatu", and if it were from ashmata, it would have to be "tushmitu".

As for His saying: ﴿and do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾ (150), Mujahid said: it refers to those who worshipped the calf.

﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ [see vol. 3, p. 431] — already discussed earlier.

Harun explained that he only stood firm out of fear for his own life from being killed. The verse indicates that one who fears being killed for himself when changing wrong may remain silent. The explanation of this has already been given in Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 47.]]. Ibn al-'Arabi: In it is evidence that anger does not alter rulings, as some people claim, for Musa, peace be upon him, did not let his anger change any of his actions; rather, they proceeded on their course: the throwing of a tablet, the reproach of a brother, and the slapping of an angel. Al-Hadawi: because his anger was for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and his silence toward the Children of Israel was out of fear that they would fight one another or scatter.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: Son of my mother﴾ (150). He was the son of his mother and father, but this is a word of gentleness and tenderness. Al-Zajjaj said: It was said that Harun was Musa's brother by the mother, not by the father. It is read with fatha and kasra on the mim. Whoever reads with fatha makes "ibn umma" one word, like "khamsata 'ashara" (fifteen), so it is like your saying: "O fifteen, come forward." Whoever reads with kasra makes it an annexation to the first-person pronoun, then deletes the annexed ya' because the structure of the vocative is on deletion, and leaves the kasra on the mim to indicate the annexation, like his saying: "O My servants" (39:10). What indicates this is Ibn al-Sumayqa's reading "Ya ibna ummi" with the ya' retained in its original form. Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd said: "Ibn umma" with fatha, its estimate being "ya ibna ummaha." The Basrans said: this view is wrong, because the alif is light and is not deleted, but the two nouns were made one noun. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim said: "Ibn umma" with kasra, as you say "ya ghulam, ghulam, aqbil," and this is an anomalous dialect and reading with it is remote. This only applies to what is annexed to you; but for what is annexed to something annexed to you, the correct form is to say "ya ghulam ghulami" and "ya ibn akhi." They permitted "ya ibn umma" and "ya ibn 'amm" because they are common in speech. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas said: But it has a good and fine construction, in which "ibn" with "umm" and with "amm" is made one name, just as in your saying "ya khamsata 'ashara aqbilu," so the ya' is deleted as it is deleted from "ya ghulam." "Indeed the people deemed me weak" (7:150): they humiliated me and counted me weak. "And they nearly killed me," meaning they came close to it. "Do not let the enemies rejoice over me" (7:150): do not make them glad. Shamatah (gloating) is joy at what befalls your brother of calamities in religion and in worldly life, and it is forbidden and prohibited. In a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not show gloating over your brother, lest Allah grant him health and afflict you." The Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge from it and say: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the evil of decree, from the snare of misery, and from the gloating of enemies." Al-Bukhari and others recorded it. The poet said:

When time drags its heavy burdens over people, it brings down others as well.
So say to those who gloat over us: Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we met.

Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an (Commentary on surah 7, verses 150–151, part 2 of 2):

Mujahid and Malik ibn Dinar read "tashmatu" with a fatha on the ta' (tashmata) and a fatha on the mim, and "al-a'da'" in the nominative (al-a'da'u). The meaning is: do not do to me what would make the enemies rejoice, that is, let them not rejoice at something you do to me. It is also related from Mujahid that he read "tashmata" with a fatha on both (the ta' and the mim) and "al-a'da'a" in the accusative. Ibn Jinni said: the meaning is "fa-la tashmat bi anta ya Rabb" (so do not let the enemies rejoice over me, You, O Lord). This is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿Allah mocks at them﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 207] and similar. Then he returned to the intended meaning and supplied a verb, governing "al-a'da'" in the accusative, as if he said: "wa la tushmit bi ya, al-a'da'" (and do not make the enemies rejoice over me).

Abu Ubayd said: I have also related from Humayd: "fa-la tushmit" with a kasra on the mim. Al-Nahhas said: there is no sound basis for this reading, because if it were from shamita, it would have to be "tashmatu", and if it were from ashmata, it would have to be "tushmitu".

As for His saying: ﴿and do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾ (150), Mujahid said: it refers to those who worshipped the calf.

﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ [see vol. 3, p. 431] — already discussed earlier.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 152–153:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [as a deity] will be overtaken by anger from their Lord﴾. Al-ghadab (anger) from Allah is punishment. "And humiliation in the life of this world," because they were commanded to kill one another. It was also said: the humiliation is the jizyah (poll tax).

But this is far-fetched, because the jizyah was not taken from them; it was taken from their descendants. Then it was said: this is part of the speech of Musa, peace be upon him, which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related from him, and the speech ended there. Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We recompense the fabricators﴾. This statement by Musa, peace be upon him, was made before the people repented by killing themselves. When they repented and Allah pardoned them after the great killing had taken place, as its explanation has already been given in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 401], He informed them that whoever among them died slain is a martyr, and whoever remained alive is forgiven. It was also said: there was a group whose hearts were saturated with love of the calf, and they did not repent, so they are the ones meant by ﴿those who took the calf﴾. It was also said: it refers to those among them who died before Musa returned from the appointed meeting. It was also said: it refers to their descendants, and this is what happened to Qurayzah and al-Nadir, meaning that it would overtake their descendants. And Allah knows best.

﴿And thus We recompense the fabricators﴾, that is, as We did to these people, so We do to the fabricators. Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "There is no innovator but you will find humiliation above his head," then he recited, "Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by anger from their Lord," up to his words, "And thus We recompense the fabricators," meaning the innovators. It was also said: Musa was commanded to slaughter the calf, and blood flowed from it; he filed it down with a file and threw it with the blood into the sea, and commanded them to drink from that water. Whoever worshipped that calf and drank it, a trace of it appeared on the edges of his mouth, and by this the worshippers of the calf were recognized. This has passed in al-Baqarah. Then Allah, Exalted, informed that Allah accepts the repentance of the one who repents from shirk and other than it. The place of ﴿And those who did evil deeds﴾, that is, disbelief and sins.

﴿Then repent after them﴾, that is, after committing them.

﴿And believe; indeed your Lord, after them﴾, that is, after the repentance, is surely Forgiving and Merciful.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 152–153:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [as a deity] will be overtaken by anger from their Lord﴾. Al-ghadab (anger) from Allah is punishment. "And humiliation in the life of this world," because they were commanded to kill one another. It was also said: the humiliation is the jizyah (poll tax).

But this is far-fetched, because the jizyah was not taken from them; it was taken from their descendants. Then it was said: this is part of the speech of Musa, peace be upon him, which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related from him, and the speech ended there. Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We recompense the fabricators﴾. This statement by Musa, peace be upon him, was made before the people repented by killing themselves. When they repented and Allah pardoned them after the great killing had taken place, as its explanation has already been given in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 401], He informed them that whoever among them died slain is a martyr, and whoever remained alive is forgiven. It was also said: there was a group whose hearts were saturated with love of the calf, and they did not repent, so they are the ones meant by ﴿those who took the calf﴾. It was also said: it refers to those among them who died before Musa returned from the appointed meeting. It was also said: it refers to their descendants, and this is what happened to Qurayzah and al-Nadir, meaning that it would overtake their descendants. And Allah knows best.

﴿And thus We recompense the fabricators﴾, that is, as We did to these people, so We do to the fabricators. Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "There is no innovator but you will find humiliation above his head," then he recited, "Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by anger from their Lord," up to his words, "And thus We recompense the fabricators," meaning the innovators. It was also said: Musa was commanded to slaughter the calf, and blood flowed from it; he filed it down with a file and threw it with the blood into the sea, and commanded them to drink from that water. Whoever worshipped that calf and drank it, a trace of it appeared on the edges of his mouth, and by this the worshippers of the calf were recognized. This has passed in al-Baqarah. Then Allah, Exalted, informed that Allah accepts the repentance of the one who repents from shirk and other than it. The place of ﴿And those who did evil deeds﴾, that is, disbelief and sins.

﴿Then repent after them﴾, that is, after committing them.

﴿And believe; indeed your Lord, after them﴾, that is, after the repentance, is surely Forgiving and Merciful.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses﴾, meaning it calmed down (sakana). Mu'awiya ibn Qurra also read it as "sakana" with a nun. The original sense of sukut (silence) is stillness and restraint. It is said: "The valley flowed three times, then it calmed (sakana)," meaning it stopped flowing. Ikrima said: "Moses fell silent from the anger (sakata ʿan al-ghadab)," and this is an inversion (al-maqlub, a figure of speech where the order of words is reversed). Like your saying: "I put the finger into the ring," and "I put the ring onto the finger," and "I put the cap onto my head," and "I put my head into the cap."

﴿Took up the tablets﴾, which he had thrown down.

﴿And in their copy is guidance and mercy﴾: that is, "guidance" from misguidance, and "mercy" from punishment. Naskh (copying, transferring) is the transfer of what is in one book to another book. The original from which something is copied is called nuskha, and the copy is also called nuskha. It is said that when the tablets were broken, Moses fasted forty days, and then those tablets were returned to him and restored to him in two tablets, without losing anything from them. This was related by Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Qushayri said: according to this, "in their copy" means: in what was copied from the broken tablets and transferred to the new tablets is guidance and mercy. ʿAta' said: "in what remained of them." That is because only one-seventh of them remained, and six-sevenths were lost, but nothing of the prescribed limits and rulings was lost. It is also said: the meaning of "in their copy" is: in what was copied for him from them from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) is guidance. And it is said: the meaning is that in what was written for him in them is guidance and mercy, so there is no need for an original from which to copy. This is like saying: "Copy what so-and-so says," meaning, record it in your book.

The Almighty's words: ﴿for those who fear their Lord﴾, meaning, who are in awe (yarhabun) of them. Regarding the lam there are three opinions. The view of the Kufans is that it is extra (za'ida). Al-Kisa'i said: "A man who heard al-Farazdaq say told me: 'I paid for her a hundred dirhams,' meaning, I paid them (naqadtu lahā = naqadtuhā)." It is also said that it is the lam of purpose (lam ajl), meaning: "those who, for the sake of their Lord, fear, out of showing-off and not for reputation," related from al-Akhfash. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: it is connected to a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "for those whose awe is directed to their Lord." It is also said: since the object was placed before the verb, the lam became acceptable, as in the saying: ﴿If you are interpreters of dreams﴾. When the governed element, which is the object, was placed first, the action of the verb weakened, and so it took the position of an intransitive verb.

The Qur'an verse (7:155) on the seventy men chosen by Musa (Moses). Al-Qurtubi's commentary, from *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*:

Allah's words: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time﴾ — the verb has two objects. One of them has had the preposition *min* ("from") omitted. Sibawayh cited:

*"Among us is the one who was chosen from among men for generosity ... and kindness when the fierce winds blow."* [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, as in Sibawayh's *Shawahid*. In his *Diwan* the reading is *wa-kheyran* ("and good").]]

Al-Ra'i also said, praising a man:

*"I chose you from among the people when their characters had decayed, and whoever was hoped for in need had failed."* [[*Ikhtalla*: became poor.]]

He means: "I chose you from among the people." The original form of *ikhtara* was *ikhtiyara*. When the *ya'* carried a vowel and had a *fatha* before it, it was changed to an *alif*, as in *qala* and *baa'a*.

Allah's words: ﴿So when the earthquake seized them﴾ — meaning they died. *Al-Rajfa* in the language means a severe quake. It is related that they were shaken until they died.

Allah's words: ﴿He said, "My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me as well"﴾ — meaning, "You would have caused them to die." This is like Allah's saying, "If a man perishes [...]" [[See vol. 6, p. 28.]]. "And me as well" is a conjunction. The meaning is: "Had You willed, You would have caused us to die before we went out to the appointed time in the presence of the Children of Israel, so that they would not accuse me."

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba narrated to us: Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Umara ibn 'Abd, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: Musa and Harun (may Allah's blessings be upon them both) set out, and Shabbar and Shabbir set out — they were the two sons of Harun. They came to a mountain on which there was a couch, and Harun stood upon it, and his soul was taken. Musa returned to his people, and they said, "You killed him! You were jealous of us for his gentleness and his character," or words similar to this (the doubt is from Sufyan). He said, "How could I kill him when his two sons are with me?" They said, "Choose whomever you wish." So they chose ten from each tribe. He said: this is Allah's saying, "And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time." They came to him and said, "Who killed you, O Harun?" He said, "No one killed me, but Allah took my soul." They said, "O Musa, [...] (the report reads: *ma tu'sa*, "what is disobeyed"; in one manuscript: *ma tuqda*)." Then the earthquake seized them, and they began to move back and forth to the right and to the left, and he said: "*Had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me as well. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? This is only Your trial*." He said: then He revived them, and made them all prophets.

It is also said that the earthquake seized them because of their saying, "Show us Allah plainly," as Allah the Exalted said: "And when you said, 'O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah plainly,' the thunderbolt seized you," as explained earlier in *al-Baqara* [[See vol. 1, p. 403.]].

Ibn 'Abbas said: The earthquake seized them only because they did not forbid those who worshipped the calf, and they did not disapprove of its worship.

It is also said: these seventy were not the same as those who said, "Show us Allah plainly."

Wahb said: They did not die. Rather, the earthquake seized them out of awe, until their joints nearly came apart, and Musa feared that they would die. It has been mentioned in *al-Baqara*, from Wahb, that they died for a day and a night. Other explanations have been given for the cause of their being seized by the earthquake, and Allah knows best the soundness of these.

The intended meaning of the interrogative in His saying, "*Will You destroy us*," is denial: that is, "You are not doing that." This is common in Arabic speech. When an interrogative has the sense of negation, it carries the sense of affirmation, as the poet said:

*"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of all the world in giving?"* [[*Al-Rah*: plural of *rahah*, the palm of the hand.]]

It is also said that its meaning is supplication and request: that is, "Do not destroy us," and he attributed it to himself. The intended people are those who died from the earthquake. Al-Mubarrad said: the interrogative is meant as an interrogative of magnification, as if he were saying, "Do not destroy us," while Musa knew that Allah does not destroy anyone for the sin of another. Rather, it is like the saying of 'Isa: "*If You punish them, they are Your servants*" [[See vol. 6, p. 377.]].

It is also said: the foolish ones refers to the seventy, and the meaning is: "Will You destroy the Children of Israel for what these foolish ones did in their saying, 'Show us Allah plainly'?" ﴿This is only Your trial﴾ — meaning, "This is nothing but Your testing and examination." He attributed the trial to Allah the Exalted and did not attribute it to himself, just as Ibrahim said: "*And when I am ill, it is He who cures me*" [[See vol. 13, p. 110.]], attributing the illness to himself and the cure to Allah the Exalted. Yusha' said: "*And none caused me to forget it except Satan*" [[Note: this is a quotation attributed in the text to Yusha', as printed.]]. Musa, peace be upon him, derived this understanding from Allah's saying to him: "*We have indeed tried your people after you*" [[See vol. 11, p. 232.]] [20:85].

When he returned to his people and saw the calf set up for worship, and it had a lowing sound, he said: ﴿It is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will﴾ — meaning, by the trial.

This is a refutation of the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination).

(And prescribe for us good in this world) meaning: enable us to do righteous deeds through which good deeds will be recorded for us.

(And in the Hereafter) 20, meaning: as a reward for them.

(Indeed, we have turned back to You) meaning: we have repented. This was said by Mujahid, Abu al-Aliyah, and Qatadah. Al-hawd (repentance) is tawbah, and it was discussed earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 423.]].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said: "My punishment I inflict on whom I will"﴾, meaning: on those who deserve it. That is, this quake and thunderbolt is a punishment from Me, which I inflict on whom I will. It was also said that the meaning of "whom I will" is: whom I will to lead astray.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾. This is general in meaning: it has no limit, meaning that whoever enters it, it does not fail to reach him. It was also said: it encompasses every created thing, to the extent that even an animal has mercy and tenderness toward its young. Some of the exegetes said: Through this verse, every thing hoped for it, even Iblis, so he said: "I am a thing." Then Allah the Exalted said: "So I will prescribe it for those who are mindful of God," and the Jews and Christians said: "We are mindful of God." Then Allah the Exalted said: "Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered," and the verse continued. Thus the verse was excluded from generality, and praise be to God. Hammad ibn Salamah narrated from Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, prescribed it for this Ummah."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, Verse 157:**

There are ten issues in this verse.

**First issue:** Yahya ibn Abi Kathir narrated from Nawf al-Bikali al-Himyari: When Musa (Moses) chose seventy men from his people for the appointed time of his Lord, God the Exalted said to Musa: "Indeed, I shall make the earth for you a place of prostration (masjid) and a purifier (tahur). You may pray wherever the prayer overtakes you, except at a latrine, a bathhouse, or a grave. I shall place tranquility (sakinah) in your hearts, and I shall make you recite the Torah from memory. Each of you will recite it, man and woman, free and slave, young and old."

Musa told this to his people, and they said: "We do not want to pray except in churches. We cannot bear the tranquility in our hearts. We want it to be as it was in the ark (tabut). We cannot recite the Torah from memory; we want to read it only by looking at it."

God the Exalted said: "So I will prescribe it for those who fear God..." up to His words "...the successful" (﴿فَسَأَكْتُبُها لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ... ﴿الْمُفْلِحُونَ﴾). So He gave it to this community (ummah).

Musa said: "O my Lord, make me their prophet." He said: "Their prophet is from among them." He said: "My Lord, make me [one of] them." He said: "Indeed, you will not reach them." Musa said: "O my Lord, I brought You the delegation of the Children of Israel, and You made the delegation of others." Then God the Mighty and Majestic revealed: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾ [7:159]. Musa was content.

Nawf said: "So praise God who made the delegation of the Children of Israel to be yours."

Abu Nu'aym also related this story through al-Awza'i, who said: Yahya ibn Abi Amr al-Sibani [in al-Taqrib: with a fatha on the first letter, sukun on the ya, followed by a single ba; Sibaan is a clan of Himyar. Al-Tahdhib.] narrated to me, Nawf al-Bikali told me: [in manuscripts j, z, k, and y: "Abu 'Amr al-Bikali used to say, when he began an admonition..." Abu 'Amr is Nawf's kunya, and he may be narrating about himself.] When he began an admonition, he would say: "Will you not praise your Lord, who protected your absent ones, took on your behalf after your arrow (i.e., after your loss), and made the delegation of the people (the Children of Israel) belong to you?" That was because Musa, peace be upon him, led a delegation of the Children of Israel, and God said to them: "Indeed, I have made the earth for you a place of prostration; wherever you pray in it, I accept your prayer, except in three places: the graveyard, the bathhouse, and the latrine." They said: "No, only in the church." He said: "And I have made dust for you a purifier when you do not find water." They said: "No, only with water." He said: "And I have made it so that whenever a man prays alone, I accept his prayer." They said: "No, only in congregation."

**Second issue:** God's words: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the Unlettered﴾. These words, as we mentioned, excluded the Jews and Christians from the shared inclusion that appears in His words, "So I will prescribe it for those who fear God," and this promise became exclusive to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and others. "Follow" means in his law, his religion, and what he brought.

"Messenger" (rasul) and "Prophet" (nabi, one who receives news from God) are two names with two meanings: the messenger is more specific than the prophet. The messenger is mentioned first because of concern for the meaning of the message (risalah), though by the meaning of prophethood, it would be the earlier. For this reason, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) corrected al-Bara' when he said: "And in your Messenger whom you sent." He told him: "Say: I believe in your Prophet whom you sent." This was recorded in the Sahih. Also, in the phrase "and in your Messenger whom you sent," the message is repeated, and this is one meaning, so it would be like filler with no benefit. Unlike the phrase "and in your Prophet whom you sent," where there is no repetition. Based on this, every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger, because the messenger and the prophet share a general matter, which is news (naba'), and differ in a specific matter, which is the message (risalah). So when you say, "Muhammad is a messenger from God," that includes that he is a prophet and the messenger of God. The same applies to the other prophets, may God's blessings and peace be upon them.

**Third issue:** God's words: ﴿the Unlettered (ummi)﴾. It is derived from the "unlettered nation" (al-ummah al-ummiyyah), which remains in its original state of birth, not having learned writing or reading. Ibn 'Aziz [or 'Aziz; a scholar of the Maliki school. In manuscript l: Ibn Jarir. In k: Ibn al-'Arabi] said so. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: "Your Prophet (ﷺ) was unlettered; he did not write, read, or calculate." God the Exalted said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ [29:48]. It is related in the Sahih from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not calculate," and the hadith continues. It was also said that the Prophet (ﷺ) was called "unlettered" in reference to Mecca, the Mother of Cities (Umm al-Qura). This was mentioned by al-Nahhas.

**Fourth issue:** God's words: ﴿whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾. Al-Bukhari narrated, saying: Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated to us, saying: Fulayh narrated to us, saying: Hilal narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, who said: I met 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, and I said: "Tell me about the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the Torah." He said: "Yes, by God, he is indeed described in the Torah with some of his description in the Qur'an: 'O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, and a warner' [33:45], and a protection for the unlettered. You are My servant and My messenger. I have named you 'the one who relies (al-mutawakkil).' He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor loud in the markets. He does not repel evil with evil, but pardons and forgives. God will not take him until he establishes with him the crooked religion, by having them say, 'There is no god but God,' and opens with it blind eyes, deaf ears, and closed hearts."

Outside al-Bukhari [in manuscripts b, j, k, and y]: 'Ata' said: "Then I met Ka'b and asked him about that, and they did not differ in a single letter, except that Ka'b said in his own language: 'ghulufiyyan' for hearts, 'sumumiyyan' for ears, and 'umumiyyan' for eyes." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "I think this is a mistake or a foreign word." It has also been reported from Ka'b that he said: "qulubvarious ghuluf, aadhanan sumum, and a'yunan umumiyyan." Al-Tabari said: "It is a Himyari dialect." Ka'b added in describing the Prophet (ﷺ): "His birth is in Mecca, his migration (hijrah) is to Taba (Taybah, i.e., the city of Medina), and his kingdom is in Syria. His community are the praisers, who praise God in every state and in every place. They wash their extremities and wear their waist-wrappers to mid-shin. They are the shepherds of the sun. They pray the prayers wherever they are overtaken, even on the dunghill. Their rows in battle are like their rows in prayer." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, God loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, as if they were a well-set structure﴾ [61:4].

**Fifth issue:** God's words: ﴿He commands them what is right and forbids them what is wrong﴾. 'Ata' said: "He commands them what is right": to renounce rivals (of God) and to practice noble character and maintaining family ties. "He forbids them what is wrong": worshipping idols and severing family ties.

**Sixth issue:** God's words: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things﴾. The school of Malik holds that the "good things" (al-tayyibat) are the lawful things (al-muhallalat). It is as if He described them as good, since this word carries praise and honor. Accordingly, we say concerning the "wicked things" (al-khaba'ith) that they are the forbidden things (al-muharramat). This is why Ibn 'Abbas said: "The wicked things are pork, usury, and others." Based on this, Malik made lawful the disgusting things, such as snakes, scorpions, beetles, and similar creatures. The school of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, holds that the "good things" are good in terms of taste; however, the term, in his view, is not to be taken in its full generality. Its generality in this sense, in terms of taste, would require making wine and pork lawful. Rather, he holds that it applies specifically to what the law has made lawful. He takes the "wicked things" as a general term covering both what the law forbids and what is disgusting. Thus he forbids scorpions, beetles, geckos, and what is similar. People hold these two positions. This meaning was already discussed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 207].

**Seventh issue:** God's words: ﴿He removes from them their burden (isr)﴾. The isr is the weight. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Jubayr. Isr also means a covenant (ahd), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Hasan. This verse includes both meanings: a covenant was taken from the Children of Israel that they would perform heavy duties, and so God removed from them, through Muhammad (ﷺ), that covenant and the weight of those duties. Among them: washing away urine, prohibiting the spoils of war, avoiding sitting with, eating with, or sleeping with a menstruating woman. If urine touched a man's garment, he would cut it off. It is also related that he would cut off his skin. When they gathered spoils, a fire would descend from heaven and consume them. When a woman menstruated, they would not approach her, and so on, of what is established in the sound hadith and elsewhere [from manuscript 'ayn].

**Eighth issue:** God's words: ﴿and the shackles that were upon them﴾. The "shackles" (aghlal) are a metaphor for those burdens. Among the burdens is abstaining from work on Saturday. It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, saw a man carrying reeds on the Sabbath, and he struck off his neck. This is the view of the majority of exegetes, and there was no blood money (diyah) among them, only retaliation (qisas). They were also commanded to kill themselves as a sign of their repentance, and so on. This is compared to shackles, as the poet said:

"It is not like the old covenant of the abode, O Umm Malik,
but the chains have encircled the necks."

"The youth became like the elder, saying nothing
except justice, so the blamers rested."

He compared the limits (hudud) of Islam and its prohibitions that prevent transgression into forbidden things to chains encircling the necks. From this meaning is the saying of Abu Ahmad ibn Jahsh to Abu Sufyan:

"Take her away, take her away,
you have worn her as a dove wears a collar."

That is, her shame has clung to you. It is said: "So-and-so was collared with such-and-such" if it clings to him.

**Ninth issue:** If it is said: how can "shackles" (aghlal, plural) be conjoined with "burden" (isr, singular)? The answer: isr is a verbal noun (masdar) that can refer to many things. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿āṣārahum﴾ in the plural, like "their deeds" (a'malahum), so that the plural reflects the diversity of sins. The rest read it in the singular, because it is a verbal noun that denotes both the few and the many of its kind while its wording remains singular. They all agreed on the singular in His words: ﴿and do not lay upon us a burden (isran)﴾ [2:286]. And thus whenever this meaning occurs to you, as in ﴿and over their hearing﴾ [2:7] and ﴿their gaze will not return to them﴾ [14:43] and ﴿from a hidden glance﴾ [42:45], all of them carry the meaning of plurality.

**Tenth issue:** God's words: ﴿So those who believed in him and honored him﴾, i.e., revered him and supported him. Al-Akhfash said: al-Jahdari and 'Isa read ﴿wa 'azarahu﴾ with a lighter pronunciation. Similarly, ﴿wa 'azartumuhum﴾ [48:9]. It is said: 'azarahu, ya'zuruhu and ya'uzzuruhu. ﴿The light (al-nur)﴾ is the Qur'an. ﴿The success (al-falah)﴾ is attaining what is sought. This has already been discussed [here].

It is mentioned that Musa gave glad tidings of him (the Prophet ﷺ), and that Isa gave glad tidings of him. Then Allah commanded him to say of himself: ﴿Indeed, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾. And ﴿His words﴾ refers to the words of Allah, the Exalted, His Books: from the Torah, the Gospel (al-Injil), and the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 159:

﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it they act justly.﴾ (7:159)

That is, they call people to guidance. The phrase ﴿yaʿdilun﴾ (they act justly) means in judgment. It is said in the tafsir: these are a people beyond China, beyond the river of sand (nahr al-Raml), who worship Allah with truth and justice. They believed in Muhammad and abandoned the Sabbath (al-sabt), they face our qibla, and none of them reaches us nor do any of us reach them.

It is related that when disagreement arose after Musa, there was among them a community who guided by the truth, but they were unable to remain among the Children of Israel, so Allah brought them out to a region of His earth, isolated from creation. A tunnel (sarab) appeared for them in the earth, and they walked in it for a year and a half until they emerged beyond China, and they remain upon the truth until now. Between the people and them there is a sea, by which they cannot be reached.

Jibril took the Prophet (ﷺ) to them on the night of the Mi'raj, and they believed in him. He taught them some surahs of the Qur'an and said to them: "Do you have a measure (mikyal) and a balance (mizan)?" They said: "No." He said: "Then from where do you obtain your livelihood?" They said: "We go out to the wilderness and sow, and when we harvest we place it there, and when any of us needs it, he takes his need." He said: "Then where are your women?" They said: "In a region apart from us, and when any of us needs his wife, he goes to her at the time of need." He said: "Does any of you lie in his speech?" They said: "If any of us did that, Laza would seize him; indeed the fire descends and burns him." He said: "Then what is the matter with your houses being level?" They said: "So that none of us rises above another." He said: "Then what is the matter with your graves being at your doors?" They said: "So that we do not become heedless of the remembrance of death."

Then, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to the world on the night of the Isra', there was revealed to him: ﴿And among those whom We created is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ [[See p. 329 of this part. Consider this together with the fact that the verse is Medinan by consensus.]] Meaning the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him). It informs him that what I gave Musa among his people, I give you among your community. It was also said: they are those among the People of the Book who believed in our Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It was also said: they are a people from the Children of Israel who adhered to the law of Musa before its abrogation, and who did not alter nor kill the prophets.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 160–162:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes (asbat), as nations﴾ [7:160]. He enumerated His blessings upon the Children of Israel, and made them into tribes (asbat) so that the affair of each tribe would be known through its leader (ra'is), and so the matter would be lighter upon Musa. In the Revelation: ﴿And We raised up from them twelve chiefs (naqib)﴾ [5:12], and this has already been discussed [see vol. 6, p. 112].

As for His saying, "twelve (ithnata 'ashrata)": the word sibt (tribe) is masculine, because after it comes "umaman (nations)," so the feminine form was applied to umam. Had he said "ithna 'ashar" to match the masculine sibt, it would have been permissible, according to al-Farra'.

It was also said: he meant by asbat the clans (qaba'il) and factions (firaq), and for this reason the number was made feminine. The poet said:

"Indeed, Quraysh, all of it, is ten butun (clans),
and you are innocent of its ten clans."

He took the word batn (clan) to mean the tribe and the subdivision, and for this reason made the number feminine. The word batn is masculine, just as asbat is the plural of a masculine noun.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "We divided them into twelve groups (firqah)." Asbatan is a substitute (badal) for ithnata 'ashrata, and umaman is an attribute (na't) of asbat.

Al-Mufaddal related from 'Asim: "wa qatta'nahum" with a light (takhfif) pronunciation.

"Asbatan": the asbat among the descendants of Ishaq hold the position of the qaba'il among the descendants of Isma'il, peace be upon them both. The word asbat is derived from sabat, which is a tree that camels feed upon. This was already discussed fully in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 140].

Ma'mar related from Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So those who did wrong among them changed the word to other than what had been said to them﴾ [7:162]. He said: "They said: 'A grain in a hair.'" And it was said to them: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾ [7:161], and they entered squatting on their buttocks (mutawarrikin 'ala astahim).

﴿For what they used to do wrongfully﴾ [7:162] is in the nominative (marfu') because it is an imperfect verb (fi'l mustaqbal), and its position is accusative (nasb). And "ma" is in the sense of the verbal noun (masdar), i.e., "for their wrongdoing."

What the meanings and rulings of this verse are has already passed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 409].

And all praise is due to Allah.

And ask them about the town, meaning the people of the town. He referred to them by the town because it was their dwelling place or the cause of their gathering. Its counterpart is ﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾. And his saying, peace be upon him: "The Throne shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh," meaning the people of the Throne among the angels, out of joy and gladness at his arrival, may Allah be pleased with him. That is, ask the Jews who are your neighbours about the reports of their forefathers and what Allah transformed of them into apes and swine. This is a question of confirmation and rebuke. This was a sign of the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ, since Allah informed him of these matters without his having learned them. They used to say: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved, for we are from the tribe of His friend Abraham, from the tribe of Israel, who is the firstborn of Allah, from the tribe of Moses, the one who spoke with Allah, and from the tribe of his son 'Uzayr, so we are their descendants." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to His Prophet: "Ask them, O Muhammad, about the town, [to see] whether He punished them for their sins," and that is by changing a branch of the branches of the Shari'ah.

The identity of this town has been disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi said: it is Ayla. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: it is Madyan, between Ayla and Tur. Al-Zuhri said: Tiberias. Qatadah and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is a coastal town on the coasts of Syria, between Madyan and 'Aynun, called Maqnah. The Jews used to conceal this story because of the disgrace it contained for them.

﴿Which was by the sea﴾, that is, it was near the sea. You say: "I was in the vicinity (hadrah) of the house," meaning near it. [The phrase "by the sea" carries a sense of honour. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: it may mean the sense of "the town" in the sense of honouring it, that is, it was the principal town among the towns of the sea, etc.]

﴿When they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾, that is, they hunted fish, though they had been forbidden from it. It is said: "the Jews sabbatized (sabata)," meaning they abstained from work on their Sabbath. "Sabata al-rajul" in the passive means he was seized by sabat, from paralysis. "Asbata" means he became still and did not move. "Al-qawm" means they entered the Sabbath. "Al-yahud" means they entered the Sabbath, which is the well-known day. It derives from rest and cessation. Its plural is asbut, subut and asbat. In a report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever cups himself on Saturday and is afflicted with leprosy, let him blame none but himself." Our scholars said: that is because the blood congeals on Saturday, so if you draw it out to extract it, it does not flow, and it turns into leprosy. The recitation of the community is ﴿ya'dunna﴾. Abu Nuhayk recited "yu'iddunna" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the 'ayn and a shaddah on the dāl. The first is from transgression (i'tida') and the second is from preparation (i'dad), meaning they prepare the equipment for catching them. Ibn al-Sumayqa recited "fi al-asbat," as the plural of sabt. [It was also read as "yawma asbatihim."] ﴿When their fish come to them on their Sabbath day﴾, and it was read as "asbatihim." ﴿Openly﴾, that is, appearing in great numbers upon the water. Al-Layth said: "Fish shura'" means fish raising their heads. It was also said: the meaning is that the fish of the sea used to come on Saturday in droves (unuq) from the sea and crowd Ayla. Allah inspired them that they should not be hunted on Saturday, because of His prohibiting the Jews from hunting them. It was also said: they used to appear at their doors like white rams with their heads raised. This was related by some later scholars. So they transgressed and took them on the Sabbath, as al-Hasan said. It was also said: it was on Sunday, and this is the most correct view, as will be explained.

﴿And on the day they do not keep the Sabbath﴾, that is, they do not observe the Sabbath. It is said: "sabata yasbutu" when one honours the Sabbath. Al-Hasan read "yusbituna" with a damma on the yā', meaning they enter into the Sabbath, as one says: "ajma'na, azhharna, ash'arna," meaning we entered into Friday, noon and the month. ﴿They do not come to them﴾, that is, their fish. ﴿Thus We test them﴾, that is, We impose hardship on them in worship and test them. The kāf is in the accusative position. ﴿Because they were defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, because of their defiance.

Husayn ibn al-Fadl was asked: "Do you find in the Book of Allah that the lawful comes to you only as sustenance, while the unlawful comes to you in abundance, abundance?" He said: "Yes, in the story of Dawud and Ayla: ﴿When their fish come to them on their Sabbath day, openly, and on the day they do not keep the Sabbath they do not come to them﴾." It is related in the narratives of this verse that it was in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, and that Iblis inspired them, saying: "You were only forbidden to take them on Saturday, so make pools." They used to drive the fish into them on Friday, and the fish would remain there, unable to come out because of the scarcity of water, and they would take them on Sunday. Ashhab related from Malik who said: Ibn Rumman claimed that a man would take a cord and put on it a noose (wahqah) [The wahq, with the vowel or sukun on the hā', is a rope with a slipknot at its end, cast around the neck of an animal or a person until it is seized. The uqshuwanah is a knot that is easy to undo; when one takes hold of one of its ends it opens, like the knot of a drawstring.] and cast it into the fish's tail, and at the other end of the cord he would place a peg, leaving it so until Sunday. Then people, seeing that the one who did this was not being tested, began to act likewise, until fish became plentiful and were carried about in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted them. Then a group from the Children of Israel stood up, forbade it, openly admonished, and withdrew. It was also said: the forbidders said, "We will not live with you," and they divided the town with a wall. One day the forbidders woke up in their assemblies, and none of the transgressors had come out. They said: "The people have some affair." So they climbed the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the door and went in to them. The apes recognised their kin among the humans, but the humans did not recognise their kin among the apes. The apes began to come to their relatives among the humans, sniffing their clothes and weeping. He would say, "Did we not forbid you?" and it would nod its head, "Yes." Qatadah said: the young men became apes and the elders became swine. Only those who forbade were saved, and the rest perished. According to this view, the Children of Israel divided only into two groups. The meaning of His saying, "And when a community among them said, 'Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy or punish with a severe punishment?'" would be: those who committed the transgression said to the admonishers when they admonished them: "If you know that Allah will destroy us, why do you admonish us?" So Allah transformed them into apes.

﴿They said: "An excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they may fear Him."﴾ That is, the admonishers said: "Our admonition to you is an excuse (ma'dhirah) [to your Lord], that is, it is incumbent upon us to admonish you so that perhaps you may be mindful." Al-Tabari attributed this saying to Ibn al-Kalbi. The majority of exegetes said: the Children of Israel divided into three groups, and this is the apparent meaning from the pronouns in the verse. One group was preserved (from wrongdoing) and refrained from hunting; they numbered about seventy thousand. Another group withdrew, neither forbidding nor disobeying, and this group said to the forbidders: "Why do you admonish a people, meaning the disobedient ones, whom Allah will destroy or punish, based on a strong supposition, and in light of what is known of Allah's dealings with disobedient nations at that time?" The forbidders replied: "Our admonition is an excuse to Allah, perhaps they may be mindful." Had they been two groups, the forbidders would have said to the disobedient: "perhaps you (plural, with the kāf) may be mindful." Then scholars differed after this. One group said that the group which neither forbade nor disobeyed perished along with the disobedient as a punishment for abandoning the forbidding, as Ibn 'Abbas said. He also said: "I do not know what was done to them," and this is the apparent meaning of the verse. 'Ikrimah said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas, when he said "I do not know what was done to them": "Do you not see that they disliked what those people were doing and opposed them, saying: 'Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy?'" I kept at him until I made him understand that they had been saved, and he clothed me in a robe. This is the view of al-Hasan. Among what shows that only the transgressing group perished is His saying: "And We seized those who did wrong," and His saying: "And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath," and the verse following.

'Isa and Talhah read "ma'dhiratan" in the accusative. According to al-Kisa'i, its accusative has two aspects: first, as a verbal noun (masdar); second, as implying "We did that as an excuse." This is the recitation of Hafs from 'Asim. The rest read it in the nominative, which is the preferred reading, because they did not want to offer an excuse that is an independent new statement about a matter for which they were being blamed. Rather, they were asked: "Why do you admonish?" and they replied: "Our admonition is an excuse." If a man said to another, "An excuse to Allah and to you for such-and-such," meaning an excuse, it would be in the accusative. This is the statement of Sibawayh.

The verse indicates the view of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i') to what is forbidden. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah). It was also discussed there whether a transformed person (mamsukh) reproduces or not, explained in detail [see vol. 1, p. 439 onward]. And praise be to Allah. In Al 'Imran and al-Ma'idah, the command to do good and the prohibition of wrong were discussed [see vol. 4, p. 46, and vol. 6, p. 253]. In al-Nisa' the withdrawal from corrupt people and avoiding them was discussed, and that whoever sits with them becomes like them, so there is no point in repeating it [see vol. 5, p. 417 onward].
