﴿Which was by the sea﴾, that is, it was near the sea. You say: "I was in the vicinity (hadrah) of the house," meaning near it. [The phrase "by the sea" carries a sense of honour. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: it may mean the sense of "the town" in the sense of honouring it, that is, it was the principal town among the towns of the sea, etc.]

﴿When they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾, that is, they hunted fish, though they had been forbidden from it. It is said: "the Jews sabbatized (sabata)," meaning they abstained from work on their Sabbath. "Sabata al-rajul" in the passive means he was seized by sabat, from paralysis. "Asbata" means he became still and did not move. "Al-qawm" means they entered the Sabbath. "Al-yahud" means they entered the Sabbath, which is the well-known day. It derives from rest and cessation. Its plural is asbut, subut and asbat. In a report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever cups himself on Saturday and is afflicted with leprosy, let him blame none but himself." Our scholars said: that is because the blood congeals on Saturday, so if you draw it out to extract it, it does not flow, and it turns into leprosy. The recitation of the community is ﴿ya'dunna﴾. Abu Nuhayk recited "yu'iddunna" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the 'ayn and a shaddah on the dāl. The first is from transgression (i'tida') and the second is from preparation (i'dad), meaning they prepare the equipment for catching them. Ibn al-Sumayqa recited "fi al-asbat," as the plural of sabt. [It was also read as "yawma asbatihim."] ﴿When their fish come to them on their Sabbath day﴾, and it was read as "asbatihim." ﴿Openly﴾, that is, appearing in great numbers upon the water. Al-Layth said: "Fish shura'" means fish raising their heads. It was also said: the meaning is that the fish of the sea used to come on Saturday in droves (unuq) from the sea and crowd Ayla. Allah inspired them that they should not be hunted on Saturday, because of His prohibiting the Jews from hunting them. It was also said: they used to appear at their doors like white rams with their heads raised. This was related by some later scholars. So they transgressed and took them on the Sabbath, as al-Hasan said. It was also said: it was on Sunday, and this is the most correct view, as will be explained.

﴿And on the day they do not keep the Sabbath﴾, that is, they do not observe the Sabbath. It is said: "sabata yasbutu" when one honours the Sabbath. Al-Hasan read "yusbituna" with a damma on the yā', meaning they enter into the Sabbath, as one says: "ajma'na, azhharna, ash'arna," meaning we entered into Friday, noon and the month. ﴿They do not come to them﴾, that is, their fish. ﴿Thus We test them﴾, that is, We impose hardship on them in worship and test them. The kāf is in the accusative position. ﴿Because they were defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, because of their defiance.

Husayn ibn al-Fadl was asked: "Do you find in the Book of Allah that the lawful comes to you only as sustenance, while the unlawful comes to you in abundance, abundance?" He said: "Yes, in the story of Dawud and Ayla: ﴿When their fish come to them on their Sabbath day, openly, and on the day they do not keep the Sabbath they do not come to them﴾." It is related in the narratives of this verse that it was in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, and that Iblis inspired them, saying: "You were only forbidden to take them on Saturday, so make pools." They used to drive the fish into them on Friday, and the fish would remain there, unable to come out because of the scarcity of water, and they would take them on Sunday. Ashhab related from Malik who said: Ibn Rumman claimed that a man would take a cord and put on it a noose (wahqah) [The wahq, with the vowel or sukun on the hā', is a rope with a slipknot at its end, cast around the neck of an animal or a person until it is seized. The uqshuwanah is a knot that is easy to undo; when one takes hold of one of its ends it opens, like the knot of a drawstring.] and cast it into the fish's tail, and at the other end of the cord he would place a peg, leaving it so until Sunday. Then people, seeing that the one who did this was not being tested, began to act likewise, until fish became plentiful and were carried about in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted them. Then a group from the Children of Israel stood up, forbade it, openly admonished, and withdrew. It was also said: the forbidders said, "We will not live with you," and they divided the town with a wall. One day the forbidders woke up in their assemblies, and none of the transgressors had come out. They said: "The people have some affair." So they climbed the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the door and went in to them. The apes recognised their kin among the humans, but the humans did not recognise their kin among the apes. The apes began to come to their relatives among the humans, sniffing their clothes and weeping. He would say, "Did we not forbid you?" and it would nod its head, "Yes." Qatadah said: the young men became apes and the elders became swine. Only those who forbade were saved, and the rest perished. According to this view, the Children of Israel divided only into two groups. The meaning of His saying, "And when a community among them said, 'Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy or punish with a severe punishment?'" would be: those who committed the transgression said to the admonishers when they admonished them: "If you know that Allah will destroy us, why do you admonish us?" So Allah transformed them into apes.

﴿They said: "An excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they may fear Him."﴾ That is, the admonishers said: "Our admonition to you is an excuse (ma'dhirah) [to your Lord], that is, it is incumbent upon us to admonish you so that perhaps you may be mindful." Al-Tabari attributed this saying to Ibn al-Kalbi. The majority of exegetes said: the Children of Israel divided into three groups, and this is the apparent meaning from the pronouns in the verse. One group was preserved (from wrongdoing) and refrained from hunting; they numbered about seventy thousand. Another group withdrew, neither forbidding nor disobeying, and this group said to the forbidders: "Why do you admonish a people, meaning the disobedient ones, whom Allah will destroy or punish, based on a strong supposition, and in light of what is known of Allah's dealings with disobedient nations at that time?" The forbidders replied: "Our admonition is an excuse to Allah, perhaps they may be mindful." Had they been two groups, the forbidders would have said to the disobedient: "perhaps you (plural, with the kāf) may be mindful." Then scholars differed after this. One group said that the group which neither forbade nor disobeyed perished along with the disobedient as a punishment for abandoning the forbidding, as Ibn 'Abbas said. He also said: "I do not know what was done to them," and this is the apparent meaning of the verse. 'Ikrimah said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas, when he said "I do not know what was done to them": "Do you not see that they disliked what those people were doing and opposed them, saying: 'Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy?'" I kept at him until I made him understand that they had been saved, and he clothed me in a robe. This is the view of al-Hasan. Among what shows that only the transgressing group perished is His saying: "And We seized those who did wrong," and His saying: "And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath," and the verse following.

'Isa and Talhah read "ma'dhiratan" in the accusative. According to al-Kisa'i, its accusative has two aspects: first, as a verbal noun (masdar); second, as implying "We did that as an excuse." This is the recitation of Hafs from 'Asim. The rest read it in the nominative, which is the preferred reading, because they did not want to offer an excuse that is an independent new statement about a matter for which they were being blamed. Rather, they were asked: "Why do you admonish?" and they replied: "Our admonition is an excuse." If a man said to another, "An excuse to Allah and to you for such-and-such," meaning an excuse, it would be in the accusative. This is the statement of Sibawayh.

The verse indicates the view of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i') to what is forbidden. This has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah). It was also discussed there whether a transformed person (mamsukh) reproduces or not, explained in detail [see vol. 1, p. 439 onward]. And praise be to Allah. In Al 'Imran and al-Ma'idah, the command to do good and the prohibition of wrong were discussed [see vol. 4, p. 46, and vol. 6, p. 253]. In al-Nisa' the withdrawal from corrupt people and avoiding them was discussed, and that whoever sits with them becomes like them, so there is no point in repeating it [see vol. 5, p. 417 onward].

Al-Nisyan (forgetting) is applied to one who is heedless (al-sahi). And al-'amid (the deliberate one) is one who abandons, based on His Exalted saying: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, meaning they abandoned it intentionally. From this is the saying: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 199.]]. The meaning of ﴿with a grievous punishment﴾ is severe.

Regarding it there are eleven readings (qira'at). The first: the reading of Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, "bai'is" (بَئِيسٍ), on the pattern fa'il (فَعِيلٍ). The second: the reading of the people of Makkah, "bi'is" (بِئِيسٍ), with the bā' kasrah, and the pattern is the same. The third: the reading of the people of Madinah, "bis" (بِيسٍ), with the bā' kasrah, followed by a sākin yā', followed by a kasrah sīn with tanwin, and concerning it there are two opinions. Al-Kisa'i said: the original form is "bai'is" with a light hamzah, so two yā's met and one was deleted, and its first letter was kasrah, as is said: raghif and shahid. It was also said: he intended "ba'is" (بَئِسَ) on the pattern fa'il (فَعِلَ), so he kasrahed its first letter, lightened the hamzah and deleted the kasrah, as is said: raḥima and riḥm. The fourth: the reading of al-Hasan, the bā' kasrah, followed by a sākin hamzah, followed by a fatḥah sīn. The fifth: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri' read "ba'isin" (بَئِسٍ), with the bā' fatḥah, the hamzah kasrah and the sīn kasrah with tanwin. The sixth: Ya'qub al-Qari said: it came from some of the readers "bi'ais" (بِعَذَابٍ بَئِسَ), with the bā' fatḥah, the hamzah kasrah and the sīn fatḥah. The seventh: the reading of al-A'mash "bay'is" (بَيْئِسٍ) on the pattern fay'al (فَيْعَلٍ). It was narrated from him "bay'is" on the pattern fay'al. It was also narrated from him "ba'iss" (بَئِّسٍ) with a fatḥah bā', a shaddah and kasrah hamzah, and the sīn in all of these is kasrah with tanwin, I mean the reading of al-A'mash. The tenth: the reading of Nasr ibn 'Asim [[Nasr ibn 'Asim al-Laythi al-Basri.]] "bi'adhabin bayyis" (بِعَذَابٍ بَيِّسٍ), with the bā' fatḥah, the yā' shaddah, without hamzah. Ya'qub al-Qari said: it came from some of the readers "bi'yis" (بِئْيَسٍ), with the bā' kasrah, followed by a sākin hamzah, followed by a fatḥah yā'. These are the eleven readings mentioned by al-Nahhas.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: the Arabs say "ja'a bi-banatin bis" (جَاءَ بِبَنَاتٍ بِيسٍ), meaning with something bad (radi'). So the meaning of "bi'adhabin bis" is with a bad punishment.

As for the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Hatim claimed that it has no basis, saying: "One does not say 'marartu bi-rajulin bi'sa' (I passed by a man, bi'sa) until one says 'bi'sa al-rajulu' or 'bi'sa rajulan.'" Al-Nahhas said: this is rejected from the words of Abu Hatim; the grammarians have related: "in fa'alta kadha wa kadha fa-biha wa ni'mat" (if you do such and such, then with it, and how excellent it is), meaning "fiha wa ni'mati al-khasla" (in it, and how excellent is the quality). The estimated reading of al-Hasan is: "bi-'idhabin bi'sa al-'adhab" (with a punishment, how wretched the punishment is).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when they transgressed against what they had been forbidden﴾, meaning: when they went beyond bounds in disobeying Allah.

(We said to them: "Be apes, despised and rejected.") It is said: "khasa'tuhu fakhasa'," meaning: I removed him and drove him away. This has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 443]. And it indicates that sins are the cause of retribution, and this is not hidden. It is said: He said this to them in an audible speech, and so they became that way. And it is said: the meaning is "We made them apes."

And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict on them the worst torment. Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful. ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed...﴾ (7:167)

That is, He informed their forefathers that if they altered (the Torah) and did not believe in the Unlettered Prophet, God would send against them those who would punish them.

Abu ʿAli said: "ādhana" with the long vowel (ā) means "to inform" (aʿlama). And "adhdhana" with the doubled letter (shaddah) means "to call out" (nādā). Some people said: "ādhana" and "adhdhana" have the same meaning as "aʿlama," just as one says "ayqana" and "tayaqqana" (both meaning "to be certain"). Zuhayr said:

"I said, 'Know that for the game there is a blind spot; if you do not lay it aside, you will surely be its killer.'"

Another said:

"Know that the worst of people is alive, proclaimed by the name of Yasar in their battle-cry."

That is, "iʿlam" (know). [[Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: "It was treated as a verb of oath, and therefore it is answered with what is used to answer an oath. Al-Zamakhshari also said this."]]

The meaning of "yasumuhum" is "to make them taste" (yudhiquhum), and it has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 384.]]).

It was said: the intended people are Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar). It was said: the Arabs. It was said: the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the most apparent, for they are the ones who will remain until the Day of Resurrection. And God knows best.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Worst of torment" (sūʾ al-ʿadhāb) here means the imposition of the jizya (poll tax). If it is said: they were transformed (into apes and swine), so how is the jizya taken from them? The answer is that it is taken from their sons and their offspring, and they are the most humiliated of people, and they are the Jews.

Regarding Saʿid ibn Jubayr, "worst of torment" he said: it is the kharaj (land tax). No prophet ever collected the kharaj except Musa, peace be upon him. He was the first to impose the kharaj, so he collected it for thirteen years, then stopped. And our Prophet, peace be upon him.

We divided them into groups throughout the land. He meant by this the scattering of their affairs, so that no single word was gathered for them.

(Among them are the righteous) is in the nominative case, as the subject of a nominal sentence. What is meant is those who believed in Muhammad (peace be upon him), and those who did not change and died upon the law of Musa (Moses). Or they are those beyond China, as has already been mentioned.

(And among them are others below that) is in the accusative case, functioning as an adverb of place (ẓarf). Al-Nahhas said: "We do not know of anyone who put it in the nominative." What is meant are the disbelievers among them.

(And We tested them) that is, We examined them.

(With good things) that is, with abundance and well-being.

(And bad things) that is, with barrenness and hardships.

(So that they might return) so that they would turn back from their disbelief.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾. He means the descendants of those whom He had dispersed over the earth. Abu Hatim said: "*Al-khalf*" (with a sukun on the lam) means descendants, and the singular and plural are the same in it. "*Al-khalaf*" (with a fatha on the lam) means a replacement, whether a son or a stranger. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "*Al-khalaf*" with a fatha means the righteous, and with a sukun means the wicked. Labid said:

*Gone are those among whose flanks one used to live,*
*and I remain among a successor like the skin of a mangy camel.*

From this comes the saying about poor speech: *khalf*. And from it comes the well-known proverb: "He kept silent for a thousand and spoke a *khalf*." So *khalf* with a sukun is used in dispraise, and *khalaf* with a fatha is used in praise. This is the common and well-known usage. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This knowledge will be carried by the trustworthy ones of every *khalaf*." Each of the two may be used in place of the other. Hassan ibn Thabit said:

*The first step toward You is ours, and our successors*
*follow our first ones in obedience to God.*

Another said:

*Indeed we found a successor, an evil successor,*
*who shut his door against us and then swore an oath.*

[[As these verses are given in the sources: the reading in the original texts is as above, while in *Lisan al-Arab* under the root *kh-d-f* it reads:

*Indeed we found a successor, an evil successor,*
*a servant who, when he is burdened with a load, bends down.*

*He shut his door against us and then swore an oath,*
*and the doorkeeper admits only one he recognizes.*]]

*The doorkeeper admits only one he recognizes,*
*a servant who, when he is burdened with a load, stands still.*

It is also transmitted as *khadafa*, meaning he broke wind (*radama*). [[*Al-radm*: flatulence.]] The purpose of the verse is dispraise.

(﴿They inherited the Book﴾) The exegetes said: they are the Jews, who inherited the Book of God, read it and knew it, yet opposed its ruling and committed its prohibited acts despite their studying it. This was a rebuke and a reproof to them. ﴿They take the goods of this lower world﴾. Then He informed about them that they take whatever worldly goods come to them, because of their intense greed and avidity.

(﴿And they say: "We shall be forgiven"﴾) while they do not repent. This indicates that they do not repent.

The verse: ﴿And if goods like it come to them, they will take them﴾. *Al-'arad* is the goods of this world, with a fatha on the ra'. With a sukun, it means any property other than dirhams and dinars. The reference in this verse is to bribes and corrupt earnings. Then He censured them for their delusion in their saying (﴿We shall be forgiven﴾), and that they are in a state where, if the opportunity came again, they would commit it. Thus they were certain of forgiveness through their delusion while persisting in sin, whereas only one who has desisted and regretted says "We shall be forgiven."

I say: this quality for which God censured these people exists among us. Abu Muhammad al-Darimi transmitted with a chain of narration (*isnad*) [[*Isnad*: the chain of transmitters of a report.]]: Muhammad ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, Sadaqa ibn Khalid narrated to us, from Ibn Jabir, from a shaykh known as Abu Amr, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may God be pleased with him), who said: "The Qur'an will decay in the hearts of people as a garment decays and falls apart. They will recite it without finding in it any desire or pleasure. They will wear sheepskins over wolves' hearts. Their deeds will be greed mixed with no fear. If they fall short, they say: 'We shall reach it.' And if they do evil, they say: 'We shall be forgiven. Indeed we do not associate anything with God.'"

It is also said that the pronoun in "*ya'tihim*" refers to the Jews of Medina, meaning: and if there comes to the Jews of Yathrib, who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), goods like it, they will take them, just as their forefathers took them.

The verse: ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they should not say about God except the truth, and that they studied what is in it? And the Last Abode is better for those who fear God. Will you not then reason?﴾ There are two issues in it.

The first: His saying ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them﴾ means the Torah. This is an emphasis on the obligation to speak the truth in the law and the rulings, and that rulers should not incline to falsehood through bribery. I say: what was obligatory for these people, and for which a covenant was taken from them to speak the truth, is obligatory for us too, through the tongue of our Prophet (ﷺ) and the Book of our Lord, as its explanation has already been given in (*al-Nisa*) [[See vol. 6, p. 7 onward.]]. There is no disagreement about it in all the sacred laws, and praise be to God.

The second: His saying (﴿and they studied what is in it﴾), that is, they read it, while they were recent in their knowledge of it. Abu Abd al-Rahman read *wa-darasu* [with a doubled dal, as in *wa-iddarasu*], so the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*. [[As in the source text, the reading is given as it stands in the manuscripts; the explanation in *al-Bahr* is that the original was *tadarasu*, i.e., it was assimilated.]] Ibn Zayd said: the one who was in the right would come to them with a bribe, and they would bring out the Book of God for him and rule in his favour according to it. When the wrongdoer came, they would take a bribe from him, bring out for him their own book that they had written with their own hands, and rule in his favour. Ibn Abbas said: "that they should not say about God except the truth" — yet they said falsehood about the forgiveness of their sins, which they claimed as necessary and asserted with certainty. Ibn Zayd said: it means in the rulings they pass, as we have mentioned. Some scholars said that the meaning of "*wa-darasu ma fihi*" is that they erased it, by abandoning acting on it and understanding it, from your saying: "The wind effaced the traces" when it erased them, and "a line of writing is effaced and a campsite is effaced" when its trace has vanished and faded. This meaning agrees [*muwati'*, i.e., is consistent] with His saying: ﴿A group of those who were given the Book threw the Book of God behind their backs﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 41.]] — the verse — and His saying: ﴿So they threw it behind their backs﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 304.]], as its explanation has already been given in (*al-Baqara*).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 170:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾ (wa-alladhina yumassikuna bil-kitab), i.e., to the Torah, meaning by acting upon it. It is said: "massaka bihi" and "tamassaka bihi," meaning "istamsaka bihi" (he held fast to it).

Abu al-Aliyah and ʿAsim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "yumsikuna" with the light form (takhfif), from "amsaka yumsiku" (to grasp). The first reading is preferable, because it carries the sense of repetition and intensification in holding fast to the Book of Allah, exalted is He, and to His religion; by this they are praised. Holding fast to the Book of Allah and to the religion requires constancy and repeated practice of it.

Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

*Fa-ma tamassaka bil-ʿahdi alladhi zaʿamta*
*illa kama tumsiku al-ma'a al-gharabil*

He brought it in his own natural style, censuring the frequent breaking of covenants.

"Qur'an 7:171: (And [recall] when We raised the mountain above them) — "nataqna" (نَتَقْنَا) means "raised" (rafa'na). Its explanation has already been given in al-Baqarah. "As if it were a canopy" — i.e., because of its height, it was as if it were a cloud providing shade. "Take what We have given you with strength" — i.e., with earnestness. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 436.]] up to the end of the verse."

There are six issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words ﴿And when your Lord took...﴾. The meaning is: "Remind them, along with what has already been mentioned of the covenants in their Scripture, of the covenant I took from the servants on the Day of Dhar (the Day of Atoms)." This verse is difficult (mushkilah), and the scholars have spoken about its interpretation (ta'wil) and its rulings (ahkam). We will mention what they said, as far as we have come to know it. Some said: the meaning of the verse is that God, exalted is He, brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam some of them from others. They said: the meaning of "He made them testify concerning themselves: 'Am I not your Lord?'" is that He pointed them, through His creation, to His oneness, since every adult knows by necessity that he has one Lord. "Am I not your Lord?" means: He said. This took the place of making them testify and of their acknowledgment, just as He said concerning the heavens and the earth: ﴿We come willingly﴾ (See vol. 15, p. 344.). This was the view of al-Qaffal, who elaborated on it at length. It was also said that He, glorified is He, brought forth the souls (arwah) before creating the bodies, and placed in them such knowledge that by it they knew when He addressed them. I say: a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ indicates other than these two views, namely that God brought forth the forms (ashbah) with the souls in them from the back of Adam, peace be upon him. Malik narrated in his Muwatta' that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about this verse: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ being asked about it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, created Adam, then wiped his back with His right hand and brought forth from it offspring. He said: 'I created these for Paradise, and they will act with the deeds of the people of Paradise.' Then He wiped his back and brought forth from it offspring, and said: 'I created these for Paradise, and they will act with the deeds of the people of Paradise.' Then He wiped his back and brought forth from it offspring, and said: 'I created these for the Fire, and they will act with the deeds of the people of the Fire.'" A man said: "Then what is the point of deeds?" He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, when Allah creates a servant for Paradise, He makes him act with the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of Paradise, and so He admits him into Paradise. And when He creates a servant for the Fire, He makes him act with the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of the Fire, and so Allah admits him into the Fire." Abu 'Umar said: This hadith has a discontinuous chain of transmission (munqati' al-isnad), because Muslim ibn Yasar did not meet 'Umar. Yahya ibn Ma'in said concerning it: Muslim ibn Yasar is not known; between him and 'Umar is Nu'aym ibn Rabi'ah, whom al-Nasa'i mentioned, and Nu'aym is not known for bearing knowledge. However, the meaning of this hadith has been authentically related from the Prophet ﷺ through many firm channels, from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them all, and others. al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sound, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Allah created Adam, He wiped his back, and there fell from his back every soul (nasamah) that He would create from his offspring until the Day of Resurrection. He placed between the eyes of each man among them a gleam of light. Then He presented them to Adam, and he said: 'O Lord, who are these?' He said: 'These are your descendants.' He saw a man among them and was pleased by the gleam between his eyes, and he said: 'O my Lord, who is this?' He said: 'This is a man from the last of the nations from your descendants, called Dawud.' He said: 'My Lord, how long have You made his life?' He said: 'Sixty years.' In another narration: "He saw among them the weak and the rich, the poor and the humiliated, the afflicted and the healthy. Adam said to Him: 'O Lord, what is this? Why did You not make them equal?' He said: 'I wished to be thanked.'" 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "They were taken from his back as a comb is drawn through hair." And Allah gave them intellects like the ant of Sulayman, and took from them the covenant that He is their Lord and that there is no god but Him. They acknowledged this and bound themselves to it, and He informed them that He would send them messengers, so some of them bore witness against others. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: He also called the seven heavens to witness against them. So there is no one born until the Day of Resurrection except that the covenant has been taken from him. There are four opinions regarding the place where the covenant was taken when they were brought forth. Ibn 'Abbas said: in Batn Nu'man, a valley beside 'Arafah. And it is related from him that it was in Rahba, a land in India, where Adam descended. Yahya ibn Sallam said that Ibn 'Abbas said concerning this verse: God lowered Adam to India, then wiped his back and brought forth from it every soul that He would create until the Day of Resurrection, then said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes, we testify.﴾ Yahya said: al-Hasan said: Then He returned them into the loins of Adam, peace be upon him. al-Kalbi said: between Makkah and al-Ta'if. al-Suddi said: in the lowest heaven, when he was brought down from Paradise to it. He wiped his back and brought forth from the right side of his back offspring white like pearls, and said to them: "Enter Paradise by My mercy." And he brought forth from the left side of his back offspring black, and said to them: "Enter the Fire, and I do not care." Ibn Jurayj said: every soul created for Paradise came forth white, and every soul created for the Fire came forth black. The second issue: Ibn al-'Arabi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "If it is asked: how is it permissible for Him to punish creatures when they have not sinned, or to punish them for what He willed of them, decreed for them, and drove them toward? We say: From where is that prohibited, by reason or by revelation? If it is said: because the merciful and wise among us may not do that, we say: because above him is one who commands him and one who forbids him, whereas our Lord, exalted is He, 'is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned' (﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾). The creation may not be measured by the Creator, and the acts of servants may not be attributed to the acts of God. In reality all acts belong to Allah, majestic is His majesty, and all creation belongs to Him. He directs them as He wills, and judges among them by what He wills. What a human finds in himself is only prompted by tenderness of nature, compassion for his kind, and love of praise and commendation, because of the benefit he expects from it; but the Creator, exalted is He, is sanctified above all that. So it is not permissible to take him as an example." It has been disputed whether this verse is specific (khassah) or general (‘ammah). It was said: the verse is specific, because He said: "from the Children of Adam, from their loins," so whoever was of Adam's descendants through his own loins is included, and whoever was not is excluded from this hadith. And He, majestic and mighty, said: ﴿Or lest you should say: "Only our fathers associated partners before, and we were descendants after them."﴾ So every person who did not have polytheist fathers is excluded from it. It was also said: it is specific to those upon whom the covenant was taken through the tongues of the prophets. It was also said: rather, it is general for all people, because everyone knows that he was once a child who was nourished and raised, and that he has a manager and creator. This is the meaning of "He made them testify concerning themselves." And the meaning of ﴿They said: "Yes"﴾ is that this is obligatory upon them. When creation acknowledged for God, glorified is He, that He is the Lord, and then they became heedless of Him, He reminded them through His prophets, and concluded the reminder with the best of His chosen ones, so that His proof would be established against them. He said to him: ﴿So remind, for you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller﴾. Then He empowered him to control, gave him authority, and established his religion in the land. al-Turtushi said: This covenant binds humankind even if they do not remember it in this life, just as divorce binds the one against whom it was witnessed even if he has forgotten it. The fourth issue: Those who said that whoever dies in childhood enters Paradise have used this verse as evidence, because of his acknowledgment in the first covenant; and whoever reaches the age of reason is not exempted by the first covenant. This speaker says that the children of polytheists are in Paradise, and this is the sound view in this matter. This question is disputed because of the differing reports, and the sound view is what we have mentioned. The discussion of this will come under "al-Rum" (See vol. 14, p. 24 ff.), God willing. We have dealt with it in the book al-Tadhkirah, and praise be to Allah. The fifth issue: God's words ﴿from their loins﴾ are a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "from the Children of Adam." The wording of the verse implies that the taking was from the Children of Adam, and there is no mention of Adam in the verse by its wording. The order of the words on this view is: "And when your Lord took from the loins of the Children of Adam their descendants." He did not mention the loins of Adam because it is known that they are all his children and that they were brought forth on the Day of the Covenant from his loins. So the mention was dispensed with by His saying: "from the Children of Adam." ("Their descendants") The Kufans and Ibn Kathir read it in the singular with a fatha on the ta' (dhurriyyatahum), and the word can be used for both singular and plural. God said: ﴿Grant me from Yourself a good descendant﴾ (See vol. 4, p. 69 ff.). This is singular, because he asked only for a son, and he was given the good news of Yahya. The readers agreed on the singular in His saying: ﴿of the descendants of Adam﴾ (See vol. 11, p. 120.), and there is nothing more numerous than the descendants of Adam. And He said: ﴿And We were a descendant after them﴾, and this is plural. The rest read "dhurriyyatihim" in the plural, because "dhurriyyah" can be used for the singular, so they used a form that cannot be used for the singular, namely the plural, so that the word would reach its intended meaning without anything else sharing in it, which is plurality. For from the loins of the Children of Adam many numerous descendants were brought forth, generation after generation, whose number none knows except Allah, so the plural was used for this meaning. The sixth issue: God's words ﴿Yes﴾ were discussed in al-Baqarah at His saying ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾ in full, so reflect upon it there (See vol. 2, p. 11.).

Qur'anic quotations are in ﴿ ﴾ per the instructions.

(أن يقولوا) "أو يقولوا": Abu 'Amr read both with the ya' (يقولوا as "yaqulu"). He returned them to the third-person form used repeatedly before them, namely His words: ﴿from the children of Adam, from their backs, their offspring, and He made them testify concerning themselves﴾. His words ﴿They said, "Yes"﴾ are also in the third-person form, and likewise ﴿and we were offspring after them﴾ and ﴿lest﴾. So he carried them on what came before and after them, which is in the third-person form.

The rest read both with the ta' (تقولوا), returning them to the second-person address that precedes in His words: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said, "Yes." And ﴿We testify﴾ would then be the words of the angels. When they said "Yes," the angels said: ﴿We testify﴾, lest you say, or "lest you say" (i.e., so that you would not say). It is also said that the meaning is that when they said "Yes," acknowledging His lordship, Allah the Exalted said to the angels: "Bear witness." They said: "We bear witness, by your acknowledgment, lest you say or you say." This is the view of Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: His words ﴿We testify﴾ are the words of the children of Adam, and the meaning is: "We testify that You are our Lord and our God." Ibn 'Abbas also said: He made some of them testify against others. So the meaning on this view is: they said "Yes, some of us testified against others." When it is the words of the angels, one pauses on "Bala" (بلى, "Yes"). It is not good to pause on it if it is the words of the children of Adam, because "an" (أن, "lest") is connected to what comes before "Bala" in His words ﴿and He made them testify concerning themselves﴾, meaning "lest they say."

Mujahid related from Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their backs, their offspring, as a comb is drawn through hair. He said to them, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes.' The angels said, 'We testify,' lest you say..." (i.e., we testify against you to your acknowledgment of His lordship, lest you say). This indicates the ta'. Makki said: This is the preferred reading for the soundness of its meaning and because the community (al-jama'ah) agrees upon it.

It has also been said that His words ﴿We testify﴾ are the words of Allah the Exalted and the angels, and the meaning is: "So We testify to your acknowledgment." This was said by Abu Malik, and it is also related from al-Suddi.

(وَكُنَّا ذُرِّيَّةً مِنْ بَعْدِهِمْ) meaning: we followed them.

﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ Its meaning: "You would not do this." And there is no excuse for the imitator (muqallid) in matters of tawhid.

The passage recounts a story that the People of the Book knew from the Torah. Concerning the identity of the one who was given the signs, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: he is Balʿam ibn Bāʿūrāʾ, and it is said his name was Nāʿim, from the Children of Israel in the time of Moses, peace be upon him. He was such that when he looked, he could see the Throne. He is the one meant by the words ﴿And recite to them the news of him to whom We gave Our signs﴾, and it does not say "a sign." In his assembly there were twelve thousand inkwells for the students who wrote down from him. Then he reached a state in which he was the first to compose a book (stating) that "the world has no maker." Malik ibn Dinar said: Balʿam ibn Bāʿūrāʾ was sent to the king of Madyan to invite him to faith. The king gave him gifts and land, so he followed the king's religion and abandoned the religion of Moses. It was concerning him that these verses were revealed.

Al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān narrated from his father, who said: Balʿam had been given prophethood, [[Note on the words "given prophethood": consider how one could be given prophethood and then go astray, for this contradicts the infallibility of the prophets, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them.]] and his supplications were answered. When Moses came with the Children of Israel intending to fight the tyrants (al-Jabbārīn), the tyrants asked Balʿam ibn Bāʿūrāʾ to curse Moses. He stood up to invoke a curse, but his tongue turned to cursing his own companions. When he was asked about this, he said: "I cannot do more than what you hear." His tongue hung out upon his chest. He said: "Now I have lost both this world and the next, and nothing remains except deceit, cunning and trickery. I will devise a plan for you. I think you should send your young women out to them, for Allah hates fornication. If they fall into it, they will be destroyed." They did so, and the Children of Israel fell into fornication, so Allah sent a plague upon them, and seventy thousand of them died. Al-Tha'labi and others have related this report in full.

It is also narrated that Balʿam ibn Bāʿūrāʾ prayed that Moses would not enter the city of the tyrants. His prayer was granted, and they remained in the wilderness of al-Tih. [[Al-Tih: a place between Egypt and al-ʿAqaba.]] Moses said: "My Lord, for what sin have we remained in al-Tih?" He said: "Because of the supplication of Balʿam." He said: "Just as You heard his supplication against me, hear my supplication against him." So Moses prayed that Allah would remove from him the Greatest Name, and Allah stripped from him what he had possessed.

Abu Hamid, at the end of his book Minhaj al-ʿArifin, said: "I heard some of the knowers (ʿarifin) say that one of the prophets asked Allah, the Exalted, about the matter of Balʿam, who had been cast out after those signs and marvels. Allah the Exalted said: 'He never once thanked Me for what I gave him, and if he had thanked Me for it even once, I would not have taken it from him.'"

ʿIkrima said: Balʿam was a prophet and was given a scripture. Mujahid said: he was given prophethood, but his people bribed him to remain silent, so he did so, and left them in the state they were in. Al-Mawardi said: this is not sound, because Allah the Exalted does not choose for His prophethood anyone whom He knows will depart from His obedience to disobedience.

ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi. He had read the scriptures and knew that Allah would send a messenger at that time, and he wished that he himself would be that messenger. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), he envied him and disbelieved in him. He is the one about whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "His poetry believed, but his heart disbelieved."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it was revealed concerning Abu ʿAmir ibn Sayfi, who used to wear hair shirts (al-masuh) in the pre-Islamic period, and he disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ). The reason was that he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in Madina and said: "O Muhammad, what is this that you have brought?" He said: "I have brought the hanifiyya, the religion of Abraham." He said: "I am upon it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You are not upon it, because you have introduced into it what is not part of it." Abu ʿAmir said: "May Allah cause the liar among us to die, alone and exiled." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes, may Allah cause the liar among us to die in that manner." He said this only as an allusion to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he left Mecca. Abu ʿAmir then went out to Syria and passed by Caesar, and he wrote to the hypocrites: "Prepare yourselves, for I will come to you from Caesar with an army to expel Muhammad from Madina." He died in Syria alone. Concerning him was revealed: ﴿and as a lookout for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before﴾. [[See vol. 8, p. 252 onward.]] It will come in Bara'a (Surah 9).

Ibn ʿAbbas said in one narration: it was revealed concerning a man who had three supplications that would be answered for him. He had a wife called al-Basus, and he had a child by her. She said: "Make one supplication for me." He said: "One is for you. What do you command?" She said: "Pray to Allah that He makes me the most beautiful woman among the Children of Israel." When she learned that there was no one among them like her, she turned away from him, so he prayed against her that Allah would make her a barking female dog. Two of his supplications were used up. Her sons came and said: "We cannot bear this, for our mother has become a dog, and people taunt us with her. Pray to Allah that He returns her as she was." He prayed, and she returned to her former state, and the supplications were used up concerning her.

The first view is more well-known and is held by most scholars.

ʿUbada ibn al-Samit said: it was revealed concerning Quraysh. Allah gave them His signs which He sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), but they withdrew from them and did not accept them.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Balʿam was from the city of the tyrants. It is also said: he was from Yemen.

﴿Then he withdrew from them﴾ means: from the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted; that is, the knowledge that he used to possess was taken from him. There is a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Knowledge is of two kinds: knowledge in the heart, which is beneficial knowledge, and knowledge on the tongue, which is the proof of Allah, the Exalted, against the son of Adam." This is like the knowledge of Balʿam and those like him; we seek refuge in Allah from it, and we ask for success and for dying in truth. Al-Insilakh means departure: it is said, "the snake withdrew from its skin," meaning it came out of it. It is also said that this is an inverted usage, meaning the signs withdrew from him.

﴿So Satan pursued him﴾ means: he caught up with him. It is said, "I pursued the people," meaning I caught up with them. It is also said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians, who awaited the coming out of Muhammad (ﷺ) and then disbelieved in him.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verses 176–177:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾. He means Balʿam (Balaam). That is, had We willed, We would have caused him to die before he disobeyed, and We would have raised him to Paradise.

(*Bihā*) means: by acting upon them.

(*Wa-lākinnahu akhlada ilā al-arḍ*) means: he clung (*rakana*) to the earth. This is related from Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi. Mujahid said: he settled (*sakana*) into it, that is, he settled into its pleasures. The root of *ikhlād* is staying in place. It is said: "Fulan *akhlada* in the place" when he dwelt there and remained in it. Zuhayr said:

*"For whom are these dwellings, which were covered by al-Gharqad*
*like the writing in the stone-bed of the flowing channel, long-lasting?"*

[[Al-Gharqad: this is Baqi' al-Gharqad, a cemetery in Medina. In his Diwan, the word is "al-Fadfad," which is a place of rough, raised ground. *Al-wahy* means writing, and he placed it in the stone-bed of the channel because that is harder. From the commentary on the Diwan.]]

He means the one who remains. It is as if the meaning were: he adhered to the pleasures of the earth, and so it was expressed by "the earth," because the enjoyments of this world are upon the surface of the earth.

(*Wa-ittaba'a hawāhu*) means: he followed what Satan made attractive to him. It is also said: his desire was with the disbelievers. And it is said: he followed the pleasure of his wife, who had desired wealth, until she drove him to invoke (a curse) against Musa (Moses).

(*Fa-mathaluhu ka-mathali al-kalb*): this is a subject and predicate (*ibtida' wa-khabar*).

(*In taḥmil ʿalayhi yalhath*): this is a conditional clause and its answer. It occupies the position of a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*), meaning: so his likeness is that of the dog, panting. The meaning is that he is in one state and does not desist from disobedience, like the dog whose condition is this. So the meaning is that he pants in every state, whether you drive him away or do not drive him away. Ibn Jurayj said: the dog has a severed heart, having no heart. If you pursue it, it pants; if you leave it, it pants. Likewise, the one who abandons guidance has no heart; his heart is severed. Al-Qutaybi said: every creature pants only from exhaustion or thirst, except the dog, which pants in a state of fatigue, in a state of rest, in a state of illness, in a state of health, in a state of satiety, and in a state of thirst. So God struck this as an example for the one who denied His signs. He said: if you admonish him he goes astray, and if you leave him he goes astray. He is like the dog: if you leave it, it pants, and if you chase it, it pants. This is like His saying: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you; it is the same for you whether you call them or you are silent﴾. [[See p. 341 of this part.]]

Al-Jawhari said: *lahatha al-kalb* (with a fatha) *yalhathu lahthan wa-luhāthan* (with a damma) means when the dog puts out its tongue from weariness or thirst, and likewise a man when he is exhausted. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿In taḥmil ʿalayhi yalhath﴾ is because, if you chase the dog, it barks and turns to flee, and if you leave it, it attacks you and barks. So it exhausts itself, coming toward you and turning away from you, and then what befalls it is what befalls it when thirsty, namely the protruding of the tongue.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said in *Nawadir al-Usul*: He compared him to the dog specifically among the beasts of prey because the dog has a dead heart, and its panting is due to the death of its heart. The other beasts of prey are not like this, so they do not pant. The dog became like this because, when Adam (ﷺ) descended to the earth, the enemy rejoiced over him, and went to the beasts of prey and incited them against Adam. The dog was among the most eager of them in pursuit. Then Gabriel descended with the staff that had been given to Musa in Madyan, which had been made a sign for him to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and in which was a great authority. It was from the wood of Paradise (*Ās*). He gave it to Adam (ﷺ) on that day, so that he could drive the beasts of prey away from himself. It is reported that he commanded him to draw near to the dog and place his hand upon its head. From this, the dog became accustomed to him, and its heart died because of the authority of the staff. It became attached to him and his offspring until this day, because of his placing his hand upon its head, and it became one of the guardians of his offspring. When it is disciplined and taught hunting, it becomes disciplined and accepts instruction. This is His saying: ﴿You teach them of what God has taught you﴾. [[See vol. 6, pp. 65 and 183.]]

Al-Suddi said: after that, Balaam would pant as the dog pants.

This example, according to many of the people of knowledge of interpretation, is general to everyone who was given the Qur'an but did not act upon it. It is also said: it applies to every hypocrite. The first view is more sound.

Mujahid said, concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So his likeness is that of the dog: if you chase him he pants, or if you leave him he pants﴾, meaning: if you chase him with your mount or with your foot, he pants; or if you leave him, he pants. Likewise is the one who reads the Book and does not act upon what is in it.

Others said: this is the worst of comparisons, because he resembles it in that his desire has overcome him until he no longer controls harm or benefit for himself. He is like a panting dog forever: whether it is chased or not chased, he cannot control for himself the cessation of panting.

It is also said: among the characteristics of the dog is that it attacks the one who does not frighten it, starting with harshness, and then its agitation calms down once it obtains any base reward (*ʿiwaḍ*, in one manuscript: *gharaḍ*, aim). God struck this as an example for the one who accepted a bribe in religion until he stripped himself away from the signs of his Lord.

The verse indicates to whoever reflects upon it that no one should be deceived by his deed or his knowledge, since he does not know with what his life will be concluded. It also indicates the prohibition of taking a bribe to nullify a right or to alter it. Its explanation has already passed in *al-Ma'ida*. [[See vol. 6, pp. 65 and 183.]]

It also indicates the prohibition of blindly following a scholar (*taqlid*) except with a proof that he explains, because God, may He be exalted, informed us that He gave this man His signs, and he stripped himself of them. Therefore it is obligatory to fear the same for others, and not to accept from anyone except with proof.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories; perhaps they will reflect. Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and they were wronging themselves﴾. That is, it is the likeness of all disbelievers.

As for His saying, ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people﴾: it is said: *sāʾa al-shayʾu* means the thing became ugly, and this is intransitive. *Sāʾa yasūʾu masāʾatan* is transitive. That is, their likeness is ugly. Its underlying construction is: "Evil is the likeness, the likeness of the people," so the first noun was elided, and *mathalan* was put in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*). Al-Akhfash said: the "likeness" was made to refer to "the people" metaphorically (*majāzan*). "The people" is in the nominative, either as a subject (*mubtada'*) or by supposing an implied subject. The estimated sense is: "the likeness is evil, being the likeness of the people." Abu ʿAli estimated it as: "Evil is the likeness of the people." And ʿAsim al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read *sāʾa mathalu al-qawm* with *mathalun* in the nominative, as the agent of *sāʾa*.
