Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said in *Nawadir al-Usul*: He compared him to the dog specifically among the beasts of prey because the dog has a dead heart, and its panting is due to the death of its heart. The other beasts of prey are not like this, so they do not pant. The dog became like this because, when Adam (ﷺ) descended to the earth, the enemy rejoiced over him, and went to the beasts of prey and incited them against Adam. The dog was among the most eager of them in pursuit. Then Gabriel descended with the staff that had been given to Musa in Madyan, which had been made a sign for him to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and in which was a great authority. It was from the wood of Paradise (*Ās*). He gave it to Adam (ﷺ) on that day, so that he could drive the beasts of prey away from himself. It is reported that he commanded him to draw near to the dog and place his hand upon its head. From this, the dog became accustomed to him, and its heart died because of the authority of the staff. It became attached to him and his offspring until this day, because of his placing his hand upon its head, and it became one of the guardians of his offspring. When it is disciplined and taught hunting, it becomes disciplined and accepts instruction. This is His saying: ﴿You teach them of what God has taught you﴾. [[See vol. 6, pp. 65 and 183.]]

Al-Suddi said: after that, Balaam would pant as the dog pants.

This example, according to many of the people of knowledge of interpretation, is general to everyone who was given the Qur'an but did not act upon it. It is also said: it applies to every hypocrite. The first view is more sound.

Mujahid said, concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So his likeness is that of the dog: if you chase him he pants, or if you leave him he pants﴾, meaning: if you chase him with your mount or with your foot, he pants; or if you leave him, he pants. Likewise is the one who reads the Book and does not act upon what is in it.

Others said: this is the worst of comparisons, because he resembles it in that his desire has overcome him until he no longer controls harm or benefit for himself. He is like a panting dog forever: whether it is chased or not chased, he cannot control for himself the cessation of panting.

It is also said: among the characteristics of the dog is that it attacks the one who does not frighten it, starting with harshness, and then its agitation calms down once it obtains any base reward (*ʿiwaḍ*, in one manuscript: *gharaḍ*, aim). God struck this as an example for the one who accepted a bribe in religion until he stripped himself away from the signs of his Lord.

The verse indicates to whoever reflects upon it that no one should be deceived by his deed or his knowledge, since he does not know with what his life will be concluded. It also indicates the prohibition of taking a bribe to nullify a right or to alter it. Its explanation has already passed in *al-Ma'ida*. [[See vol. 6, pp. 65 and 183.]]

It also indicates the prohibition of blindly following a scholar (*taqlid*) except with a proof that he explains, because God, may He be exalted, informed us that He gave this man His signs, and he stripped himself of them. Therefore it is obligatory to fear the same for others, and not to accept from anyone except with proof.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories; perhaps they will reflect. Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and they were wronging themselves﴾. That is, it is the likeness of all disbelievers.

As for His saying, ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people﴾: it is said: *sāʾa al-shayʾu* means the thing became ugly, and this is intransitive. *Sāʾa yasūʾu masāʾatan* is transitive. That is, their likeness is ugly. Its underlying construction is: "Evil is the likeness, the likeness of the people," so the first noun was elided, and *mathalan* was put in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*). Al-Akhfash said: the "likeness" was made to refer to "the people" metaphorically (*majāzan*). "The people" is in the nominative, either as a subject (*mubtada'*) or by supposing an implied subject. The estimated sense is: "the likeness is evil, being the likeness of the people." Abu ʿAli estimated it as: "Evil is the likeness of the people." And ʿAsim al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read *sāʾa mathalu al-qawm* with *mathalun* in the nominative, as the agent of *sāʾa*.

It has already been explained (its meaning) in more than one other place. This verse also refutes the Qadariyya, as has already been mentioned, and it refutes those who say that Allah the Exalted guided all the accountable persons and that it is not permissible for Him to lead anyone astray.

Allah, exalted is He, informed that He created for Hellfire a people (ahl) by His justice. Then He described them, saying: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾, which is the status of one who does not understand, because they do not benefit from them, and they do not reason about reward, nor do they fear punishment.

﴿Eyes with which they do not see﴾ the guidance.

﴿And they have ears with which they do not hear﴾ the admonitions. The purpose is not to negate perception from their senses altogether, as we explained in (al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 214]).

﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ because they do not find their way to reward. So they are like livestock, meaning their concern is eating and drinking, and they are further astray because livestock perceive their benefits and harms and follow their owner, whereas they are the opposite of that. ʿAṭāʾ said: "Livestock know Allah, while the disbeliever does not know Him." It was also said: "Livestock obey Allah, exalted is He, while the disbeliever does not obey."

﴿Those are the heedless﴾, meaning they abandoned reflection and turned away from Paradise and Hellfire.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 180:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [7:180]. In it are six issues.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [7:180], is a command to make worship sincerely for Allah, and to keep away from the polytheists and the atheists (al-mulhidin). Muqatil and other exegetes said: the verse was revealed concerning a man among the Muslims who used to say in his prayer: "O Most Merciful, O Most Merciful." A man from the polytheists of Makkah said: "Does Muhammad and his companions not claim that they worship one Lord? Then what is the matter with this one, calling upon two lords?" So Allah, glorified and exalted, revealed: "And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them [7:180]."

The second issue: There came in the book of al-Tirmidhi and the Sunan of Ibn Majah and others a hadith from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), explicitly stating: "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; in one of them there is what is not in the other." We have explained this in (al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna) [The Most Excellent Book on Explaining the Beautiful Names of Allah]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said, mentioning the hadith of al-Tirmidhi: "That hadith is not mutawatir (widely transmitted), although Abu 'Isa said of it: 'This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except from the hadith of Safwan ibn Salih, and he is trustworthy according to the people of hadith.' What is mutawatir from it is his (ﷺ) saying: 'Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever enumerates them enters Paradise.'" The meaning of "enumerates them" (ahsaha) is to count them and to memorize them. Other things have been said besides this, which we have explained in our book. There we mentioned the authentication of the hadith of al-Tirmidhi, and we mentioned from the names what has been agreed upon and what has been disputed, of what we found in the books of our imams, amounting to more than two hundred names. Before specifying them, we mentioned in the introduction of the book thirty-two sections concerning their rulings; whoever wishes it will find them there and in other books composed on this subject. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is right, there is no lord but Him.

The third issue: The scholars differed on this topic regarding the name and the named (al-ism wa'l-musamma), and we have mentioned what the scholars hold on that in "al-Kitab al-Asna." Ibn al-Hassar said: In this verse there occurs the use of "ism" for the named and its use for the naming. His saying "wa-Lillah" (and to Allah) refers to the named, and his saying "al-asma'" (the names), which is the plural of ism, refers to the namings. What supports the correctness of what we have said is His saying: "so call upon Him by them [7:180]." The pronoun in "fad'uhu" (so call upon Him) returns to the named, glorified and exalted, for He is the one called upon. The pronoun in "bihā" (by them) returns to the names, which are the namings by which one calls upon Him and by which He is called upon, not by other than them. This is what the Arabic language requires. Similar to this is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I have five names: I am Muhammad and Ahmad..." the hadith. Some of this has preceded in al-Baqarah [see the second issue, vol. 1, p. 281]. What the people of truth hold is that the ism is the musamma, or an attribute of it connected to it, and that it is other than the tasmiyah (the act of naming). Ibn al-'Arabi, in his discussion of the saying of the Exalted, "And to Allah belong the most beautiful names [7:180]," said: There are three opinions. Some of our scholars said: In this there is evidence that the ism is the musamma, for if it were other than it, the names would have to belong to other than Allah, the Exalted. The second: Others said: What is meant is the namings, because He is one and "asma'" is plural. I say: Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned in his tafsir that the "asma'" in the verse, in the sense of namings, is a consensus among the commentators, and nothing other than it is permissible. Qadi Abu Bakr said in the book al-Tamhid: The interpretation of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them enters Paradise," means that He has ninety-nine namings without disagreement, and these are expressions of Allah being upon various attributes, some of which He deserves for Himself and some of which He deserves for an attribute connected to Him. His names that return to Himself are He Himself, and what is connected to an attribute of His is names for Him. Some are attributes of His essence, and some are attributes of actions. This is the interpretation of His saying: "And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them [7:180]," that is, the beautiful namings. The third: Others said: What is meant is the attributes, "And to Allah belong the attributes."

The fourth issue: Allah, glorified, named His names "the most beautiful" because they are beautiful to the ears and hearts, for they indicate His oneness, His generosity, His bounty, His mercy and His grace. "Al-husna" is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective. It is also permissible to parse "al-husna" as fu'la, the feminine of "al-ahsan" (the most beautiful), like "al-kubra," the feminine of "al-akbar"; its plural is "al-kubar" and "al-husan." On the first view, it is used in the singular as the attribute of non-rational things is used in the singular, as He said: "other uses (ma'arib ukhra)" [20:18] and "O mountains, echo with him" [34:10].

The fifth issue: His saying, ﴿So call upon Him by them﴾ [7:180], that is, ask of Him by His names, so each name is invoked with what befits it. You say: "O Merciful, have mercy on me; O Wise, judge for me; O Provider, provide for me; O Guide, guide me; O Opener, open for me; O Relenting, relent toward me," and so on. If you call by a general name, you say: "O Sovereign, have mercy on me; O Mighty, judge for me; O Gentle, provide for me." And if you call by the most comprehensive and greatest name, and say: "O Allah," it includes every name. And you do not say: "O Provider, guide me," unless you mean: "O Provider, provide me with good." Ibn al-'Arabi said: So arrange your supplication and you will be among the sincere. The conditions of supplication have preceded in al-Baqarah [vol. 2, p. 308], and also in this surah [see p. 223 of this part]. Praise be to Allah.

The sixth issue: Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi included several names among the names of Allah, glorified, such as "Perfecter of His light," "Best of the inheritors," "Best of the schemers," "Fourth of three," "Sixth of five," "al-Tayyib" (the Good), "al-Mu'allim" (the Teacher), and similar. Ibn al-Hassar said: In this he followed Ibn Barjan [Barjan (with fatha on the ya and shadda on the ra): 'Abd al-Salam ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Rahhal Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, Abu al-Hakam al-Lakhmi al-Ifriqi, then al-Ishbili, the Sufi exegete. He died in Marrakesh in 536 AH (from Tabaqat al-Mufassirin)], for he mentioned among the names "al-Nazif" (the Pure) and other things that have not come in a Book or a Sunnah. I say: As for what was mentioned from his saying "what has not come in a Book or Sunnah," then "al-Tayyib" has come in Sahih Muslim. And al-Tirmidhi transmitted "al-Nazif." And he transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in his supplication: "My Lord, help me and do not help against me, support me and do not support against me, scheme for me and do not scheme against me..." the hadith, and he said of it: "a hasan sahih hadith." On this basis it is permissible to say: "O Best of the schemers, scheme for me and do not scheme against me." And Allah knows best. We have mentioned "al-Tayyib" and "al-Nazif" in our book and elsewhere, among what has been mentioned in the reports and from the pious predecessors, and what may be named by and called upon, what may be named by but not called upon, and what may neither be named by nor called upon, according to what Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari mentioned. There it will become clear to you, God willing, Exalted is He.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names; they will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ [7:180]. In it are two issues.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿yulhidun﴾ [7:180]. Al-ilhad is inclination and abandoning the right course; it is said: "alhada al-rajul fi al-din" (the man deviated in religion), and "alhada" when he inclined. From it comes "al-lahd" in the grave, because it is in its side. It is recited "yalhadun" and "yulhidun," two dialects. Ilhad occurs in three ways. The first: by altering the names, as the polytheists did, for they diverted them from what they are, naming their idols by them: they derived "al-Lat" from "Allah," "al-'Uzza" from "al-'Aziz," and "Manat" from "al-Mannan," as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The second: by adding to them. The third: by subtracting from them, as do the ignorant who invent supplications in which they name Allah, the Exalted, by other than His names, and mention Him by other than what is mentioned of His actions, and other things unfitting for Him. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "So beware of them. Let none of you call upon anything except what is in the Book of Allah and the five books, which are al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i. These are the books on which Islam revolves, and what is in the Muwatta', which is the origin of compositions, has entered into them. Leave aside what is other than them. Let none of you say, 'I choose the supplication of such and such,' for Allah has chosen for him, and sent His Messenger (ﷺ) to the creation with that."

The second issue: The meaning of addition in the names is assimilation (tashbih), and the meaning of subtraction is denial (ta'til). The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) described Him with what He did not permit, and the Mu'attilah (denialists) stripped Him of what He is described by. For this reason the people of truth said: "Our religion is a path between two paths, neither by likening nor by denial." Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Bushanji was asked about tawhid and said: "Affirming an essence not likened to essences, nor void of attributes."

It has been said concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And leave those who deviate [7:180]﴾ that its meaning is: leave them, do not argue with them, and do not confront them. On this view the verse is abrogated by fighting, as said by Ibn Zayd. It has also been said that its meaning is a threat, like His saying: "Leave Me with whom I created, alone [74:11]," and His saying: "Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves [15:3]." This is the apparent meaning of the verse, by the saying of the Exalted: "they will be recompensed for what they used to do [7:180]." And Allah knows best.

In the report, the Prophet ﷺ said: "They are this Ummah." It is also narrated that he said: "This [verse] is for you, and Allah has given the people of Musa a like of it," and he recited this verse and said: "Indeed, among my Ummah there will be a group upon the truth until 'Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary) descends."

The verse thus indicates that Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, does not leave the world, at any time or in any era, without a caller who calls to the truth.

Al-Qurtubi, Al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, on Surah 7, verse 182:

God, exalted is He, informed concerning those who denied His signs that He would gradually draw them on (yastadrijuhum). Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are the people of Makkah." Al-istidraj (gradual drawing-on, a gradual leading toward ruin) is taking someone step by step, one station after another. Al-darj means folding something up: one says adraktuhu and darrajtuhu (I folded it). From this comes the expression "udrija al-mayyit fi akfanihi" (the dead person was wrapped in his shrouds). It was also said that it derives from al-darajah (rank or degree), so al-istidraj means lowering someone one degree after another until he reaches the intended end. Al-Dahhak said: "Whenever they renew a act of disobedience for Us, We renew a blessing for them."

It was said to Dhu al-Nun: "What is the most effective means by which a servant can be deceived?" He said: "By kindnesses and honours." For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿We shall draw them on gradually from where they do not know﴾. (It means:) We shower blessings upon them and make them forget gratitude. They also recited:

You thought well of your days when they were good, and you did not fear the evil that fate might bring.

The nights kept faith with you, so you were deceived by them, yet at the clear calm of the nights, turbidity arises.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 183:

Allah's words: ﴿And I give them respite﴾, meaning: I prolong their term, grant them time, and delay their punishment.

(﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾), meaning: My scheme (makr) is strong.

(Matin) means: powerful and strong. Its root is from al-matn (the spine), which is the thick flesh alongside the backbone (al-sulb). It was said: this was revealed concerning the mockers among the Quraysh, whom Allah destroyed in a single night after granting them respite for a period. Its parallel is Allah's words: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 425]. And it has already been discussed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 184:

His words, exalted is He: (Have they not reflected?) That is, upon what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought them. Stopping at "yatafakkarū" (they reflect) is acceptable (ḥasan). Then He said: "There is no madness in their companion" (mā bi-ṣāḥibihim min jinnah), a refutation of their saying: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad" [[See vol. 10, p. 4.]]. It was also said that it was revealed because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood one night upon al-Safa calling the Quraysh clan by clan, saying: "O sons of so-and-so," warning them of the punishment and retribution of Allah. Then one of them said: "Indeed this companion of theirs is mad; he stayed up calling out until morning."

In it are four issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have they not considered?﴾ It is a matter of wonder at their turning away from reflecting on His signs, so that they might come to know the perfection of His power, as we have explained in Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 185.]]. And malakut (sovereignty, dominion) is of the forms of intensification, and its meaning is the great kingdom. It has already been mentioned [[See p. 23 of this part.]].

The second: This verse, and what is similar to it, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Consider what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 386.]] [10:101], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it?﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 5.]] [50:6], and His saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 34.]] — the verse — and His saying: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 40.]] — have been used by those who say that reflection upon His signs and taking lessons from His creatures is obligatory. They said: God, exalted is He, has censured those who do not reflect, and deprived them of benefiting from their senses, saying: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ — the verse. The scholars have differed about the first of the obligations: is it reflection and inference, or faith, which is the assent present in the heart, for which knowledge is not a condition of its validity? The judge (al-Qadi) and others held that the first obligation is reflection and inference, because God, blessed and exalted is He, cannot be known by necessity, but is known only through reflection and inference with the proofs He has set up for knowing Him. To this view went al-Bukhari, may God have mercy on him, when he entitled a chapter in his book: "The chapter on knowledge before speech and action, based on the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿So know that there is no god but God﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 241.]]." The judge said: Whoever is not knowing of God is ignorant, and whoever is ignorant of Him is an unbeliever. Ibn Rushd said in his Muqaddimat: "This is not clear, because faith is valid with the certainty that may arise for one whom God has guided through imitation, and through the first glance of consideration of what God has directed to be considered in more than one verse." He said: al-Baji argued against those who say that reflection and inference are the first obligations, by the consensus of Muslims in all eras in calling the common folk and the imitator believers. He said: If what they held were correct, it would not be valid to call anyone a believer except one who has knowledge of reflection and inference. He said: Also, if faith were not valid except after reflection and inference, it would be permissible for the unbelievers, when the Muslims overcome them, to say to them: "Killing us is not lawful for you, because it is part of your religion that faith is not valid except after reflection and inference, so delay us until we reflect and infer." He said: This leads to leaving them in their disbelief, and not being fought until they reflect and infer. I say: This is the correct view on the matter. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I have been commanded to fight people until they say, 'There is no god but God,' and believe in me and in what I have brought. When they do that, they protect their blood and property from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with God." Ibn al-Mundhir entitled in his book al-Ashraf: "Mention of the description of the perfection of faith": "All scholars from whom knowledge is preserved have agreed that when an unbeliever says: 'I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, and that everything Muhammad brought is true, and I disavow every religion that opposes the religion of Islam,' while being mature and sound of mind, he is a Muslim. If he returns after that and manifests disbelief, he is an apostate, and what is obligatory upon an apostate becomes obligatory upon him." Abu Hafs al-Zinjani said, and our shaykh, the judge Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Simnani, used to say: "The first of the obligations is faith in God, His Messenger, and all that he brought, then reflection and inference, which lead to the knowledge of God, exalted is He. Thus, for him, the obligation of faith in God precedes knowledge of God." He said: This is closer to the truth and gentler on creation, for most of them do not know the reality of knowledge, reflection and inference. If we said that the first obligation is knowledge of God, it would lead to the declaring of disbelief upon a vast multitude and a great number, and that only a few individuals would enter Paradise; and that is far-fetched, because the Messenger ﷺ affirmed that most of the people of Paradise are his community, and that the communities of all the prophets are one row, while his community is eighty rows. This is clear, with no difficulty in it. And praise be to God.

The third: Some of the later and earlier theologians have held that whoever does not know God through the paths they have traversed and the investigations they have set out, his faith is not valid and he is an unbeliever. It follows from this that most Muslims are declared unbelievers, and the first to be declared so would be their fathers, their ancestors and their neighbors. This was put to some of them, and he said: "Do not condemn me for the multitude of the people of the Fire," or as he said. I say: This statement can only come from one ignorant of the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Prophet, for it narrows the vast mercy of God upon a small handful of theologians, and they have plunged into declaring the general body of Muslims to be unbelievers. This is like the saying of the Bedouin who uncovered his private parts to urinate, and the companions of the Prophet ﷺ rebuked him, and he said: "O God, have mercy on me and on Muhammad, and have mercy on no one with us." The Prophet ﷺ said: "You have restricted something vast." It was related by al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and others among the imams. Do you think this Bedouin knew God through evidence, proof, argument and demonstration? And that His mercy encompasses everything? How many like him are judged to be believers! Indeed, the Prophet ﷺ was content from many who embraced Islam with only the pronouncement of the two testimonies, and even was content with a gesture in that. Do you not see that when he said to the black woman: "Where is God?" She said: "In the heaven." He said: "Who am I?" She said: "You are the Messenger of God." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer." There was no reflection or inference there; rather he judged their faith from the first moment, even if there was heedlessness there regarding reflection and knowledge. And God knows best.

The fourth: Reflection and consideration are also not to be applied to the beautiful faces of beardless youths and women. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: Abu al-Tayyib Tahir ibn Abd Allah al-Tabari said: It has reached me concerning this group who attend the listening sessions (sama') that they add to it the gazing upon the face of the beardless youth, and sometimes they adorn him with jewelry and colored garments, and they claim that they intend by it an increase in faith through reflection, consideration, and inference from the made thing to the maker. And this is the extreme of following desire, deceiving the intellect, and opposing knowledge. Abu al-Faraj said: Imam Abu al-Wafa ibn Aqil said: God has not permitted gazing except upon forms toward which the soul has no inclination and in which desire has no share, but rather as a lesson not mixed with lust nor accompanied by pleasure. For this reason God, glorified is He, did not send a woman with the message, nor made her a judge, nor an imam, nor a muezzin; all of this is because she is a locus of desire and temptation. Whoever says, "I find lessons in attractive forms," we deny him. And whoever distinguishes himself with a nature that takes him out of our natures, we deny him; these are only the deceptions of Satan for those who claim. Some of the wise said: Everything in the greater world has a counterpart in the lesser world, and for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We created man in the best of stature﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 113.]], and said: ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not see?﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 40.]]. We have already explained the aspect of the comparison at the beginning of al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 387.]]. So the intelligent person should look at himself and reflect upon his creation from the time he was a gushing water to the time he became a well-formed creature, nourished with food, reared with gentleness, and guarded with softness until he acquires strength and reaches maturity. Then he says, "I, I," and forgets that a time passed over him when he was not a thing worth mentioning, and he will return to being buried; so woe to him if he is one who is wretched. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay. Then We made him a drop in a firm lodging﴾ — up to His saying — ﴿you will be resurrected﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 108.]]. Then he should see that he is a servant, reared and charged, warned with punishment if he falls short, hoping for reward if he obeys; so he turns to the worship of his Master, even if he does not see Him, He sees him; and he does not fear people, while God is more worthy that he should fear Him, and he does not act proudly toward any of God's servants, for he is composed of filth, filled with defilements, heading toward Paradise if he obeys, or toward the Fire. Ibn al-Arabi said: Our shaykhs used to recommend that a person look at the wise verses which gathered these attributes of knowledge:

How can he who has dung for a bed for all time be proud, ... his companion and his suckling are the same

He is from it and to it, ... and his brother and his nursling.

And he calls it to the privy (hash) with smallness, so it gives it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what God has created of things﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: and in what God has created of things.

(And that perhaps their term has drawn near) meaning: and in their terms, which may have drawn near; it is in the genitive position, coordinated with what precedes it. Ibn Abbas said: By the drawing near of the term he meant the Day of Badr and the Day of Uhud.

(Then in what statement after this will they believe?) meaning: in what Qur'an other than what Muhammad ﷺ brought will they believe? It was said: the pronoun refers to the term, in the sense of: in what statement after the term will they believe, at a time when faith will not benefit, because the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation.

He explained that their turning away is because Allah has led them astray. And this is a refutation of the Qadariyya (the Qadariyya, an early school that denied divine predestination).

(And He leaves them in their transgression) is in the nominative, as a resumed statement (isti'naf). It has also been read in the jussive, taking it as a response to the position of the fa' and what follows it.

(wandering blindly) means they are bewildered. It is also said: they hesitate. This has already been discussed fully at the beginning of al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 209.]].

**Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 7 (al-A'raf), verse 187**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it take place?﴾ "Ayyan" is a question about time, like "mata" (when). The rajiz (poet) said:

*When will my need be fulfilled, when?*
*Do you not see that its success has its time?*

The Jews used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you are a prophet, then tell us when the Hour will arise." It is also related that the polytheists said this out of extreme denial. "Mursaha" is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada') according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is "ayyan." It is an adverb of time built on fatha, and it is built because it carries the meaning of interrogation. "Mursaha" with a damma on the mim is from "arsaha Allah," meaning He established it, i.e., when its establisher (i.e., its occurrence) will be, meaning when its occurrence will be. With a fatha on the mim it is from "rasat," meaning it became firm and stood still, and from it comes ﴿and fixed cooking pots﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 376]. Qatada said: meaning, firmly fixed.

(﴿Say: its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾) is a beginning and a predicate, meaning He has not made it clear to anyone, so that the servant may always be on guard. (﴿None will reveal it at its time but He﴾) meaning none will manifest it. "Li-waqtiha" means at its time, "illa Hu." Al-tajliya is the manifestation of a thing; it is said: "Fulan jalla li al-khabar" when he made the news manifest and clear. The meaning of (﴿It is heavy in the heavens and the earth﴾) is that its knowledge is hidden from the people of the heavens and the earth. Whatever's knowledge is hidden is heavy upon the heart. It was also said: its coming is great upon the people of the heavens and the earth, related from al-Hasan and others. Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi said: its occurrence is grave upon the people of the heavens and the earth. Qatada and others said: the meaning is that the heavens and the earth cannot bear it because of its magnitude, for the sky will split, the stars will scatter, and the seas will dry up. It was also said: the meaning is that the question about it is burdensome.

(﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾) meaning unexpectedly, a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). (﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it﴾) meaning, as if you were knowing of it, asking about it often. Ibn Faris said: al-ḥafiyy is one who knows a thing, and al-ḥafiyy is one who presses in questioning. al-A'sha said:

*If you ask about me, then many a questioner*
*Has been kept in ignorance of al-A'sha wherever he ascended.*

It is said: "aḥfā fi al-mas'ala wa fi al-ṭalab," so he is *muḥfin* and *ḥafiyy* in intensive form, like *mukhsib* and *khaṣīb*. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: the meaning is "they ask you as if you were insistent in asking about it," i.e., persistent. He holds that there is no inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the sentence. But Ibn Abbas and others said: it is by inversion, and the meaning is: "They ask you about it as if you were fond of them," i.e., fond of their goodness and delighted by their question. That is because they said: "Between us and you there is kinship, so disclose to us the time of the Hour."

(﴿Say: its knowledge is only with Allah, but most people do not know﴾) This is not a repetition, but one (statement) refers to its occurrence and the other to its precise nature (kunh).

"Say: 'I have no power over any benefit or harm to myself, except as Allah wills.'" — Qurtubi's gloss: "That is, I have no power to bring good to myself or to ward off evil from myself, so how could I possess knowledge of the Hour?" It was also said: "I have no power over my own guidance or misguidance."

"Except as Allah wills" — the phrase (illa ma sha'a Allah) is in the accusative place as an exception. The meaning is: "except what Allah wills that He empower me to do." Sibawayh cited the verse: "Whatever he wills he does with people" (mahma sha'a bi-l-nasi yaf'alu) — the second half of a line by al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur: "Is there not for this age a restrainer of its people? ... whatever [it] wills."

"And if I knew the unseen, I would have acquired much of good" — the meaning: if I knew what Allah intends for me before He informs me of it, I would have done it. It was also said: if I knew when victory in war would come to me, I would have fought and not been defeated. Ibn Abbas said: if I knew the year of drought, I would have prepared for it in the time of plenty what would suffice me. It was also said: the meaning is, if I knew the trade that would profit, I would have bought it at the time of its slump. It was also said: the meaning is, if I knew when I would die, I would have increased my righteous deeds, related from al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj. It was also said: the meaning is, if I knew the unseen, I would have answered every question I am asked. All of these are intended, and Allah knows best.

"And harm did not touch me. I am only a warner and a bringer of good tidings to a people who believe" — this is a resumption of speech, meaning: I am not possessed by madness, for they attributed madness to him. It was also said: it is connected, and the meaning is: if I knew the unseen, no harm would have touched me and I would have taken precautions. This is indicated by the words of Allah: "I am only a clear warner" (in ja, the reading is: "I am only a warner and a bringer of good tidings").

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, verses 189–190:**

This passage contains seven issues.

**The first issue** concerns God's words: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul﴾. The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir, the classical Qur'anic commentary) said: by "the single soul" is meant Adam.

(And made from it its mate) means Eve.

(That he might dwell in tranquility with her) means that he might be at ease with her and find rest. All of this took place in Paradise. Then he began with another state, one which occurs in this world after their descent, and said: (When he covers her) is a metaphor for intercourse.

(She bore a light burden) Anything that is inside a womb or on the top of a tree is called *haml* with a fatha (*ḥamal*). When something is on the back or on the head, it is called *ḥiml* with a kasra (*ḥimil*). Ya'qub (al-Sikkiti) related the kasra for the fruit of the palm tree. Abu Sa'id al-Sirafi said: for a woman's pregnancy one says *ḥaml* and *jaml*; the first is used because the fetus is hidden, like the burden inside a woman, and the second because it protrudes and becomes visible, like the load on a beast. The word *ḥaml* is also the verbal noun of *ḥamala 'alayhi yaḥmilu ḥamlan*, meaning he attacked him.

(Then she went about with it) means the *mani* (the seed), that is, she continued with that light burden. She would stand, sit, and turn about without being troubled by its weight until it became heavy. This is related from al-Hasan, Mujahid, and others. It was said that the meaning is: the burden continued with her, and this is an inversion (*maqlub*), as when you say, "I put the cap on my head." Abdullah ibn Umar read *famarat bihi* (فَمَارَتْ بِهِ) with an alif and light pronunciation, from *māra yamūru*, meaning to go, come, and move about. Ibn Abbas and Yahya ibn Ya'mar read *famarat bihi* (فَمَرَتْ بِهِ) with light pronunciation, from *al-miryah* (doubt), meaning she doubted what had befallen her, whether it was a pregnancy, an illness, or something similar.

**The second issue** concerns God's words: ﴿Then when she became heavy﴾, meaning she became one with a heavy burden, as you say, "the palm tree bore fruit" (*athmara*). It was also said that she entered into heaviness, as you say, "he became in the morning and in the evening" (*aṣbaḥa wa-amsā*).

(They both called upon Allah, their Lord) The pronoun in *da'awā* (they both called) refers to Adam and Eve. According to this view, it is narrated in the stories of this verse that when Eve bore her first child she did not know what it was. This strengthens the reading of those who read *famarat bihi* with light pronunciation. She was therefore distressed, and Iblis found his way to her. Al-Kalbi said: Iblis came to Eve in the form of a man when she became heavy at the beginning of her pregnancy and said, "What is this in your womb?" She said, "I do not know!" He said, "I fear that it may be an animal." She told Adam, peace be upon him, of this, and they both remained in worry over it. Then he returned to her and said, "It comes from Allah in a certain station. If I call upon Allah and you give birth to a human being, will you name him after me?" She said, "Yes." He said, "Then I will call upon Allah." He came to her after she had given birth and said, "Name him after me." She said, "And what is your name?" He said, "al-Harith." Had he named himself to her, she would have recognized him. So she named him Abd al-Harith. Something similar to this is mentioned in weak hadith (*ḍa'if al-ḥadith*) in al-Tirmidhi and elsewhere. There is much in the Isra'iliyyat (narratives taken from Jewish and Christian sources) that has no firm basis, so one who has a sound heart should not rely upon them. Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, were deceived, though the Deceiver deceived them by means of Allah; yet the believer is not stung twice from the same hole. Furthermore, this has been written down and recorded. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "He deceived them twice: (deceived them) in Paradise and deceived them on earth." This is supported by the reading of al-Sulami: *a-tushrikūna* (أَتُشْرِكُونَ) with a *ta'*. The meaning of (righteous) is: a sound, well-formed child.

(But when He gave them a righteous child, they both ascribed to Him partners in that which He had given them.) (190) The scholars differed in interpreting the *shirk* (association) attributed to Adam and Eve.

**The third issue:** The exegetes said that it was an association in naming and attribute, not in worship and lordship. The scholars of meaning (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: they did not hold that al-Harith was their lord by naming their child Abd al-Harith. Rather, they intended that al-Harith was the cause of the child's deliverance, so they named him after him, just as a man calls himself "the servant of his guest" as an expression of humility toward him, not because the guest is his lord. As Hatim said:

*"Indeed I am the servant of the guest as long as he remains,*
*and there is nothing in me but that trait of the servant."*

Others said: this refers to the human race in general and clarifies the state of the polytheists among the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, and this is the view to rely upon. Thus His words *"they ascribed partners"* (190) refer to the disbelieving male and female, and by it is meant the two kinds (the species). This is indicated by (Exalted is Allah above what they associate) and not "what they both associate." This is a good opinion. It was also said: the meaning of (He who created you from a single soul) is from a single form and one shape, (and made from it its mate) means of its own kind, (when he covers her) refers to the two kinds. According to this view, Adam and Eve are not mentioned in the verse. When He gives them a child who is righteous, sound, and well-formed as they wished, they turn him away from the natural disposition (*fitra*) to association, and this is the act of the polytheists. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the natural disposition" (in another narration, "upon this religion"), "and his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian." Ikrimah said: this is not specific to Adam; rather it is general to all creation after Adam. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this is more pleasing to the people of reflection, because the first view attributes great matters to the Prophet of Allah, Adam.

The people of Medina and 'Asim read *shirkan* (شِرْكًا) in the singular. Abu 'Amr and the rest of the people of Kufa read it in the plural, following the pattern *fu'alā'*, the plural of *sharīk* (partner). Al-Akhfash Sa'id denied the first reading, though it is correct by omitting the modified noun: the meaning is "they made for Him one having association," like "ask the village" (Yusuf 12:82). The meaning thus returns to: they made for Him partners.

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates that pregnancy is one of the illnesses. Ibn al-Qasim and Yahya related from Malik that he said: "The beginning of pregnancy is ease and joy, and its end is an illness among the illnesses." Malik's saying that "it is an illness among the illnesses" is suggested by the apparent meaning of His words *"they both called upon Allah, their Lord."* This condition is observed in pregnant women. Because of the greatness of the matter and the severity of the calamity, a pregnant woman's death was made a martyrdom, as occurs in the hadith: "Martyrdom is of seven kinds besides being killed in the way of Allah: one who dies of plague is a martyr, one who drowns is a martyr, one who has pleurisy is a martyr, one who dies of abdominal illness is a martyr, one who dies in a fire is a martyr, one who dies under a collapsed building is a martyr, and a woman who dies in childbirth is a martyr." That is, she dies while carrying a child in her womb. Related by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim.

[[In the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Martyrdom is seven..." (as above).]]

If this is established from the apparent meaning of the verse, then the state of the pregnant woman is the state of the sick person in his actions. There is no disagreement among the scholars of the major cities that the actions of a sick person in giving gifts and favours are valid only from one third of his estate. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: this applies to a pregnant woman only at the time of labour; before that it does not. They argued that pregnancy is a normal condition and that in it safety is the general rule. We reply: likewise, most illnesses are generally safe, yet one who has no illness may still die.

**The fifth issue:** Malik said: if six months have passed for a pregnant woman from the day she conceived, she may not dispose of her property except within one third. If a man divorces his wife while she is pregnant with an irrevocable divorce (*talaq ba'in*), and six months pass over her, and then he wishes to take her back, he may not do so, because she is then in the condition of a sick woman, and the marriage of a sick woman is not valid.

**The sixth issue:** Yahya said: I heard Malik say about a man who attends battle: when he advances in the line for combat, he may not dispose of anything of his property except within one third. He is in the same position as the pregnant woman and the sick person whose life is in danger in that state. Included with this is the one imprisoned for execution in retaliation (*qisas*). Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and others disagreed with this. Ibn al-'Arabi said: when you consider the matter fully, there is no doubt that the one held for execution is in a more severe condition than the sick person, and denying this is a lapse in reasoning, for the cause of death is present in both, just as illness is a cause of death. Allah, the Exalted, said: *"And you used to wish for death before you met it; now you have seen it while you were looking on"* (Al Imran 3:143). Ruwaishid al-Ta'i said:

*"O rider who urges on his mount,*
*ask the Banu Asad what this sound is?*
*And tell them: hurry to make excuses and seek*
*words that will clear you; I am indeed Death."*

[[*Al-sawt* (the sound) is masculine. He made it feminine here because he meant by it the clamour and uproar, in the sense of a cry or a plea for help.]]

Among what indicates this is His saying: *"When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats"* (Al Ahzab 33:10) [[See vol. 14, p. 144.]]. How then can al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa say that the severe condition is only that of single combat, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has informed us of the confrontation with the enemy and the approach of the two groups in this supreme state, in which hearts reach the throats, evil thoughts about Allah arise, and hearts are shaken and disturbed? Is this a condition seen in the sick person or not? No fair-minded person doubts this, and it applies to one who is firm in belief, strives in Allah with true striving, and witnesses the Messenger and his signs. So what then of us?

**The seventh issue:** Our scholars differed about a passenger on the sea at the time of terror: is his ruling that of a healthy person or that of a pregnant woman? Ibn al-Qasim said: his ruling is that of the healthy person. Ibn Wahb and Ashhab said: his ruling is that of a pregnant woman once she has reached six months. The Qadi Abu Muhammad said: their view is more analogous, because it is a state of fear for the self, like the burden of pregnancy. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ibn al-Qasim never boarded the sea, nor did he see a worm on a plank. Whoever wishes to be certain of Allah, that He alone is the Doer and there is no doer with Him, and that means are weak and the certain believer should not depend on them, and so that trust (*tawakkul*) and reliance (*tafwid*) may be realized, let him board the sea.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: when you consider the matter fully, there is no doubt that the one held for execution is in a more severe condition than the sick person, and denying this is a lapse in reasoning, for the cause of death is present in both, just as illness is a cause of death. Allah, the Exalted, said: *"And you used to wish for death before you met it; now you have seen it while you were looking on"* (Al Imran 3:143). Ruwaishid al-Ta'i said:

*"O rider who urges on his mount,*
*ask the Banu Asad what this sound is?*
*And tell them: hurry to make excuses and seek*
*words that will clear you; I am indeed Death."*

[[*Al-sawt* (the sound) is masculine. He made it feminine here because he meant by it the clamour and uproar, in the sense of a cry or a plea for help.]]

Among what indicates this is His saying: *"When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats"* (Al Ahzab 33:10) [[See vol. 14, p. 144.]]. How then can al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa say that the severe condition is only that of single combat, when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has informed us of the confrontation with the enemy and the approach of the two groups in this supreme state, in which hearts reach the throats, evil thoughts about Allah arise, and hearts are shaken and disturbed? Is this a condition seen in the sick person or not? No fair-minded person doubts this, and it applies to one who is firm in belief, strives in Allah with true striving, and witnesses the Messenger and his signs. So what then of us?

**The seventh issue:** Our scholars differed about a passenger on the sea at the time of terror: is his ruling that of a healthy person or that of a pregnant woman? Ibn al-Qasim said: his ruling is that of the healthy person. Ibn Wahb and Ashhab said: his ruling is that of a pregnant woman once she has reached six months. The Qadi Abu Muhammad said: their view is more analogous, because it is a state of fear for the self, like the burden of pregnancy. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ibn al-Qasim never boarded the sea, nor did he see a worm on a plank. Whoever wishes to be certain of Allah, that He alone is the Doer and there is no doer with Him, and that means are weak and the certain believer should not depend on them, and so that trust (*tawakkul*) and reliance (*tafwid*) may be realized, let him board the sea.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verses 191–192:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they associate with Him that which creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ That is: do they worship what is not able to create anything?

(﴿while they themselves are created﴾) That is, the idols (al-asnam) are created. He said "يُخْلَقُونَ" with the wāw and nūn (the masculine sound plural ending) because they believed that the idols harm and benefit, so they were treated as people are treated, as in His saying: ﴿in an orbit they swim﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 286 and vol. 15, p. 32.]], and His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 169.]].

(﴿And they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves﴾) That is, the idols cannot help, nor can they be helped.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 193:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you call them to guidance, they will not follow you﴾. Al-Akhfash said: That is, "If you call the idols to guidance, they will not follow you."

(﴿It is the same for you whether you call them or you are silent﴾). Ahmad ibn Yahya said: This is because it is the end of a verse (ra's ayah). He means that He said "am antum samitun" (or you are silent) and did not say "am samatum" (or you have been silent). According to Sibawayh, "samitun" and "samatum" are one and the same. It was also said: what is meant is those whom God's knowledge had already determined would not believe. It is also read "la yattabi'ukum" with the doubled ta' (tashdid) and without it (takhfif); both are two dialects with the same meaning. Some of the lexicographers said: "atba'ahu" (without doubling) means he went after him but did not catch up with him, while "attaba'ahu" (with doubling) means he went after him and caught up with him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 194–196:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke besides Allah are servants like you﴾. He is arguing with them regarding the worship of idols. "Tad'una" (you invoke) means "ta'buduna" (you worship). It is also said: you call them gods. "Min dun Allah" means "min ghayr Allah" (other than Allah). The idols were called "ibad" (servants) because they are owned by Allah and subjected to Him. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that the idols are created, like you. When the polytheists believed that the idols could harm and benefit, He treated them as people, saying: (so call upon them).

He did not say "fad'uhunna" (call upon them, feminine), and He said "ibad" (servants) and "inna alladhina" (indeed, those who, masculine) and did not say "inna allati" (feminine). The meaning of "fad'uhum" is: [[min j.]] so seek from them benefit and harm, that the worship of idols benefits. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning of "fad'uhum" is "fa-'buduhum" (so worship them). Then Allah rebuked them and mocked their intellects, saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk, or do they have hands with which they strike, or do they have eyes with which they see, or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ and so on. That is: you are better than them, so how can you worship them? The purpose is to show their ignorance, because the one worshipped is characterized by limbs. Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: "Inna alladhina tad'una min dun Allahi ibadun amthalukum" with the "inna" lightened and kasrah (vowelled with kasra) because of the meeting of two sukun, and "ibad" in the accusative with tanwin, and "amthalakum" in the accusative. The meaning: "ma alladhina tad'una min dun Allahi ibadan amthalukum," that is, they are stone and wood, and you worship what you are more noble than.

Al-Nahhas said: This is a reading that should not be recited for three reasons. First: it contradicts the written text (al-sawad). Second: Sibawayh prefers the nominative in the predicate of "inna" when it has the meaning of "ma," so one says "inna Zaydun munṭaliqun," because the action of "ma" is weak, and "inna" with its meaning is even weaker than it. Third: al-Kisa'i claimed that "in" hardly occurs in the speech of the Arabs with the meaning of "ma" unless it is followed by an affirmative, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾. [[See vol. 18, p. 218.]]

﴿So let them answer you﴾: the original is that the lam should be kasra, but the kasra was elided because it is heavy. Then it is said: there is an ellipsis in the speech; the meaning is: so call upon them to follow you, so let them answer you, if you are truthful that they are gods.

Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read "am lahum aydin yabtushuna biha" with a damma on the ta', and this is a dialect. The "yad" (hand) and "rijl" (foot) are feminine nouns, diminutives of which take the ha'; a ya' is added to "yad" in the diminutive, returned to its origin, so it is said: "yudayyah," with shadda because of the meeting of the two ya's.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Call upon your partners﴾, that is, the idols.

(Then plot against me) you and they.

(And give me no respite) that is, do not delay me. The original is "kidunni" (plot against me), the ya' was elided because the kasra indicates it, and likewise "fala tunzirun." "Al-kayd" means plotting, and "al-kayd" also means war; it is said: he raided and did not meet any war (kayd).

(Indeed my guardian is Allah, who sent down the Book) that is, the One who takes charge of my victory and protection is Allah. The "wali" of a thing is the one who guards it and keeps harm away from it. "Al-Kitab" is the Qur'an.

(And He takes charge of the righteous) that is, He protects them. In Sahih Muslim, from Amr ibn al-As, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say openly, more than once: "Behold, the family of Abi, – he meant So-and-so – are not my guardians; my guardian is only Allah and the righteous among the believers." Al-Akhfash said: it was read "Inna waliyya Allahi alladhi nazzala al-kitab," meaning Jibril. Al-Nahhas said: this is the reading of Asim al-Jahdari. But the first reading is clearer, due to His saying: "wa huwa yatawalla al-salihin."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 197–198:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those whom you invoke besides Him﴾. He repeated it to make clear that what they worship neither benefits nor harms.

(وَإِنْ تَدْعُوهُمْ إِلَى الْهُدى) is a conditional clause, and the response is (لا يَسْمَعُوا).

(وَتَراهُمْ) is a new (resumptive) clause.

(يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It means the idols. The meaning of "naẓar" is the opening of the eyes toward the thing looked at, and "wa-tarāhum" is as if they were looking at you. He referred to them with the plural of the masculine rational (wāw) even though they are inanimate objects that do not see, because the report was framed according to the action of those who have intellect. It was also said: they had eyes made of crafted jewels, and for this reason He said "wa-tarāhum yanẓurūna." It was also said: what is meant is the polytheists, and He informed about them that they do not see, since they did not benefit from their eyesight.
