There are three issues in this verse.

The first concerns the verse's three phrases, which together contain the foundations of the Shariah regarding commands and prohibitions. His words, "Take what is easy and forgiving" (khudh al-'afw), include maintaining ties with those who cut you off, pardoning wrongdoers, showing gentleness to the believers, and other good conduct of the obedient. In his words, "and enjoin what is good" (wa'mur bil-'urf), are included maintaining ties of kinship, fearing Allah regarding the lawful and the unlawful, lowering the gaze, and preparing for the Abode of Settlement (the Hereafter). In his words, "and turn away from the ignorant" (wa'ridh 'anil-jahilin), there is encouragement to cling to knowledge, turning away from the people of wrongdoing, keeping oneself clear of disputing with fools, not equating oneself with ignorant and dull-witted people, and other praiseworthy characteristics and upright deeds.

I say: These qualities need elaboration, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered them for Jabir ibn Sulaym. Jabir ibn Sulaym, Abu Juray, said: "I mounted my riding-camel and came to Makkah, and I sought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I made my camel kneel at the gate of the mosque, and they directed me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He was sitting wearing a woolen cloak with red stripes. I said: 'Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'And upon you peace.' I said: 'We are a people of the desert, a folk among whom there is coarseness, so teach me words by which Allah may benefit me.' He said: 'Come closer,' three times. I drew near, and he said: 'Repeat to me.' I repeated to him, and he said: '(Fear Allah, and do not belittle anything of what is good; and meet your brother with a cheerful face; and pour from your bucket into the vessel of one who seeks water; and if a man reviles you for something he does not know of you, do not revile him for something you know of him, for Allah will give you a reward for it and a burden upon him; and do not revile anything that Allah has entrusted to you.)'" Abu Juray said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, I never reviled a sheep or a camel after that." Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated it in his Musnad with this meaning.

Abu Sa'id al-Maqburi narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed you will not embrace people with your wealth, but what embraces them from you is a cheerful face and good character."

Ibn al-Zubayr said: "Allah did not reveal this verse except concerning the characters of people." Al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, concerning His words "Take what is easy and forgiving and enjoin what is good": he said: "Allah did not reveal this verse except concerning the characters of people."

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: "Jibril descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'I do not know until I ask the scholar.'" In another narration: "until I ask my Lord." So he went off, remained for an hour, then returned and said: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, commands you to pardon those who wrong you, to give to those who deprive you, and to maintain ties with those who cut you off."

Some poets versified this, saying:

The noble qualities of character are in three, and whoever has them all perfected, that is the young man (or: the wealthy one):
Giving to the one who withholds from you, and joining the one who cuts you off, and pardoning the one who transgresses against you.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: "Allah commanded His Prophet with the noble qualities of character in this verse, and there is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities of character than this verse." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was sent to perfect noble character."

The poet said:
All affairs pass away from you and come to an end,
except praise, which remains for you.

And if I were given the choice of every virtue,
I would choose nothing but the noble qualities of character.

Sahl ibn 'Abdullah said: "Allah spoke to Musa at Mount Sinai." It was said to him: "With what did He instruct you?" He said: "With nine things: fear (of Allah) in secret and in public; the word of truth in contentment and in anger; moderation in poverty and in wealth; He commanded me to join the one who cuts me off, to give to the one who deprives me, to pardon the one who wrongs me; that my speech be remembrance, my silence reflection, and my gaze a lesson."

I say: It has been narrated from our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) that he said: "My Lord commanded me with nine: sincerity in secret and in public; justice in contentment and in anger; moderation in wealth and in poverty; that I pardon the one who wrongs me, join the one who cuts me off, give to the one who deprives me; that my speech be remembrance, my silence reflection, and my gaze a lesson."

It was said: the meaning of His words "Take what is easy and forgiving" is zakat, because it is a small portion of much. But this is distant, because 'afw comes from 'afa, meaning to become effaced (or: to be obliterated). It may also be said: "Take the easy from him," i.e., do not press him, and be lenient with him. The occasion of revelation rejects this, and Allah knows best. For when He commanded him to dispute with the polytheists, He guided him to the noble qualities of character, for these are the means of drawing the polytheists toward faith. That is: accept from people what is easy for you of their characters and what is facilitated. You say: "I took my right easily and clearly," meaning with ease.

The second issue concerns His words, ﴿and enjoin what is good﴾, i.e., "bil-ma'ruf" (with what is known to be good). 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "al-'urufi" with two damma, like "al-hulm", and both are dialects. Al-'urf, al-ma'ruf and al-'arifah are every good quality which the intellects approve of and to which the souls are at ease. The poet said:

Whoever does good will not lack its rewards;
good custom does not perish between Allah and the people.

'Ata' said: "'And enjoin what is good' means: 'There is no god but Allah.'"

The third issue concerns His words, ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾, i.e., when you have established the proof against them and commanded them with what is good, but they act ignorantly toward you, then turn away from them, to preserve yourself from them and to elevate your rank above responding to them. Although this is an address to His Prophet (peace be upon him), it is a disciplining of all of His creation. Ibn Zayd and 'Ata' said: it is abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of the sword. Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is non-abrogated (muhkamah), and this is the correct view, due to what al-Bukhari narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Uyaynah ibn Hisn ibn Hudhayfah ibn Badr arrived and stayed with his nephew al-Hurr ibn Qays ibn Hisn. He was among the group whom 'Umar would bring near, and the reciters (of the Qur'an) were the companions of 'Umar's gatherings and his consultations, whether they were elderly or young. 'Uyaynah said to his nephew: 'O nephew, do you have standing with this Amir, so that you may seek permission for me to see him?' He said: 'I will seek permission for you to see him.' So he sought permission for 'Uyaynah. When he entered he said: 'O son of al-Khattab, by Allah, you do not give us the abundance, nor do you judge between us with justice!' So 'Umar became angry until he was about to strike him. Then al-Hurr said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, indeed Allah said to His Prophet (peace be upon him): "Take what is easy and forgiving, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant," and this man is one of the ignorant.' By Allah, 'Umar did not go beyond it when he recited it to him, and he was one who stopped at the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

I say: 'Umar's employment of this verse and al-Hurr's citing of it indicate that it is muhkamah, not mansukhah. Likewise al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib employed it, as will be explained. If the rudeness toward the ruler is deliberate and shows contempt for his right, then he may discipline him (ta'zir). If it is other than that, then turning away, overlooking and pardoning are (appropriate), as the just caliph did.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 200:

There are two issues here. The first: when the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿Take what is easy and forgiving﴾ were revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "How, O Lord, when there is anger?" Then it was revealed: "And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you [to anger], then seek refuge in Allah" (7:200). The "nazgh" of Satan means his whisperings (waswasa). There are two forms of the word: nazgh and nagh (نَغْز). It is said: "Beware of the nazzaa and the naggaaz," meaning those who stir up discord (al-muwarrishun) [[al-tawrish: incitement; it is said: warrasha bayna al-qawm and arrasha, meaning he set them against each other.]]. Al-Zajjaj said: the nazgh is the slightest movement, and from Satan it is the slightest whisper. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "I witnessed 'Uthman and 'Ali, and there was a nazgh of Satan between them, so neither of them left anything of the other's [honour] unsaid. Then they did not part until each of them asked forgiveness for the other." The meaning of ﴿yanzaghannaka﴾ (7:200) is: it will befall you and a whisper of what is not lawful will present itself to you at the time of anger.

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾ (7:200), i.e., seek deliverance from that through Allah. Thus Allah commanded that the whisper be repelled by turning to Him and seeking refuge in Him, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness. One seeks refuge from dogs only with the Lord of the dogs. It is related from one of the early scholars that he said to his student: "What do you do with Satan when he tempts you to sins?" He said: "I struggle against him." He said: "And if he returns?" He said: "I struggle against him." He said: "And if he returns?" He said: "I struggle against him." He said: "This will go on long. Suppose you passed by a flock and its dog barked at you and prevented you from crossing; what would you do?" He said: "I would endure it and repel it with all my effort." He said: "This will be long for you. Rather, call upon the owner of the flock to restrain it from you."

The second issue: nagh (النَّغْز), nazgh (النَّزْغ), hamz (الهَمْز) and waswasa (الوَسْوَسَة) are the same. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the promptings of the devils﴾ (23:97–98) [[See vol. 12, p. 148.]], and He said: ﴿From the evil of the whisperer, who withdraws﴾ (114:4) [[See vol. 20, p. 261.]]. The original meaning of nazgh is corruption; it is said: "Nazagha baynana," meaning he sowed discord between us. From this is his saying: "Satan sowed discord (nazagha) between me and my brothers" [[See vol. 9, p. 264.]], meaning he corrupted them. It is also said that nazgh is incitement and provocation, and the meanings are close.

I say: The parallel to this verse is what is in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Satan comes to one of you and says: Who created such-and-such? until he says: Who created your Lord? When he reaches that, let him seek refuge in Allah and desist." And in the same source, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about waswasa and said: "That is the pure essence of faith" (mahd al-iman). And in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "That is the clear faith" (sarih al-iman); and sarih means pure and unmixed.

This is not to be taken literally, since the whisper itself cannot be faith, for faith is certainty. Rather, the reference is to what they found of fear of Allah the Exalted, lest they be punished for what occurred in their souls. It is as if he said: your aversion to this is the pure essence of faith and its purest form, given the soundness of your faith and your knowledge of its corruption. He called the whisper "faith" because repelling it, turning away from it, rejecting it, not accepting it, and recoiling from it proceed from faith. As for his command to seek refuge, it is because those whisperings are among the effects of Satan. As for the command to desist, it is from inclining to them and turning towards them. Whoever has sound faith and acts upon what his Lord and his Prophet commanded, it benefits him and he profits by it. But whoever is seized by doubt, overcome by sensory impressions, and cannot free himself from them, must be addressed with rational proof, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the one whose mind was troubled by the doubt about camels with mange, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no contagion" (la 'adwa). A Bedouin said: "Then what about camels that are in the sand like gazelles, and when a mangy camel enters among them it causes them to be mangy?" He (ﷺ) said: "Then who infected the first?" Thus he uprooted the doubt from its source.

When Satan despaired of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) through incitement and misguidance, he began to disturb their times with those inventions. The waswasa are trivialities; their hearts recoiled from them, and their occurrence among them weighed heavily upon them. So they came, as in the Sahih, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we find in ourselves what one of us considers too grave to speak of." He said: "Have you indeed found it?" They said: "Yes." He said: "That is the clear faith, a humiliation for Satan," in accordance with what the Qur'an stated in His words: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (15:42) [[See vol. 10, p. 38 and p. 28 onward.]]. So the passing thoughts that are not settled and were not drawn in by doubt are those repelled by turning away from them, and it is upon such that the name waswasa is applied. And Allah knows best. This meaning has already passed at the end of al-Baqarah [[See vol. 3, p. 428 onward.]], and praise be to Allah.

There are two issues here. The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who fear Allah﴾ [7:201]. He means: those who avoid shirk and sins.

(When an apparition from Satan touches them) This is the reading of the people of Basra and Makkah. The reading of the people of Madinah and Kufa is "ṭāʾif." It is also reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr as "ṭayyif" with a doubled yāʾ. Al-Nahhas said: "The usage of the Arabs in such a case is "ṭayf" with a single yāʾ, as a verbal noun (maṣdar) of ṭāfa, yaṭīfu." Al-Kisa'i said: "It is a shortened form of "ṭayyif," like mayyit and mayt." Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning of "ṭayf" in the language is what is imagined in the heart or seen in sleep, and likewise the meaning of ṭāʾif." Abu Hatim said: "I asked al-Asmaʿi about ṭayf, and he said: 'There is no faʿl pattern among the maṣādir.'" Al-Nahhas said: "It is not a maṣdar, but it carries the meaning of ṭāʾif. The meaning is: those who fear Allah, the sins, when something befalls them, reflect on the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and on His favour towards them, and so they abandon disobedience." It was also said: "ṭayf" and "ṭāʾif" are two different meanings. The first means imagination, and the second means Satan himself. The first is the maṣdar of "al-khayal ṭāfa yaṭūfu ṭayfan," and they did not say from this an active participle "ṭāʾif." Al-Suhayli said: "Because it is an imagining with no real existence." As for His saying: "Then there came upon it a visitation (ṭāʾif) from your Lord" [[See vol. 18, p. 238 onward.]], it is not said "ṭayf" in that case, because it is truly an active participle, and it is said that it refers to Jibril. Al-Zajjaj said: "Ṭuftu ʿalayhim, aṭūfu, and ṭāfa al-khayal, yaṭīfu." Hassan said:

"Leave this aside, but who will deal with the phantom (ṭayf) that keeps me awake when the night prayer has passed?"

Mujahid said: "The ṭayf is anger. Madness, anger and whispering are also called ṭayf, because it is a passing thought from Satan, likened to the passing of an imagined image (khayal) through the heart."

(Then, behold, they see clearly) That is, they stop. It was also said: "Then, behold, they are upon insight." Saʿid ibn Jubayr read "tadhakkarū" with a doubled dhāl, but it has no basis in Arabic grammar, as mentioned by al-Nahhas.

The second issue: ʿIsam ibn al-Mustaliq said: "I entered Madinah and saw al-Hasan ibn ʿAli, peace be upon them both. I was impressed by his bearing and his fine manner, and envy stirred in me the hatred that my breast had been concealing towards his father. So I said: 'You are the son of Abu Talib!' He said: 'Yes.' I went to extremes in insulting him and his father. He looked at me with a gaze of tenderness and compassion, then said: 'I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate: "Take what is pardoned, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant."' He recited up to His saying: 'Then, behold, they see clearly.' Then he said to me: 'Be at ease. I ask Allah's forgiveness for me and for you. If you seek our help, we will help you; if you seek our provision, we will provide for you; if you seek our guidance, we will guide you.' He perceived in me regret for what had escaped from me, and said: 'There is no reproach upon you today; Allah will forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful' [[See vol. 9, p. 255 onward.]]. Are you from the people of al-Sham?" I said, "Yes." He said:

"A disposition I recognise from Akhzam [[Al-shinshinah (with a kasra on the shin): habit and nature. Al-Asmaʿi said: this is a rajaz verse, which was cited for Abu Akhzam al-Ta'i, and it is:

'Indeed, my sons have clothed me in blood,
A disposition I recognise from Akhzam,
Whoever meets the lions of men will be wounded.'

Ibn Burri said: Akhzam was undutiful to his father. When he died, he left sons who were undutiful to their grandfather, struck him and made him bleed, so he said that, meaning they resembled their father in disobedience.]]

May Allah greet you and make you welcome, and grant you well-being and assistance [[His saying "ḥayyāka Allāh wa-bayyāka" means: Allah made you king and chose you with greeting. "Bayyāka" means "bawwāka" (given you a dwelling), but since it came with "ḥayyāka," its hamza was dropped and its waw changed to yāʾ... "Ādāka": aided you and helped you.]]. Be at ease with us in your needs and whatever befalls you; you will find us at the best of your expectations, if Allah wills." ʿIsam said: "The earth became too narrow for me despite its vastness, and I wished that it would swallow me up. Then I slipped away from him in hiding [[Al-liwadh: concealment.]], and there was nothing on the face of the earth more beloved to me than him and his father."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And their brothers (the devils) extend them in error, then they do not cease﴾ [7:202]. It was said: the meaning is that the brothers of the devils, namely the wicked among the misguided humans, are extended by the devils in error. It was also said that the wicked are called brothers of the devils because they accept from them. The mention of Satan has preceded in this verse. This is the best that has been said about it, and it is the view of Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. The meaning of "then they do not cease" is that they do not repent and do not return. Al-Zajjaj said: there is inversion and displacement in the speech, and the meaning is: "Those you invoke besides Him are unable to help you or themselves to be helped, and their brothers extend them in error, because the disbelievers are the brothers of the devils." The meaning of the verse is: when the believer is touched by an apparition from Satan, he quickly takes heed, whereas the polytheists are extended by Satan. As for "then they do not cease," it was said: it refers to the disbelievers according to both views. It was also said it may refer to Satan. Qatadah said: the meaning is, "then they do not cease from them, nor do they show mercy to them." Al-iqsar means refraining from something; that is, the devils do not cease in extending the disbelievers in error. As for His saying "in error," it may be connected to "they extend them," and it may be connected to "the brothers." Al-ghayy means ignorance. Nafi' read "yumiddūnahum" with a damma on the yāʾ and a kasra on the mīm; the rest read with a fatha on the yāʾ and a damma on the mīm. Both are dialectal forms: madda and amadda, and madda is more common, without the alif, as Makki said. Al-Nahhas said: a group of the grammarians, including Abu Hatim and Abu ʿUbayd, deny the reading of the people of Madinah. Abu Hatim said: "I do not know a basis for it, unless the meaning is that they increase them in error." A group of lexicographers, including Abu ʿUbayd, related that when one increases a thing by itself one says "madda," and when one increases it by means of another one says "amadda," as in His saying: "Your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked [for battle]" [[See vol. 4, p. 160.]]. It is related from Muhammad ibn Yazid that he argued for the reading of the people of Madinah, saying: one says "maddadtu lahu fi kadhā," meaning I adorned it for him and urged him to do it; and "amdadtuhu fi kadhā," meaning I helped him with an opinion or otherwise. Makki said: the preferred reading is with the fatha, because one says "maddadtu fi al-sharr" and "amdadtu fi al-khayr," and Allah the Exalted said: "And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly" [[See vol. 1, p. 207.]]. This indicates the strength of the fatha in this letter, since it is in evil, and ghayy is evil, and because the majority read it so. ʿAsim al-Jahdari read "yumadduwnahum fi al-ghayy." ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read "yaqsurūn" with a fatha on the yāʾ, a damma on the ṣād and a lightened qāf; the rest read "yaqsurūn" with the opposite vowels, and both are dialects. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Has longing come upon you after it had ceased?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 7, verse 203:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign﴾ (203), meaning: when you do not recite it to them.

(They say, "Why do you not fabricate it?") "Lawla" here has the sense of "halla" (why not), and in this meaning it is followed only by a verb, either expressed or implied. The discussion of it has already been given in full in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 91]. The meaning of "ijtabaytaha" is: you invented it yourself. So He informed them that the signs come from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that he recites to them only what has been revealed to him. It is said: "ijtabaytu al-kalam" meaning "irtajaltahu" (I composed it extemporaneously), "ikhtalaqtahu" (I fabricated it), and "ikhtra'tahu" (I originated it), when you bring it from your own self.

(Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord.") That is, from Allah, not from myself.

(This is insight from your Lord) meaning the Quran, the plural of "basirah" (insight), which is indication and lesson; that is, this which I have shown you as evidence that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is One. "Basa'ir" means that by which one gains insight. Al-Zajjaj said: "Basa'ir" means ways (paths), and the "basa'ir" are the paths of the religion. Al-Ju'fi said:

They carried their insights upon their shoulders... and my insight runs with it, a swift steed.

[see p. 57 of this part]

"And guidance" means right direction and clarification. "And mercy" means and blessing.

**Issue One:** Regarding the words of the Most High, ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, then listen to it and be silent﴾ (20). It is said that this was revealed concerning the prayer. This is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Jabir, al-Zuhri, Ubayd Allah ibn Umayr, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. Sa'id said: "The polytheists used to come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he prayed, and some of them would say to others in Mecca, 'Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it.'" So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed in reply to them: "When the Qur'an is recited, then listen to it and be silent" (20).

It is also said that it was revealed concerning the sermon (khutbah). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ata', Amr ibn Dinar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah, Muslim ibn Yasar, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak. This view is weak, because the Qur'an recited in the sermon is little, whereas silence is obligatory throughout it. This was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

Al-Naqqash said: The verse is Meccan (Makki), and there was no sermon or Friday prayer (Jumu'ah) in Mecca.

Al-Tabari also reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that this refers to silence on the day of Adha, the day of Fitr, and the day of Friday, and in what the imam recites aloud. The general sense is the sound view, because it encompasses everything this verse and other Sunnah texts require regarding silence.

Al-Naqqash said: The people of tafsir (exegesis) are agreed that this listening applies in the obligatory prayer and in the non-obligatory prayer.

Al-Nahhas said: In the language, it must apply to everything, unless some evidence specifies a particular case.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "then listen to it and be silent" (20) means: act upon what is in it, and do not transgress it.

Al-Insat (silence) means keeping quiet in order to listen, attend, and observe. One says: anṣata yunṣitu inṣatan, and also naṣata. The poet said:

"The Imam said: 'The command of your leader is upon you,'
so we did not oppose, and we fell silent as they both spoke."

And it is said: "Anṣitūhu" and "anṣitū lahu" (listen to him). The poet said:

"When Hadhām speaks, then be silent to her,
for the saying is what Hadhām has said."

Some of them said regarding His words, "then listen to it and be silent" (20): This was specific to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so that his companions might retain it from him. I say: This is far-fetched, and the sound view is that it is general, due to His words, "that you may receive mercy." Specification requires evidence.

Abd al-Jabbar ibn Ahmad said in his book *Fawa'id al-Qur'an*: The polytheists used to increase noise and uproar, out of frivolity and obstinacy, as God related of them: "Those who disbelieved said: 'Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may prevail'" (26:26). So God commanded the Muslims, at the time of the revelation's recitation, to be the opposite of this state and to listen. He praised the jinn for this, saying: "And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an..." (46:29), to the end of the verse.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited in the prayer, those behind him would respond to him. When he said, "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," they would say the same as he said, until he finished the Opening Chapter (al-Fatihah) and the surah. He remained like that for as long as God willed, and then this was revealed: "When the Qur'an is recited, then listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy" (20). So they were silent. This indicates that what is meant by silence is abandoning raising the voice, as they had been doing by responding to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Qatadah said regarding this verse: A man would come while they were in the prayer and ask them, "How many have you prayed? How many remain?" So God, Exalted, revealed: "When the Qur'an is recited, then listen to it and be silent" (20).

Also from Mujahid, on the same: They used to speak in the prayer about their needs, so the words of the Most High were revealed: "that you may receive mercy."

The disagreement regarding the recitation of the follower behind the imam has already passed in the commentary on the Opening Chapter (al-Fatihah). The ruling on the sermon will come in the commentary on *al-Jumu'ah* (Friday), God willing.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 7, verse 205:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear﴾ 20. Its counterpart is "Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly" [[See p. 223 of this volume.]] "and this has already been discussed." Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: There is no disagreement that the meaning of "And remember your Lord within yourself" 20 refers to supplication (du'a'). I say: It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he meant by the remembrance (dhikr) the recitation during prayer. It has also been said: the meaning is to recite the Qur'an with reflection and contemplation.

"Tadarru'an" (humbly) is a verbal noun (masdar, a noun derived from the verb's action), and it may also occupy the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). "Khifatan" (with fear) is conjoined to it (ma'tuf 'alayhi). The plural of khifah is khiwaf, because it has the meaning of khawf (fear); this was mentioned by al-Nahhas. The original form of khifah is khiwfah; the waw was changed to ya' because the letter before it is kasra. One says: khafa al-rajulu yakhafu khawfan, khifatan, and makhafatan; so he is khA'if (fearful). The plural qawm khuwwaf follows the original form, and khuyyaf follows the pronounced form. Al-Farra' related that the plural of khifah is also said to be khif. Al-Jawhari said: al-Jifah means fear, its plural is khif, and its root is a waw.

(And below the loud voice) 20 That is, below raising the voice in speech; i.e., let yourself hear it, as He said: ﴿And seek a path between that﴾ 110, meaning between loudness and quietness. This indicates that raising the voice in remembrance is forbidden, as has been stated in more than one place.

(In the mornings and the evenings) 20 Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: al-Asal means the evenings (al-'ashiyyat). Al-Ghuduww is the plural of ghadwah. Abu Mijlaz recited "bil-ghuduwwi wal-asal" 20, and it is the verbal noun of asalna, meaning we entered into the evening. Al-Asal is the plural of usul, like tunub and atnab, so it is a plural of a plural; the singular is asil, and it is said to be the plural of asal, according to al-Zajjaj.

Al-Akhfash said: al-Asal is the plural of asil, like yamin and aiman. Al-Farra' said: usul is the plural of asil, and it may also be a singular, as the poet said:

"Nor is any more beautiful than her when the evening (al-usul) approaches."

Al-Jawhari said: al-Asil is the time after the afternoon prayer until sunset; its plural is usul, asal, and asa'il, as if it were the plural of asilah. The poet said:

"By my life, you are indeed the House; I honor its people,
and I sit in its shade in the evenings (bil-asa'il)."

It is also pluralized as usalan, like ba'ir and bu'ran. Then they made the plural diminutive, saying usayлан, then they replaced the nun with a lam, saying usayyalal. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I stood there at dusk (usayyalan), asking it;
it was unable to answer, and there was no one in the enclosure."

Al-Lihyani related: "I met him at dusk (usayyalan)."

(And do not be among the heedless) 20 That is, heedless of the remembrance.

**First issue:** Concerning this there are eight questions.

**The first:** God's statement ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [20]. It means the angels, by consensus (*ijma'*, the agreement of the scholars). He said "with your Lord [20]," though God is in every place, because they are close to His mercy, and everyone close to the mercy of God, Mighty and Majestic is, in that sense, "with Him." This is from al-Zajjaj. Others said that it is because they are in a place where only God's command takes effect. It was also said that they are God's messengers, as one says, "Near the caliph is a large army." It was also said that this is a mark of honour for them, and that they are in an honoured station, so it is an expression of their nearness in honour, not in distance. ﴿And they glorify Him [20]﴾, that is, they magnify Him and declare Him free of every imperfection. ﴿And to Him they prostrate [20]﴾. It was said: they pray. It was also said: they humble themselves, unlike the people of sins.

**The second:** The majority of scholars hold that this is a place of prostration (*sujud*) for the reciter. The scholars differed over the number of prostrations of the Qur'an. The highest number stated is fifteen: the first is the final verse of al-A'raf and the last is the final verse of al-'Alaq. This is the view of Ibn Habib, Ibn Wahb (in one narration), and Ishaq. Some scholars added the prostration of al-Hijr, God's statement ﴿and be among the prostrators﴾, as will be explained later, if God wills. On this view there are sixteen. It was also said there are fourteen, as stated by Ibn Wahb in the other narration from him, dropping the second prostration of al-Hajj. This is the view of the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*, the Hanafis). The sound view is that it is dropped, because no hadith establishing it has been authenticated. Ibn Majah and Abu Dawud related in their *Sunan* from Abd Allah ibn Muneen of the Banu Abd Kulal, from Amr ibn al-As, that the Messenger of God ﷺ taught him fifteen prostrations in the Qur'an, three of them in the *Mufassal* and two in al-Hajj. Abd Allah ibn Muneen is not relied upon as a source of hadith, as Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq said. Abu Dawud also mentioned from the hadith of Uqba ibn Amir, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, are there two prostrations in the Surah of al-Hajj?' He said: 'Yes, and whoever does not prostrate for them should not recite them.'" Its chain includes Abd Allah ibn Lahi'a, who is very weak. Al-Shafi'i affirmed the two prostrations and dropped the prostration of Sad. It was also said there are eleven prostrations, dropping the last of al-Hajj and the three of the *Mufassal*. This is the well-known view of Malik, and it is reported from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and others. In the *Sunan* of Ibn Majah, from Abu al-Darda, who said: "I prostrated with the Prophet ﷺ eleven prostrations, none of them from the *Mufassal*: al-A'raf, al-Ra'd, al-Nahl, Bani Isra'il, Maryam, the prostration in al-Hajj, al-Furqan, Sulayman (the Surah of al-Naml), al-Sajdah, Sad, and the prostrations of the Ha Mims." It was also said there are ten, dropping the last of al-Hajj, Sad, and the three of the *Mufassal*, as reported from Ibn Abbas. It was also said there are four: the prostration of Alif Lam Mim Tanzil, Ha Mim Tanzil, al-Najm, and al-'Alaq. The cause of the disagreement is the variation in the transmitted reports and in practice, and their disagreement over the general term "prostration" in the Qur'an, whether it means the prostration of recitation (*sujud al-tilawa*) or the obligatory prostration within prayer?

**The third:** They differed over whether the prostration of recitation is obligatory. Malik and al-Shafi'i said it is not obligatory. Abu Hanifa said it is obligatory. He relied on the fact that an unqualified command to prostrate implies obligation, and on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "When the son of Adam recites a prostration and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping, saying: 'Woe is him!'" In the narration of Abu Kurayb it is "Woe is me!" He also relied on the Prophet's ﷺ saying, reporting about Iblis (may God curse him): "The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is Paradise; I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so for me is the Fire." Related by Muslim. Also, the Prophet ﷺ was constant in it. Our scholars relied on the authentic hadith of Umar, related by al-Bukhari, that he recited a verse of prostration on the pulpit and came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. Then he recited it on the next Friday, and the people prepared to prostrate, so he said: "O people, take it easy! God did not prescribe it for us unless we wish." This was in the presence of the Companions (may God be pleased with them all) from the Ansar and the Muhajirun, and no one objected to him, so the consensus on this was established. As for the saying, "The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate," it is a report about obligatory prostration. And the Prophet's ﷺ constancy indicates recommendation. And God knows best.

**The fourth:** There is no disagreement that the prostration of the Qur'an requires what prayer requires: purity from minor and major impurity, intention, facing the qibla, and the proper time. Except what al-Bukhari reported from Ibn Umar, that he would prostrate without purity. Ibn al-Mundhir also reported it from al-Sha'bi. On the view of the majority, does it require the opening takbir (*tahrim*), raising the hands at its beginning, takbir, and the taslim? They differed on this. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq held that one says takbir and raises the hands for it. It is reported in a narration from Ibn Umar that when the Prophet ﷺ prostrated he said takbir, and likewise when he rose he said takbir. The well-known view of Malik is that one says takbir for it in lowering and raising during prayer. He differed from himself regarding takbir for it outside prayer. The majority of jurists say takbir for it. The majority hold that there is no taslim for it. A group of the early scholars and Ishaq held that one makes taslim from it. On this view it is established that the takbir at its beginning is the opening takbir. On the view of those who say there is no taslim, it is for prostration only. The first view is preferable, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "The key to prayer is purity, its opening is takbir, and its ending is taslim." This is an act that has takbir, so it has a closing like the funeral prayer, indeed more so, because this is an action, while the funeral prayer is speech. This is the preference of Ibn al-Arabi.

**The fifth:** As for its time, it was said: one prostrates at all times without restriction, because it is a prayer with a cause. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and a group. It was also said: as long as dawn has not brightened, or as long as the sun has not yellowed after the afternoon prayer. It was said: one does not prostrate after the dawn prayer nor after the afternoon prayer. It was said: one prostrates after the dawn prayer but not after the afternoon prayer. These three views are in our school. The cause of the disagreement is the conflict between the prostration's occasion, which requires prostration upon reciting it, and the general prohibition of prayer after the afternoon and after the dawn prayers. Also their disagreement about the reason for which prayer is forbidden at these two times. And God knows best.

**The sixth:** When he prostrates, he says in his prostration: "O God, remove from me through it a burden, write for me through it a reward, and make it for me with You a treasure." Ibn Abbas related it from the Prophet ﷺ, and Ibn Majah mentioned it.

**The seventh:** If he recites it in prayer: if it is a voluntary prayer, he prostrates if he is alone, or in congregation if he is safe from confusion in it. If he is in congregation and not safe from that, the established ruling is that it is permitted. It was also said he does not prostrate. As for the obligatory prayer, the well-known view of Malik is the prohibition of it therein, whether the prayer is silent or aloud, in congregation or alone. This is because it would be an addition to the number of prostrations of the obligatory prayer. It was also said that the reason is the fear of confusion among the congregation, and this is more likely. On this view, the one praying alone is not prevented from it, nor is the congregation in which confusion is not feared.

**The eighth:** Al-Bukhari related from Abu Rafi, who said: "I prayed the 'Atamah (night prayer) behind Abu Hurayrah, and he recited 'When the sky splits asunder' and prostrated. I said: 'What is this?' He said: 'I prostrated in it behind Abu al-Qasim ﷺ, so I will not cease to prostrate in it until I meet him.'" Al-Bukhari alone related it. In it: "It was said to Imran ibn Husayn: 'A man hears the prostration but did not sit for it?' He said: 'What do you think if he had sat for it!'" As if he did not make it obligatory for him. Salman said: "This is not what we came out for." Uthman [in one manuscript: Umar] said: "The prostration is only upon one who listens to it." Al-Zuhri said: "He does not prostrate unless he is pure. When you prostrate while at home, face the qibla; if you are riding, it does not matter, wherever your face is." Al-Sa'ib did not prostrate for the prostration of the storyteller (*qass*: one who recites stories, news, and admonitions, not intending the recitation of the Qur'an). And God knows best.
